# Overview



Rosetta is a comprehensive **biomolecular modeling suite** developed collaboratively by the RosettaCommons — a consortium of over 100 academic research groups with more than two decades of continuous development. The software provides algorithms for computational modeling and analysis of protein structures, enabling scientific advances in de novo protein design, enzyme design, ligand docking, and structure prediction of biological macromolecules. This page introduces the repository's architecture, its key subsystems, and the logical pathways for getting started as a new developer.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L20)

## Repository at a Glance

The Rosetta repository is a large, multi-module C++ codebase hosted on GitHub under the `RosettaCommons/rosetta` organization. Despite being publicly hosted, **Rosetta is not "Open Source" in the OSI (Open Source Initiative) sense** — commercial use requires a separate license obtained from the University of Washington. This distinction is critical for anyone planning to build on or redistribute Rosetta-derived software.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L42-L46), [LICENSE.md](LICENSE.md#L1-L6)

The top-level repository layout reflects three primary concerns: the **C++ source tree** under `source/`, the **runtime database** under `database/`, and several **git submodules** that provide documentation, demos, example scripts, and external dependencies.

```
rosetta/                          ← Repository root
├── source/                       ← C++ source tree & build system
│   ├── src/                      ← Core library, protocols, apps, utilities
│   ├── test/                     ← Compiled unit tests
│   ├── SConstruct                ← SCons build entry point
│   ├── cmake/                    ← CMake configuration (PyRosetta, extras)
│   └── external/                 ← Vendored dependencies (auto-fetched)
│
├── database/                     ← Runtime data (rotamers, scoring params, etc.)
│   ├── chemical/                 ← Chemical component definitions
│   ├── scoring/                  ← Energy function parameters
│   ├── rotamer/                  ← Rotamer libraries
│   ├── sampling/                 ← Fragment & sampling data
│   ├── sequence/                 ← Sequence profiles
│   └── protocol_data/            ← Protocol-specific data files
│
├── tests/                        ← Integration & scientific tests
│   ├── integration/              ← End-to-end protocol tests
│   ├── scientific/               ← Scientific validation benchmarks
│   └── benchmark/                ← Performance benchmarks
│
├── docker/                       ← Reference Dockerfiles
├── documentation/                ← [submodule] Online documentation source
├── demos/                        ← [submodule] Usage demos
├── tools/                        ← [submodule] Helper scripts & utilities
├── rosetta_scripts_scripts/      ← [submodule] Example RosettaScripts XML
├── pyrosetta_scripts/            ← [submodule] Example PyRosetta scripts
└── PyRosetta.notebooks/          ← [submodule] Jupyter notebooks for PyRosetta
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L122-L161)

## High-Level Architecture

Rosetta's architecture follows a layered design: **foundational types and utilities** at the bottom, a **core modeling engine** (Pose, ScoreFunction, kinematics) in the middle, and **domain-specific protocols** and **application executables** on top. Extensibility is achieved through three primary interfaces: C++ protocol development, XML-based RosettaScripts, and Python bindings via PyRosetta.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "User Interfaces"
        CLI["CLI Applications<br/>(source/src/apps/public)"]
        RS["RosettaScripts XML<br/>(protocols/rosetta_scripts)"]
        PY["PyRosetta Python API<br/>(source/src/python/PyRosetta)"]
    end

    subgraph "Protocol Layer"
        P1["De Novo Design"]
        P2["Structure Relaxation"]
        P3["Ab Initio Folding"]
        P4["Ligand Docking"]
        P5["ML Integration<br/>(trRosetta, ProteinMPNN)"]
        P6["120+ Protocol Modules"]
    end

    subgraph "Core Engine"
        Pose["Pose & Conformation<br/>(core/pose)"]
        SF["ScoreFunction<br/>(core/scoring)"]
        MOV["Movers & Filters"]
        MC["Monte Carlo Sampling"]
        PK["Side-Chain Packing<br/>(core/pack)"]
    end

    subgraph "Foundation"
        UT["Utility Library<br/>(utility/)"]
        BS["Basic Infrastructure<br/>(basic/)"]
        NUM["Numeric & Math<br/>(numeric/)"]
        OXF["ObjexxFCL<br/>(Array/Vector types)"]
    end

    CLI --> P1 & P2 & P3 & P4
    RS --> P1 & P2 & P3 & P4 & P5
    PY --> P1 & P2 & P3 & P4

    P1 & P2 & P3 & P4 & P5 --> MOV & MC & PK
    MOV --> Pose & SF
    MC --> Pose & SF
    PK --> Pose & SF

    Pose --> UT & BS & NUM & OXF
    SF --> UT & BS & NUM & OXF
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L122-L141), [source/src/core](source/src/core), [source/src/protocols](source/src/protocols)

## Core Subsystem Breakdown

The C++ source tree under `source/src/` is organized into several major directories, each with a distinct responsibility within the modeling pipeline.

### `core/` — The Modeling Kernel

The `core/` directory contains the fundamental data structures that every protocol depends on. It is divided into approximately 20 subdirectories, each encapsulating a domain of the modeling problem:

| Subdirectory | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `core/pose/` | The **Pose** class — the central data structure representing a macromolecular structure (atomic coordinates, residues, energies, PDB metadata) |
| `core/scoring/` | The **ScoreFunction** framework — energy terms, scoring methods, and the energy graph used to evaluate and minimize structures |
| `core/conformation/` | **Conformation** data — internal coordinate representation, fold trees, and residue geometry |
| `core/chemical/` | **ResidueType** and atom type definitions — the chemical vocabulary of the system |
| `core/pack/` | **Side-chain packing** — rotamer placement and optimization algorithms |
| `core/kinematics/` | **Kinematics** — fold trees, jumps, and coordinate transformations |
| `core/fragment/` | **Fragment picking** — selecting structural fragments for ab initio folding |
| `core/id/` | **Identifier types** — AtomID, ResidueIndex, DOF_ID used throughout |
| `core/import_pose/` | PDB and structure file import utilities |
| `core/optimization/` | Numerical optimization algorithms (minimizers) |

The foundational type aliases used across all of Rosetta (e.g., `Real`, `Size`, `Length`) are declared in [core/types.hh](source/src/core/types.hh#L30-L50), providing a uniform type system built on platform-specific definitions.

Sources: [source/src/core](source/src/core), [core/types.hh](source/src/core/types.hh#L30-L50)

### `protocols/` — The Protocol Library

The `protocols/` directory is where the vast majority of Rosetta's scientific algorithms live. With over 120 subdirectories, it represents decades of accumulated research. Each subdirectory typically corresponds to a specific modeling task or research domain. Key protocol areas include:

| Protocol Directory | Modeling Domain |
|---|---|
| `protocols/relax/` | Full-atom and centroid structure relaxation |
| `protocols/abinitio/` | Ab initio (de novo) protein folding |
| `protocols/docking/` | Protein-protein and protein-ligand docking |
| `protocols/denovo_design/` | De novo protein structure design |
| `protocols/ligand_docking/` | Small molecule ligand docking |
| `protocols/rosetta_scripts/` | XML protocol parsing and execution engine |
| `protocols/trRosetta/` | Deep learning-based contact prediction integration |
| `protocols/protein_mpnn/` | ProteinMPNN inverse folding model integration |
| `protocols/symmetry/` | Symmetric complex modeling |
| `protocols/membrane/` | Membrane protein modeling |
| `protocols/enzdes/` | Enzyme design |
| `protocols/rna/` | RNA structure prediction and design |
| `protocols/loops/` | Loop modeling and rebuilding |
| `protocols/simple_moves/` | Fundamental structural manipulation movers |
| `protocols/filters/` | Structure evaluation and filtering |
| `protocols/task_operations/` | Residue-level design task specifications |

Sources: [source/src/protocols](source/src/protocols)

### `apps/public/` — Command-Line Applications

The `source/src/apps/public/` directory contains the source for Rosetta's public command-line executables. Each `.cc` file compiles into a standalone binary (e.g., `relax`, `AbinitioRelax`, `minimize`, `rosetta_scripts`). These executables serve as the most common entry point for running Rosetta protocols, particularly for users who prefer CLI-driven workflows over Python or XML interfaces.

Sources: [source/src/apps/public](source/src/apps/public)

### `utility/` and `basic/` — Infrastructure Libraries

The **utility** library provides cross-cutting concerns: string manipulation, file I/O, option parsing (`utility/options/`), pointer management, graph data structures (`utility/graph/`), threading utilities, JSON support, and the factory pattern implementation (`utility/factory/`). The **basic** library provides runtime infrastructure: the `Tracer` logging system, database resource management (`basic/database/`), random number generation, MPI support, TensorFlow integration hooks, and the citation manager that tracks which scientific methods are used during a run.

Sources: [source/src/utility](source/src/utility), [source/src/basic](source/src/basic)

## Extensibility Interfaces

Rosetta provides three distinct interfaces for extending and composing modeling workflows, each targeting a different audience and level of customization:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "C++ Development"
        CPP["Custom Mover<br/>in C++"]
        CPP --> BLD["Compile with SCons"]
        BLD --> EXE["New CLI Binary"]
    end

    subgraph "RosettaScripts"
        XML["XML Protocol File"]
        XML --> PARSER["RosettaScripts Parser<br/>(ParsedProtocol)"]
        PARSER --> ENGINE["Compose existing<br/>Movers & Filters"]
    end

    subgraph "PyRosetta"
        PY1["Python Script"]
        PY1 --> BIND["PyRosetta Bindings"]
        BIND --> API["Full C++ API<br/>in Python"]
    end

    style CPP fill:#e8f5e9
    style XML fill:#e3f2fd
    style PY1 fill:#fff3e0
```

**C++ protocol development** offers the deepest control — developers can create new `Mover` and `Filter` subclasses, register them with the factory system, and compile them as new applications or as dynamically loaded extras. **RosettaScripts** enables no-compilation workflow composition through XML files that declaratively chain together existing movers and filters. **PyRosetta** provides Python bindings to essentially the entire C++ API, enabling interactive exploration, rapid prototyping, and integration with the Python scientific ecosystem.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L100-L108), [protocols/rosetta_scripts](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts), [PyRosetta](source/src/python/PyRosetta)

## Machine Learning Integration

Rosetta has integrated deep learning approaches alongside its traditional physics-based methods. Two notable integrations are present in the protocols layer:

- **trRosetta** ([`protocols/trRosetta/`](source/src/protocols/trRosetta)) — Integrates the trRosetta deep learning model for predicting inter-residue distance and orientation distributions from multiple sequence alignments, which can then guide structure prediction.
- **ProteinMPNN** ([`protocols/protein_mpnn/`](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn)) — Provides a Mover and metric for the ProteinMPNN inverse folding neural network, enabling sequence design conditioned on protein backbone geometry.

Both integrations expose themselves through the standard Mover/Filter interface, making them composable via RosettaScripts and PyRosetta alongside traditional protocols.

Sources: [source/src/protocols/trRosetta](source/src/protocols/trRosetta), [source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn)

## Runtime Database System

The `database/` directory provides the **runtime data files** that Rosetta loads during execution. Unlike compiled code, these files contain parameter tables, statistical potentials, and structural data that are read from disk at startup. Key subdirectories include `database/scoring/` (energy function parameters), `database/rotamer/` (rotamer libraries for side-chain packing), `database/chemical/` (residue type and parameter definitions), and `database/sampling/` (fragment libraries and sampling data). The database is tightly coupled to specific code versions — the build system and versioning infrastructure in [source/version.py](source/version.py#L1-L50) help ensure compatibility between compiled binaries and the correct database revision.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L131-L133), [database](database), [source/version.py](source/version.py#L1-L50)

## Getting Rosetta Running

There are three primary paths to obtaining a working Rosetta installation:

| Method | Effort Level | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| **Docker** | Lowest | Quick start, tutorials, reproducible environments |
| **Conda** | Low | Pre-built binaries for standard workflows |
| **Source compilation** | Highest | Development, customization, new protocols |

The official Docker images (available at Docker Hub as `rosettacommons/rosetta`) ship with both Rosetta and PyRosetta pre-installed. The [docker/](docker) directory contains reference Dockerfiles for multiple Ubuntu versions and a machine-learning variant with `libtorch` and TensorFlow support. For Conda, pre-built binaries are available through the RosettaCommons Conda channel. For full source compilation, the build is driven by SCons (`source/SConstruct`) and requires only a C++ compiler and Python.

> [!TIP]
> **Docker is the recommended starting point for new users.** The images include both Rosetta CLI and PyRosetta with Jupyter, letting you run tutorials immediately without wrestling with build dependencies. The Dockerfiles in `docker/` also serve as templates for local installation.
>
> **Git submodules are not fetched by default.** A fresh `git clone` leaves submodule directories empty. The SCons build system auto-fetches build-critical submodules, but for demos, documentation, or tools you need to run `git submodule update --init --recursive` or target specific submodules.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L63-L80), [docker/README.md](docker/README.md#L1-L19)

## Contributing to Rosetta

Rosetta uses a **fork-and-pull-request** model. Contributors fork the repository under their own GitHub account, develop on branches, and submit PRs against the `main` branch of `RosettaCommons/rosetta`. Before contributions can be merged, contributors must sign the **Rosetta Contributor License Agreement (CLA)** — a legal agreement that grants the RosettaCommons a perpetual, royalty-free license to the contributed code while allowing contributors to retain their own rights to use their contributions independently. This hybrid licensing approach (restrictive for the existing codebase, permissive for inbound contributions) preserves the RosettaCommons' ability to maintain commercial licensing revenue while enabling community contributions.

Sources: [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#L1-L25), [CLA.md](CLA.md#L1-L18)

# Quick Start



This page gets you from zero to running your first Rosetta computation as quickly as possible. Whether you prefer pre-built binaries, containerized environments, or compiling from source, Rosetta offers multiple paths to get started. By the end of this guide, you will have a working Rosetta installation and understand how to run its core applications on protein structure data.

Before proceeding, make sure you have reviewed the [Overview](1-overview) page for context on what Rosetta is, and the [Licensing Model](3-licensing-model) page for the specific license terms that govern your use of the software. Rosetta is **not** OSI Open Source — commercial use requires a paid license from the University of Washington.

## Prerequisites

The Rosetta build process has minimal host dependencies. The codebase vendors most of its runtime libraries as git submodules, so you only need a C++ compiler (g++ or clang) and Python 2.7+ installed on your system. The build system itself — SCons — is bundled with the repository, eliminating the need for a separate installation step.

| Requirement | Minimum Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| C++ Compiler | GCC 4.9+ or Clang 3.5+ | Compiling Rosetta from source |
| Python | 2.7 or 3.x | Build scripting and PyRosetta |
| Git | Any recent version | Cloning the repository and submodules |
| Disk Space | ~15 GB free | Source tree, build artifacts, and runtime database |
| RAM | 8 GB+ recommended | Compilation can be memory-intensive with parallel jobs |

For PyRosetta specifically, you will also need the [Ninja](https://github.com/ninja-build/ninja) build tool and CMake, both of which are available through your system package manager or Conda.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L161), [source/readme.txt](source/readme.txt#L1-L111)

## Repository Architecture at a Glance

Understanding the top-level layout before you clone will help you navigate the codebase with confidence. Rosetta is organized into three conceptual layers: the **source tree** (compilable C++ code), the **runtime database** (parameter files loaded at execution time), and the **submodule ecosystem** (documentation, demos, scripts, and external dependencies).

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["rosetta/ (repo root)"] --> B["source/"]
    A --> C["database/"]
    A --> D["demos/ (submodule)"]
    A --> E["documentation/ (submodule)"]
    A --> F["tools/ (submodule)"]
    A --> G["docker/"]
    A --> H["pyrosetta_scripts/ (submodule)"]
    A --> I["rosetta_scripts_scripts/ (submodule)"]
    A --> J["PyRosetta.notebooks/ (submodule)"]

    B --> B1["src/ — C++ source code"]
    B --> B2["bin/ — Built executables (symlinks)"]
    B --> B3["build/ — Compiled libraries"]
    B --> B4["test/ — Unit tests"]
    B --> B5["external/ — Vendored dependencies"]

    B1 --> B1a["core/ — Core data structures & scoring"]
    B1 --> B1b["protocols/ — Application protocols"]
    B1 --> B1c["apps/ — Executable entry points"]
    B1 --> B1d["utility/ — Utility libraries"]
    B1 --> B1e["python/ — PyRosetta bindings"]

    B1c --> B1c1["public/ — Published protocols"]
    B1c --> B1c2["pilot/ — Work-in-progress"]
    B1c --> B1c3["benchmark/ — Performance benchmarks"]

    C --> C1["scoring/ — Score function params"]
    C --> C2["chemical/ — Residue type params"]
    C --> C3["rotamer/ — Rotamer libraries"]

    style A fill:#1a73e8,color:#fff
    style B fill:#4285f4,color:#fff
    style C fill:#4285f4,color:#fff
    style B1 fill:#5e97f6,color:#fff
    style B1c fill:#7baaf7,color:#fff
```

A critical distinction: the `database/` directory is **not** source code — it contains parameter files that Rosetta executables load at runtime. Without it, no Rosetta application will function. The `source/src/apps/public/` directory holds all officially published protocol executables, while `source/src/apps/pilot/` contains experimental work that has not yet been released.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L130-L161), [source/src/apps/README](source/src/apps/README#L1-L22)

## Path 1: Clone and Build from Source

This is the most flexible option and the one you need if you plan to modify Rosetta or run protocols that are not available in the pre-built packages.

### Step 1 — Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/RosettaCommons/rosetta.git
cd rosetta
```

The default clone does **not** pull down git submodules — the demo scripts, documentation, and example notebooks will appear as empty directories. This is intentional; the build system will automatically fetch only the submodules required for compilation. If you want all submodules (for demos and documentation), run:

```bash
git submodule update --init --recursive
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L42-L161)

### Step 2 — Compile with SCons

SCons is Rosetta's primary build system. It is distributed within the repository itself, so there is nothing to install. Navigate to the `source/` directory and invoke the build:

```bash
cd source
./scons.py -j<NumOfJobs> mode=release bin
```

Replace `<NumOfJobs>` with the number of CPU cores available on your machine (e.g., `-j8` for 8 cores). The `mode=release` flag is essential — without it, SCons builds in debug mode, which produces executables that are approximately **10× slower** than release builds. The `bin` target tells SCons to create executable symlinks in `source/bin/`.

**Common build variants:**

| Command | What It Does |
|---|---|
| `./scons.py -j8 mode=release bin` | Standard production build (recommended) |
| `./scons.py -j8 mode=release extras=static bin` | Statically linked binaries (more portable) |
| `./scons.py -j8 mode=release extras=mpi,serialization bin` | Build with MPI parallelism support |
| `./scons.py -j8 mode=release extras=cxx11thread bin` | Build with C++11 multi-threading |
| `./scons.py -j8 mode=release extras=tensorflow bin` | Build with TensorFlow ML integration |
| `./scons.py -j8 cat=test bin` then `python test/run.py` | Build and run the unit test suite |

The compilation of the full Rosetta source tree is substantial — expect it to take between 30 minutes and several hours depending on your hardware. The resulting executables will appear in `source/bin/` with descriptive names like `relax.linuxgccrelease`.

Sources: [source/SConstruct](source/SConstruct#L62-L206), [source/readme.txt](source/readme.txt#L1-L111)

> [!TIP]
> **Build speed tip**: Use `./scons.py --nover -j8 mode=release bin` during rapid development iterations. The `--nover` flag skips the versioning script and submodule update, preventing unnecessary recompilation of files that depend on version headers. Never use `--nover` for production builds.

### Step 3 — Verify the Build

After compilation completes, confirm that executables were produced:

```bash
ls source/bin/ | head -20
```

You should see a large number of executables. A quick smoke test:

```bash
./source/bin/relax.linuxgccrelease --help
```

If the executable prints its usage information, your build is working correctly.

## Path 2: Docker (Fastest to Get Running)

Docker provides the fastest path to a working Rosetta environment with zero compilation required. The RosettaCommons maintains official images on Docker Hub that ship with both Rosetta and PyRosetta pre-installed, including Jupyter notebook setups for interactive exploration.

Pull and run the official image:

```bash
docker pull rosettacommons/rosetta:latest
docker run -it rosettacommons/rosetta:latest /bin/bash
```

The Docker Hub repository provides several image variants:

| Image Variant | Description |
|---|---|
| `serial` | Standard single-threaded Rosetta build |
| `mpi` | MPI-enabled Rosetta build for cluster use |
| `pyrosetta` | PyRosetta with standard Python environment |
| `pyrosetta-jupyter` | PyRosetta with full Jupyter notebook setup |
| `ml` | PyRosetta with libtorch and TensorFlow integration |

If you need to customize the build environment, reference Dockerfiles are provided in the `docker/` directory of the repository. These files serve as templates showing exactly which system packages are needed — they do **not** clone or build Rosetta themselves. You mount your cloned repository into the container and run the build commands manually.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L80-L95), [docker/README.md](docker/README.md#L1-L19), [docker/rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile#L1-L43)

## Path 3: Conda Pre-built Binaries

For users who prefer Conda environments over Docker, Rosetta distributes pre-compiled binaries via the RosettaCommons Conda channel. All Conda binaries are built with `serialization` and `cxx11thread` extras enabled.

Configure your `~/.condarc` to point to one of the two mirror channels:

```yaml
# US West Coast (recommended default)
channels:
  - https://conda.rosettacommons.org
  - conda-forge

# US East Coast alternative
channels:
  - https://conda.graylab.jhu.edu
  - conda-forge
```

Then install:

```bash
conda create -n rosetta rosetta
conda activate rosetta
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L57-L75)

## Building PyRosetta from Source

If you need PyRosetta but want to build it from the source tree rather than using the Docker or Conda packages, the process requires Ninja and CMake in addition to the standard C++ compiler:

```bash
cd source/src/python/PyRosetta
python3 build.py -j<NumOfJobs> --create-package $HOME/my_pyrosetta_package
cd $HOME/my_pyrosetta_package/setup
python3 setup.py install
```

This produces a standard Python package that can be installed into your current environment. Verify the installation with:

```bash
python3 -c "import pyrosetta; pyrosetta.init()"
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L96-L109)

## Running Your First Rosetta Application

With a working build (or Docker/Conda installation), you can immediately run Rosetta's most commonly used protocols. All Rosetta applications follow a consistent command-line pattern: they accept PDB files as input via flags and produce structure files as output.

### Structure Relaxation

The `relax` application performs energy minimization and side-chain optimization to improve the physical realism of a protein structure:

```bash
# Using a source build
./source/bin/relax.linuxgccrelease -s input.pdb -relax:fast

# Using Docker
docker run -v $(pwd):/data rosettacommons/rosetta relax.linuxgccrelease \
  -s /data/input.pdb -relax:fast
```

Key flags: `-s` specifies the input PDB file, `-relax:fast` selects the fast (less thorough) relaxation protocol. The `-out:path:all` flag controls where output files are written.

### RosettaScripts (XML-driven Protocols)

RosettaScripts allows you to compose complex protocols from XML configuration files without writing C++ code. The `rosetta_scripts` application interprets these XML definitions:

```bash
./source/bin/rosetta_scripts.linuxgccrelease \
  -s input.pdb \
  -parser:protocol my_protocol.xml
```

XML schema files for validation (`RosettaScripts.xsd`, `RosettaScripts.rnc`) are located alongside the application source in [source/src/apps/public/rosetta_scripts/](source/src/apps/public/rosetta_scripts/).

Sources: [source/src/apps/public/relax.cc](source/src/apps/public/relax.cc#L1-L50), [source/src/apps/public/rosetta_scripts/README.txt](source/src/apps/public/rosetta_scripts/README.txt#L1-L4)

### Common Application Reference

| Application | Source File | Primary Use |
|---|---|---|
| `relax` | [relax.cc](source/src/apps/public/relax.cc) | Structure refinement and energy minimization |
| `AbinitioRelax` | [AbinitioRelax.cc](source/src/apps/public/AbinitioRelax.cc) | Ab initio folding followed by relaxation |
| `rosetta_scripts` | [rosetta_scripts.cc](source/src/apps/public/rosetta_scripts/rosetta_scripts.cc) | XML-driven protocol composition |
| `minimize` | [minimize.cc](source/src/apps/public/minimize.cc) | Pure energy minimization |
| `docking_protocol` | [docking/](source/src/apps/public/docking/) | Protein-protein docking |
| `ligand_docking` | [ligand_docking/](source/src/apps/public/ligand_docking/) | Small molecule docking |
| `fragment_picker` | [fragment_picker.cc](source/src/apps/public/fragment_picker.cc) | Fragment library generation for ab initio |
| `ddg_monomer` | [ddg/](source/src/apps/public/ddg/) | Stability change (ΔΔG) calculations |

## The Runtime Database

Every Rosetta executable requires access to the `database/` directory at runtime. This directory contains score function parameters, rotamer libraries, chemical residue definitions, and other essential data files. By default, Rosetta locates the database by searching relative to the executable's location, but you can override this with the `-database` flag:

```bash
./source/bin/relax.linuxgccrelease -database /path/to/rosetta/database -s input.pdb
```

The database directory contains 14 subdirectories covering scoring parameters, rotamer libraries, membrane protein data, symmetry definitions, and more. The [Runtime Database System](23-runtime-database-system) page explores this in depth.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L130-L140)

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

| Problem | Likely Cause | Solution |
|---|---|---|
| `database not found` error | Executable cannot locate `database/` | Pass `-database /path/to/rosetta/database` explicitly |
| Slow executable performance | Built in debug mode instead of release | Rebuild with `mode=release` flag |
| Missing submodules (empty dirs) | Submodules not initialized | Run `git submodule update --init --recursive` |
| Compiler errors on older GCC | Advanced C++ features required | Upgrade to GCC 7+ or Clang 6+ |
| Python version errors during build | Python 2.7+ or 3.x required | Ensure a compatible Python is in your PATH |
| MPI applications not available | Built without MPI extras | Rebuild with `extras=mpi,serialization` |

For questions not covered here, the [RosettaCommons forums](https://www.rosettacommons.org/forum) are the primary support channel. For build system internals, consult `tools/build/README` within the source tree.

Sources: [source/readme.txt](source/readme.txt#L1-L111), [README.md](README.md#L42-L161)

## Contributing to Rosetta

If your Quick Start journey leads you to fix bugs or add features, Rosetta uses a **Fork-and-PR** development model. Fork the repository under your own GitHub account, develop on a branch, and open a Pull Request against the `main` branch of RosettaCommons/rosetta. Before your first contribution is accepted, you must sign the [Contributor License Agreement (CLA)](https://www.rosettacommons.org/forms/cla) — a one-time requirement that grants the RosettaCommons permission to distribute your code under the Rosetta license while you retain full rights to your original work.

Note that modifying submodule content (documentation, demos, tools) requires forking the respective submodule repository separately, not the main `rosetta` repo.

Sources: [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#L1-L73), [CLA.md](CLA.md#L1-L64)

## What to Explore Next

Now that you have a working Rosetta installation, your learning path depends on your goals:

- **Understand the codebase structure** → [Codebase Architecture](5-codebase-architecture) for a deep dive into how the C++ source is organized across `core/`, `protocols/`, and `apps/`.
- **Master the build system** → [SCons Build System](6-scons-build-system) for advanced build configuration and [CMake Build Configuration](7-cmake-build-configuration) for the alternative CMake-based build path.
- **Explore Docker and Conda in depth** → [Docker and Conda Setup](4-docker-and-conda-setup) for containerized workflows and environment management.
- **Learn the fundamental data model** → [Pose and Conformation](8-pose-and-conformation) to understand Rosetta's core representation of protein structures.
- **Start scripting protocols** → [RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework) for composing protocols declaratively, or [PyRosetta Python Bindings](16-pyrosetta-python-bindings) for programmatic control.
- **Run your first scientific protocol** → [Structure Relaxation](18-structure-relaxation) is the natural next step after verifying your build works.

# Licensing Model



Understanding Rosetta's licensing model is one of the most important first steps before you write a single line of code. Unlike many scientific tools you may have encountered, Rosetta is **not Open Source** according to the Open Source Initiative (OSI) definition. This means the source code is publicly visible on GitHub, but its use is governed by a specific license agreement that restricts certain activities—most notably, commercial use. This page walks you through every dimension of the licensing model so you can confidently determine how Rosetta fits into your project.

## License Architecture Overview

Rosetta's licensing model is organized into three distinct layers, each governing a different relationship between you and the software. The diagram below illustrates how these layers connect:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph License["License Tiers"]
        direction TB
        Academic["Academic (Non-Commercial) License<br/>Free for qualifying institutions"]
        Commercial["Commercial License<br/>Fee-based via UW CoMotion"]
    end

    subgraph Contribution["Contribution Layer"]
        direction TB
        CLA["Contributor License Agreement<br/>Required for all external PRs"]
        ForkPR["Fork-and-PR Workflow<br/>Code stays in your fork until accepted"]
    end

    subgraph Constraints["Key Constraints"]
        direction TB
        NoDist["No redistribution of<br/>modified or unmodified copies"]
        Citation["Mandatory citation of<br/>protocol-specific papers"]
        GPLIncompatible["Incompatible with GPL<br/>and share-alike licenses"]
    end

    Academic --> Constraints
    Commercial --> Constraints
    CLA --> ForkPR
```

The two license tiers—academic and commercial—sit at the top of the hierarchy and determine how you may *use* the software. The contribution layer operates independently and governs how you may *give back* code. Both layers share a set of common constraints that apply regardless of which tier you fall under.

Sources: [LICENSE.md](LICENSE.md#L1-L6), [README.md](README.md#L1-L161)

## Academic (Non-Commercial) License

The academic license is the pathway most developers will encounter first. It grants free access to Rosetta and PyRosetta for non-commercial, non-profit research use. However, the definition of "Non-Commercial User" is precise and worth understanding fully, as exceeding its boundaries can have legal implications.

### Who Qualifies as a Non-Commercial User

The license defines a Non-Commercial User as someone who falls into one of two categories, each with explicit exclusions:

| Category | Included | Excluded |
|----------|----------|----------|
| **Institutional** | Employees of not-for-profit research institutions, government laboratories, and universities | (a) Commercial services; (b) Contract research for a for-profit company where resulting IP is owned by that company |
| **Individual** | Individual researchers acting in a non-commercial capacity | (a) Any use by, for, or on behalf of a for-profit entity; (b) Any use intended for commercial advantage or monetary compensation |

The key distinction is **intent and IP ownership**, not just your employer's tax status. For example, a university researcher performing contract research where the resulting intellectual property transfers to a for-profit company would fall outside the academic license, even though they work at an academic institution.

### What the Academic License Grants

Non-Commercial Users are granted the rights to **perform, display, reproduce, and modify** the Software—this includes both source and executable copies—solely for internal non-commercial purposes. This is broad enough to cover typical academic research activities: running simulations, modifying scoring functions, developing new protocols, and publishing results.

### Obtaining an Academic License

As of April 2026, the academic license text has been temporarily removed from the GitHub repository while the University of Washington conducts an export control review. Users seeking academic licenses should contact `license@uw.edu` directly and follow the instructions provided once the review process completes. This is a procedural pause, not a policy change—academic licensing remains available.

Sources: [LICENSE.md](LICENSE.md#L1-L6), [LICENSE.PyRosetta.md](LICENSE.PyRosetta.md#L1-L64)

## Commercial License

If your use case falls outside the non-commercial definition—or if you represent a for-profit entity—you need a commercial license. This is the licensing tier that sustains the RosettaCommons financially, as all profits from commercial licenses fund the scientific mission of the collaborative.

### How to Obtain a Commercial License

Commercial licenses for both Rosetta and PyRosetta are administered by **UW CoMotion**, the University of Washington's technology transfer office. You can initiate the licensing process through two channels:

| Method | Details |
|--------|---------|
| **Email** | Contact `license@uw.edu` directly |
| **Web Portal** | Rosetta: `https://els2.comotion.uw.edu/product/rosetta` |
| | PyRosetta: `https://els2.commotion.uw.edu/product/pyrosetta` |

The commercial license grants broader usage rights appropriate for pharmaceutical companies, biotech firms, and other for-profit organizations that wish to use Rosetta's capabilities in their pipelines.

### The Commercial/Academic Boundary

A common source of confusion is determining exactly where the boundary lies between academic and commercial use. The contributing FAQ provides explicit guidance on several edge cases:

- **Using Rosetta as a library** in another program does not exempt you from Rosetta's licensing terms. Any combination of Rosetta with another program must maintain Rosetta licensing terms for those portions containing Rosetta code.
- **Charging a fee** for programs that contain Rosetta code counts as commercial use, even if the fee is nominally for "your" code rather than Rosetta's.
- **Combining with GPL-licensed code** is not permitted, as the Rosetta license is explicitly incompatible with GPL and other share-alike provisions.

> [!TIP]
> Before deciding your license tier, carefully evaluate whether any aspect of your project involves IP transfer to a for-profit entity, fee-based services, or commercial advantage. When in doubt, contact `license@uw.edu` for a determination—it is far cheaper than discovering a license violation after the fact.

Sources: [LICENSE.md](LICENSE.md#L1-L6), [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#L46-L73)

## Contributor License Agreement (CLA)

If you plan to contribute code back to Rosetta—whether bug fixes, new protocols, or documentation improvements—you must sign a Contributor License Agreement before any Pull Request can be merged. This is a critical piece of the licensing architecture that exists specifically because Rosetta is **not** OSI Open Source.

### Why a CLA Instead of "Inbound = Outbound"

Many open-source projects use a simple "inbound equals outbound" model, meaning contributions are accepted under the same license as the existing codebase. Rosetta cannot do this because its license must preserve the RosettaCommons' ability to charge commercial license fees. If inbound contributions were licensed under the same restricted terms, it would create an "incompatible mess"—particularly problematic if the project ever attempted to change its license in the future.

Instead, the CLA asks contributors to grant more **permissive terms** on their inbound contributions, creating flexibility for future licensing transitions while preserving the commercial licensing model for the existing codebase.

### What the CLA Grants and Preserves

The CLA is structured to balance the interests of contributors, the RosettaCommons, and downstream users:

| Aspect | What It Means |
|--------|--------------|
| **Copyright License** | You grant UW a perpetual, worldwide, non-exclusive, royalty-free, irrevocable license to reproduce, modify, display, perform, sublicense, and distribute your contributions |
| **Patent License** | You grant the same terms for patent claims necessarily infringed by your contribution (alone or combined with Rosetta) |
| **Ownership Retention** | You retain all right, title, and interest in your contributions—you can still use your own code under any terms you wish |
| **Patent Retaliation** | If anyone sues alleging your contribution infringes their patent, their patent license under the CLA terminates |
| **Scope Limitation** | UW agrees not to use your contributions in a way inconsistent with the RosettaCommons' mission of developing and broadly sharing protein modeling software |

### Signing the CLA

You sign the CLA **once** at [https://www.rosettacommons.org/forms/cla](https://www.rosettacommons.org/forms/cla), and it applies to all your future contributions. Important details:

- If you are contributing as an employee or graduate student, confirm with your institution that you are authorized to sign on their behalf.
- If you change employers, you must re-sign the CLA with your new employer's information.
- RosettaCommons lab members follow a separate Developers Agreement process through their PI.
- Third-party code (code you did not write) must be submitted separately, clearly identified with its source and any applicable license restrictions.

Sources: [CLA.md](CLA.md#L1-L64), [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#L1-L45)

## License Restrictions and Responsibilities

Regardless of which license tier you fall under, there are several responsibilities and restrictions that apply universally. Understanding these upfront prevents surprises later.

### Core Restrictions

The following table summarizes the binding constraints that apply to all Rosetta users:

| Restriction | Academic Users | Commercial Users |
|-------------|---------------|-----------------|
| **No redistribution** of the Software or modifications | ✅ Enforced | ✅ Enforced |
| **Retain all copyright/trademark notices** in copies and modifications | ✅ Enforced | ✅ Enforced |
| **Cite Rosetta** in publications | ✅ Enforced | ✅ Enforced |
| **Software provided "AS IS"** with no warranty | ✅ Enforced | ✅ Enforced |
| **No commercial use** | ✅ Enforced | ❌ Covered by license fee |

The "no redistribution" clause is particularly notable—it means you cannot share Rosetta binaries or modified source code with colleagues at other institutions. Each institution must obtain their own license directly from UW CoMotion.

### Citation Requirements

The license requires you to acknowledge the contribution of the Developers and cite appropriate references in your publications. Importantly, there is no single "The Rosetta Citation." Rosetta is composed of many sub-protocols, each described in its own paper. You should cite the specific papers that describe the protocols you actually used.

Rosetta sometimes prints citation information at the end of a run, but this list is **not exhaustive** and may contain outdated or incomplete references. The recommended approach is to trace back to where you learned about the protocol (documentation, tutorials, or other papers) and cite accordingly.

Several landmark papers serve as starting points for citation searches, including the foundational methods paper by Leaver-Fay et al., the RosettaScripts paper by Fleishman et al., the All-Atom Energy Function paper by Alford et al., and the 2020 Nature Methods overview by Leman et al.

### External Library Compatibility

When incorporating external libraries into Rosetta or combining Rosetta with other software, license compatibility must be verified:

| License Type | Compatible with Rosetta? |
|-------------|------------------------|
| MIT | ✅ Yes |
| OSI-approved BSD | ✅ Yes |
| GPL (any version) | ❌ No |
| Other share-alike licenses | ❌ No |
| Uncertain | Open a GitHub issue to discuss |

Sources: [LICENSE.PyRosetta.md](LICENSE.PyRosetta.md#L1-L64), [CITING_ROSETTA.md](CITING_ROSETTA.md#L1-L37), [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#L46-L73)

## Quick-Start Decision Guide

If you are a new developer trying to figure out where you fit, use this flowchart to determine your licensing path:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start["I want to use Rosetta"] --> Question1{"Are you at a non-profit<br/>institution or acting<br/>as an individual researcher?"}
    Question1 -->|No| Commercial["Contact license@uw.edu<br/>for a Commercial License"]
    Question1 -->|Yes| Question2{"Is your work for<br/>commercial services<br/>or IP transfer to a for-profit?"}
    Question2 -->|Yes| Commercial
    Question2 -->|No| Question3{"Do you want to<br/>contribute code?"}
    Question3 -->|Yes| AcademicCLA["Academic License + Sign CLA<br/>at rosettacommons.org/forms/cla"]
    Question3 -->|No| AcademicOnly["Academic License<br/>Contact license@uw.edu<br/>(temporarily off GitHub)"]
    AcademicCLA --> PR["Open a PR against<br/>main branch of<br/>RosettaCommons/rosetta"]
    AcademicOnly --> Use["Clone, build, and use Rosetta<br/>for non-commercial research"]
    Commercial --> UseCommercial["Obtain license, then<br/>clone, build, and use Rosetta"]
```

> [!TIP]
> Even if you only plan to *use* Rosetta and never contribute code, clone the repository via `git clone https://github.com/RosettaCommons/rosetta` and review the LICENSE.md and LICENSE.PyRosetta.md files yourself. These are legal documents, and this guide is for informational purposes only—your actual rights and obligations are defined by the license agreements themselves.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L161), [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#L1-L45)

## Next Steps

Now that you understand the licensing landscape, here is the recommended reading progression based on your goals:

- **Ready to start using Rosetta?** → Move to [Quick Start](2-quick-start) for installation and your first build.
- **Prefer containerized environments?** → Jump to [Docker and Conda Setup](4-docker-and-conda-setup) for pre-built images and Conda packages.

# Docker and Conda Setup



Rosetta provides two primary pathways for environment provisioning that bypass the complexities of manual compilation: **Docker containers** for fully isolated, reproducible builds and **Conda packages** for pre-built binary distributions. Both approaches abstract away compiler toolchain configuration, external dependency management, and the notoriously time-consuming Rosetta build process itself. This page covers the architecture of each approach, their configuration variants, and practical workflows for getting Rosetta or PyRosetta running with minimal friction.

## Environment Provisioning Architecture

The two provisioning paths serve complementary needs. Docker images are **self-contained build environments** — they provide the toolchain and dependencies but expect you to supply a cloned Rosetta source tree via volume mount. Conda packages, by contrast, deliver **pre-compiled Rosetta binaries** ready for direct execution without any build step. Understanding this distinction is critical for choosing the right approach.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Docker Path
        A[Select Dockerfile] --> B[Build Image]
        B --> C[Clone Rosetta]
        C --> D[Volume Mount into Container]
        D --> E[Run scons or build.py Inside Container]
        E --> F[Rosetta/PyRosetta Binaries]
    end

    subgraph Conda Path
        G[Configure ~/.condarc Channel] --> H[conda install rosetta]
        H --> I[Pre-built Rosetta Binaries]
        I --> J[Ready to Run]
    end

    F --> K[Use Rosetta]
    J --> K
```

| Criterion | Docker Images | Conda Packages |
|---|---|---|
| **What you get** | Build environment (compiler + deps) | Pre-compiled binary executables |
| **Requires source clone** | Yes — mounted at runtime | No |
| **Requires compilation** | Yes — you run the build | No — binaries are pre-built |
| **Isolation** | Full container isolation | Shares host environment |
| **PyRosetta included** | Yes (in most images) | Yes (as separate package) |
| **ML support** | Yes (via `rosetta-ml` image) | Depends on package variant |
| **Best for** | Developers modifying Rosetta | Users running existing protocols |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L63-L161), [docker/README.md](docker/README.md#L1-L19)

## Docker Setup

### Official Images vs. Reference Recipes

The Docker ecosystem in this repository has two layers. The **official Docker Hub images** at `rosettacommons/rosetta` ship with Rosetta and PyRosetta pre-installed, including serial and MPI builds, Jupyter environments, and experimental ML-enabled builds. These are the fastest path to a working Rosetta environment. The **reference Dockerfiles** in the `docker/` directory serve as templates for building custom environments — they provide the toolchain and dependencies but **do not clone or build Rosetta**. You must mount your own source tree and run the build commands yourself.

Sources: [docker/README.md](docker/README.md#L1-L19)

### Available Dockerfile Variants

Each Dockerfile in `docker/` targets a specific combination of base OS and feature set:

| Dockerfile | Base Image | Purpose | Python | MPI | ML Libraries |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile#L1-L43) | `ubuntu:22.04` | Primary reference — Rosetta + PyRosetta | Python 3 | MPICH | No |
| [rosetta-ubuntu-20.04.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-ubuntu-20.04.dockerfile#L1-L40) | `ubuntu:20.04` | Legacy reference build | Python 3 | MPICH | No |
| [rosetta-ubuntu-18.04.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-ubuntu-18.04.dockerfile#L1-L33) | `ubuntu:18.04` | Python 2.7 compatible build | Python 2.7 + 3 | No | No |
| [rosetta-alpine-3.9.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-alpine-3.9.dockerfile#L1-L19) | `alpine:3.9` | Minimal footprint build | Python 3 | No | No |
| [rosetta-ml.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-ml.dockerfile#L1-L48) | `ubuntu:22.04` | ML-enabled PyRosetta | Python 3 | No | TensorFlow + libtorch |

### Shared Dependency Stack (Ubuntu variants)

The Ubuntu-based Dockerfiles (22.04, 20.04, ML) share a common dependency foundation consisting of four layers. The first layer provides **core build tools** — `git`, `curl`, `cmake`, `ninja-build`, `build-essential`, and `clang` ([rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile#L21-L26)). The second layer adds **system library development headers** required by Rosetta's C++ core — `zlib1g-dev`, `libssl-dev`, `libbz2-dev`, `libreadline-dev`, `libsqlite3-dev`, `liblzma-dev`, and `libffi-dev` ([rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile#L28-L28)). The third layer installs the **Python 3 runtime and scientific stack** — `python3`, `python3-dev`, `python3-numpy`, `python3-setuptools`, and `python3-venv` ([rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile#L30-L30)). Finally, optional layers add **static analysis tools** (`clang-tidy`, `clang-format`) and **documentation tooling** (`doxygen`, `graphviz`) ([rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile#L38-L42).

The 22.04 variant is the most complete reference, adding MPI support via `mpich` and `mpi-default-dev`, plus the `python-dev-is-python3` convenience package ([rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile#L37-L40).

### ML Image Specifics

The `rosetta-ml` Dockerfile extends the standard Ubuntu 22.04 stack with two deep learning frameworks critical for Rosetta's ML-enabled protocols. It downloads and installs **TensorFlow 1.15.0** (CPU-only) by extracting the pre-built C library to `/usr/local/lib/` and configuring `LIBRARY_PATH` and `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` ([rosetta-ml.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-ml.dockerfile#L34-L39)). It then installs **PyTorch 2.0.1** (CPU, C++11 ABI, shared with deps) by downloading `libtorch`, extracting it to a temporary location, and copying its contents into `/usr/local` ([rosetta-ml.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-ml.dockerfile#L42-L44). These libraries enable the `--torch` and `--tensorflow` flags in the PyRosetta build system ([source/src/python/PyRosetta/build.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/build.py#L875-L876).

Sources: [rosetta-ml.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-ml.dockerfile#L1-L48)

### Building and Running a Docker Environment

The workflow for using reference Dockerfiles follows a three-step pattern: build the image, clone the source, then compile inside the container.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["docker build -f docker/rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile -t rosetta-dev ."] --> B["git clone your Rosetta fork"]
    B --> C["docker run -v /path/to/rosetta:/rosetta -it rosetta-dev"]
    C --> D{What to build?}
    D -->|Rosetta| E["cd /rosetta/source && ./scons.py -j8 mode=release bin"]
    D -->|PyRosetta| F["cd /rosetta/source/src/python/PyRosetta && python3 build.py -j8"]
    E --> G[Ready to use]
    F --> G
```

The key principle is that the Docker container provides the **build environment** while the host volume provides the **source code**. After building, the compiled binaries live inside the container's filesystem. To persist them, you can either commit the container to a new image or mount additional volumes for output directories.

> [!TIP]
> The `DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive` environment variable set in all Ubuntu Dockerfiles prevents `tzdata` and other packages from prompting for interactive input during `apt-get install`, which would hang in non-TTY Docker builds ([rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile#L12-L12).

> [!TIP]
> All Ubuntu Dockerfiles comment out the final cleanup layer (`apt-get clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`) by default. Uncommenting this line significantly reduces image size but prevents installing additional packages in derived images ([rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile](docker/rosetta-ubuntu-22.04.dockerfile#L43-L43).

## Conda Setup

### Channel Configuration

Rosetta distributes pre-compiled binaries through its own Conda channel, with two geographic mirrors for reliability. All binaries are built with `serialization` and `cxx11thread` extras enabled. Configuration requires editing the `~/.condarc` file to add the appropriate channel URL.

**US West coast mirror** (recommended default):
```yaml
channels: 
  - https://conda.rosettacommons.org
  - conda-forge
```

**US East coast mirror**:
```yaml
channels: 
  - https://conda.graylab.jhu.edu
  - conda-forge
```

The `conda-forge` channel is specified as a fallback, providing access to supplementary packages like `ninja` and `cmake` that may be needed for development work even when using the pre-built binaries ([README.md](README.md#L86-L100).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L86-L100)

### Installing Rosetta via Conda

Once the channel is configured, installation is a single command:

```bash
conda install rosetta
```

This installs pre-compiled Rosetta executables and the runtime database, eliminating the need for any C++ compilation. The `serialization` build extra means that Rosetta's checkpointing and object serialization capabilities are available out of the box, and `cxx11thread` enables modern C++ threading support.

### Conda vs. Docker Decision Guide

| Scenario | Recommended Approach | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Running existing Rosetta protocols | **Conda** | Pre-built binaries, fastest setup |
| Following Rosetta tutorials | **Docker Hub** | Self-contained with Jupyter + PyRosetta |
| Modifying Rosetta C++ source | **Docker reference** | Full compiler toolchain in isolated env |
| Reproducing published results | **Docker Hub** | Version-pinned, reproducible images |
| Multi-user shared cluster | **Conda** | No root/Docker privileges required |
| ML-augmented protocols (trRosetta, ProteinMPNN) | **Docker ML image** | TensorFlow + libtorch pre-installed |
| Minimal disk footprint | **Conda** | Downloads only the package, not full OS |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L63-L161)

## From Setup to Execution

After provisioning your environment through either Docker or Conda, the natural next step depends on your goal. If you want to understand how Rosetta's build system works under the hood (relevant when using Docker reference images for compilation), proceed to the [SCons Build System](6-scons-build-system) page. For an architectural overview of Rosetta's internal organization, see [Codebase Architecture](5-codebase-architecture). If you're specifically interested in PyRosetta's Python bindings and how they connect to the C++ core, the [PyRosetta Python Bindings](16-pyrosetta-python-bindings) page covers the binding generation pipeline. For ML-enabled workflows using the Docker ML image, the [trRosetta Deep Learning](21-trrosetta-deep-learning) and [ProteinMPNN Integration](22-proteinmpnn-integration) pages detail those specific integrations.

# Codebase Architecture



Rosetta is a monolithic C++ software suite for macromolecular modeling and design, organized around a strict layered library architecture. Understanding this architecture is essential before diving into individual subsystems, as the dependency flow dictates what can import what, where new code belongs, and how the build system orchestrates compilation across millions of lines of code. This page maps the structural skeleton — the top-level directories, the internal library layering, the shared programming idioms, and the data flow that binds it all together.

Sources: [SConstruct](source/SConstruct#L1-L8), [core/types.hh](source/src/core/types.hh#L30-L70)

## Top-Level Directory Map

The repository root divides into five functional zones. The **source/** directory is the heart of the project, containing all C++ source code, the build system, and external dependencies. The **database/** directory holds runtime data files — scoring parameters, rotamer libraries, chemical definitions — that Rosetta loads at startup rather than embedding in binary. The **tests/** directory contains integration and scientific validation tests. The **tools/** and **demos/** directories provide standalone scripts and tutorial materials, while **docker/** ships pre-configured container environments for reproducible builds.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Repository Root"
        SRC["source/<br/>C++ source, build system,<br/>external deps"]
        DB["database/<br/>Runtime data files<br/>(scoring, rotamers, chemical)"]
        TESTS["tests/<br/>Integration &amp; scientific tests"]
        TOOLS["tools/<br/>Utility scripts"]
        DEMOS["demos/<br/>Tutorials &amp; examples"]
        DOCKER["docker/<br/>Container configs"]
    end
    
    SRC --> EXT["external/<br/>boost, gemmi, rdkit,<br/>libxml2, pybind11, tensorflow"]
    SRC --> CORE_SRC["src/<br/>Layered C++ libraries"]
    SRC --> BUILD["SConstruct / cmake/<br/>Dual build system"]
    
    CORE_SRC --> APPS["apps/<br/>Public &amp; pilot binaries"]
```

Sources: [get_repo_structure source/](source/SConstruct), [get_repo_structure database/](database), [get_repo_structure source/external/](source/external)

## The Library Layer Hierarchy

All C++ code lives under `source/src/` and is organized into strictly ordered layers. Each layer may only depend on layers below it — never above. This dependency discipline is enforced by the build system through `.src.settings` files that declare inter-library linkages. The layers, from bottom to top, are:

**ObjexxFCL** — A vendored Fortran-compatible array library providing `FArray1D`, `FArray2D`, and other N-dimensional fixed-size arrays. Originally derived from the Objexx project, it bridges Rosetta's scientific computing heritage with modern C++. Its header at [ObjexxFCL/FArray2D.hh](source/src/ObjexxFCL/FArray2D.hh) is included throughout the scoring system for statistical potential tables.

**numeric** — Pure mathematical primitives: vectors (`xyzVector`), matrices (`xyzMatrix`), transformations (`xyzTransform`), quaternions, interpolation, clustering, and spatial data structures (KD-trees, voxel grids). These are the atomic units of geometric computation that every higher layer consumes. Critically, `numeric::xyzVector<core::Length>` is typedef'd as `core::PointPosition` in [core/types.hh](source/src/core/types.hh#L67-L69).

**utility** — The foundation for all Rosetta programming idioms: smart pointers ([owning_ptr.hh](source/src/utility/pointer/owning_ptr.hh)), the polymorphic base class `VirtualBase` ([VirtualBase.hh](source/src/utility/VirtualBase.hh#L37-L56)), the CRTP-based `SingletonBase` ([SingletonBase.hh](source/src/utility/SingletonBase.hh#L27-L54)), the factory/registration pattern ([factory/](source/src/utility/factory)), serialization, exception hierarchies, graph data structures, thread-safe MPI utilities, JSON spirit, and ubiquitous string/vector type aliases like `vector1` (1-indexed). The comment in `VirtualBase.hh` makes the architectural contract explicit: every polymorphic class in Rosetta must inherit from `VirtualBase` to guarantee a virtual destructor.

**basic** — Cross-cutting infrastructure that doesn't belong to any specific domain: the `Tracer` logging system, the global initialization gate ([basic/init.cc](source/src/basic/init.cc#L20-L29)), the option system (`basic/options/`), the resource manager, random number generators, profiling utilities, and the citation manager. The `init()` function sets a global flag that downstream code checks to detect forgotten initialization.

**core** — The central modeling engine. Due to its massive size, it is split across six compilation units (`core.1` through `core.6`) for parallel builds. It defines the fundamental data model of Rosetta: chemical types, poses, conformations, scoring, kinematics, energy methods, fragment picking, and packing. This is the domain of [Pose](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L10-L25), [Conformation](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L10-L17), [ScoreFunction](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L10-L17), and the `EnergyMethod` hierarchy. The comment in `Pose.hh` — *"almost every file in Rosetta #includes Pose.hh"* — underscores that this class is the gravitational center of the entire codebase.

**protocols** — Concrete modeling algorithms organized by scientific domain. With over 180 subdirectories, this is by far the largest layer. It implements everything from ab initio folding and relaxation to ligand docking, antibody design, membrane modeling, RNA structure prediction, and machine learning integration (trRosetta, ProteinMPNN). Each protocol directory typically contains Movers, Filters, and TaskOperations following the [Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy) pattern. Like core, it is split across multiple compilation units for build parallelism.

**apps** — Executable entry points split into `public/` (stable, documented applications like `relax`, `minimize`, `rosetta_scripts`) and `pilot/` (experimental code organized by developer). Each public app is a thin `main()` that delegates to the protocol layer through the Job Distributor.

**python** — PyRosetta bindings built with pybind11, living under `source/src/python/PyRosetta/`. This is covered in depth on the [PyRosetta Python Bindings](16-pyrosetta-python-bindings) page.

> [!TIP]
> The `.src.settings` files at each layer level (e.g., `core.1.src.settings`, `protocols.3.src.settings`) declare compile flags and link dependencies. If you introduce a new library or move code between layers, you must update the corresponding settings file — the build will fail with cryptic linker errors if the dependency graph has cycles.

Sources: [core/types.hh](source/src/core/types.hh#L30-L69), [VirtualBase.hh](source/src/utility/VirtualBase.hh#L21-L56), [SingletonBase.hh](source/src/utility/SingletonBase.hh#L19-L54), [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L16-L25), [basic/init.cc](source/src/basic/init.cc#L15-L31), [SConscript](source/src/SConscript.src)

## Core Namespace Anatomy

The `core` namespace is the single largest namespace in the codebase and serves as the domain model for structural biology. Its subdirectories under `source/src/core/` map directly to conceptual subsystems:

| Namespace | Directory | Responsibility |
|-----------|-----------|----------------|
| `core::id` | `core/id/` | Typed identifiers: `AtomID`, `TorsionID`, `DOF_ID`, `JumpID`, `SequenceMapping` — the address system for every degree of freedom |
| `core::chemical` | `core/chemical/` | Residue types, atom types, element types, orbital types, and the `ChemicalManager` singleton that loads type definitions |
| `core::conformation` | `core/conformation/` | `Residue`, `Conformation` (the geometric state container), `AtomTree`, membrane info |
| `core::kinematics` | `core/kinematics/` | `FoldTree`, `Jump`, `Stub`, `RT` (rigid-body transforms), `AtomTree` traversal, DOF management |
| `core::pose` | `core/pose/` | `Pose` (the full modeling container), `PDBInfo`, `MiniPose`, pose utilities, variant types |
| `core::scoring` | `core/scoring/` | `ScoreFunction`, `ScoreType` enum, `EnergyMap`, `Energies`, `ScoringManager`, `NeighborList`, `EnergyGraph` |
| `core::scoring::methods` | `core/scoring/methods/` | The `EnergyMethod` class hierarchy — the extensibility point for new energy terms |
| `core::pack` | `core/pack/` | Rotamer packing, rotamer sets, interaction graphs, packing statistics |
| `core::fragment` | `core/fragment/` | Fragment picker framework for ab initio folding |
| `core::optimization` | `core/optimization/` | Minimization algorithms (LBFGS, conjugate gradient, atom-tree minimizer) |
| `core::io` | `core/io/` | PDB and mmCIF file parsers (now via gemmi), silent-file I/O |
| `core::import_pose` | `core/import_pose/` | Pose loading utilities wrapping core::io |
| `core::simple_metrics` | `core/simple_metrics/` | Reusable metric calculators (RMSD, SASA, etc.) |
| `core::select` | `core/select/` | Residue selectors — logical predicates for choosing subsets of residues |

The `core::id` subsystem deserves special attention because it is the universal addressing scheme. An `AtomID` is a `(residue_number, atom_within_residue)` pair; a `DOF_ID` is a `(atom_id, dof_type)` pair; a `TorsionID` identifies a torsional degree of freedom by its structural context (BB, CHI, JUMP). This typed-ID pattern prevents the subtle index bugs that plague positionally-indexed code in other molecular modeling frameworks.

Sources: [core/id/](source/src/core/id), [core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L1-L54), [core/types.hh](source/src/core/types.hh#L47-L69)

## The Pose-Centric Data Flow

Everything in Rosetta revolves around the `Pose` object. It is not just a data container — it is an event-bus that coordinates updates between its constituent subsystems. Understanding the Pose's internal composition is the single most important architectural insight for working with Rosetta.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Pose
        CONF["Conformation<br/>Geometry &amp; topology<br/>AtomTree, FoldTree"]
        ENERGY["Energies<br/>Score cache &amp;<br/>EnergyGraph"]
        PDBI["PDBInfo<br/>Chain/RESSEQ/<br/>occupancy mapping"]
        CACHE["BasicDataCache<br/>Arbitrary key-value<br/>attachments"]
        CST["ConstraintSet<br/>User-defined<br/>restraints"]
        METRICS["PoseMetricContainer<br/>Lazy-evaluated<br/>metrics"]
    end
    
    CONF --> |"xyz changes"| ENERGY
    CONF --> |"signals"| CST
    ENERGY --> |"triggered by"| SCOREFN["ScoreFunction<br/>weights + methods"]
    SCOREFN --> |"evaluates"| ENERGY
    MOVER["Mover::apply()"] --> |"modifies"| Pose
    FILTER["Filter::apply()"] --> |"reads"| ENERGY
    FILTER --> |"reads"| METRICS
```

The `Pose` aggregates five major subsystems. The **Conformation** holds the actual 3D coordinates, managed through an `AtomTree` kinematic forest rooted at the FoldTree topology. When a Mover changes a torsion angle, the AtomTree propagates the coordinate update efficiently to only the downstream atoms. The **Energies** object caches the results of the last scoring evaluation in a dense neighbor-aware `EnergyGraph`, avoiding redundant computation. The **PDBInfo** maps Rosetta's internal residue numbering back to the author-assigned chain IDs and residue numbers, ensuring round-trip fidelity with PDB files. The **ConstraintSet** holds user-defined spatial restraints (distance, angle, dihedral). The **BasicDataCache** provides extensible storage for arbitrary data that protocols want to attach to a Pose.

The comment block at the top of `Pose.hh` reveals an important architectural constraint: because "almost every file in Rosetta #includes Pose.hh," any heavy header added to Pose.hh triggers a massive recompilation cascade. Only lightweight forward declarations and enum typedefs are permitted in its header — everything else must be forward-declared or placed in implementation files.

Sources: [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L16-L25), [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L10-L17), [ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L10-L54)

## The Mover-Filter-Job Runtime Pattern

The execution model follows a three-stage pipeline: **input → processing → output**, each governed by a pluggable factory. The `protocols::jd2` (Job Distributor 2) namespace orchestrates this pipeline, with concrete implementations for filesystem, MPI, BOINC, and multi-threaded execution backends.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    INPUT["JobInputter<br/>(PDB, SilentFile,<br/>mmCIF, SerializedPose)"] --> JD["JobDistributor<br/>( jd2 / jd3 )"]
    JD --> PROTOCOL["Protocol<br/>(Movers + Filters)"]
    PROTOCOL --> OUTPUT["JobOutputter<br/>(PDB, SilentFile,<br/>mmCIF, ScoreOnly)"]
    
    subgraph "Factory Registration"
        JIF["JobInputterFactory"] --> INPUT
        JOF["JobOutputterFactory"] --> OUTPUT
        JDF["JobDistributorFactory"] --> JD
    end
```

The Job Distributor iterates over input structures (each wrapped in a `Job` object), applies the user-specified protocol (a sequence of Movers), evaluates Filters, and writes results through the outputter. Each of these three points is extensible through a factory: `JobInputterFactory`, `JobDistributorFactory`, and `JobOutputterFactory`. The `jd2` namespace contains 15+ inputter and outputter implementations, from PDB/Silent file I/O to MPI-parallel and BOINC-volunteer computing backends.

> [!TIP]
> The "Creator" pattern is pervasive throughout Rosetta. For every pluggable component (Movers, Filters, JobInputters, ScoreTypes, EnergyMethods), there is a corresponding `*Creator` class and a `*Factory` that maintains a registry. Registration happens through static initialization — each translation unit defines a static `*Registrator` object whose constructor calls `Factory::register_creator()`. This means simply linking a new `.cc` file into the binary automatically makes its components available to the XML parser and the C++ API.

Sources: [protocols/jd2/](source/src/protocols/jd2), [utility/factory/Factory.hh](source/src/utility/factory/Factory.hh)

## Shared Programming Idioms

Rosetta enforces several coding conventions that are deeply embedded in its architecture and build infrastructure:

**1-indexed vectors everywhere.** The `utility::vector1<T>` template (an adapter around `std::vector` that shifts indices to start at 1) is used throughout the codebase instead of `std::vector`. This eliminates the off-by-one errors endemic to 0-indexed molecular modeling code, where residue 1 is the first residue, not residue 0.

**Forward declarations over includes.** The `.fwd.hh` pattern is mandatory across the entire codebase. For every `Foo.hh`, there is a `Foo.fwd.hh` containing only forward declarations and `OP`/`COP`/`AP` typedefs. This is not optional — the build system and code review process enforce it to keep compilation times manageable in a codebase where a single `.hh` can be transitively included by thousands of translation units.

**Singleton pattern via CRTP.** The `SingletonBase<T>` template ([SingletonBase.hh](source/src/utility/SingletonBase.hh#L27-L54)) provides thread-safe singleton semantics using C++11 function-scope static initialization. The `ScoringManager`, `ChemicalManager`, and dozens of other managers derive from it. The derived class must have a private constructor and declare `SingletonBase<T>` as a friend.

**XML-driven protocol composition.** The `protocols::rosetta_scripts` subsystem provides an XML parser that instantiates Movers, Filters, TaskOperations, and ScoreFunctions by name from the factory registries. This decouples protocol definition from protocol implementation and is the primary interface for non-C++-developers. The full framework is described on the [RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework) page.

**Option system.** The `basic/options/` system provides a hierarchical, type-safe command-line option framework. Options are declared as static `BooleanOptionKey`, `RealOptionKey`, `IntegerOptionKey`, `StringOptionKey`, etc., organized by namespace (e.g., `OptionKeys::relax::fast`). The option system is initialized during `core::init::init()` and is accessible globally.

Sources: [SingletonBase.hh](source/src/utility/SingletonBase.hh#L19-L54), [VirtualBase.hh](source/src/utility/VirtualBase.hh#L21-L56), [utility/factory/](source/src/utility/factory)

## External Dependencies

Rosetta vendors a significant number of third-party libraries under `source/external/` to ensure build reproducibility across platforms. The key dependencies are:

| Dependency | Location | Purpose |
|-----------|----------|---------|
| **boost_submod** | `external/boost_submod/` | Smart pointers, filesystem, containers (C++11-era subset) |
| **gemmi_repo** | `external/gemmi_repo/` | PDB and mmCIF file parsing (replacing the legacy parser) |
| **libxml2** | `external/libxml2/` | XML parsing for RosettaScripts |
| **rdkit** | `external/rdkit/` | Chemical informatics for ligand handling |
| **pybind11** | `external/pybind11/` | Python bindings for PyRosetta |
| **tensorflow** | `external/tensorflow/` | Deep learning inference (trRosetta, ProteinMPNN) |
| **libzmq** | `external/libzmq/` | ZeroMQ for distributed computing |
| **zlib** | `external/zlib-1.2.8/` | Compression for silent files |
| **scons-local** | `external/scons-local/` | Vendored SCons build tool |
| **ObjexxFCL** | `src/ObjexxFCL/` | Fortran-compatible array library (internal vendoring) |

The `*.external.settings` files in `source/external/` control which optional dependencies are enabled. For example, `rdkit.external.settings` configures the RDKit integration, while `bcl.external.settings` controls the BCL library for membrane protein folding. These settings feed into both the SCons and CMake build systems.

Sources: [external/](source/external), [external SConscript](source/external/SConscript.external)

## Build System Architecture

Rosetta supports two build systems that coexist: **SCons** (primary, used for production and release builds) and **CMake** (secondary, used for PyRosetta, IDE integration, and some CI workflows). Both share the same source layout and produce equivalent binaries.

The SCons build is orchestrated from `source/SConstruct`, which loads project settings, configures the compiler toolchain, and delegates to per-directory `SConscript` files. The `source/cmake/` directory contains over 40 build configuration presets (e.g., `build_release/`, `build_debug/`, `build_torch/`, `build_sharedmpi/`) that generate platform-specific CMake configurations. These are described in detail on the [SCons Build System](6-scons-build-system) and [CMake Build Configuration](7-cmake-build-configuration) pages.

The parallel compilation of the `core` and `protocols` layers (split into `core.1`–`core.6` and `protocols.1`–`protocols.8`, plus domain-specific sub-groups) is one of the key build optimizations that makes this multi-million-line codebase practical to compile. Each compilation unit is a separate shared library with its own `.src.settings` declaring its dependencies, allowing independent incremental builds.

Sources: [SConstruct](source/SConstruct#L1-L80), [cmake/](source/cmake)

## Where to Go Next

Now that you understand the architectural skeleton, the natural next step is to examine the build system that assembles it, or to dive into the core data structures that define Rosetta's computational model:

- **[SCons Build System](6-scons-build-system)** — How Rosetta compiles across platforms and manages its massive dependency graph
- **[Pose and Conformation](8-pose-and-conformation)** — A deep dive into the central data object that drives all computation
- **[ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework)** — How energy terms are composed, weighted, and evaluated
- **[Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy)** — The protocol composition pattern that makes Rosetta extensible
- **[RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework)** — The declarative interface for assembling protocols without writing C++

# SCons Build System



Rosetta's build system is built on top of [SCons](https://scons.org/), an open-source software construction tool implemented in Python. Rather than relying on a simple Makefile hierarchy, Rosetta wraps SCons with a sophisticated multi-layer settings cascade that resolves compiler flags, platform paths, and project configurations through an algorithmic merge of dozens of `.settings` files. This architecture allows a single invocation of `scons` to produce platform-aware builds across Linux, macOS, Windows, and various HPC environments without manual Makefile editing. The entire build infrastructure lives under `source/tools/build/`, with the two top-level orchestrators — `source/SConstruct` and `source/SConscript` — serving as the entry points that bootstrap and dispatch the build graph.

Sources: [SConstruct](source/SConstruct#L1-L206), [SConscript](source/SConscript#L1-L76)

## Architecture Overview

The SCons build system operates as a multi-stage pipeline. When you invoke `scons`, control flows through a carefully ordered sequence: option parsing → settings resolution → environment construction → project dispatch → compilation. The following diagram illustrates this architecture at a macro level.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["scons [options] [targets]"] --> B["SConstruct (entry point)"]
    B --> C["tools/build/setup.py :: setup()"]
    C --> D["copy_template_files()"]
    C --> E["setup_build_options()"]
    C --> F["setup_build_settings()"]
    C --> G["setup_environment()"]
    C --> H["setup_platform_path()"]
    C --> I["setup_projects()"]
    E --> E1["basic.options (defaults)"]
    E --> E2["site.options / user.options"]
    E --> E3["options.settings (validation)"]
    F --> F1["basic.settings (~3000 lines)"]
    F --> F2["site.settings"]
    F --> F3["user.settings"]
    F --> F4["Algorithmic key merging"]
    G --> G1["SCons Environment construction"]
    H --> I
    I --> J["SConscript (main dispatcher)"]
    J --> K{"project kind?"}
    K -->|src (apps/pilot_apps)| K1["src/SConscript.apps → executables"]
    K -->|src (lib projects)| K2["src/SConscript.src → libraries"]
    K -->|test| K3["test/SConscript.test"]
    K -->|external| K4["external/SConscript.external"]
    K -->|doc| K5["doc/SConscript.doc"]
    K1 & K2 & K3 & K4 & K5 --> L["build/&lt;mode&gt;/&lt;platform&gt;/"]
```

The `BuildState` object — defined in [settings.py](source/tools/build/settings.py#L437-L452) — is the central data structure threading through every stage. It carries the resolved environment, platform path, option set, project list, and all accumulated build settings from the top-level `SConstruct` down into every sub-project `SConscript`.

Sources: [settings.py — BuildState](source/tools/build/settings.py#L437-L452), [setup.py — setup()](source/tools/build/setup.py#L497-L516)

## Build Configuration Pipeline

### Prerequisites and Invocation

The build system requires **SCons ≥ 0.98.1** and **Python ≥ 2.7** ([SConstruct#L8-L12](source/SConstruct#L8-L12)). The canonical production build command is:

```bash
./scons.py -j 8 mode=release bin
```

where `-j 8` controls parallel compilation threads and `bin` is the target that installs all executables into the output directory. The basic invocation form follows this pattern:

```
scons [flags] [<options>] [<targets>]
```

SCons flags (prefixed with `-`) control the SCons engine itself (e.g., `-j`, `-D`, `-H`), while Rosetta options are `key=value` pairs that configure the build type. Targets specify which projects or directories to compile.

Sources: [SConstruct — help text](source/SConstruct#L63-L178)
