### Options System

Build options are defined across three layers, each with increasing specificity:

| File | Purpose | Modified by |
|---|---|---|
| `basic.options` | Default values for all options | **Never** — repository-controlled |
| `site.options` | Site-wide defaults (cluster-specific) | System administrators |
| `user.options` | Per-developer defaults | Individual developers |
| Command line | Runtime overrides | Build invocation |

The supported option keys and their permissible values are enumerated in [options.settings](source/tools/build/options.settings#L9-L196). The six primary option dimensions are:

| Option | Description | Key Values |
|---|---|---|
| `cxx` | C++ compiler family | `gcc`, `clang`, `icc`, `msvc`, `xlc` |
| `cxx_ver` | Compiler version | e.g., `5.1`, `6.3`, `*` (auto-detect) |
| `os` | Target operating system | `linux`, `macos`, `windows`, `cygwin` |
| `arch` | Processor architecture | `x86`, `amd`, `ppc`, `arm`, `aarch64` |
| `mode` | Build optimization level | `debug`, `release`, `release_native`, `release_symbols`, `profile`, `coverage`, `addsane`, `memsan`, `tsan`, `ubsan` |
| `cat` | Build category | `src`, `external`, `test`, `doc` |

Options use `*` as a wildcard, resolved automatically by [setup_platforms.py](source/tools/build/setup_platforms.py). For instance, macOS 10.9+ (Darwin kernel version ≥ 13) defaults to `clang` rather than `gcc` ([basic.options#L23-L27](source/tools/build/basic.options#L23-L27)).

Sources: [basic.options](source/tools/build/basic.options#L1-L46), [options.settings](source/tools/build/options.settings#L9-L196)

### Settings Cascade and Resolution

The settings system is the most architecturally distinctive component. Rather than using static Makefile rules, Rosetta resolves compiler flags through an **algorithmic cascade** that merges settings dictionaries based on a computed set of identifier keys. The resolution process works as follows:

1. A set of **possible setting IDs** is generated from combinations of the current options — for example `"gcc, linux, release"`, `"gcc, 6.3, linux, release"`, `"gcc, x86, 64"`, etc.
2. Each ID is looked up in the aggregated settings pool (from `basic.settings`, `site.settings`, and `user.settings`).
3. Matching settings are wrapped in `BuildSettingsCombined` objects, each carrying four merge strategies: **prepends**, **appends**, **overrides**, and **removes**.
4. These are applied sequentially to a fresh `SCons Environment` in [setup_environment()](source/tools/build/setup.py#L440-L494).

The merge precedence (last writer wins) follows this order, from lowest to highest priority:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["base"] --> B["os"]
    B --> C["os, os_ver"]
    C --> D["compiler"]
    D --> E["compiler, version"]
    E --> F["compiler, os"]
    F --> G["compiler, ver, os, ver"]
    G --> H["compiler, arch, size"]
    H --> I["compiler, mode"]
    I --> J["compiler, os, arch"]
    J --> K["compiler, extra"]
    K --> L["site.settings"]
    L --> M["user.settings"]
```

The `basic.settings` file spans over **3,000 lines** and defines everything from base include paths and preprocessor defines ([basic.settings#L66-L104](source/tools/build/basic.settings#L66-L104)) to per-compiler flag sets — for instance, the GCC configuration includes `-std=c++0x`, warning flags (`-Wall -Wextra -Werror`), and `-isystem` directives for suppressing warnings from external headers like Boost ([basic.settings#L145-L193](source/tools/build/basic.settings#L145-L193)).

> [!TIP]
> When adding a new external dependency, use `overrides` in `user.settings` to add include/library paths, or `appends` to add linker flags. Never modify `basic.settings` directly — it is repository-controlled and shared across all developers.

Sources: [basic.settings — merge order documentation](source/tools/build/basic.settings#L9-L56), [basic.settings — base settings](source/tools/build/basic.settings#L66-L193), [setup.py — setup_build_settings()](source/tools/build/setup.py#L212-L328)

### Environment Construction

The `setup_environment()` function ([setup.py#L440-L494](source/tools/build/setup.py#L440-L494)) translates the merged `BuildSettingsCombined` objects into a concrete SCons `Environment`. This is where the four merge strategies take effect:

- **`appends`**: Adds flags to the end of existing lists (e.g., adding `-O2` to the existing optimization flags).
- **`prepends`**: Adds flags to the beginning of existing lists (e.g., putting a custom include path before system defaults).
- **`overrides`**: Replaces existing values entirely (e.g., setting a specific compiler command).
- **`removes`**: Strips individual values from existing lists (e.g., removing a conflicting `-D` define).

The `BuildSettings.symbols()` method ([settings.py#L260-L349](source/tools/build/settings.py#L260-L349)) converts the high-level flag categories (`cc`, `cxx`, `compile`, `link`, `warn`, `mode`) into SCons-native symbols like `CCFLAGS`, `CXXFLAGS`, `CFLAGS`, `LINKFLAGS`, `CPPPATH`, `LIBPATH`, and `LIBS`. It also handles SCons version-specific bugs (#846 and #1971) by branching on the detected SCons version.

Sources: [setup.py — setup_environment()](source/tools/build/setup.py#L440-L494), [settings.py — BuildSettings.symbols()](source/tools/build/settings.py#L260-L349)

## Extras System

The `extras` option ([options.settings#L71-L196](source/tools/build/options.settings#L71-L196)) is the primary extension mechanism for enabling optional features. Extras are specified as a comma-separated list and each one injects additional compiler flags, library dependencies, and preprocessor defines through the settings cascade. Multiple extras can be combined in a single build:

```bash
scons mode=release extras=mpi,serialization bin
```

The following table summarizes the most commonly used extras:

| Extra | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `static` | Static linking instead of shared libraries | More portable, larger binaries |
| `mpi` | MPI-based parallelism | Requires MPI runtime installed |
| `serialization` | Boost serialization support | Needed for distributed protocols |
| `cxx11thread` | C++11 threading utilities | Multi-threaded execution support |
| `omp` | OpenMP parallelism | Compiler-specific OpenMP flags |
| `python` | Link to Python interpreter | For embedded Python extensions |
| `cuda` / `opencl` | GPU computing support | Requires CUDA/OpenCL toolkits |
| `hdf5` | HDF5 data stores | For structured data I/O |
| `tensorflow` / `tensorflow_gpu` | TensorFlow integration | ML extension linking |
| `torch` / `torch_gpu` | LibTorch integration | PyTorch C++ backend |
| `cxx14` / `cxx17` / `cxx20` | C++ standard level | Defines `CXX14_OR_LATER`, etc. |
| `boinc` | BOINC support | Used by Rosetta@home |
| `valgrind` | Valgrind-compatible build | Adds `--valgrind` flags |
| `lto` | Link-time optimization | Slower build, faster runtime |

Each extra activates a corresponding settings key in `basic.settings` (e.g., `"gcc, mpi"` or `"clang, cuda"`) that appends the necessary flags and libraries to the build environment.

Sources: [options.settings — extras list](source/tools/build/options.settings#L71-L196), [SConstruct — examples](source/SConstruct#L150-L177)

## Platform Path Convention

The build output directory follows a structured platform path generated by `setup_platform_path()` ([setup.py#L331-L349](source/tools/build/setup.py#L331-L349)). The format is:

```
build/<mode>/<os>/<os_ver>/<arch_size>/<arch>/<cxx>/<cxx_ver>/<extras>
```

For example, a release build with GCC 6.3 on 64-bit Linux would produce:

```
build/release/linux/x86_64/64/x86/gcc/6.3/default/
```

The `<os_ver>` component is omitted when set to `*` (auto-detected), and `<extras>` defaults to `"default"` when no extras are specified. This naming convention ensures that builds for different platforms, compiler versions, and feature sets never collide in the same source tree, enabling simultaneous multi-configuration builds.

Sources: [setup.py — setup_platform_path()](source/tools/build/setup.py#L331-L349)

## Project Dispatch and SConscript Hierarchy

The top-level `SConscript` ([source/SConscript](source/SConscript#L1-L76)) is responsible for dispatching the build to sub-project SConscripts. Before dispatching, it performs three critical pre-build steps:

1. **Version generation** — runs `version.py` to embed the SVN/Git revision into `src/core/svn_version.cc` (skippable with `--nover`)
2. **Options update** — executes `update_options.sh` to synchronize option definitions
3. **Submodule initialization** — runs `update_submodules.sh` to fetch required git submodules

Each project kind is then dispatched to its own SConscript with a `variant_dir` mapping that redirects build artifacts into the platform-specific `build/` subdirectory:

```python
SConscript(script, exports=["build", "project"],
           variant_dir=build_path, duplicate=False)
```

The `duplicate=False` parameter is significant — it tells SCons to reference source files in-place rather than copying them into the build directory, keeping the build tree shallow.

Sources: [SConscript — dispatch logic](source/SConscript#L46-L68)

## User Customization

Developers customize their builds through two mechanisms that sit at the top of the settings cascade:

**`user.settings`** — Created from `user.settings.template` ([user.settings.template](source/tools/build/user.settings.template#L1-L52)), this file allows you to prepend, append, override, or remove any build setting. Common use cases include adding custom include paths for external libraries, importing the full OS environment (`"ENV" : os.environ`), or enabling experimental preprocessor defines.

**`user.options`** — Created from `user.options.template`, this file sets default option values so you don't need to specify them on every `scons` invocation. For example, a developer on a cluster with Intel MPI might set `extras = "mpi"` here.

Both files are gitignored and never checked into the repository. Template files are auto-copied on first build via `copy_template_files()` in [setup.py#L17-L23](source/tools/build/setup.py#L17-L23).

> [!TIP]
> During rapid development iteration, use `scons --nover` to skip the versioning and submodule update scripts. This avoids recompiling files that depend on `svn_version.cc` and can significantly reduce incremental build times — but **never** use it for production builds.

Sources: [user.settings.template](source/tools/build/user.settings.template#L1-L52), [setup.py — copy_template_files()](source/tools/build/setup.py#L17-L23)

## Core Settings Classes

The settings infrastructure is implemented through a class hierarchy in [settings.py](source/tools/build/settings.py#L1-L452) that provides structured, validated access to build configuration:

| Class | Purpose | Key Slot Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `Settings` | Base dictionary with attribute access | Dynamic via `__slots__` |
| `BuildOptionsSupported` | Enumerates all valid option values | `cxx`, `os`, `arch`, `mode`, `cat`, `extras` |
| `BuildOptions` | Resolved options for current build | `cxx`, `cxx_ver`, `os`, `os_ver`, `arch`, `arch_size`, `mode`, `cat`, `extras` |
| `BuildFlags` | Categorized compiler flags | `cc`, `cxx`, `compile`, `link`, `shlink`, `mode`, `warn` |
| `BuildSettings` | Single setting layer with symbols | `flags`, `defines`, `include_path`, `library_path`, `libraries` |
| `BuildSettingsCombined` | Wraps a setting with merge strategy | `id`, `appends`, `prepends`, `overrides`, `removes` |
| `ProjectSettings` | Per-project settings from `.src.settings` | `sources`, `defines`, `include_path`, `libraries` |
| `BuildState` | Global build state passed through SConscripts | `environment`, `platform`, `options`, `projects`, `settings` |

All classes inherit from Python's `dict` and use `__slots__` to enforce a fixed schema, catching typos at attribute-access time rather than silently storing incorrect keys.

Sources: [settings.py — class hierarchy](source/tools/build/settings.py#L65-L452)

## Common Build Recipes

The following table provides a quick reference for typical build scenarios:

| Goal | Command |
|---|---|
| Default debug build | `scons` |
| Production release build | `scons -j 8 mode=release bin` |
| Build a specific project | `scons mode=release <project_name>` |
| Build a specific executable | `scons mode=release bin/<exec_name>` |
| Enable MPI + serialization | `scons mode=release extras=mpi,serialization bin` |
| Static linking (portable binaries) | `scons mode=release extras=static bin` |
| Build unit tests | `scons cat=test` then `python test/run.py` |
| Fast incremental dev build | `scons --nover` |
| Debug logging of build decisions | `scons log=toplevel,platform,options,settings` |
| Native-optimized (run on compile machine only) | `scons mode=release_native bin` |

## Relationship to CMake

Rosetta also ships with a CMake-based build configuration. The SCons system is the older, more established build path and remains the default for many HPC and cluster environments. The CMake system provides a more conventional alternative that may be preferred for IDE integration and cross-platform workflows. For a full comparison and CMake-specific guidance, see [CMake Build Configuration](7-cmake-build-configuration).


# CMake Build Configuration



Rosetta's CMake build system operates as a two-stage code-generation pipeline: Python scripts read SCons-style `.src.settings` files to emit intermediate `.cmake` project definitions, which CMake then consumes alongside a layered chain of shared configuration modules. This architecture allows the CMake system to coexist with the legacy SCons build while leveraging CMake's superior IDE integration and Ninja's parallelism. This page documents every layer of that pipeline, from project scaffolding scripts down to per-compiler flag matrices.

Sources: [README](source/cmake/README), [ninja_build.py](source/ninja_build.py)

## Build Pipeline Architecture

The CMake system is not a standalone build definition — it is a *consumer* of the same `.src.settings` manifests that SCons uses. A Python preprocessing step (`make_project.py`) reads these manifests and generates per-library and per-application `.cmake` files into `source/cmake/build/`. The build directory's `CMakeLists.txt` then stitches these generated files together with a shared chain of configuration includes.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Stage 1: Code Generation"
        SS["src/*.src.settings<br/>src/*.test.settings"] --> MP["make_project.py"]
        MP --> GC["cmake/build/*.cmake<br/>(libraries, apps, tests)"]
    end

    subgraph "Stage 2: CMake Configuration"
        GC --> BDIR["build_*/CMakeLists.txt<br/>(sets MODE, LINK_RULES)"]
        BDIR --> COMP["compiler.cmake<br/>Auto-detect compiler"]
        BDIR --> PRE["build.pre.cmake<br/>Platform & includes"]
        BDIR --> LINK["shared/static.build.cmake<br/>Link strategy"]
        BDIR --> SETTINGS["build.settings.cmake<br/>Compiler+mode flags"]
        BDIR --> POST["build.post.cmake<br/>Library definitions & link order"]
        BDIR --> APPS["apps.all.cmake / pilot_apps.all.cmake"]
        BDIR --> TEST["build.test.cmake"]
        BDIR --> INST["install.cmake"]
    end

    subgraph "Stage 3: Build & Install"
        COMP & PRE & LINK & SETTINGS & POST & APPS & TEST & INST --> NINJA["ninja (or make)"]
        NINJA --> BIN["bin/<app>.<platform><compiler><mode>"]
        NINJA --> UTEST["unit test executables"]
    end
```

The three-stage design means that **any change to source file membership** (adding a new `.cc` file to a library, registering a new application) requires re-running `make_project.py` before CMake will see it. This is the most common source of "file not found" errors for developers migrating from SCons.

Sources: [make_project.py](source/cmake/make_project.py), [build_release/CMakeLists.txt](source/cmake/build_release/CMakeLists.txt)

## Build Variant Catalog

Rosetta ships with over 30 pre-configured build directories under `source/cmake/build_*/`, each containing a minimal `CMakeLists.txt` that sets the `MODE` and `LINK_RULES` variables and then includes the shared build chain. This table catalogs the most commonly used variants.

| Build Directory | MODE | LINK_RULES | Compiler Override | Key Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `build_release` | `release` | `shared` | Auto-detect | Standard optimized build |
| `build_debug` | `debug` | `shared` | Auto-detect | Debug + unit tests (default) |
| `build_clang` | `release` | `shared` | `clang`/`clang++` | Clang-specific release |
| `build_omp` | `release` | `shared` | `gcc` (forced) | OpenMP parallelism (`-fopenmp`) |
| `build_release_static` | `release_static` | `static` | Auto-detect | Static linking for portability |
| `build_sharedmpi` | `release` | `shared` | Auto-detect | MPI with shared libraries |
| `build_staticmpi` | `release` | `static` | Auto-detect | MPI with static linking |
| `build_cxx11` | `release` | `shared` | Auto-detect | Explicit C++11 build |
| `build_cxx11_omp` | `release` | `shared` | Auto-detect | C++11 + OpenMP |
| `build_graphics` | `release` | `shared` | Auto-detect | Graphics/visualization support |
| `build_cxx11_windows_vs` | `release` | `shared` | `cl` (MSVC) | Windows Visual Studio |
| `build_torch` | `release` | `shared` | Auto-detect | PyTorch/ML integration |
| `build_zeromq` | — | `shared` | Auto-detect | ZeroMQ messaging layer |
| `build_clangSA` | `release` | `shared` | `clang` | Clang Static Analyzer |
| `build_clang_tidy` | `release` | `shared` | Auto-detect | Clang-Tidy linting |
| `build_PyRosetta.release` | `release` | `shared` | Auto-detect | PyRosetta Python bindings |
| `build_PyRosetta.debug` | `debug` | `shared` | Auto-detect | PyRosetta debug bindings |

Each variant's `CMakeLists.txt` follows an identical include sequence, differing only in the values of `MODE`, `LINK_RULES`, and optional compiler overrides. The full include chain for a standard variant is:

Sources: [build_release/CMakeLists.txt](source/cmake/build_release/CMakeLists.txt#L1-L34), [build_debug/CMakeLists.txt](source/cmake/build_debug/CMakeLists.txt#L1-L39)

```
INCLUDE(../build/compiler.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/build.pre.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/${LINK_RULES}.build.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/build.settings.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/build.post.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/apps.all.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/pilot_apps.all.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/build.test.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/install.cmake)
```

## Project Scaffolding: make_project.py

The `make_project.py` script is the bridge between Rosetta's SCons-era file manifests and the CMake build. It executes four preparatory steps before generating build files:

1. **`update_version()`** — Runs `version.py` to regenerate version strings
2. **`update_options()`** — Runs `update_options.sh` to regenerate option registration code
3. **`update_submodules()`** — Runs `update_submodules.sh` to fetch external dependencies
4. **`update_ResidueType_enum_files()`** — Regenerates ResidueType enumeration files

It then reads the `.src.settings` files and writes three categories of `.cmake` output into `source/cmake/build/`:

- **Library `.cmake` files** — Each library (e.g., `core.1`, `protocols.3`) gets a `<library>.cmake` file setting `<library>_files` as a list of source paths
- **Application `.cmake` files** — Each app under `src/apps/` gets a `<app>.cmake` file with `ADD_EXECUTABLE`, `TARGET_LINK_LIBRARIES`, compile/link property assignments, and symlinking rules
- **Test `.cmake` files** — Unit test manifests for CxxTest integration, setting `*_testfiles`, `*_testdirectories`, `*_testheaders`, and `*_testinputs`

The application `.cmake` generator also creates symlink targets that place executables into `source/bin/` with Rosetta's naming convention: `<app>.<platform><compiler><mode>` (e.g., `relax.linuxgccrelease`).

Sources: [make_project.py](source/cmake/make_project.py#L90-L188)

## Core Configuration Modules

The shared build infrastructure lives in `source/cmake/build/` and is organized into a strict include ordering. Each module has a specific responsibility in the configuration pipeline.

### compiler.cmake — Compiler Auto-Detection

Rather than letting build variants hardcode the compiler, `compiler.cmake` inspects `CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_ID` and maps it to a `COMPILER` variable used by downstream modules. The detection logic follows a priority chain:

- If the compiler ID matches `.*[Cc][Ll][Aa][Nn][Gg].*` → sets `COMPILER clang`
- If `WIN32` is set → sets `COMPILER cl`
- Otherwise → sets `COMPILER gcc`

Crucially, this file **does not change which compiler CMake uses** — it only sets the Rosetta-internal `COMPILER` string that drives flag selection in `build.settings.cmake` and the executable extension suffix. To actually change compilers, you must set `$CC`/`$CXX` environment variables or pass `-DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER` — and perform a clean rebuild, because CMake caches the compiler choice.

Sources: [compiler.cmake](source/cmake/build/compiler.cmake#L1-L43)

### build.pre.cmake — Platform and Include Setup

This module declares the project (`minirosetta`), sets archive creation policies (to fix linker issues on some platforms), and configures include paths. It handles platform detection via `APPLE`, `UNIX`, and `WIN32` conditionals, adding platform-specific directories under `src/platform/` and setting corresponding preprocessor defines (`-DMAC`, `-DLINUX`, `-DWIN32`). External dependency include paths are set with the `SYSTEM` directive to suppress warnings from third-party headers.

Sources: [build.pre.cmake](source/cmake/build/build.pre.cmake#L1-L50)

### build.settings.cmake — Compiler and Mode Flag Matrix

This is the largest and most critical configuration file at 704 lines. It defines a comprehensive flag matrix organized as a two-dimensional lookup: **compiler × build mode**. Each combination specifies compile flags, warning flags, preprocessor defines, and linker flags.

For **GCC**, the flag categories are:

| Category | Debug Mode | Release Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Optimization | `-O0` | `-O3 -ffast-math -fno-finite-math-only -funroll-loops -finline-functions -finline-limit=20000 -s` |
| Debug info | `-g -ggdb -ffloat-store` | (none) |
| Warnings | `-Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Werror -Wno-long-long -Wno-strict-aliasing` | Same + `-Wno-unused-variable -Wno-unused-parameter` |
| Defines | `-D_DEBUG -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` | `-DNDEBUG` |
| Base compile | `-pipe -ffor-scope -ftemplate-depth-256 -fPIC` | Same |
| Language | `-std=c++11` | `-std=c++11` |

For GCC versions above 8.1, the configuration additionally appends `-Wl,--no-as-needed` to both compile and link flags and removes the now-obsolete `-ffor-scope`.

For **Clang**, the release configuration uses `-O3 -w -std=c++11 -Qunused-arguments -DUNUSUAL_ALLOCATOR_DECLARATION -ftemplate-depth-256` with platform-specific standard library selection (`-stdlib=libstdc++` on Linux, `-stdlib=libc++` on macOS).

For **MSVC** (`cl`), the configuration uses `-permissive- -bigobj` with a curated set of warning suppressions (`-wd4018`, `-wd4101`, `-wd4244`, `-wd4251`, `-wd4267`, `-wd4275`, `-wd4305`, `-wd4996`) and defines `-DNOMINMAX -DWIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN -DBOOST_ERROR_CODE_HEADER_ONLY -DBOOST_SYSTEM_NO_DEPRECATED -DBOOST_ALL_NO_LIB`. A global job pool of 4 link processes is enforced to prevent the MSVC linker from consuming all physical memory during parallel builds of Rosetta's massive static libraries.

> [!TIP]
> The `-Werror` flag is enabled for both GCC and Clang in the default `build.settings.cmake`. If you are building against a newer compiler version that introduces new warnings, you may need to either remove `-Werror` from the `warn` list or add specific `-Wno-<warning>` suppressions. The `build_release_werror` variant exists specifically to isolate this concern for CI workflows.

Sources: [build.settings.cmake](source/cmake/build/build.settings.cmake#L1-L200), [build.settings.cmake](source/cmake/build/build.settings.cmake#L200-L500)

### shared.build.cmake vs static.build.cmake — Linking Strategy

The `LINK_RULES` variable set in each variant's `CMakeLists.txt` determines which link module is included. The **shared** variant sets `LINK_TYPE SHARED` and links against `z dl stdc++` as external system libraries. It also configures RPATH handling for relocatable binaries — setting `CMAKE_INSTALL_RPATH` to search `${CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX}/lib`, `$ORIGIN/../lib`, and `@executable_path/../lib`, which allows Rosetta executables to find their shared libraries after installation.

The **static** variant sets `LINK_TYPE STATIC` and links against `z.a libcppdb-static.a`. On MSVC, it uses `zlib ws2_32` instead. Static builds are preferred for HPC environments and containerized deployments where library portability matters more than incremental link times.

Sources: [shared.build.cmake](source/cmake/build/shared.build.cmake#L1-L21), [static.build.cmake](source/cmake/build/static.build.cmake#L1-L9)

### build.post.cmake — Library Chaining and Target Hierarchy

After flags are set, `build.post.cmake` iterates over the `LIBRARIES` list (generated by `make_project.py` from the `.src.settings` files), includes each library's `.cmake` definition, creates the library target, and chains them into a sequential link order. The chaining is critical: each library depends on the previous one via `ADD_DEPENDENCIES`, and `TARGET_LINK_LIBRARIES` passes the accumulated link chain forward. This produces a deterministic link order that mirrors the SCons dependency resolution.

The module also defines the **build target hierarchy** used by Ninja/Make:

| Custom Target | Dependencies | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `libs` | `BUILD_ROSETTA_LIBS` | Build all Rosetta libraries only |
| `apps` | `BUILD_ROSETTA_LIBS` | Build public applications |
| `pilot_apps` | `BUILD_ROSETTA_LIBS` | Build pilot/experimental applications |
| `bin` | `apps` + `pilot_apps` | Build all executables |
| `unit` | `BUILD_ROSETTA_LIBS` | Build all unit test executables |

Sources: [build.post.cmake](source/cmake/build/build.post.cmake#L1-L36)

### external.cmake — Third-Party Dependency Management

Rosetta vendors its critical external dependencies in `source/external/` and builds them as part of the CMake pipeline. The `external.cmake` module iterates over `EXTERNAL_LIBRARIES`, reads each `external_<lib>.cmake` definition, and builds them with suppressed warnings (`-Wno-error -w` on non-MSVC compilers). The key vendored dependencies built here include:

- **cppdb** — A C++ database connectivity layer wrapping SQLite3
- **sqlite3** — Built from source with `SQLITE_OMIT_LOAD_EXTENSION`, `SQLITE_OMIT_DISABLE_LFS`, and `SQLITE_THREADSAFE=0`
- **zlib** — Compression library (platform-specific compile flags on MSVC: `-DZLIB_DLL=1 -DZLIB_WINAPI=1`)

The module also applies version-specific workarounds for GCC 4.9 and GCC 5.x/6.x/7.x to fix cppdb linking errors via `-fno-strict-aliasing -ldl` and `-Wl,--no-as-needed -ldl`.

Sources: [external.cmake](source/cmake/build/external.cmake#L1-L169)

## Unit Test Infrastructure

Unit tests use the **CxxTest** framework, vendored in `source/external/cxxtest/`. The `build.test.cmake` module automates the complete test lifecycle:

1. **Test registration** — Reads `test_<library>.cmake` files (generated by `make_project.py`) containing lists of test source files, directories, headers, and input files
2. **Code generation** — For each test `.cc` file, invokes `cxxtestgen.py --have-std --part` to generate a CxxTest runner
3. **Main wrapper** — Generates a root test runner per library using `cxxtestgen.py --error-printer --root`
4. **Compilation** — Builds each library's test as a single executable linked against all Rosetta libraries
5. **Input staging** — Copies test input files into the build tree using `CMAKE_COMMAND -E copy`

The Windows path uses `cmd /c` to invoke `cxxtestgen.py` due to CMake's `EXECUTE_PROCESS` requiring a binary executable on that platform.

Sources: [build.test.cmake](source/cmake/build/build.test.cmake#L1-L53)

## Building with ninja_build.py (Recommended)

The `ninja_build.py` script at `source/ninja_build.py` is the officially recommended entry point for CMake builds. It orchestrates the full pipeline — project generation, CMake configuration, and Ninja invocation — through a single command with intuitive abbreviations.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CLI["ninja_build.py <build> [options]"] --> |"-remake"| MP["make_project.py all/my"]
    CLI --> |"-remake"| CM["cmake -G Ninja"]
    MP --> CM
    CM --> NJ["ninja -C build_<name> [targets]"]
    NJ --> SYM["bin/ symlinks"]
    NJ --> UT["unit test executables"]
```

**First-time build:**
```bash
cd rosetta/main/source/
./ninja_build.py release -remake
```

**Subsequent incremental builds** (after editing `.cc`/`.hh` files but NOT `.src.settings`):
```bash
./ninja_build.py r
```

**After modifying `.src.settings` files:**
```bash
./ninja_build.py r -remake
```

### Command Reference

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `release` / `r` | Optimized release build |
| `debug` / `d` | Debug build with unit tests |
| `rs` | Release with static linking |
| `z` | ZeroMQ messaging build |
| `m` | C++11 threading build |
| `-remake` | Re-run `make_project.py` + `cmake` |
| `-my` | Use `*.src.settings.my` instead of `*.src.settings.all` |
| `-t <target>` | Build specific target(s): `bin`, `apps`, `pilot_apps`, `unit`, `relax`, etc. |
| `-j <N>` | Override Ninja's auto-detected parallelism |
| `-k` | Keep building on errors (up to 5000) |
| `-v` | Verbose output (show actual compiler commands) |
| `-clean` | Remove all generated files in build directory |
| `-install <path>` | Install relocatable binaries to given path |

The script validates that both `cmake` and `ninja` are on `PATH` before proceeding and provides clear error messages if prerequisites are missing.

Sources: [ninja_build.py](source/ninja_build.py#L1-L138)

## Manual CMake Workflow

For developers who prefer direct control over CMake, the manual workflow follows three steps:

```bash
cd rosetta/main/source/cmake/

# Step 1: Generate CMake project files from src.settings
./make_project.py all          # or "my" for restricted build

# Step 2: Configure with CMake
cd build_release/
cmake -G Ninja                 # or "cmake ." for Make

# Step 3: Build
ninja                          # or "make"
ninja -v                       # verbose compiler commands
ninja relax                    # build single application
ninja core                     # build single library sub-target
```

For Make-based builds, the `/fast` suffix skips dependency checking for already-built libraries:
```bash
make myapp/fast    # rebuild only myapp, skip dependency checks
make VERBOSE=1     # show full compiler commands
```

> [!TIP]
> CMake caches the compiler selection from the first invocation in a clean build directory. Changing `$CC`/`$CXX` or `-DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER` on subsequent runs will have no effect — you must delete the build directory contents and re-run from scratch. This is a fundamental difference from SCons, which re-evaluates compiler selection on every invocation.

Sources: [README](source/cmake/README#L18-L135)

## Installation and Relocation

The `install.cmake` module configures a relocatable installation layout. Running `ninja install` (or `cmake --install .`) produces:

```
<install_prefix>/
├── bin/          # All executables
├── lib/          # Shared/static libraries
└── database/     # Full Rosetta database (copied from source)
```

During installation, the `score` application is automatically executed against a test PDB to generate binary Dunbrack rotamer files — a post-install step that ensures the database is in a usable state. The `CMAKE_SKIP_INSTALL_ALL_DEPENDENCY` policy is set to `TRUE`, allowing partial installations (e.g., `ninja rosetta_scripts && ninja install`) without triggering a full rebuild.

Sources: [install.cmake](source/cmake/build/install.cmake#L1-L25)

## Creating Custom Build Configurations

The `make_new_build.py` script (located at `source/cmake/make_new_build.py`) scaffolds new build variant directories. For manual creation, the pattern is straightforward — create a new `build_<name>/CMakeLists.txt` with the desired configuration variables:

```cmake
CMAKE_MINIMUM_REQUIRED(VERSION 2.6)
SET(MODE release)           # "release", "debug", or custom
SET(LINK_RULES shared)      # "shared" or "static"
SET(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS 1)

INCLUDE(../build/compiler.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/build.pre.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/${LINK_RULES}.build.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/build.settings.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/build.post.cmake)

INCLUDE(../build/apps.all.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/pilot_apps.all.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/build.test.cmake)
INCLUDE(../build/install.cmake)
```

For build variants that need non-standard flags (like the OpenMP variant), the generated flags from `build.settings.cmake` can be overridden by setting `COMPILE_FLAGS`, `CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS`, and `CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS` directly in the variant's `CMakeLists.txt` after including the standard chain.

Sources: [build_omp/CMakeLists.txt](source/cmake/build_omp/CMakeLists.txt#L1-L25), [build_clang/CMakeLists.txt](source/cmake/build_clang/CMakeLists.txt#L1-L25)

## SCons Coexistence and Migration Context

The CMake build system was designed to coexist with the SCons build system documented in [SCons Build System](6-scons-build-system). Both systems read the same `.src.settings` manifest files, ensuring source file lists remain synchronized. The key architectural difference is that SCons evaluates its build graph dynamically on every invocation, while CMake requires explicit regeneration via `make_project.py` when source membership changes.

The `gen_cmake_build.py` utility at `source/cmake/gen_cmake_build.py` demonstrates the original bridge concept: it parses `tools/build/basic.settings` (the SCons configuration) and extracts settings matching a given build tag, providing a reference for how SCons settings map to CMake equivalents. This script is primarily of historical interest now, as `build.settings.cmake` has evolved to be independently maintained.


# Pose and Conformation



The **Pose** is the central data structure in all of Rosetta — the atomic unit of computation that flows through every protocol, mover, and scorer. Understanding Pose and its Conformation subsystem is prerequisite to effective work in any domain of the codebase. This page dissects their architecture, the relationship between internal (torsion/DOF) and external (Cartesian) coordinates, the observer pattern that binds them together, and the extension points available to developers.

## Architectural Overview

Pose is not a monolithic class. It is a **coordinating façade** that composes four major subsystems — Conformation (geometry and kinematics), Energies (scoring cache), PDBInfo (file-format metadata), and a signal network (observer notifications). The header itself carries a stark warning: nearly every file in Rosetta includes Pose.hh, so unnecessary includes here trigger massive recompilation [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L16-L25).

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Pose["Pose (core::pose::Pose)"]
        direction TB
        Conf["Conformation<br/>geometry + kinematics"]
        Energy["Energies<br/>scoring cache"]
        PDB["PDBInfo<br/>file metadata"]
        Cache["BasicDataCache<br/>arbitrary user data"]
        ObsCache["ObserverCache<br/>indexed observers"]
        RefPos["ReferencePoseSet<br/>residue mapping"]
        Constraints["ConstraintSet<br/>restraints"]

        Conf --> Residues["ResidueOPs<br/>residues_"]
        Conf --> FT["FoldTree<br/>topology"]
        Conf --> AT["AtomTree<br/>kinematics"]
        FT --> AT

        Residues --> Res1["Residue 1"]
        Residues --> Res2["Residue N"]
        Res1 --> Atoms["Atom[]<br/>xyz + type"]
    end

    subgraph Signals["Signal Hubs"]
        GE["GeneralEvent"]
        CE["ConformationEvent"]
        EE["EnergyEvent"]
        DE["DestructionEvent"]
    end

    Pose -.->|"fires"| Signals
    Conf -.->|"fires"| CE
```

The class declaration at line 162 makes this composition explicit: Pose inherits from `utility::VirtualBase` and `enable_shared_from_this<Pose>`, providing both polymorphic ownership and safe weak-pointer access [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L162-L163).

## Core Responsibilities of Pose

The official documentation in the Pose header enumerates three responsibilities [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L117-L142):

| Responsibility | Description | Key Methods |
|---|---|---|
| **Kinematic** | (a) Update xyz coordinates when internal DOFs change; (b) Update internal coordinates when xyz changes | `set_phi()`, `set_xyz()`, `set_jump()`, `dof()`, `set_dof()` |
| **Scoring** | (a) Track what parts changed since last evaluation; (b) Cache residue and residue-pair energies | `energies()`, `scoring_begin()`, `scoring_end()` |
| **Container** | Single object for passing molecular systems; copying whole molecules or stretches between Poses | `assign()`, `detached_copy()`, `clone()`, `append_pose_by_jump()` |

> [!TIP]
> Calling `pose.residue(seqpos)` triggers a **refold** if torsions or coordinates are out-of-date. In contrast, `pose.residue_type(seqpos)` does not trigger a refold. This distinction matters in performance-critical loops — use the lighter accessor when you only need type information.

## Conformation: The Geometry Engine

`core::conformation::Conformation` is defined as "a container of Residues and the kinematics to manage them" [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L90-L91). It inherits from `utility::VirtualBase` and `enable_shared_from_this<Conformation>`, mirroring Pose's ownership model [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L91).

### Private Data Layout

The Conformation's private data section reveals its internal architecture [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L1710-L1800):

| Member | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `residues_` | `ResidueOPs` | Owning container of all residues |
| `residue_type_sets_` | `CacheableResidueTypeSets` | Conformation-specific residue type definitions (copy-on-write) |
| `chain_endings_` | `vector1<Size>` | Positions marking chain boundaries |
| `fold_tree_` | `FoldTreeOP` | Topological connectivity of residues |
| `atom_tree_` | `AtomTreeOP` | Kinematic tree for DOF propagation |
| `membrane_info_` | `MembraneInfoOP` | Membrane protein environment data |
| `tree_set_observer_` | `GlycanTreeSetObserverOP` | Carbohydrate tree connectivity |
| `parameters_set_` | `vector1<ParametersSetOP>` | Parametric conformation generation data |
| `contains_carbohydrate_residues_` | `bool` | Carbohydrate presence flag |
| `residue_coordinates_need_updating_` | `bool mutable` | Dirty flag for coordinate sync |
| `residue_torsions_need_updating_` | `bool mutable` | Dirty flag for torsion sync |
| `dof_moved_` | `AtomID_Mask` | Tracks which DOFs changed (for energy caching) |
| `xyz_moved_` | `AtomID_Mask` | Tracks which xyz coords changed |
| `structure_moved_` | `bool mutable` | Global movement flag since last reset |
| `secstruct_` | `vector1<char>` | Per-residue secondary structure assignments |

The five signal hubs at the bottom (`connection_obs_hub_`, `general_obs_hub_`, `identity_obs_hub_`, `length_obs_hub_`, `xyz_obs_hub_`) form the observer backbone [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L1786-L1800).

### Chain Management

Chains in Rosetta are tracked via the `chain_endings_` vector. The relationship between chain numbers, chain letters, and jumps is carefully documented in the Pose header [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L1370-L1399):

- **Chain numbers (ids)** belong to Conformation — sequentially numbered positive integers for consecutively numbered residues that are chemically connected.
- **Chain letters** belong to PDBInfo — arbitrary single characters with no ordering guarantees.
- **Jumps** belong to FoldTree — specify how movement propagates; a single chain may span multiple jumps.

Key accessors delegate directly to Conformation: `chain_begin(chain)`, `chain_end(chain)`, `num_chains()` [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L292-L322).

### Mode Detection

Conformation provides convenience methods for detecting the representation level [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L253-L266):

| Method | Returns true when |
|---|---|
| `is_fullatom()` | Majority of residues use `FULL_ATOM` typeset |
| `is_centroid()` | Majority of residues use `CENTROID` typeset |
| `is_mixed_mode()` | Residues span multiple typeset modes |
| `is_membrane()` | `membrane_info_` is non-null |
| `contains_carbohydrate_residues()` | Carbohydrate flag is set |

## Residue Manipulation API

Pose provides a rich vocabulary for structural modification, divided into append, insert, replace, and delete operations [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L456-L619):

### Append Operations

| Method | Connection Type | Key Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `append_residue_by_jump()` | Rigid-body jump | anchor residue, anchor/root atoms, start_new_chain |
| `append_residue_by_bond()` | Covalent bond | build_ideal_geometry, connection number, anchor residue/connection |
| `append_residue_by_atoms()` | Covalent by atom name | connect_atom, anchor atom names (wraps `append_residue_by_bond`) |
| `append_pose_by_jump()` | Whole pose by jump | Source pose, anchor residue |
| `append_polymer_residue_after_seqpos()` | Polymer bond after position | build_ideal_geometry |
| `prepend_polymer_residue_before_seqpos()` | Polymer bond before position | build_ideal_geometry |

### Replace and Delete

`replace_residue(seqpos, new_rsd, orient_backbone)` swaps a residue at a given position, optionally reorienting the backbone to match the existing frame [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L563-L569). An overload accepts explicit atom-pair mappings for superposition [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L574-L580).

Deletion is available via `delete_polymer_residue(seqpos)` (fast, polymer-only) and `delete_residue_slow(seqpos)` (general, handles jumps/root) [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L606-L616).

## Atom: The Coordinate Primitive

The `conformation::Atom` class is deliberately minimal — a stark contrast to `chemical::Atom` which describes chemical properties. The header explicitly notes this distinction [Atom.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Atom.hh#L33-L37):

> This atom class differs from chemical::Atom, AtomType, and AtomTypeSet in that it only contains the information about the xyz coordinates.

The class holds exactly three data members [Atom.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Atom.hh#L129-L143):

| Member | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `xyz_` | `numeric::xyzVector<Real>` | 3D position in Angstroms |
| `type_` | `ShortSize` | Rosetta atom type index (for Lennard-Jones) |
| `mm_type_` | `ShortSize` | MM atom type index (for CHARMM LJ) |

`chemical::Atoms` are stored in `chemical::ResidueType` (the ResidueGraph), while `conformation::Atoms` are stored in `conformation::Residue` — the former defines the template, the latter the instance [Atom.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Atom.hh#L36-L38).

## Torsion Angle Access

Pose provides two tiers of torsion access: **convenience methods** for standard backbone/sidechain angles, and **generic access** through `TorsionID`.

### Backbone Torsions (Peptides)

Convenience methods `phi()`, `psi()`, `omega()` operate on residue sequence positions and return/accept degrees [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L1008-L1083). For non-standard backbones, `theta()` (beta-amino acids, oligoureas) and `mu()` (oligoureas) are provided [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L1085-L1143).

### Nucleic Acid Torsions

Six backbone torsions — `alpha()`, `beta()`, `gamma()`, `delta()`, `epsilon()`, `zeta()` — cover the nucleic acid backbone [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L1145-L1299).

### Sidechain and Generic Access

Chi angles use `chi(chino, seqpos)` for peptides/saccharides and `chi(seqpos)` for nucleic acids [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L1305-L1363). The generic `torsion(TorsionID)` and `set_torsion(TorsionID, setting)` methods provide uniform access for any torsion type [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L1571-L1586).

### AtomTree DOF Access

Below the torsion level, raw DOFs are accessible via `dof(DOF_ID)` and `set_dof(DOF_ID, setting)` [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L1592-L1606). Cartesian coordinates are accessed through `xyz(AtomID)`, `set_xyz(AtomID, point)`, and batch variants `batch_set_xyz()`/`batch_get_xyz()` for performance [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L1616-L1671).

## Coordinate System Duality

The relationship between internal coordinates (torsions/DOFs) and Cartesian coordinates (xyz) is mediated by the AtomTree and guarded by dirty flags in Conformation.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Internal["Internal Coordinates"]
        DOF["DOF_ID<br/>bond angles, lengths,<br/>torsions"]
        TORS["TorsionID<br/>phi, psi, chi, etc."]
    end

    subgraph KIN["Kinematics Layer"]
        AT["AtomTree<br/>forward kinematics"]
        DIRTY_T["torsions_need_updating<br/>(mutable bool)"]
        DIRTY_X["coordinates_need_updating<br/>(mutable bool)"]
    end

    subgraph External["Cartesian Coordinates"]
        XYZ["Atom xyz_<br/>Vector positions"]
    end

    DOF -->|"set_dof()"| AT
    TORS -->|"set_torsion()"| AT
    AT -->|"forward kinematics"| XYZ
    DIRTY_T -.->|"invalidates"| AT
    DIRTY_X -.->|"invalidates"| AT
    XYZ -->|"set_xyz()"| AT
```

When `set_phi()` or `set_dof()` is called, Conformation marks `residue_coordinates_need_updating_` as true [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L1754-L1755). The next call to `residue(seqpos)` or `xyz()` triggers the AtomTree refold. Conversely, when `set_xyz()` modifies coordinates, `residue_torsions_need_updating_` is set [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L1757-L1758).

## Observer and Signal Architecture

Both Pose and Conformation use a signal/hub pattern for loose coupling between subsystems. Pose exposes four signal attachment points [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L1857-L1899):

| Signal Hub | Event Type | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| `destruction_obs_hub_` | `DestructionEvent` | Pose destruction |
| `general_obs_hub_` | `GeneralEvent` | Any derived signal (superset) |
| `energy_obs_hub_` | `EnergyEvent` | Scoring state changes |
| `conformation_obs_hub_` | `ConformationEvent` | Structural changes |

Conformation adds five more [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L1786-L1800):

| Signal Hub | Event Type | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| `connection_obs_hub_` | `ConnectionEvent` | Observer attachment/detachment |
| `general_obs_hub_` | `GeneralEvent` | Any conformation signal |
| `identity_obs_hub_` | `IdentityEvent` | Residue identity changes |
| `length_obs_hub_` | `LengthEvent` | Insertions/deletions |
| `xyz_obs_hub_` | `XYZEvent` | Coordinate changes |

> [!TIP]
> Conformation's `general_obs_hub_` is a `PausableSignalHub`, unlike the `BufferedSignalHub` used for other event types. This allows bulk operations to temporarily suppress general notifications, then fire a single summary event — a critical optimization for fragment insertion and large-scale remodels.

## I/O and Serialization

Pose supports export to multiple formats through a unified `dump_file()` method that dispatches based on file extension [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L1790-L1801):

| Method | Format | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `dump_pdb(filename)` | PDB | Returns bool for success |
| `dump_pdb(ostream)` | PDB | Stream variant |
| `dump_pdb(ostream, residue_indices)` | PDB | Subset output |
| `dump_scored_pdb(filename, scorefxn)` | PDB + scores | Includes per-residue energy annotations |
| `dump_cif(filename)` | mmCIF | |
| `dump_mmtf(filename)` | MMTF | Binary format |
| `dump_file(filename)` | Auto-detected | Dispatches by extension |

Both Pose and Conformation support Cereal serialization via `save()`/`load()` template methods, enabled by the `SERIALIZATION` preprocessor guard [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L106-L109), [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L79-L82).

## Pose Subsystems at a Glance

The `source/src/core/pose/` directory reveals the full scope of Pose's supporting infrastructure:

| Subdirectory/Module | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `datacache/` | `ObserverCache`, `CacheableDataType`, `CacheableObserver` hierarchy |
| `metrics/` | `PoseMetricCalculatorBase`, `CalculatorFactory` for runtime structural metrics |
| `reference_pose/` | `ReferencePoseSet` — residue index mapping across structural changes |
| `signals/` | `ConformationEvent`, `DestructionEvent`, `EnergyEvent`, `GeneralEvent` |
| `full_model_info/` | RNA/protein modeling parameters for stepwise assembly |
| `rna/` | RNA-specific data: base pairs, base stacks, suite names |
| `copydofs/` | `CopyDofs` — selective DOF copying between poses |
| `symmetry/` | Symmetric pose utilities |
| `carbohydrates/` | Carbohydrate pose manipulation utilities |

## Deep Copy vs. Assignment

Pose provides two distinct copying semantics with critical differences [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L226-L233):

- `operator=(src)` performs a **shallow-aware copy** where two Poses may share non-bitwise-constant data through the AtomTree observer system. This is fast but creates coupling.
- `detached_copy(src)` performs a **deep copy** guaranteeing no shared mutable data. The resulting Pose is fully independent.

The same pattern exists on Conformation with `operator=` vs. `detached_copy()` [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L163-L172). Always use `detached_copy()` when passing poses across protocol boundaries that modify structure independently.

## Specialized Conformations

Conformation is designed for extension through inheritance. The codebase includes notable derived classes in `source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/`:

- **`SymmetricConformation`** — extends Conformation with symmetry-aware kinematics via `SymmetryInfo` [symmetry/SymmetricConformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetricConformation.hh)
- **`MirrorSymmetricConformation`** — handles mirror symmetry constraints

The `same_type_as_me()` virtual method enables runtime type checking between Conformation instances [Conformation.hh](source/src/core/conformation/Conformation.hh#L208-L210), and `set_new_conformation(ConformationCOP)` on Pose allows swapping the entire conformation backend [Pose.hh](source/src/core/pose/Pose.hh#L298-L301).

## Where to Go Next

Having understood Pose and Conformation, the natural progression follows the data flow through Rosetta's architecture. The [ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework) describes how the `Energies` object within Pose gets populated and used. The [Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy) shows how protocols transform Pose objects. For the kinematic underpinnings — FoldTree and AtomTree — consult [Monte Carlo Sampling](12-monte-carlo-sampling) which depends heavily on jump manipulation. Finally, [Symmetry Modeling](24-symmetry-modeling) and [Membrane Protein Modeling](25-membrane-protein-modeling) demonstrate how specialized Conformation subclasses extend this architecture for domain-specific needs.

# ScoreFunction Framework



The ScoreFunction is the central nervous system of Rosetta's energy evaluation — the object that decides *what* physics to compute, *how much* each term matters, and *when* to invoke expensive calculations. Every protocol that evaluates, compares, or optimizes protein structures ultimately passes through a ScoreFunction. This document dissects the framework's architecture, its extension mechanisms, and the practical patterns you'll encounter when customizing or debugging scoring behavior across Rosetta's codebase.

## Architectural Overview

At its highest level, the ScoreFunction framework follows a **weighted-sum composition pattern**: a `ScoreFunction` object holds an `EMapVector` of per-term weights and a categorized collection of `EnergyMethod` instances. When `score(pose)` is called, only methods whose corresponding weight is non-zero are evaluated — this zero-weight culling is the framework's primary performance lever. The result is a single scalar (the total score) plus a rich decomposition stored in the `Pose`'s `Energies` object.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "ScoreFunction Creation"
        SF_Factory["ScoreFunctionFactory<br/>(Singleton)"]
        WeightsFile["database/scoring/weights/<br/>*.wts + *.wts_patch"]
        SM["ScoringManager<br/>(Singleton)"]
        SF_Factory -->|"loads weights & options"| ScoreFunction
        SM -->|"factory_register()"| SF_Factory
        SM -->|"lazy-loads potentials"| ScoreFunction
    end

    subgraph "ScoreFunction (core)"
        Weights["EMapVector weights_<br/>per-ScoreType scalars"]
        EMOpts["EnergyMethodOptions<br/>etables, hbond config, etc."]
        Methods["Categorized EnergyMethods<br/>CI_2B, CD_2B, CI_1B, CD_1B<br/>LR_2B, WS"]
        ScoreFunction
        ScoreFunction --> Weights
        ScoreFunction --> EMOpts
        ScoreFunction --> Methods
    end

    subgraph "Scoring Pipeline"
        Pose["Pose"]
        Energies["Energies<br/>(cached in Pose)"]
        EnergyGraph["EnergyGraph<br/>(pairwise residues)"]
        ScoreFunction -->|"score( pose )"| Pose
        Pose --> Energies
        Energies --> EnergyGraph
    end

    WeightsFile -->|"add_weights_from_file"| ScoreFunction
```

This diagram illustrates the two-phase lifecycle: **construction** (factory creates, loads weights, instantiates methods) followed by **evaluation** (pose is scored, energies cached in its `Energies` object). The key insight is that weights drive method selection — setting a weight to zero effectively disables that term without removing the method.

## Core Classes and Their Relationships

### ScoreFunction

The `ScoreFunction` class, defined in [ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L91-L120), inherits from `utility::VirtualBase` and `enable_shared_from_this`. It is the user-facing orchestrator. Its constructor delegates to `reset()`, which clears all weights and calls `initialize_methods_arrays()` to prepare categorized method containers. The class explicitly makes its copy constructor and assignment operator private — you must use `clone()` instead, which preserves subclass information through virtual dispatch ([ScoreFunction.cc](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.cc#L136-L142)).

The categorized method typedefs reveal the framework's taxonomy for energy computations:

| Category | Typedef | Evaluation Scope |
|---|---|---|
| **CI_2B_Methods** | `ContextIndependentTwoBodyEnergyOP` | Pairwise, residue-level, no environment dependence |
| **CD_2B_Methods** | `ContextDependentTwoBodyEnergyOP` | Pairwise, residue-level, depends on structural context |
| **CI_1B_Methods** | `ContextIndependentOneBodyEnergyOP` | Per-residue, no environment dependence |
| **CD_1B_Methods** | `ContextDependentOneBodyEnergyOP` | Per-residue, depends on structural context |
| **CI_LR_2B / CD_LR_2B** | `ContextIndependentLRTwoBodyEnergyOP` | Long-range pairwise (beyond neighbor cutoff) |
| **WS_Methods** | `WholeStructureEnergyOP` | Global terms over the entire pose |

The distinction between **context-independent** and **context-dependent** is critical for caching. Context-independent two-body energies are cached in the `EnergyGraph` and reused across scoring rounds; context-dependent energies must be recomputed when the structural context changes. This categorization is declared at [ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L102-L117).

### ScoreType Enumeration

Every energy term in Rosetta corresponds to a `ScoreType` enum value defined in [ScoreType.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreType.hh#L35-L120). The enum starts at `fa_atr = 1` (for `utility::vector1` compatibility) and extends to several hundred types covering full-atom physics (`fa_atr`, `fa_rep`, `fa_sol`), electrostatics (`fa_elec`), hydrogen bonding (`hbond_sr_bb`, `hbond_lr_bb`), knowledge-based terms (`rama_prepro`, `p_aa_pp`), and domain-specific terms (RNA, membrane, DNA). The comment block at the top of the file warns that any new `ScoreType` must also be registered in `ScoreTypeManager.cc` with its string name for serialization and weights-file parsing ([ScoreType.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreType.hh#L25-L30)).

### EMapVector (EnergyMap)

The `EMapVector` class in [EnergyMap.hh](source/src/core/scoring/EnergyMap.hh#L43-L99) is a fixed-size `std::array<Real, n_score_types>` that provides ScoreType-indexed access to energy values. Its critical operation is the `dot()` method ([EnergyMap.hh](source/src/core/scoring/EnergyMap.hh#L153-L161)), which computes the weighted sum over non-zero terms — this is how the total score is calculated from the component energy map. The `zero()` method is essential between uses since the same `EMapVector` objects are often reused across residue pairs to avoid allocation overhead.

## ScoreFunctionFactory and Weight Files

### Factory Pattern

`ScoreFunctionFactory` is a `SingletonBase` ([ScoreFunctionFactory.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunctionFactory.hh#L90-L91)) that provides static `create_score_function()` overloads. These accept a weights tag (e.g., `"ref2015"`), an optional patch tag, and an optional `OptionCollection` for thread-local configuration. The factory uses a `ScoreFunctionKey` struct ([ScoreFunctionFactory.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunctionFactory.hh#L55-L87)) — a tuple of weights filename, comma-separated patches, and a raw pointer to the `OptionCollection` — to cache previously loaded score functions in a `std::map`. Each call returns a `clone()` of the cached instance, making repeated constructions from the same weights tag essentially free.

The `_add_weights_from_stream()` method ([ScoreFunction.cc](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.cc#L263-L349)) parses weight files, which support a rich set of directives beyond simple weight assignments:

| Directive | Effect |
|---|---|
| `ETABLE <name>` | Selects the Etable (Lennard-Jones + solvation) parameterization |
| `METHOD_WEIGHTS <type> <w1> <w2>...` | Sets per-method sub-weights for multi-component terms |
| `NO_PROTEIN_PROTEIN_FA_ELEC` | Excludes protein-protein electrostatic interactions |
| `NO_HB_ENV_DEP` | Disables environment-dependent hydrogen bond scoring |
| `PUT_INTRA_INTO_TOTAL` | Includes intra-residue energies in the total score |
| `PATHTYPE` | Selects atom-pair path type for etable computation |

### Weight File Ecosystem

The `database/scoring/weights/` directory contains over 150 weight files spanning Rosetta's history and application domains. The major families include:

| Weight Set | Era | Primary Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| `ref2015` / `ref2015_cart` | Current standard | General-purpose full-atom scoring, relaxation |
| `talaris2013` / `talaris2014` | Predecessor to ref2015 | Legacy protocols, backward compatibility |
| `beta_nov16` / `beta_jan25` | Centroid scoring | Ab initio folding, low-resolution staging |
| `score12` / `score13` | Historical | Older published protocols |
| `mm_std` / `mm_std_cart` | Molecular mechanics | MM-based refinement |
| `membrane_highres` / `mpframework_*` | Membrane protein | Transmembrane protein modeling |
| `docking` / `interface` | Protein-protein interactions | Docking and interface design |
| `ligand` / `ligand_soft_rep` | Small molecule | Ligand docking and design |

Patches (files ending in `.wts_patch`) apply incremental modifications on top of base weight sets — for example, `docking.wts_patch` adjusts weights specifically for docking scenarios. The factory's `create_score_function("ref2015", "patch_name")` overload handles patch composition.

> [!TIP]
> When debugging scoring discrepancies, always check which weight set your protocol is actually using. The `ScoreFunction::show()` method prints all non-zero weights, and `serialize_weights()` returns them as a string. A common mistake is applying a patch that accidentally zeros out a critical term.

## EnergyMethod Hierarchy

### Base Class and Lifecycle

The `EnergyMethod` base class ([EnergyMethod.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethod.hh#L53-L64)) is itself a `VirtualBase` that takes an `EnergyMethodCreatorOP` at construction — this creator links the method to its factory registration. The base class defines a rich set of virtual lifecycle hooks that the scoring pipeline calls in strict order:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["setup_for_scoring(pose)"] --> B["setup_for_derivatives(pose)"]
    B --> C["residue_pair_energy(rs1, rs2)"]
    C --> D["evaluate_rotamer_pair(...)"]
    B --> E["residue_energy(rsd)"]
    E --> F["eval_atom_derivative(...)"]
    
    A2["setup_for_packing(pose, ...)"] --> A3["setup_for_packing_with_rotsets(pose, rotsets)"]
    A3 --> A4["prepare_rotamers_for_packing(pose, rotset)"]
    A4 --> A5["update_residue_for_packing(pose, resid)"]
    A5 --> A6["rotamer_energy(rotamer)"]
    A6 --> A7["rotamer_pair_energy(rot1, rot2)"]
    
    B2["setup_for_minimizing(pose, minmap)"] --> B3["setup_for_minimizing_for_node(node, rsd)"]
    B3 --> B4["eval_atom_derivative(atomid, rsd)"]
```

The packing setup sequence ([EnergyMethod.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethod.hh#L69-L101)) follows a strict five-step protocol: `setup_for_packing` → rotamer construction → `setup_for_packing_with_rotsets` → `prepare_rotamers_for_packing` → energy evaluation. Methods that need to precompute data (like `ApproximateBuriedUnsatPenalty`, which identifies compatible rotamers) use the `setup_for_packing_with_rotsets` hook for this purpose.

### EnergyMethodCreator and Registration

Every concrete `EnergyMethod` must have a corresponding `EnergyMethodCreator` subclass ([EnergyMethodCreator.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethodCreator.hh#L42-L58)) that implements two pure virtual methods: `create_energy_method(options)` and `score_types_for_method()`. The creator is auto-registered with the `ScoringManager` at static initialization time via the `EnergyMethodRegistrator<T>` template ([EnergyMethodRegistrator.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethodRegistrator.hh#L31-L53)), which inherits from `utility::factory::WidgetRegistrator<ScoringManager, T>`.

The `ScoringManager` singleton ([ScoringManager.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoringManager.hh#L149-L164)) serves a dual role: it acts as the factory registry for energy method creators via `factory_register()`, and it provides lazy-loaded, thread-safe access to scoring potentials (Ramachandran distributions, P_AA statistics, hydrogen bond potentials, etc.). The thread-safety of lazy loading is implemented using `utility::thread::safely_create_load_once_object_by_OP`.

> [!TIP]
> If you add a new energy method, you must create an `EnergyMethodCreator` subclass and add a static `EnergyMethodRegistrator<YourCreator> registrator_instance` in your `.cc` file. Without this, the ScoringManager will never know your method exists, and it won't be instantiated even if its weight is non-zero.

## The Scoring Pipeline

When `ScoreFunction::operator()(pose)` is called ([ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L255-L263)), the framework executes a multi-phase evaluation:

1. **ScoreFunctionInfo validation** — The `info()` method ([ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L275-L276)) creates a fingerprint object that the `Energies` class uses to detect stale cached data. If the pose's cached state matches the current ScoreFunction's info, short-circuiting may occur.

2. **Long-range energy setup** — Long-range methods (electrostatics, constraints) initialize their `LREnergyContainer` objects, which store pairwise energies for residue pairs beyond the neighbor graph cutoff.

3. **Context graph construction** — `indicate_required_context_graphs()` ([ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L283-L284)) signals which context graphs (e.g., 10Å or 12Å neighbor graphs) the energy methods require.

4. **Two-body evaluation** — Short-range two-body energies are evaluated for neighbor residue pairs, with context-independent results cached in the `EnergyGraph` for reuse.

5. **One-body evaluation** — Per-residue energies (dihedral, Ramachandran, reference) are computed independently for each residue.

6. **Whole-structure evaluation** — Global terms (constraint scores, buried unsatisfied penalties) are computed over the entire pose.

The final total score is computed as the dot product of the weights vector with the accumulated energy map, filtered to only non-zero weight indices via the `nonzero_weights_` list ([ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L356-L360)).

## Minimization Integration

The ScoreFunction framework provides specialized pathways for gradient-based minimization through `setup_for_minimizing()` ([ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L501-L506)) and its symmetry-aware variants `asym_setup_for_minimizing()` / `sym_setup_for_minimizing()`. These methods populate a `MinimizationGraph` (distinct from the scoring `EnergyGraph`) with nodes that store per-residue one-body energies and edges that store two-body energies with their analytical derivatives. The `setup_for_minimizing_for_node()` method ([ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L534-L544)) initializes individual graph nodes and optionally accumulates fixed-position energies. After minimization completes, `finalize_after_minimizing()` ([ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L528-L530)) allows methods to perform cleanup operations.

## Practical Patterns

### Creating and Customizing ScoreFunctions

The most common usage pattern uses the factory to load a preset and then adjusts individual weights:

```
scorefxn = create_score_function("ref2015")
scorefxn.set_weight(fa_sol, 0.8)       # Reduce solvation weight
scorefxn.set_weight(hbond_sr_bb, 1.5)  # Strengthen short-range H-bonds
total = scorefxn(pose)                 # Score the pose
```

For programmatic construction, `initialize_from_file()` ([ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L205-L206)) resets the ScoreFunction and loads weights from a file path. The `add_extra_method()` method ([ScoreFunction.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.hh#L483-L496)) allows injection of non-standard energy methods — useful for protocol-specific scoring that doesn't warrant full framework integration.

### Weight Perturbation for Benchmarking

The `perturb_weights()` method ([ScoreFunction.cc](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreFunction.cc#L216-L237)) adds Gaussian noise to each non-zero weight with a standard deviation of `weight / 8`, enforcing non-negativity. This is used in benchmarking to generate ensembles of slightly different score functions, testing protocol robustness. The method's documentation notes the resulting distribution: 68% of weights change by less than 12.5%, 26% by 12.5–25%, and 4% by more than 25%.

### EnergyMethodOptions Configuration

The `EnergyMethodOptions` object ([EnergyMethodOptions.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethodOptions.hh#L60-L82)) held by each ScoreFunction controls fine-grained behavior of all energy methods — everything from the etable parameterization to hydrogen bond exclusion rules to per-domain composition setup files. When you call `set_energy_method_options()`, the ScoreFunction triggers `reset_energy_methods()` to rebuild its method collection, ensuring method state stays consistent with the new options.

## Navigation

This page covered the ScoreFunction framework's architecture, from weight files through the energy method hierarchy to the scoring pipeline. For the next level of detail on how individual energy terms are implemented, proceed to [Energy Methods](10-energy-methods). To understand how ScoreFunctions integrate with Rosetta's protocol framework — particularly how Movers invoke scoring during Monte Carlo trajectories — see [Monte Carlo Sampling](12-monte-carlo-sampling). For the XML-based mechanism that allows non-programmers to compose and customize score functions, see [RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework).

# Energy Methods



Energy Methods constitute the computational core of Rosetta's scoring engine — the physics-based and knowledge-based functions that assign a numerical energy to a molecular conformation. Every term in a [ScoreFunction](9-scorefunction-framework) is backed by an EnergyMethod instance that knows how to evaluate, minimize, and report on its specific contribution. This page dissects the inheritance hierarchy, the factory registration mechanism, the scoring lifecycle, and the domain-specific subsystems that make up this vast framework.

## Architectural Overview

The Energy Method hierarchy follows a strict classification along two orthogonal axes: **interaction order** (one-body, two-body, whole-structure) and **context dependency** (context-independent, context-dependent). These axes determine both the computational interface a method must implement and how the ScoreFunction schedules its evaluation during scoring, packing, and minimization. The entire system is bootstrapped through a Factory pattern — each concrete energy method pairs with an `EnergyMethodCreator` that registers with the `ScoringManager` singleton before `main()` begins, ensuring all methods are available by the time the first `ScoreFunction` is constructed.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class EnergyMethod {
        <<abstract>>
        +clone() EnergyMethodOP
        +setup_for_packing(Pose)
        +setup_for_scoring(Pose, ScoreFunction)
        +setup_for_minimizing(Pose, ScoreFunction, MinimizerMap)
        +setup_for_derivatives(Pose, ScoreFunction)
        +finalize_total_energy(Pose, ScoreFunction, EnergyMap)
        +method_type() EnergyMethodType
        +score_types() ScoreTypes
        +indicate_required_context_graphs()
        +eval_atom_derivative()
        +version() Size
    }

    class OneBodyEnergy {
        <<abstract>>
        +residue_energy(Residue, Pose, EnergyMap)*
        +eval_residue_derivatives()
    }

    class TwoBodyEnergy {
        <<abstract>>
        +residue_pair_energy(Residue, Residue, Pose, ScoreFunction, EnergyMap)*
        +eval_residue_pair_derivatives()
        +evaluate_rotamer_pair_energies()
        +evaluate_rotamer_background_energies()
    }

    class WholeStructureEnergy {
        +method_type() EnergyMethodType
        +atomic_interaction_cutoff() Distance
    }

    class CI1B {
        +method_type() ci_1b
        +residue_energy(Residue, Pose, EnergyMap)*
    }

    class CD1B {
        +method_type() cd_1b
        +residue_energy(Residue, Pose, EnergyMap)*
    }

    class CI2B {
        <<abstract>>
        +method_type() ci_2b
    }

    class CD2B {
        <<abstract>>
        +method_type() cd_2b
    }

    class SR2B {
        <<abstract>>
        +atomic_interaction_cutoff()*
        +evaluate_rotamer_pair_energies()
    }

    class LR2B {
        <<abstract>>
        +long_range_type() LongRangeEnergyType*
        +defines_residue_pair_energy(Pose, Size, Size)*
    }

    EnergyMethod <|-- OneBodyEnergy
    EnergyMethod <|-- TwoBodyEnergy
    EnergyMethod <|-- WholeStructureEnergy
    OneBodyEnergy <|-- CI1B : ContextIndependentOneBodyEnergy
    OneBodyEnergy <|-- CD1B : ContextDependentOneBodyEnergy
    TwoBodyEnergy <|-- SR2B : ShortRangeTwoBodyEnergy
    TwoBodyEnergy <|-- LR2B : LongRangeTwoBodyEnergy
    CI1B <|-- CI2B : ContextIndependentTwoBodyEnergy
    CD1B <|-- CD2B : ContextDependentTwoBodyEnergy
    SR2B <|-- CI2B
    SR2B <|-- CD2B
    LR2B <|-- CI_LR2B : ContextIndependentLRTwoBodyEnergy
    LR2B <|-- CD_LR2B : ContextDependentLRTwoBodyEnergy
```

Sources: [EnergyMethod.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethod.hh#L50-L62), [OneBodyEnergy.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/OneBodyEnergy.hh#L52-L70), [TwoBodyEnergy.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/TwoBodyEnergy.hh#L63-L115), [WholeStructureEnergy.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/WholeStructureEnergy.hh#L41-L58)

## The Base EnergyMethod Interface

`EnergyMethod` is the abstract root of the entire hierarchy, defined in `core::scoring::methods`. It extends `utility::VirtualBase` and declares the full lifecycle contract that every scoring term must support — from pre-computation setup through energy evaluation to derivative computation. The constructor requires an `EnergyMethodCreatorOP`, which serves double duty: it enables polymorphic cloning via the Factory pattern and it communicates the set of `ScoreType` values the method is responsible for computing.

The lifecycle methods form a carefully ordered protocol. During packing, `setup_for_packing()` runs first, followed by rotamer construction, then `setup_for_packing_with_rotsets()` and `prepare_rotamers_for_packing()` before the actual rotamer scoring begins. During minimization, `setup_for_minimizing()` initializes cached data (such as neighbor lists), with per-residue and per-residue-pair setup hooks available. After minimization completes, `finalize_after_minimizing()` provides a teardown point. For derivative evaluation, `setup_for_derivatives()` prepares state and `finalize_after_derivatives()` cleans up.

Two critical boolean methods control minimization behavior: `minimize_in_whole_structure_context()` (which returns `true` by default, forcing legacy methods to evaluate only in `finalize_total_energy()`) and `defines_high_order_terms()` (which returns `false` by default, allowing methods that evaluate per-residue or per-residue-pair to participate in RTMin). The `method_type()` pure virtual returns one of the seven `EnergyMethodType` enum values, and `indicate_required_context_graphs()` tells the Pose which neighbor graphs to maintain.

Sources: [EnergyMethod.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethod.hh#L50-L364), [EnergyMethod.cc](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethod.cc)

## One-Body Energy Methods

One-body energies evaluate the intrinsic score of a single residue within the structural context (or without it, for context-independent variants). The `OneBodyEnergy` abstract class extends `EnergyMethod` with the pure virtual `residue_energy()` method that takes a `Residue`, a `Pose`, and an `EnergyMap` to accumulate into. Critically, the documentation emphasizes that implementations must **accumulate** into the EnergyMap, not overwrite it.

Beyond basic energy evaluation, `OneBodyEnergy` provides an extended minimization interface. The `use_extended_residue_energy_interface()` method lets derived classes opt into a faster path during minimization that uses cached `ResSingleMinimizationData`. When enabled, `setup_for_minimizing_for_residue()` populates the cache and `residue_energy_ext()` performs the actual evaluation using it. Similarly, `eval_residue_derivatives()` computes all atom derivatives for a residue at once, writing into a `vector1<DerivVectorPair>` — this batch approach avoids the overhead of per-atom virtual dispatch.

> [!TIP]
> When implementing a new one-body energy, the `defines_score_for_residue()` method can return `false` for residues where the energy is trivially zero. This allows the ScoreFunction to skip both energy evaluation and derivative computation for those residues, yielding significant speedups during minimization of large structures.

Sources: [OneBodyEnergy.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/OneBodyEnergy.hh#L52-L200)

## Two-Body Energy Methods

Two-body energies evaluate interactions between residue pairs and form the computational bottleneck of Rosetta scoring. The `TwoBodyEnergy` class declares the pure virtual `residue_pair_energy()` and a rich minimization interface mirroring the one-body pattern but with per-pair caching via `ResPairMinimizationData`. The interface documentation contains an important architectural note about the design trade-off of requiring a `Pose` parameter even for context-independent methods: this ensures a common interface for both CI and CD variants but places the burden on implementers to not accidentally access context-dependent data in methods declared context-independent.

The `defines_score_for_residue_pair()` method is particularly powerful for context-dependent two-body energies. By returning `false` when residues are not moving with respect to each other, a CD2B method can effectively behave as context-independent for stationary pairs, allowing the score caching infrastructure to avoid redundant recomputation. This optimization is critical for large-scale relaxation protocols.

The rotamer interaction methods — `evaluate_rotamer_pair_energies()` and `evaluate_rotamer_background_energies()` — enable batch computation during packing. `ShortRangeTwoBodyEnergy` overrides these with distance-based filtering logic that skips rotamer pairs whose bounding spheres exceed `atomic_interaction_cutoff()`, avoiding unnecessary residue_pair_energy calls for distant pairs.

Sources: [TwoBodyEnergy.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/TwoBodyEnergy.hh#L63-L200), [ShortRangeTwoBodyEnergy.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/ShortRangeTwoBodyEnergy.hh#L49-L129)

## Context-Independent vs. Context-Dependent Methods

The distinction between context-independent (CI) and context-dependent (CD) energy methods is a first-class architectural concept that directly impacts score caching and recomputation. Context-independent methods depend only on the intrinsic properties of the residue(s) involved — they can be evaluated once and their results reused across scoring rounds. Context-dependent methods depend on the broader structural environment and must be recomputed whenever surrounding residues change.

For one-body energies, `ContextIndependentOneBodyEnergy` overrides `residue_energy()` to omit the `Pose` parameter entirely, making the context-independence explicit in the interface signature. `ContextDependentOneBodyEnergy` retains the `Pose` parameter. Both fix their `method_type()` return values (`ci_1b` and `cd_1b` respectively) and mark the method as final to prevent override.

For two-body energies, both `ContextIndependentTwoBodyEnergy` and `ContextDependentTwoBodyEnergy` inherit from `ShortRangeTwoBodyEnergy` (or from `LongRangeTwoBodyEnergy` for the LR variants). The CI2B methods include the core statistical potentials — `fa_atr`, `fa_rep`, `fa_sol` (the Etable terms), `lk_ball`, `fa_elec`, and `mm_lj_*` terms. The CD2B methods include hydrogen bonding (`hbond_sr_bb`, `hbond_sc`), the `fa_pair` centroid interaction term, `geom_sol`, and the interface scores.

Sources: [ContextIndependentOneBodyEnergy.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/ContextIndependentOneBodyEnergy.hh#L47-L62), [ContextDependentOneBodyEnergy.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/ContextDependentOneBodyEnergy.hh#L47-L62), [ScoreType.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreType.hh#L36-L264)

## Long-Range Two-Body Energy Methods

Long-range energy methods interact with the scoring infrastructure fundamentally differently from short-range methods. While short-range energies are stored in the `EnergyGraph` edges between neighboring residues, long-range energies require their own `LREnergyContainer` data structures and are initialized during `setup_for_scoring()`. The `LongRangeTwoBodyEnergy` class adds two pure virtual methods: `long_range_type()` returns a `LongRangeEnergyType` enum value, and `defines_residue_pair_energy()` determines whether a specific residue pair should be scored by this method.
