The `LongRangeEnergyType` enumeration in [Methods.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/Methods.hh) catalogs the long-range categories: `constraints_lr`, `gen_born_lr`, `multipole_elec_lr`, `vdw_tinker_lr`, `sasa_lr`, `epr_deer_lr`, `PB_elec_lr`, `cart_bonded_lr`, `dna_dihedral_lr`, `gen_bonded_lr`, `rama2b_lr`, `ramaprepro_lr`, `rna_suite_lr`, `DFIRE`, `sym_bonus_lr`, and several electron density terms. Each type may have multiple registered energy methods that handle it. Both context-independent (`ContextIndependentLRTwoBodyEnergy`) and context-dependent (`ContextDependentLRTwoBodyEnergy`) variants exist, following the same pattern as their short-range counterparts.

Sources: [LongRangeTwoBodyEnergy.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/LongRangeTwoBodyEnergy.hh#L42-L62), [Methods.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/Methods.hh#L44-L65)

## Whole-Structure Energy Methods

Whole-structure energies evaluate properties that emerge only from the complete molecular assembly — terms like radius of gyration, buried unsatisfied hydrogen bonds, or symmetry constraints that have no meaningful per-residue decomposition. The `WholeStructureEnergy` class is deliberately minimal: it inherits from `EnergyMethod`, fixes `method_type()` to return the whole-structure enum value, and provides a default `atomic_interaction_cutoff()` of `0.0` (meaning no energy graph edges are needed unless overridden).

All computational work for whole-structure energies happens inside `finalize_total_energy()`, which is called by the ScoreFunction after all residue-level and residue-pair-level evaluations complete. This late-binding execution order means whole-structure terms can observe the results of other scoring terms if needed, and it also means they cannot participate in RTMin's residue-decomposed minimization (unless `minimize_in_whole_structure_context()` is overridden to return `false` and `defines_high_order_terms()` returns `true`).

Sources: [WholeStructureEnergy.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/WholeStructureEnergy.hh#L41-L65)

## Factory Registration: EnergyMethodCreator and EnergyMethodRegistrator

The Factory pattern that bootstraps the energy method system involves three cooperating types. `EnergyMethodCreator` is an abstract base class with two pure virtual methods: `create_energy_method()` instantiates a new `EnergyMethod` given `EnergyMethodOptions`, and `score_types_for_method()` returns the `ScoreTypes` the method computes. Each concrete energy method defines a corresponding Creator class (e.g., `MMBondLengthEnergyCreator`, `MMLJEnergyInterCreator`).

`EnergyMethodRegistrator<T>` is a templated class that performs static registration. It inherits from `utility::factory::WidgetRegistrator<ScoringManager, T>` and ensures that each Creator is registered exactly once with the `ScoringManager` singleton at static initialization time — before `main()` begins. This design centralizes thread-safety concerns in one location and prevents double-registration.

> [!TIP]
> When adding a new energy method to Rosetta, you must: (1) define a concrete `EnergyMethod` subclass, (2) define a corresponding `EnergyMethodCreator` subclass, (3) add a static `EnergyMethodRegistrator<YourCreator>` instance in a .cc file, (4) add the new `ScoreType` values to the enum in `ScoreType.hh`, and (5) register the string names in `ScoreTypeManager.cc`. Missing any of these steps will result in silent failures at runtime.

Sources: [EnergyMethodCreator.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethodCreator.hh#L40-L55), [EnergyMethodRegistrator.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethodRegistrator.hh#L38-L53)

## The ScoreType Enumeration

The `ScoreType` enum in [ScoreType.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreType.hh) is the central registry of all scoring terms in Rosetta, containing well over 200 values organized into sections. The ordering is significant: the enum uses sentinel values (e.g., `n_ci_2b_score_types`) to mark the boundaries between categories, which allows the scoring infrastructure to efficiently iterate over subsets. Each ScoreType maps to exactly one energy method, but a single energy method may claim multiple ScoreTypes.

The major categories in the enum are:

| Category | Boundary Markers | Representative Terms |
|---|---|---|
| CI Two-Body | `fa_atr` → `n_ci_2b_score_types` | `fa_atr`, `fa_rep`, `fa_sol`, `lk_ball`, `fa_elec`, `mm_lj_*`, `ch_bond`, `vdw`, `cenpack` |
| CD Two-Body | `fa_pair` → `n_cd_2b_score_types` | `fa_pair`, `hbond_sr_bb`, `hbond_sc`, `npd_hbond_*`, `geom_sol`, `cen_rot_pair*` |
| CI One-Body | `rama_prepro` → `n_ci_1b_score_types` | `rama_prepro`, `p_aa_pp`, `dunbrack`, `yaad`, `hbond_bb_sc`, `hxl_tors` |
| CD One-Body | `envsmooth` → `n_cd_1b_score_types` | `envsmooth`, `envsmooth_lr`, `bsa`, `env` |
| Whole-Structure | `atom_pair_constraint` → end | Constraint terms, density scores, interface scores, cavity scores, symmetry terms |
| RNA-specific | scattered throughout | `rna_torsion`, `rna_suite`, `rna_base_pair`, `fa_stack_*` |
| Membrane-specific | `Menv_smooth`, `Mpair`, `Msol` | Membrane environment, pair, and solvation terms |

Sources: [ScoreType.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreType.hh#L35-L264)

## Scoring Lifecycle Integration

Understanding when each lifecycle method fires is essential for implementing correct energy methods. The following diagram shows the execution order during a typical scoring-and-minimization sequence:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Scoring
        S1["setup_for_scoring(pose, sfxn)"] --> S2["Per-residue: setup_for_scoring_for_residue()"]
        S2 --> S3["OneBodyEnergy::residue_energy() per residue"]
        S3 --> S4["TwoBodyEnergy::residue_pair_energy() per neighbor pair"]
        S4 --> S5["WholeStructureEnergy::finalize_total_energy()"]
    end

    subgraph Minimization
        M1["setup_for_minimizing(pose, sfxn, minmap)"] --> M2["setup_for_minimizing_for_residue() per residue"]
        M2 --> M3["setup_for_minimizing_for_residue_pair() per pair"]
        M3 --> M4["Loop: energy eval → gradient eval → step"]
        M4 --> M5["finalize_after_minimizing(pose)"]
    end

    subgraph Packing
        P1["setup_for_packing(pose, relevant, designing)"] --> P2["Build rotamers"]
        P2 --> P3["setup_for_packing_with_rotsets()"]
        P3 --> P4["prepare_rotamers_for_packing() per RotamerSet"]
        P4 --> P5["Score all rotamers & pairs"]
        P5 --> P6["Annealing"]
        P6 --> P7["update_residue_for_packing() on acceptance"]
    end

    Scoring --> Minimization
```

During scoring, context graphs (maintained by the Pose) determine which residue pairs are neighbors. The ScoreFunction iterates over all residues for one-body evaluation and over all neighbor pairs for two-body evaluation, dispatching to the appropriate methods. The `finalize_total_energy()` call at the end is where whole-structure energies and any long-range methods using neighbor lists perform their final accumulation.

Sources: [EnergyMethod.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethod.hh#L73-L113), [EnergyMethod.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethod.hh#L127-L153), [EnergyMethod.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethod.hh#L155-L165), [EnergyMethod.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethod.hh#L297-L308)

## Domain-Specific Energy Method Subsystems

The `source/src/core/scoring/` directory contains over 40 subdirectories, each implementing a domain-specific set of energy methods. These subsystems demonstrate how the base framework scales to diverse computational biology problems.

```mermaid
graph LR
    EM["EnergyMethod Framework"] --> HB["hbonds/"]
    EM --> ELEC["elec/"]
    EM --> ETABLE["etable/"]
    EM --> RNA["rna/"]
    EM --> MEMB["membrane/"]
    EM --> DNA["dna/"]
    EM --> MM["mm/"]
    EM --> DENS["electron_density/"]
    EM --> CARB["carbohydrates/"]
    EM --> CRYST["cryst/"]
    EM --> SYM["symmetry/"]
    EM --> PACK["packing/"]
    EM --> LKB["lkball/"]
    EM --> VDW["vdwaals/"]
    EM --> NMR["nmr/"]
    EM --> CONST["constraints/"]
    EM --> ORB["orbitals/"]

    HB --> HB1["HBondEnergy\n(CD2B, LR2B)"]
    ELEC --> ELEC1["FAElecEnergy\n(CI2B)"]
    ETABLE --> ET1["EtableEnergy\n(fa_atr, fa_rep, fa_sol)\n(CI2B)"]
    RNA --> RNA1["RNA specific terms\n(torsion, suite, stacking)"]
    MM --> MM1["MMLJEnergyInter/Intra\nMMBondAngle/BondLength\n(CI2B, CI1B)"]
```

Key subsystems and their architectural roles:

| Subsystem | Directory | Primary Methods | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Etable** | `etable/` | `fa_atr`, `fa_rep`, `fa_sol` | Core van der Waals + solvation; CI2B |
| **LK Ball** | `lkball/` | `lk_ball`, `lk_ball_wtd`, `lk_ball_iso` | Lazaridis-Karplus solvation; CI2B |
| **Hydrogen Bonds** | `hbonds/` | `hbond_sr_bb`, `hbond_sc`, `hbond_lr_bb` | Geometric H-bond scoring; CD2B + LR2B |
| **Electrostatics** | `elec/` | `fa_elec`, `fa_elec_bb_bb` | Coulomb with distance-dependent dielectric; CI2B |
| **Molecular Mechanics** | `mm/` | `mm_lj_inter_*`, `mm_lj_intra_*`, `mm_bond_angle` | CHARMM-style force field terms; CI2B + CI1B |
| **RNA** | `rna/` | `rna_torsion`, `rna_suite`, `fa_stack_*` | RNA-specific scoring ~30+ terms |
| **Membrane** | `membrane/` | `Menv_smooth`, `Mpair`, `Msol` | Implicit membrane potential |
| **Constraints** | `constraints/` | Constraint scores | Whole-structure; LR2B |
| **Electron Density** | `electron_density/` | `elec_dens_*` | Cryo-EM / X-ray map fitting |
| **Carbohydrates** | `carbohydrates/` | Glycan tree scoring | Ring conformer, linkage terms |
| **Orbitals** | `orbitals/` | `pci_cation_pi`, `pci_pi_pi` | Semi-empirical orbital-based terms |

Sources: [Methods.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/Methods.hh#L35-L44), [ScoreType.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreType.hh#L120-L264)

## Minimization-Specific Interfaces

The energy method framework provides a dual-path optimization for minimization. The "standard" path uses the basic `residue_energy()` and `residue_pair_energy()` virtual calls during each minimization step. The "extended" path, activated when `use_extended_residue_energy_interface()` or `use_extended_residue_pair_energy_interface()` returns `true`, leverages cached data stored in `ResSingleMinimizationData` and `ResPairMinimizationData` objects. These caches typically hold pre-computed tables, neighbor lists, or atom-pair distance data that would be expensive to recompute every minimization step.

The `minimize_in_whole_structure_context()` method is a critical control point. Methods returning `true` (the default) are evaluated exclusively in `finalize_total_energy()` during minimization and cannot participate in RTMin (residue-trie-based minimization). Methods returning `false` can be decomposed and evaluated on a per-residue or per-residue-pair basis within the `MinimizationGraph`. The `defines_high_order_terms()` method provides a secondary signal: returning `true` indicates the method has terms that span more than two residues (e.g., multi-body constraints) and should use the MinimizationGraph for evaluation despite being decomposable at the residue level.

Derivative computation follows the F1/F2 convention from Abe et al. (1984), where F1 and F2 vectors encode the gradient of the energy with respect to atomic Cartesian coordinates. The `eval_residue_derivatives()` and `eval_residue_pair_derivatives()` methods write into `vector1<DerivVectorPair>` structures, with each entry containing the F1/F2 pair for a single atom.

Sources: [EnergyMethod.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethod.hh#L185-L208), [EnergyMethod.hh](source/src/core/scoring/methods/EnergyMethod.hh#L262-L283)

## EnergyMap and Score Accumulation

All energy methods accumulate their results into an `EnergyMap` — a fixed-size array indexed by `ScoreType` that serves as the universal container for all scoring terms. The `ScoreFunction` maintains a weight vector (also an `EnergyMap`) and computes the final weighted sum. This design allows any combination of energy methods to be active simultaneously, with zero-cost terms simply having zero weight.

The `EnergyMap` class defined in `source/src/core/scoring/EnergyMap.hh` supports element-wise arithmetic operations, enabling the ScoreFunction to separate the unweighted energy computation from the weighted total. This separation is architecturally important: the same unweighted energies can be reused across multiple ScoreFunctions with different weight sets, and the unweighted values are accessible for analysis and debugging even when the weighted total is all that matters for optimization.

Sources: [EnergyMap.hh](source/src/core/scoring/EnergyMap.hh), [ScoreType.hh](source/src/core/scoring/ScoreType.hh#L32-L38)

## Continuing the Exploration

This page has covered the architectural skeleton of the energy method system. To understand how these methods are orchestrated into a complete scoring function, continue to the [ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework). For the broader structural context these energies evaluate, see [Pose and Conformation](8-pose-and-conformation). To learn how energy methods participate in conformational search, proceed to [Monte Carlo Sampling](12-monte-carlo-sampling) and [Side-Chain Packing](13-side-chain-packing). For runtime extensibility of scoring through XML, see [RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework).

# Mover and Filter Hierarchy



Every Rosetta protocol is ultimately an orchestrated sequence of **Movers** (which mutate a `Pose`) and **Filters** (which evaluate whether a `Pose` meets acceptance criteria). Together they form the backbone of Rosetta's composable, declarative protocol system — one that scales from simple C++ pipelines to complex RosettaScripts XML choreographies. This page dissects their inheritance hierarchies, composition patterns, and the control-flow structures that bind them together.

## Architectural Overview

The Mover and Filter systems are designed around a small number of core abstractions: every Mover transforms state via `apply(Pose&)`, and every Filter judges state via `apply(Pose const&) → bool`. Both hierarchies share a parallel factory/creator architecture that enables runtime instantiation from XML tags, and both expose a `parse_my_tag()` entry point for declarative configuration. The key structural insight is that **Movers consume Filters** — filters never call movers — creating a clean unidirectional dependency graph from structural transformation to quality assessment.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class VirtualBase {
        <<utility>>
    }

    class Mover {
        <<abstract>>
        +apply(Pose&) = 0
        +get_name() = 0 : string
        +clone() : MoverOP
        +fresh_instance() : MoverOP
        +parse_my_tag(TagCOP, DataMap&)
        +get_last_move_status() : MoverStatus
        +get_additional_output() : PoseOP
        #set_last_move_status(MoverStatus)
    }

    class Filter {
        <<abstract>>
        +apply(Pose const&) = 0 : bool
        +clone() = 0 : FilterOP
        +fresh_instance() = 0 : FilterOP
        +report(ostream, Pose const&)
        +report_sm(Pose const&) : Real
        +score(Pose&) : Real
    }

    class MoverContainer {
        <<abstract>>
        +add_mover(MoverOP, Real weight)
        #movers_ : vector~MoverOP~
        #weight_ : vector~Real~
    }

    class SequenceMover
    class RandomMover
    class CycleMover
    class SwitchMover

    class TrialMover
    class RepeatMover
    class FilterMover
    class IfMover
    class WhileMover
    class JumpOutMover

    class CompoundFilter
    class FilterCollection
    class StochasticFilter
    class ContingentFilter

    class MoverCreator {
        <<abstract>>
        +create_mover() = 0 : MoverOP
        +keyname() = 0 : string
        +provide_xml_schema(XSD&)
    }

    class FilterCreator {
        <<abstract>>
        +create_filter() = 0 : FilterOP
        +keyname() = 0 : string
        +provide_xml_schema(XSD&)
    }

    VirtualBase <|-- Mover
    VirtualBase <|-- Filter
    Mover <|-- MoverContainer
    MoverContainer <|-- SequenceMover
    MoverContainer <|-- RandomMover
    MoverContainer <|-- CycleMover
    MoverContainer <|-- SwitchMover
    Mover <|-- TrialMover
    Mover <|-- RepeatMover
    Mover <|-- FilterMover
    Mover <|-- IfMover
    Mover <|-- WhileMover
    Mover <|-- JumpOutMover
    Filter <|-- CompoundFilter
    VirtualBase <|-- FilterCollection
    Filter <|-- StochasticFilter
    Filter <|-- ContingentFilter
    VirtualBase <|-- MoverCreator
    VirtualBase <|-- FilterCreator

    FilterMover --> Mover : wraps
    FilterMover --> Filter : evaluates
    TrialMover --> Mover : wraps
    TrialMover --> MonteCarlo : uses
    IfMover --> Filter : branches on
    IfMover --> Mover : true/false paths
    CompoundFilter --> Filter : composes
```

Sources: [Mover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/Mover.hh#L64-L99), [Filter.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/Filter.hh#L48-L80), [MoverContainer.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverContainer.hh#L44-L97)

## The Mover Base Class

The `protocols::moves::Mover` class is the abstract root of every structural transformation in Rosetta. It inherits from `utility::VirtualBase` and `utility::pointer::enable_shared_from_this<Mover>`, giving it both polymorphic deletion semantics and the ability to safely return shared pointers to itself — a critical requirement for nested mover compositions that must share ownership of child movers [Mover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/Mover.hh#L64).

### Core Interface Contract

Every concrete Mover must implement at minimum two pure virtual methods. The **`apply(Pose&)`** method is the primary entry point — it receives a mutable `Pose` reference and is expected to perform an in-place conformational change. The **`get_name()`** method returns a human-readable class identifier used for logging, factory lookup, and debugging. Beyond these, the base class provides two cloning strategies: **`clone()`** returns a deep copy preserving the mover's current configuration (useful for reproducing a specific protocol state), while **`fresh_instance()`** returns a default-constructed copy (used by the job distributor to obtain a clean mover for each new job) [Mover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/Mover.hh#L98-L132).

| Method | Signature | Purpose | Override Requirement |
|--------|-----------|---------|---------------------|
| `apply()` | `void apply(Pose&)` | Perform the conformational change | **Pure virtual** — must override |
| `get_name()` | `string get_name() const` | Return class name for identification | **Pure virtual** — must override |
| `clone()` | `MoverOP clone() const` | Deep copy with current state | Virtual (not pure, but expected) |
| `fresh_instance()` | `MoverOP fresh_instance() const` | Default-constructed copy | Virtual (not pure, but expected) |
| `parse_my_tag()` | `void parse_my_tag(TagCOP, DataMap&)` | Parse XML attributes | Virtual, optional |
| `get_additional_output()` | `PoseOP get_additional_output()` | Multi-output support (JD2) | Virtual, optional |

### Mover Status Protocol

After `apply()` executes, the job distributor inspects the mover's **`MoverStatus`** to determine the outcome. The status is set through the protected `set_last_move_status()` method and retrieved via `get_last_move_status()`. This five-valued enum communicates not just success or failure, but *the nature of the failure* — which the job distributor uses to decide whether to retry, skip, or abort the current job [MoverStatus.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverStatus.hh#L26-L50).

| Status Constant | Value | Semantic Meaning | Job Distributor Action |
|----------------|-------|-----------------|----------------------|
| `MS_SUCCESS` | 0 | Mover completed successfully | Accept output |
| `FAIL_RETRY` | 1 | "Science" failure — stochastic, retryable | Retry same job |
| `FAIL_DO_NOT_RETRY` | 2 | Valid job but uninteresting output | Skip, move on |
| `FAIL_BAD_INPUT` | 3 | Structurally broken input | Cancel all nstruct repeats |
| `FAIL` | 4 | Undefined/general failure | Undefined (not obeyed by JD2) |

> [!TIP]
> The distinction between `FAIL_RETRY` and `FAIL_DO_NOT_RETRY` is fundamental to Rosetta's job distribution strategy. A docking run that fails an RMSD filter receives `FAIL_RETRY` because stochastic re-sampling might escape the local minimum. A design run that produces a sequence violating residue-type constraints receives `FAIL_DO_NOT_RETRY` because the same input will deterministically produce the same invalid result.

### Reference Pose Management

Movers maintain optional references to an **input pose** (the starting structure) and a **native pose** (the reference structure for RMSD calculation) via `set_input_pose()` and `set_native_pose()`. These are propagated through container movers to their children, ensuring that nested movers deep in a protocol hierarchy can access reference structures set at the top level. The `MoverContainer` base class overrides both setters to cascade them to all contained movers, maintaining consistency across the entire composition tree [MoverContainer.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverContainer.hh#L61-L66).

Sources: [Mover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/Mover.hh#L73-L299), [MoverStatus.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverStatus.hh#L26-L50)

## The Filter Base Class

The `protocols::filters::Filter` class serves as the abstract evaluator in Rosetta's protocol framework. Where Movers *produce* conformational change, Filters *judge* it. The base class defines a minimal but expressive interface built around three layers of reporting: a boolean pass/fail, a real-valued score, and a human-readable text report [Filter.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/Filter.hh#L48-L100).

### The Three-Layer Evaluation Model

The primary method is **`apply(Pose const&)`**, which returns a boolean indicating whether the pose passes the filter's criteria. Critically, the `Pose` is passed by `const` reference — filters are **never permitted to modify the pose**. This asymmetry with Mover's mutable `apply()` is a deliberate architectural invariant that prevents side effects in the evaluation phase. The second layer, **`report_sm(Pose const&)`**, returns a `Real` value typically written to score files and silent-output columns — it represents the *magnitude* of the filter's metric (e.g., an energy threshold distance), not just a binary result. The default returns `-99999` as a sentinel, signaling "no meaningful value." The third layer, **`report(ostream&, Pose const&)`**, writes human-readable diagnostics for protocol analysis [Filter.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/Filter.hh#L54-L82).

A fourth method, **`score(Pose&)`** (note the **non-const** reference), bridges the filter and scoring worlds. It exists primarily for integration with the score-function framework and for filters that need to temporarily modify pose state during evaluation — a rare but necessary escape hatch from the const-correctness contract.

### FilterCollection

Alongside the `Filter` hierarchy, a separate **`FilterCollection`** class provides a simple aggregation mechanism. It wraps a `vector1<FilterCOP>` and evaluates each filter in sequence via its own `apply()` method. The collection uses **logical AND** semantics: all member filters must pass for the collection to pass. This is a lightweight complement to the more feature-rich `CompoundFilter` (discussed below), suitable for straightforward "all of these must pass" scenarios without needing Boolean operators [Filter.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/Filter.hh#L105-L138).

Sources: [Filter.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/Filter.hh#L48-L144)

## Container Movers: Composing Sequential and Stochastic Protocols

The `MoverContainer` class and its subclasses provide the structural backbone for building complex protocols from simpler atomic movers. Rather than hand-writing loop logic and branching in C++ or XML, developers compose container movers that encapsulate common execution patterns. The container holds a `vector0<MoverOP>` paired with a `vector0<Real>` of relative weights, enabling both ordered and probabilistic execution strategies [MoverContainer.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverContainer.hh#L44-L97).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph ContainerMovers["MoverContainer Subclasses"]
        direction TB
        SM["SequenceMover\nApplies M1 → M2 → M3\nin strict order"]
        RM["RandomMover\nPicks Mover i with\nprobability ∝ weight[i]\nRepeats nmoves_ times"]
        CM["CycleMover\nCycles M1, M2, M3 ...\none per apply() call\nRound-robin over time"]
        SWM["SwitchMover\nExecutes the single mover\nselected by name string\nScriptable via script_vars"]
    end

    SM --> M1["Mover 1"]
    SM --> M2["Mover 2"]
    SM --> M3["Mover 3"]
    RM --> W1["w=3.0"]
    RM --> W2["w=1.0"]
    RM --> W3["w=1.0"]
```

### SequenceMover

The `SequenceMover` applies each contained mover in the order it was added, sequentially modifying the pose. After each sub-mover executes, an optional `use_mover_status_` flag can trigger early termination if a child mover signals failure — otherwise, all movers execute unconditionally regardless of individual outcomes. The deep-copy constructor ensures that each `clone()` call produces independent copies of all child movers, preventing cross-protocol state contamination [MoverContainer.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverContainer.hh#L106-L178).

### RandomMover

The `RandomMover` samples from its child movers with probability proportional to their assigned weights. The `nmoves_` member controls how many random selections occur per `apply()` call (default: 1). For thermodynamic sampling accuracy, it also tracks `last_proposal_density_ratio_`, which is essential for Metropolis-Hastings acceptance in Monte Carlo protocols — the ratio accounts for the asymmetric probability of proposing forward vs. reverse moves when using weighted random selection [MoverContainer.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverContainer.hh#L182-L242).

### CycleMover

Unlike the SequenceMover which exhausts all movers in a single `apply()` call, the `CycleMover` advances an internal cursor by one position each time `apply()` is invoked, wrapping around at the end. This is specifically designed for interleaved sampling patterns — for example, performing a full repack once every eight cycles while doing rotamer trials on the other seven [MoverContainer.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverContainer.hh#L249-L269).

### SwitchMover

The `SwitchMover` provides named dispatch: it holds multiple movers with associated string names and executes only the one matching its `selected_` string. This enables a single RosettaScripts XML block to encode multiple protocol behaviors, with the active behavior selected at runtime through `parser:script_vars` or other external control mechanisms. The mover also logs which mover was selected in the output scores for traceability [MoverContainer.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverContainer.hh#L275-L316).

| Container | Execution Pattern | Per-Call Behavior | Key Use Case |
|-----------|------------------|-------------------|-------------|
| `SequenceMover` | Sequential, all movers | Runs all children | Multi-stage protocols |
| `RandomMover` | Stochastic, weighted | Samples `nmoves_` times | Monte Carlo move sets |
| `CycleMover` | Round-robin | One child per call | Interleaved sampling |
| `SwitchMover` | Named dispatch | One named child | Multi-mode scripts |

Sources: [MoverContainer.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverContainer.hh#L100-L322)

## Control-Flow Movers: Bridging Movers and Filters

The most powerful pattern in the Rosetta protocol framework is the set of control-flow movers that **consume both Movers and Filters** to implement conditional execution, retry logic, and acceptance criteria directly within the mover hierarchy. These classes eliminate the need for external loop/branch logic and enable fully declarative protocol specification.

### TrialMover — The Monte Carlo Gate

The `TrialMover` wraps a single Mover with a `MonteCarlo` acceptor, implementing the classic Metropolis criterion: apply the mover, compute the score change, and stochastically accept or reject based on the Boltzmann factor. It tracks statistics through a `StatsType` enum (all scores, accept/reject counts only, or no stats) and exposes `acceptance_rate()` and `num_accepts()` for monitoring convergence. This is the fundamental building block of nearly every Rosetta sampling protocol, from simple minimization to full ab initio folding [TrialMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/TrialMover.hh#L96-L197).

### RepeatMover — Fixed Iteration

The `RepeatMover` provides the simplest form of control flow: it invokes its child mover exactly `nmoves_` times in sequence. While trivial, it's the standard way to express "run this mover N times" in both C++ and RosettaScripts, and is commonly composed with `TrialMover` to create N independent Monte Carlo trials [RepeatMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/RepeatMover.hh#L36-L62).

### FilterMover — Retry on Rejection

The `FilterMover` applies its child mover and then evaluates its child filter. If the filter passes, execution succeeds. If the filter fails, the mover retries up to `max_tries_` times, restoring the pose between attempts. On final failure, it sets its `MoverStatus` to a configurable `ms_whenfail_` value (default: `FAIL_DO_NOT_RETRY`). This pattern is essential for protocols that require a move to satisfy a quality threshold before proceeding [FilterMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/FilterMover.hh#L33-L76).

### IfMover — Conditional Branching

The `IfMover` implements a two-way conditional branch based on filter evaluation. It holds a filter, a `true_mover_`, and a `false_mover_`. When `apply()` is called, it evaluates the filter: if true, `true_mover_` executes; if false, `false_mover_` executes. Critically, `IfMover` leverages the `get_additional_output()` mechanism to support **dual-output mode** — `get_additional_output_true_mover()` and `get_additional_output_false_mover()` can each yield a separate output pose, enabling JD2 to collect both branches of a conditional protocol [IfMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/IfMover.hh#L36-L84).

### JumpOutMover — Score-Threshold Branching

The `JumpOutMover` applies a first mover, evaluates whether the score improvement is within a `tolerance_` of the initial score using a `ScoreFunction`, and conditionally applies a second mover only if the threshold is met. This is useful for protocols where an expensive refinement step should only be attempted when a preliminary move has already achieved a sufficient energy improvement [JumpOutMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/JumpOutMover.hh#L43-L69).

### WhileMover — Pose-Condition Loops

The `WhileMover` repeatedly applies its child mover while a `PoseCondition` functor returns true, up to `nmoves_` iterations. The `PoseCondition` base class is a minimal abstract functor with `operator()(Pose const&) → bool`, allowing developers to define arbitrary termination conditions — from score thresholds to geometric criteria to convergence checks [WhileMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/WhileMover.hh#L40-L67).

Sources: [TrialMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/TrialMover.hh#L96-L197), [RepeatMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/RepeatMover.hh#L36-L62), [FilterMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/FilterMover.hh#L33-L76), [IfMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/IfMover.hh#L36-L84), [JumpOutMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/JumpOutMover.hh#L43-L69), [WhileMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/WhileMover.hh#L40-L67)

## The Creator Pattern: Runtime Factory Registration

Both the Mover and Filter hierarchies use an identical **Creator pattern** for load-time factory registration. Each concrete class pairs with a corresponding `MoverCreator` or `FilterCreator` that knows how to instantiate it and describe its XML schema. These creators self-register with their respective factories (`MoverFactory` and `FilterFactory`) at program startup through static initialization, enabling any protocol to be instantiated by name from XML without the application needing to `#include` its header [MoverCreator.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverCreator.hh#L32-L46).

### The Three-Method Creator Contract

Every Creator implementation must provide exactly three methods. **`create_mover()` / `create_filter()`** returns a fresh `OP` to a default-constructed instance. **`keyname()`** returns the string identifier used as the XML tag name (e.g., `"MinMover"`, `"InterfaceScoreFilter"`). **`provide_xml_schema()`** populates an `XMLSchemaDefinition` object with the attribute and sub-element definitions that the RosettaScripts parser will use to validate the mover's XML configuration. This schema-generation approach replaces the older hand-written parsing with type-safe, validated configuration [MoverCreator.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverCreator.hh#L32-L46), [FilterCreator.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/FilterCreator.hh#L32-L43).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant XML as RosettaScripts XML
    participant MF as MoverFactory
    participant MC as MoverCreator
    participant M as ConcreteMover

    XML->>MF: new_mover("MinMover", tag, datamap)
    MF->>MF: creators_["MinMover"]
    MF->>MC: create_mover()
    MC->>M: new MinMover()
    MC-->>MF: MoverOP
    MF->>M: parse_my_tag(tag, datamap)
    M-->>MF: configured mover
    MF-->>XML: MoverOP
```

> [!TIP]
> When implementing a new Mover for RosettaScripts, you must create three artifacts: the Mover class itself, a corresponding `MoverCreator` subclass, and a static registration call (typically via `MoverRegistrator` or `MoverFactory::CreatorRegistrer`). The Creator's `provide_xml_schema()` method must be complete and accurate — the RosettaScripts parser will reject XML that doesn't conform to the schema, and silently ignored attributes are a common source of configuration bugs.

Sources: [MoverCreator.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverCreator.hh#L32-L46), [FilterCreator.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/FilterCreator.hh#L32-L43)

## Composable Filter Patterns

Beyond the base `Filter` class, Rosetta provides several filter composition strategies that enable building complex acceptance criteria from simpler building blocks. These are particularly valuable in RosettaScripts where multi-criteria filtering is the norm.

### CompoundFilter — Boolean Logic on Filters

The `CompoundFilter` implements compound logical expressions over other filters using AND, OR, and XOR operators. Each entry in its `CompoundStatement` vector pairs a `FilterOP` with a `boolean_operations` enum value. An optional `invert()` method negates the entire compound expression. It also supports `reset_filters` — a set of stateful filters that must have their internal caches cleared before evaluation, preventing stale data from contaminating multi-iteration protocols. The `compute()` method evaluates the compound expression and returns a boolean, while `apply()` delegates to it [BasicFilters.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/BasicFilters.hh#L172-L200).

### StochasticFilter — Probabilistic Acceptance

The `StochasticFilter` passes with a configurable `confidence_` probability (the fraction of calls that return `true`). It optionally wraps a sub-filter that is evaluated only when the core stochastic check matches a `run_subfilter_on_` condition. This is useful for implementing rejection sampling protocols or for intentionally allowing occasional "bad" structures through to maintain diversity in a sampling trajectory [BasicFilters.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/BasicFilters.hh#L126-L170).

### ContingentFilter — Cross-Mover Communication

The `ContingentFilter` is a stateful filter whose pass/fail value is set externally by another mover via `set_value()`, rather than being computed from the pose. This creates a communication channel between movers and filters, enabling patterns like "mover A sets a flag that filter B reads." The value defaults to `false` and persists until explicitly changed. This is the only filter type whose `apply()` result is decoupled from the pose state [ContingentFilter.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/ContingentFilter.hh#L35-L74).

| Filter | Composition Type | Stateful? | Typical Use |
|--------|-----------------|-----------|------------|
| `TrueFilter` / `FalseFilter` | Constant | No | Testing, always-accept branches |
| `TrueFalseFilter` | Configurable constant | No | Parameterized pass-through |
| `CompoundFilter` | Boolean expression | Optional (reset_filters) | Multi-criteria acceptance |
| `StochasticFilter` | Probabilistic wrapper | No | Diversity maintenance |
| `ContingentFilter` | External state flag | Yes | Cross-mover signaling |
| `FilterCollection` | Logical AND aggregation | No | Simple multi-filter gates |

Sources: [BasicFilters.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/BasicFilters.hh#L41-L200), [ContingentFilter.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/ContingentFilter.hh#L35-L74)

## The Mover-Filter Protocol Pattern

In practice, Rosetta protocols assemble Movers and Filters into layered pipelines. A typical pattern nests container movers inside control-flow movers, with filters providing acceptance gates at multiple levels. The following diagram illustrates a canonical structure common to many RosettaScripts protocols:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    OUTER["RepeatMover (100 iterations)"]
    OUTER --> TRIAL["TrialMover"]
    TRIAL --> SEQ["SequenceMover"]
    SEQ --> M1["ShearMover"]
    SEQ --> M2["MinMover"]
    SEQ --> M3["PackRotamersMover"]
    TRIAL --> MC["MonteCarlo"]
    OUTER --> EVAL["FilterMover"]
    EVAL --> FM["FilterMover wraps:\nSequenceMover + ScoreFilter"]
    FM --> RETRY["Retries up to max_tries_"]
    
    style OUTER fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff
    style TRIAL fill:#40916c,color:#fff
    style SEQ fill:#52b788,color:#fff
    style EVAL fill:#d4a373,color:#fff
```

The outer `RepeatMover` runs 100 independent iterations. Each iteration applies a `SequenceMover` of perturbation moves (shear, minimize, repack) through a `TrialMover` that gate-keeps acceptance via Metropolis criteria. After each iteration, a `FilterMover` checks whether the result meets a quality threshold, retrying the entire sequence if it doesn't. This layered composition — iteration → acceptance → sequence → atomic moves — is the idiomatic Rosetta protocol structure, and every layer is itself a Mover that can be independently tested, configured, and reused.

## Navigating the Protocol Ecosystem

The `source/src/protocols/` directory contains **over 180 subdirectories**, each typically housing one or more specialized movers and filters for a particular modeling domain. A few key directories worth noting for further exploration: `simple_moves/` contains fundamental atomic movers (minimization, packing, side-chain movers); `relax/` implements structure relaxation protocols; `docking/` provides protein-protein and protein-ligand docking movers; and `rosetta_scripts/` contains the parser infrastructure that ties this entire hierarchy together [protocols directory](source/src/protocols/).

For a deeper understanding of how these movers integrate with Rosetta's sampling framework, see [Monte Carlo Sampling](12-monte-carlo-sampling). To learn how the Creator pattern enables XML-based protocol construction, see [RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework). For the underlying data structure that all movers consume, revisit [Pose and Conformation](8-pose-and-conformation).

# Monte Carlo Sampling



Monte Carlo (MC) sampling is the thermodynamic engine that powers nearly every Rosetta protocol—from ab initio folding to protein design to structure relaxation. Rather than exhaustively enumerating conformational space, Rosetta uses stochastic Metropolis accept/reject criteria to explore energy landscapes efficiently. This page dissects the layered MC architecture: the core `MonteCarlo` state machine, the mover-level integration via `TrialMover`, the self-contained `GenericMonteCarloMover`, and the advanced canonical sampling framework for tempering and replica exchange.

## Architecture Overview

The MC subsystem is organized into four conceptual layers, each serving a distinct role in the sampling pipeline. The core layer manages thermodynamic state, the mover layer couples perturbations to acceptance decisions, the protocol layer provides high-level iteration control, and the canonical sampling layer implements advanced sampling techniques.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Canonical Sampling Layer"
        PT[ParallelTempering]
        ST[SimulatedTempering]
        HE[HamiltonianExchange]
        MH[MetropolisHastingsMover]
    end

    subgraph "Protocol Layer"
        GMC[GenericMonteCarloMover]
        GSA[GenericSimulatedAnnealer]
        RM[MonteCarloRecover]
        MR[MonteCarloReset]
        REX[ReplicaExchangeMC]
    end

    subgraph "Mover Layer"
        TM[TrialMover]
        RM2[RepeatMover]
        MM[MixedMonteCarlo]
        DMC[DualMonteCarlo]
    end

    subgraph "Core Layer"
        MC[MonteCarlo<br/>Metropolis Criterion]
        MCS[MonteCarloStatus<br/>MCA Enum]
        TC[TrialCounter<br/>Statistics]
        MCE[MonteCarloException<br/>Converge]
    end

    PT --> MC
    ST --> MC
    HE --> MC
    MH --> MC
    GMC --> MC
    REX --> MC
    TM --> MC
    RM2 --> TM
    GMC --> TM
```

Sources: [MonteCarlo.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MonteCarlo.hh#L70-L98), [GenericMonteCarloMover.hh](source/src/protocols/monte_carlo/GenericMonteCarloMover.hh#L60-L93), [ReplicaExchangeMC.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/ReplicaExchangeMC.hh#L27-L60)

## The Core MonteCarlo Object

The `protocols::moves::MonteCarlo` class is the heart of Rosetta's sampling engine. It extends `utility::VirtualBase` and is responsible for all major functions needed in a Monte Carlo simulation: applying the Metropolis Criterion, tracking the lowest-energy and last-accepted conformations, and maintaining simulation statistics. It is constructed from three fundamental inputs: an initial `Pose`, a `ScoreFunction`, and a temperature value.

Sources: [MonteCarlo.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MonteCarlo.hh#L51-L98)

### Constructors and Initialization

The `MonteCarlo` class provides three constructor variants, each addressing a different initialization scenario. The primary constructor takes a full `Pose`, `ScoreFunction`, and temperature—it scores the initial pose and sets both `last_accepted_pose_` and `lowest_score_pose_` to it. A second constructor accepts an externally computed score instead of a `ScoreFunction`, useful when scoring logic lives outside Rosetta's standard framework. A third "deferred" constructor accepts only a `ScoreFunction` and temperature, requiring a subsequent `reset(pose)` call before the first trial.

Sources: [MonteCarlo.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MonteCarlo.hh#L94-L118)

### The Boltzmann Accept/Reject Criterion

The `boltzmann()` method is the central decision point of every MC trial. It is overloaded in four variants, each accommodating different calling patterns. The primary variant accepts a `Pose&`, evaluates its score via the internal `ScoreFunction`, and then applies the Metropolis criterion. The returned `bool` indicates acceptance, and the `MCA` enum (stored internally and retrievable via `mc_accepted()`) encodes the *reason* for acceptance at four granularity levels.

Sources: [MonteCarlo.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MonteCarlo.hh#L174-L229)

### Acceptance States: The MCA Enum

The `MCA` enum in `MonteCarloStatus.hh` defines a four-level acceptance taxonomy. This granularity is critical for diagnostics and for protocols that need to distinguish between energetically favorable moves and thermally uphill ones.

| MCA Value | Constant | Meaning |
|-----------|----------|---------|
| 3 | `MCA_accepted_score_beat_low` | Accepted: score is the new global best |
| 2 | `MCA_accepted_score_beat_last` | Accepted: score improved over last accepted |
| 1 | `MCA_accepted_thermally` | Accepted: score worsened but passed Boltzmann probability |
| 0 | `MCA_rejected` | Rejected: move did not pass acceptance test |

This enum is hierarchical—each value implies the properties of all lower values—enabling callers to filter acceptance statistics at the desired granularity.

Sources: [MonteCarloStatus.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MonteCarloStatus.hh#L21-L31)

### Pose State Management

The `MonteCarlo` object maintains three independent pose snapshots: the **last accepted pose** (used as the reference for the next Boltzmann evaluation), the **lowest score pose** (the global best encountered across all trials), and the **working pose** (the input to each `boltzmann()` call). Several methods govern transitions between these states: `recover_low(pose)` copies the lowest-score conformation into the working pose and updates the last-accepted state; `reset(pose)` reinitializes both reference poses to the current conformation; `eval_lowest_score_pose()` evaluates the current pose against the lowest without invoking full Boltzmann logic.

Sources: [MonteCarlo.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MonteCarlo.hh#L249-L404)

### Temperature Control and Annealing

Temperature is the central control knob for exploration versus exploitation. The `set_temperature()` method updates the temperature in real time, enabling simulated annealing schedules. Additionally, `set_autotemp()` enables automatic quenching: when enabled, the temperature is gradually reduced toward a user-specified `quench_temp` after each acceptance. The `change_weight()` method allows selective reweighting of individual score terms without rebuilding the entire `ScoreFunction`, providing finer-grained control during multi-stage annealing protocols.

Sources: [MonteCarlo.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MonteCarlo.hh#L132-L171)

### Convergence Monitoring

The `MonteCarloExceptionConverge` class (included conditionally on Win32) provides a mechanism to detect when a simulation has stalled—that is, when the acceptance rate drops below a useful threshold. The `show_state()`, `show_scores()`, and `show_counters()` methods provide real-time diagnostic output including temperature, scores, annealing settings, and per-move-type statistics.

Sources: [MonteCarlo.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MonteCarlo.hh#L464-L504)

> [!TIP]
> The `boltzmann()` method accepts a `proposal_density_ratio` parameter (defaulting to 1.0) that corrects for asymmetric proposal distributions—critical when using non-reversible moves like certain fragment insertions or biased perturbations. Setting this incorrectly silently biases your sampling distribution.

## Mover-Level Integration: TrialMover

The `TrialMover` bridges Rosetta's Mover hierarchy and the MonteCarlo acceptance engine. It composes any arbitrary `MoverOP` with a `MonteCarloOP`, executing the move and then delegating the accept/reject decision. This composition pattern is the standard idiom for MC-driven protocols throughout Rosetta.

Sources: [TrialMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/TrialMover.hh#L46-L117)

### Construction and Usage Pattern

A `TrialMover` is constructed with a `MoverOP` (the perturbation) and a `MonteCarloOP` (the acceptance criterion). When `apply(pose)` is called, it first invokes the inner mover's `apply()`, then calls `mc_->boltzmann(pose)`. If the move is rejected, the pose is automatically restored to the last accepted conformation. This pattern is so fundamental that it is typically wrapped in a `RepeatMover` to execute thousands of trials.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Input Pose] --> B[TrialMover.apply]
    B --> C[Inner Mover.apply]
    C --> D{MonteCarlo.boltzmann}
    D -- accepted --> E[Update last_accepted]
    D -- rejected --> F[Restore last_accepted]
    E --> G[Output Pose]
    F --> G
```

Sources: [TrialMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/TrialMover.hh#L133-L145)

### Statistics and Diagnostics

The `TrialMover` supports three statistics granularity levels via the `StatsType` enum. Setting `keep_stats_type(all_stats)` tracks per-trial energy changes, accept/reject counts, and score distributions—useful for analysis but with memory overhead. The `accept_reject` mode tracks only counts (the default for production), while `no_stats` disables tracking entirely for maximum throughput. The `acceptance_rate()` and `num_accepts()` methods expose aggregate statistics.

Sources: [TrialMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/TrialMover.hh#L64-L68), [TrialMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/TrialMover.hh#L151-L154)

### MonteCarloUtil: Reset Mover

The `MonteCarloUtil` class (defined alongside `TrialMover`) provides a lightweight Mover wrapper for MC state operations. It wraps a `MonteCarloOP` and exposes a `mode_` string that controls whether `apply()` performs a recover-low or reset operation. This is commonly used in RosettaScripts pipelines to reset MC state between protocol stages.

Sources: [TrialMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/TrialMover.hh#L73-L94)

## GenericMonteCarloMover: Self-Contained MC Protocols

The `GenericMonteCarloMover` in `protocols::monte_carlo` is a high-level, self-contained Mover that bundles an inner mover, its own `MonteCarlo`-like state, trial counters, and termination conditions into a single RosettaScripts-compatible unit. It extends `MoverApplyingMover` and provides both score-function-based and filter-based evaluation.

Sources: [GenericMonteCarloMover.hh](source/src/protocols/monte_carlo/GenericMonteCarloMover.hh#L60-L93)

### Key Features

The mover operates around a central `boltzmann()` method that accepts a pose and a vector of random numbers (enabling deterministic replay). It tracks the last accepted pose, lowest score pose, and current score independently. The `sample_type_` parameter supports both `"low"` (standard MC, minimizing energy) and `"high"` (maximizing energy) sampling directions. The `drift` parameter controls whether the last accepted pose "drifts" with each acceptance or is reset to the original at the start of each trial. The `task_scaling` parameter adjusts the number of designable residues, and the `max_accepted_trials` parameter provides an alternative convergence criterion to raw trial count.

Sources: [GenericMonteCarloMover.hh](source/src/protocols/monte_carlo/GenericMonteCarloMover.hh#L132-L166)

### Trigger API

A distinctive feature is the **trigger system**: users can register callback functions via `add_trigger()` that fire at each MC iteration. Triggers receive the current trial index and can return `true` to force rescoring—enabling adaptive schemes like dynamic score weight adjustment mid-simulation. The trigger signature binds stage and total-stage information at registration time, providing context about overall simulation progress.

Sources: [GenericMonteCarloMover.hh](source/src/protocols/monte_carlo/GenericMonteCarloMover.hh#L179-L199)

## The Monte Carlo Protocol Mover Family

Beyond the core classes, the `protocols::monte_carlo` namespace provides several specialized movers for common MC workflow patterns.

Sources: [monte_carlo/ directory](source/src/protocols/monte_carlo/)

### Mover Summary

| Mover | Purpose | Key Parameter |
|-------|---------|---------------|
| `GenericMonteCarloMover` | Full MC loop with configurable inner mover, filters, and termination | `maxtrials`, `temperature` |
| `GenericSimulatedAnnealer` | MC with automatic temperature ramping | Start/end temperature |
| `MonteCarloRecover` | Restore pose to the MC lowest-energy state | N/A |
| `MonteCarloReset` | Reset MC state (counters, poses) to a new baseline | N/A |
| `ResetBaselineMover` | Re-establish the scoring baseline for the current pose | N/A |
| `MonteCarloTest` | Diagnostic mover for testing MC acceptance behavior | N/A |
| `MonteCarloInterface` | Adapts external MC frameworks to Rosetta's Pose system | N/A |

The `MonteCarloRecover` and `MonteCarloReset` movers are particularly important in multi-stage RosettaScripts protocols. After an MC sampling stage, `MonteCarloRecover` ensures the pose is set to the best structure found (not the last trial), while `MonteCarloReset` prepares the MC object for a fresh sampling phase at a different temperature or with different weights.

Sources: [GenericMonteCarloMover.hh](source/src/protocols/monte_carlo/GenericMonteCarloMover.hh#L82-L117), [MonteCarloRecover.hh](source/src/protocols/monte_carlo/MonteCarloRecover.hh)

## Advanced Mover Composition Patterns

The `protocols::moves` namespace provides several composition movers that enable complex MC strategies beyond simple single-mover trials.

Sources: [moves/ directory](source/src/protocols/moves/)

### Composition Movers

The `RepeatMover` wraps any mover (typically a `TrialMover`) and executes it N times—forming the outer loop of virtually every MC protocol. The `MixedMonteCarlo` maintains multiple `MonteCarlo` objects and randomly selects among them at each trial, enabling multi-resolution sampling where different score functions guide different move types. The `DualMonteCarlo` extends this to two MC objects with independent temperature and score settings, commonly used for coupled backbone/sidechain sampling.

Sources: [MixedMonteCarlo.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MixedMonteCarlo.hh), [DualMonteCarlo.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/DualMonteCarlo.hh)

### ReplicaExchangeMC

The `ReplicaExchangeMC` class extends `MonteCarlo` to implement replica exchange (parallel tempering). It accepts a list of temperatures (`tlist`) and a replica exchange frequency (`nreplica_frequency`). On each call to its overridden `boltzmann()`, it periodically attempts temperature swaps between neighboring replicas according to the standard Metropolis exchange criterion. The class maintains parallel energy lists and temperature tags, supporting both serial and MPI-parallel exchange schedules.

Sources: [ReplicaExchangeMC.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/ReplicaExchangeMC.hh#L27-L76)

## Canonical Sampling Framework

The `protocols::canonical_sampling` namespace implements a comprehensive framework for thermodynamically rigorous sampling, supporting parallel tempering, simulated tempering, Hamiltonian exchange, and Metropolis-Hastings with bias corrections. This is Rosetta's most advanced MC subsystem, designed for applications requiring proper Boltzmann ensemble sampling.

Sources: [canonical_sampling/ directory](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/)

### Framework Architecture

The canonical sampling framework decomposes complex sampling protocols into three orthogonal plugin types: **ThermodynamicMovers** (perturbations), **ThermodynamicObservers** (recording), and **TemperatureControllers** (annealing). The `CanonicalSamplingMover` orchestrates these components, while `MetropolisHastingsMover` implements the generalized accept/reject criterion with support for asymmetric proposal distributions.

Sources: [CanonicalSamplingMover.hh](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/CanonicalSamplingMover.hh), [MetropolisHastingsMover.hh](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/MetropolisHastingsMover.hh), [ThermodynamicMover.hh](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/ThermodynamicMover.hh)

### Tempering Methods

| Class | Method | Description |
|-------|--------|-------------|
| `ParallelTempering` | Parallel tempering | Multiple replicas at different temperatures with periodic exchange attempts |
| `SimulatedTempering` | Simulated tempering | Single replica that randomly proposes temperature changes |
| `HamiltonianExchange` | Hamiltonian exchange | Multiple replicas with different energy functions (e.g., different score weights) |
| `AsyncMPITemperingBase` | Async MPI tempering | Asynchronous replica exchange for improved scaling on large clusters |

Each tempering method inherits from `TemperingBase`, which manages the temperature schedule, exchange logic, and MPI coordination (when enabled). The `TemperatureController` class provides automated annealing with configurable cooling schedules.

Sources: [ParallelTempering.hh](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/ParallelTempering.hh), [SimulatedTempering.hh](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/SimulatedTempering.hh), [HamiltonianExchange.hh](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/HamiltonianExchange.hh)

### Bias Energy and Well-Tempered Ensemble

The `BiasedMonteCarlo` and `BiasEnergy` classes introduce biasing potentials that reshape the effective energy landscape to enhance sampling of specific collective variables. The `WTEBiasEnergy` implements the Well-Tempered Ensemble approach, which adds a Gaussian bias centered on the current energy to flatten the energy distribution—particularly useful for escaping deep local minima.

Sources: [BiasedMonteCarlo.hh](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/BiasedMonteCarlo.hh), [WTEBiasEnergy.hh](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/WTEBiasEnergy.hh)

### Trajectory Recording

The framework provides three recording backends for capturing simulation trajectories: `PDBTrajectoryRecorder` (writes individual PDB files), `SilentTrajectoryRecorder` (writes to Rosetta's silent file format for compact storage), and `DbTrajectoryRecorder` (writes to a SQLite database for complex analysis). The `MetricRecorder` enables recording arbitrary `SimpleMetric` values at each trial, providing extensible observables beyond raw scores.

Sources: [PDBTrajectoryRecorder.hh](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/PDBTrajectoryRecorder.hh), [SilentTrajectoryRecorder.hh](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/SilentTrajectoryRecorder.hh), [MetricRecorder.hh](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/MetricRecorder.hh)

### Convergence Assessment

The `mc_convergence_checks/` subdirectory implements hierarchical convergence detection. The `HPool` (Hierarchical Pool) maintains a tree of energy pools at different resolution thresholds, enabling efficient detection of structural convergence without storing full poses. MPI variants (`MPIPool_ConvergenceCheck`, `MPIHPool_ConvergenceCheck`, `MPIBPool_ConvergenceCheck`) aggregate convergence statistics across processes for distributed sampling campaigns.

Sources: [mc_convergence_checks/](source/src/protocols/canonical_sampling/mc_convergence_checks/)

## MC in Practice: Typical Protocol Pattern

The most common MC protocol in Rosetta follows a consistent pattern: create a `MonteCarlo` object, wrap a perturbation mover in a `TrialMover`, repeat for N iterations, then recover the best structure. This pattern is used across relaxation, design, docking, and folding protocols.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["mc = MonteCarlo(pose, scorefxn, temp)"] --> B["trial = TrialMover(perturbation_mover, mc)"]
    B --> C["repeat = RepeatMover(trial, N)"]
    C --> D["repeat.apply(pose)"]
    D --> E{"Check convergence"}
    E -- not converged --> F["mc.set_temperature(new_temp)"]
    F --> D
    E -- converged --> G["mc.recover_low(pose)"]
    G --> H["Output best structure"]
```

> [!TIP]
> A critical and frequently overlooked step is calling `mc.recover_low(pose)` *after* the sampling loop. Without this, the output pose reflects the last trial's state (which may have been a rejected move restored to the last accepted conformation), not necessarily the global best encountered during sampling.

## Relationship to Other Rosetta Systems

Monte Carlo sampling does not exist in isolation—it depends on and is depended upon by several other core systems. Understanding these relationships is essential for extending or debugging MC-based protocols.

### Dependencies

| System | Relationship |
|--------|-------------|
| **[Pose and Conformation](8-pose-and-conformation)** | The `Pose` is the mutable state that MC samples; conformations are cloned internally for pose snapshots |
| **[ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework)** | Provides the energy landscape that MC explores via `MonteCarlo.boltzmann()` |
| **[Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy)** | Supplies perturbation movers for `TrialMover` and acceptance filters for `GenericMonteCarloMover` |
| **[RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework)** | All MC movers are registered via `MoverFactory` and configurable through XML tags |

### Downstream Consumers

Nearly every application-domain protocol consumes the MC infrastructure: [Structure Relaxation](18-structure-relaxation) uses temperature-ramped MC with minimization interleaving; [Ab Initio Folding](20-ab-initio-folding) uses fragment-insertion MC with stage-dependent score functions; [De Novo Protein Design](17-de-novo-protein-design) alternates backbone MC perturbation with sequence design; and [Ligand Docking](19-ligand-docking) uses rigid-body MC with soft-repulsive score functions.

Sources: [MonteCarlo.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MonteCarlo.hh#L19-L39), [TrialMover.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/TrialMover.hh#L192-L196)

## Summary

Rosetta's Monte Carlo sampling subsystem is a carefully layered architecture that scales from simple single-temperature accept/reject loops to sophisticated parallel tempering with bias corrections. The core `MonteCarlo` class implements the thermodynamic decision logic, `TrialMover` provides the composition bridge to Rosetta's mover hierarchy, `GenericMonteCarloMover` offers a self-contained protocol unit for RosettaScripts, and the canonical sampling framework delivers production-grade ensemble sampling with convergence assessment. Understanding how these layers interact—and critically, where pose state is managed and recovered—is essential for building correct and efficient sampling protocols.

For deeper understanding of the components that MC depends on, see [ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework) for energy evaluation, [Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy) for perturbation strategies, and [RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework) for configuring MC protocols declaratively. To see MC in action within specific protocols, proceed to [Structure Relaxation](18-structure-relaxation) or [Ab Initio Folding](20-ab-initio-folding).

# Side-Chain Packing



Side-chain packing is the combinatorial optimization problem at the heart of Rosetta's protein modeling pipeline: given a fixed backbone, find the set of side-chain conformations (rotamers) that minimizes the total energy. This page dissects the packing subsystem's architecture — from the task specification that governs what the packer is allowed to do, through rotamer generation and interaction graph construction, to the simulated annealing search that produces the final assignment.

## Architectural Overview

The packing system follows a strict **three-phase pipeline**: setup, search, and cleanup. Each phase is deliberately factored into independent functions so that setup (which is expensive) can be decoupled from search (which may be repeated across multiple annealing runs). The `pack_rotamers()` function in [pack_rotamers.cc](source/src/core/pack/pack_rotamers.cc#L74-L110) serves as the canonical entry point, orchestrating these phases in sequence:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Entry["pack_rotamers()"]
        A["Pose + ScoreFunction<br/>+ PackerTask"]
    end

    subgraph Phase1["Phase 1: Setup (pack_rotamers_setup)"]
        B1["pack_scorefxn_pose_handshake"]
        B2["update_residue_neighbors"]
        B3["scfxn.setup_for_packing"]
        B4["create_packer_graph"]
        B5["RotamerSets.build_rotamers"]
        B6["InteractionGraphFactory::<br/>create_and_initialize_annealing_graph"]
    end

    subgraph Phase2["Phase 2: Search (pack_rotamers_run)"]
        C1["AnnealerFactory::create_annealer"]
        C2["annealer->run()"]
        C3["Replace residues on Pose"]
    end

    subgraph Phase3["Phase 3: Cleanup"]
        D1["pack_rotamers_cleanup"]
        D2["scfxn(pose) rescore"]
    end

    A --> Phase1 --> Phase2 --> Phase3
```

This pipeline architecture is not merely organizational — it enables the `pack_rotamers_loop()` variant ([pack_rotamers.cc](source/src/core/pack/pack_rotamers.cc#L144-L190)) to reuse a single interaction graph across multiple independent annealing runs, storing the best result found. The setup phase is amortized over `nloop` iterations, which is critical for stochastic sampling protocols where you need independent decoys from the same rotamer landscape.

Sources: [pack_rotamers.cc](source/src/core/pack/pack_rotamers.cc#L74-L110), [pack_rotamers.cc](source/src/core/pack/pack_rotamers.cc#L144-L190)

## PackerTask: Specifying What the Packer May Do

The `PackerTask` class hierarchy is the **declarative specification layer** for packing. Rather than imperatively telling the packer what to change, you declare a policy: which residues may be repacked (same amino acid, new conformation), which may be redesigned (potentially different amino acid), and which are frozen entirely. The abstract interface is defined in [PackerTask.hh](source/src/core/pack/task/PackerTask.hh#L59-L150), with the concrete implementation in `PackerTask_` ([PackerTask_.hh](source/src/core/pack/task/PackerTask_.hh#L57-L99)).

The PackerTask controls packing behavior along several orthogonal dimensions:

| Dimension | Key Methods | Effect |
|-----------|-------------|--------|
| **Repacking** | `pack_residue()`, `being_packed()` | Allows side-chain conformational search at fixed identity |
| **Design** | `design_residue()`, `design_any()` | Allows amino acid identity to change during optimization |
| **Bump checking** | `bump_check()`, `max_rotbump_energy()` | Filters rotamers that clash with the backbone |
| **Interaction graph** | `linmem_ig()`, `lazy_ig()`, `double_lazy_ig()`, `precompute_ig()` | Selects which IG data structure to use |
| **Annealer** | `multi_cool_annealer()`, `smart_annealer()` | Selects which simulated annealing strategy to employ |
| **Symmetry** | `keep_sequence_symmetry()` | Constrains symmetric subunits to maintain identical sequences |
| **Rotamer links** | `rotamer_couplings_exist()`, `rotamer_links_exist()` | Enforces correlated rotamer changes across residues |

The task system is further extensible through **TaskOperations** (in [task/operation/](source/src/core/pack/task/operation/)), which modify PackerTask policies programmatically or via RosettaScripts. This is the primary extensibility point for controlling packing behavior without modifying the packer itself. Common operations include `RestrictToRepacking`, `PreventRepacking`, `OperateOnResidueSubset`, and `ClashBasedRepackShell`.

Sources: [PackerTask.hh](source/src/core/pack/task/PackerTask.hh#L59-L150), [PackerTask_.hh](source/src/core/pack/task/PackerTask_.hh#L57-L99)

## Rotamer Generation

Before the packer can optimize, it needs a **discrete set of candidate conformations** — rotamers — to consider at each position. This is the responsibility of the `RotamerSets` subsystem ([rotamer_set/](source/src/core/pack/rotamer_set/)).

### Rotamer Library Foundation

Rosetta's rotamer libraries live in [database/rotamer/](database/rotamer/) and come in several variants. The **Dunbrack rotamer library** is the primary backbone-dependent library, with implementations in [dunbrack/](source/src/core/pack/dunbrack/). Key classes include `RotamerLibrary` (the singleton manager), `RotamericSingleResidueDunbrackLibrary` for standard amino acids, and `SemiRotamericSingleResidueDunbrackLibrary` for residues where the rotameric model is only partially applicable.

### Rotamer Database Variants

| Library Path | Purpose |
|-------------|---------|
| `database/rotamer/ExtendedOpt1-5/` | Default backbone-dependent rotamers with extended optimization |
| `database/rotamer/beta_nov2016/` | Beta-sheet optimized rotamer statistics |
| `database/rotamer/corrections_conway2016/` | Corrections from Conway et al. 2016 re-derived statistics |
| `database/rotamer/shapovalov/` | Shapovalov-Dunbrack library with higher discretization levels |
| `database/rotamer/dna/` | Vector-quantized DNA rotamer libraries |
| `database/rotamer/ncaa_rotlibs/` | Non-canonical amino acid rotamer libraries |
| `database/rotamer/peptoid_rotlibs/` | Peptoid rotamer libraries |

### RotamerSet Building Pipeline

Within `pack_rotamers_setup()`, the rotamer set construction follows a precise sequence ([pack_rotamers.cc](source/src/core/pack/pack_rotamers.cc#L196-L246)):

1. **`rotsets->set_task(task)`** — Bind the PackerTask to determine which residues are packable
2. **`rotsets->initialize_pose_for_rotsets_creation(pose)`** — Prepare the pose
3. **`rotsets->build_rotamers(pose, scfxn, packer_neighbor_graph)`** — Generate candidate rotamers from the Dunbrack library, filtered by bump checking and task restrictions
4. **`scfxn.setup_for_packing_with_rotsets(pose, rotsets)`** — Allow the score function to adapt to the rotamer sets
5. **`rotsets->prepare_sets_for_packing(pose, scfxn)`** — Final preparation for energy computation

The `FixbbRotamerSets` class ([rotamer_set/FixbbRotamerSets.hh](source/src/core/pack/rotamer_set/FixbbRotamerSets.hh)) manages the mapping between "molten residues" (positions being optimized) and their rotamer collections. Additional rotamers can be injected or filtered via **RotamerSetOperations** such as `AddResiduesRotamerSetOperation`, `DeleteAllRotamerSetOperation`, `BumpSelector`, and `UnboundRotamersOperation`.

> [!TIP]
> The rotamer generation step often produces the largest number of rotamers at designed positions (where multiple amino acid types are allowed). The `RotamerSampleOptions` class in [task/RotamerSampleOptions.hh](source/src/core/pack/task/RotamerSampleOptions.hh) controls how many extra chi-angle samples are added per residue type, directly impacting the combinatorial explosion that the interaction graph must handle.

Sources: [pack_rotamers.cc](source/src/core/pack/pack_rotamers.cc#L196-L246), [database/rotamer/](database/rotamer/), [dunbrack/](source/src/core/pack/dunbrack/), [rotamer_set/](source/src/core/pack/rotamer_set/)

## Interaction Graph: Modeling Rotamer Compatibility

The **interaction graph (IG)** is the core data structure that makes combinatorial rotamer optimization tractable. Each rotamer assignment has an intrinsic (one-body) energy, and each pair of rotamers on neighboring residues has a pairwise (two-body) energy. The total energy decomposes exactly into these terms, enabling efficient simulated annealing. The interaction graph hierarchy lives in [interaction_graph/](source/src/core/pack/interaction_graph/).

### Graph Selection Logic

The `InteractionGraphFactory` ([InteractionGraphFactory.cc](source/src/core/pack/interaction_graph/InteractionGraphFactory.cc#L233-L341)) employs a sophisticated decision tree to select the most appropriate graph type based on the PackerTask settings, score function weights, and symmetry:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start["PackerTask + RotamerSets<br/>+ ScoreFunction"] --> LinMem{"linmem_ig()?"}
    LinMem -->|Yes| MakeLinMem["make_linmem_ig()<br/>(O(N) on-the-fly)"]
    LinMem -->|No| Design{"design_any()?"}
    
    Design -->|Yes| SurfaceW{"surface weight?"}
    SurfaceW -->|Yes| PDSSIG["PDSurfaceInteractionGraph"]
    SurfaceW -->|No| HPW{"hpatch weight?"}
    HPW -->|Yes| PDHPatchIG["PDHPatchInteractionGraph"]
    HPW -->|No| NPDHB{"npd_hbond weight?"}
    NPDHB -->|Yes| StdNPDHB["StandardNPDHBondInteractionGraph"]
    NPDHB -->|No| Lazy{"lazy_ig()?"}
    Lazy -->|Yes| LIG["LazyInteractionGraph"]
    Lazy -->|No| DLazy{"double_lazy_ig()?"}
    DLazy -->|Yes| DLIG["DoubleLazyInteractionGraph"]
    DLazy -->|No| Precomp{"precompute_ig()?"}
    Precomp -->|Yes| PDIG["PDInteractionGraph<br/>(O(N²) precomputed)"]
    Precomp -->|No| Auto{"auto_use_linmem_ig()<br/>(runtime estimation)"}
    Auto -->|linmem faster| MakeLinMem
    Auto -->|precompute faster| PDIG2["PDInteractionGraph"]
    
    Design -->|No| NPDHB2{"npd_hbond?"}
    NPDHB2 -->|Yes| DNPDHB["DenseNPDHBondInteractionGraph"]
    NPDHB2 -->|No| DenseIG["DensePDInteractionGraph"]
```

### Interaction Graph Type Comparison

| Graph Type | Memory | Precompute Cost | Per-Iteration Cost | Best For |
|-----------|--------|-----------------|-------------------|----------|
| `DensePDInteractionGraph` | O(N²) | O(N²) | O(1) per swap | Small repack-only jobs |
| `PDInteractionGraph` | O(N²) | O(N²) | O(1) per swap | Design with few rotamers |
| `LazyInteractionGraph` | O(N²) amortized | Lazy | O(1) cached, O(N) uncached | Design where many pairs never swap |
| `DoubleLazyInteractionGraph` | Bounded | Lazy + deferred alloc | O(1) cached | Multi-state design with memory constraints |
| `LinearMemoryInteractionGraph` | O(N) | Minimal | O(N) per swap | Large-scale design (95% less memory) |
| `OnTheFlyInteractionGraph` | O(N) | None | O(N) per evaluation | Maximum memory savings |
| `SymmLinMemInteractionGraph` | O(N) | Minimal | O(N) per swap | Symmetric packing with memory constraints |

The auto-selection logic in `auto_use_linmem_ig()` ([InteractionGraphFactory.cc](source/src/core/pack/interaction_graph/InteractionGraphFactory.cc#L120-L162)) estimates runtime using empirical scaling factors (derived from benchmarks) and compares expected precompute time against expected linear-memory per-iteration time multiplied by `nloop`. When precomputation is estimated at under 60 seconds, the precomputed graph is always preferred due to the noise in the estimation model at small scales.

> [!TIP]
> When multi-threaded builds are active (`MULTI_THREADED`), the precomputed interaction graph computation is parallelized across the requested thread count, effectively dividing the precompute time. The linear memory IG does not yet support multi-threaded construction, so the auto-selection threshold shifts accordingly. The `ig_threads_to_request` parameter on `PackerTask_` controls this.

Sources: [InteractionGraphFactory.cc](source/src/core/pack/interaction_graph/InteractionGraphFactory.cc#L233-L341), [InteractionGraphFactory.cc](source/src/core/pack/interaction_graph/InteractionGraphFactory.cc#L120-L162), [InteractionGraphFactory.cc](source/src/core/pack/interaction_graph/InteractionGraphFactory.cc#L392-L420)

## Simulated Annealing: The Search Strategy

Once the interaction graph is built and populated with energy data, the **simulated annealer** searches for the globally optimal rotamer assignment. The annealer hierarchy lives in [annealer/](source/src/core/pack/annealer/), with the factory pattern in `AnnealerFactory` ([AnnealerFactory.cc](source/src/core/pack/annealer/AnnealerFactory.cc#L42-L96)).

### Annealer Selection

The `AnnealerFactory::create_annealer()` method follows a priority chain:

| Priority | Condition | Annealer Type | Purpose |
|----------|-----------|---------------|---------|
| 1 | `keep_sequence_symmetry()` | `SequenceSymmetricAnnealer` | Maintains identical sequences across symmetric subunits |
| 2 | `rotamer_couplings_exist()` | `FixbbCoupledRotamerSimAnnealer` | Handles correlated rotamer changes via coupling specifications |
| 3 | `rotamer_links_exist()` | `FixbbLinkingRotamerSimAnnealer` | Handles rotamer link constraints |
| 4 | `multi_cool_annealer()` | `MultiCoolAnnealer` | Multiple independent cooling schedules with history-based selection |
| 5 | `smart_annealer()` | `SmartFixbbSimAnnealer` | Adaptive temperature schedule based on acceptance history |
| 6 | Default | `FixbbSimAnnealer` | Standard Metropolis simulated annealing with fixed temperature schedule |

All annealers share a common base class `SimAnnealerBase` ([SimAnnealerBase.hh](source/src/core/pack/annealer/SimAnnealerBase.hh)) and operate on the `AnnealableGraphBase` interface, making them interchangeable once the interaction graph is constructed. The annealer's `run()` method ([pack_rotamers.cc](source/src/core/pack/pack_rotamers.cc#L333-L335)) performs the stochastic search, writing the best rotamer assignment into a `bestrotamer_at_seqpos` array.

### Temperature Control

The PackerTask exposes `low_temp()` and `high_temp()` methods ([pack_rotamers.cc](source/src/core/pack/pack_rotamers.cc#L328-L329)) to override the default annealing temperature schedule. When set to values greater than 0, these override the score function's default temperature range. The `disallow_quench()` flag prevents the final low-temperature quenching step, which can be useful when you want to preserve the Metropolis acceptance dynamics at all temperatures.

Sources: [AnnealerFactory.cc](source/src/core/pack/annealer/AnnealerFactory.cc#L42-L96), [pack_rotamers.cc](source/src/core/pack/pack_rotamers.cc#L294-L336), [annealer/](source/src/core/pack/annealer/)

## Putting It All Together: The Complete Flow

The following diagram shows the full packing pipeline with all key components and their relationships:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Input
        Pose["Pose"]
        Sfxn["ScoreFunction"]
        Task["PackerTask"]
    end

    subgraph Setup["pack_rotamers_setup()"]
        PN["create_packer_graph()"]
        RS["RotamerSets<br/>.build_rotamers()"]
        IGF["InteractionGraphFactory"]
    end

    subgraph IGTypes["Interaction Graph Variants"]
        DenseIG["DensePDInteractionGraph"]
        PDIG["PDInteractionGraph"]
        LazyIG["LazyInteractionGraph"]
        LinMemIG["LinearMemoryInteractionGraph"]
        SymmIG["SymmLinMemInteractionGraph"]
    end

    subgraph Search["pack_rotamers_run()"]
        AF["AnnealerFactory"]
        Annealer["SimAnnealerBase"]
        MuxIG["MultiplexedAnnealableGraph"]
    end

    subgraph Output
        BestPose["Best Pose"]
        BestEnergy["Best Energy"]
    end

    Pose --> Setup
    Sfxn --> Setup
    Task --> Setup
    
    PN --> RS
    RS --> IGF
    IGF --> IGTypes
    Task --> IGF

    IGTypes --> MuxIG
    MuxIG --> Search
    Task --> AF
    AF --> Annealer
    Annealer --> BestEnergy
    Annealer --> BestPose
```

The `MultiplexedAnnealableGraph` ([InteractionGraphFactory.cc](source/src/core/pack/interaction_graph/InteractionGraphFactory.cc#L404-L419)) is a notable composite pattern: when the score function includes whole-structure energy methods (such as buried unsaturation penalties) that cannot be decomposed into pairwise terms, the factory wraps the two-body interaction graph together with a `ResidueArrayAnnealingEvaluator` into a multiplexed graph that combines both energy models during annealing.

## Specialized Packing Modes

The `core::pack` directory contains several specialized packing utilities beyond the standard fixed-backbone pipeline:

| Component | Location | Purpose |
|-----------|----------|---------|
| `rotamer_trials` | [rotamer_trials.hh](source/src/core/pack/rotamer_trials.hh) | Single-pass greedy rotamer optimization (no annealing) |
| `min_pack` / `rtmin` | [min_pack.hh](source/src/core/pack/min_pack.hh), [rtmin.hh](source/src/core/pack/rtmin.hh) | Rotamer minimization: continuous chi-angle optimization after discrete packing |
| `optimizeH` | [optimizeH.hh](source/src/core/pack/optimizeH.hh) | Specialized hydrogen placement optimization |
| `pack_missing_sidechains` | [pack_missing_sidechains.hh](source/src/core/pack/pack_missing_sidechains.hh) | Packs only residues that lack side-chain coordinates |
| `scmin` | [scmin/](source/src/core/pack/scmin/) | Side-chain minimization framework |
| Symmetric packing | [make_symmetric_task.hh](source/src/core/pack/make_symmetric_task.hh) | Symmetry-aware task transformation |
| RNA packing | [task/rna/](source/src/core/pack/task/rna/) | RNA-specific residue level tasks |
| Water packing | [rotamer_set/water_rotamer_building_functions.hh](source/src/core/pack/rotamer_set/water_rotamer_building_functions.hh) | Explicit water molecule placement |

Sources: [source/src/core/pack/](source/src/core/pack/)

## Integration with the Broader Rosetta Framework
