Side-chain packing is not an isolated operation — it is a fundamental subroutine called by virtually every protocol in Rosetta. Understanding its architecture is essential for working with:

- **[Structure Relaxation](18-structure-relaxation)** — Calls packing iteratively as the backbone moves
- **[De Novo Protein Design](17-de-novo-protein-design)** — Relies heavily on the design capabilities of the packer
- **[Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy)** — `PackRotamersMover` wraps the packing API as a Mover
- **[RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework)** — Exposes PackerTask configuration via XML (see [xml_util.cc](source/src/core/pack/task/xml_util.cc) and [task_op_schemas.cc](source/src/core/pack/task/operation/task_op_schemas.cc))
- **[Symmetry Modeling](24-symmetry-modeling)** — Uses `SymmetricRotamerSets` and symmetry-aware interaction graphs
- **[ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework)** — Provides energy terms that populate the interaction graph; `setup_for_packing()` prepares context-dependent evaluation

For the next step in understanding Rosetta's protocol architecture, see [Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy) to learn how packing is exposed as a composable protocol step, or [Structure Relaxation](18-structure-relaxation) to see how packing integrates with backbone optimization.

# RosettaScripts XML Framework



RosettaScripts is Rosetta's declarative protocol construction system — an XML-driven framework that lets you compose Movers, Filters, ScoreFunctions, and other components into executable pipelines without writing C++. Rather than compiling custom applications, you define entire computational protocols as structured XML documents that the parser translates into a chain of C++ objects at runtime. This page dissects the architecture that makes that translation possible.

## Architectural Overview

The RosettaScripts framework forms a bridge between declarative XML and imperative C++ execution. At its core, a **RosettaScriptsParser** reads an XML file, resolves includes and script variables, validates the structure against a generated XML Schema, and then walks the tag tree to instantiate objects through a set of singleton **Factory** registries. The resulting object graph is packaged into a **ParsedProtocol** — itself a Mover — whose `apply()` method executes each protocol step sequentially. All instantiated objects share state through a **DataMap**, a keyed container that acts as the dependency injection mechanism for the framework.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Input
        XML["XML Script File<br/><ROSETTASCRIPTS>"]
        INCL["xi:include Files"]
        SV["-parser:script_vars<br/>%%variable%% substitution"]
    end

    subgraph "RosettaScriptsParser"
        A["read_in_and_recursively_replace_includes()"] --> B["create_tag_from_xml()"]
        B --> C["RosettaScriptsSchemaValidator"]
        C --> D["Tag Tree (boost property_tree)"]
        D --> E["initialize_data_map()"]
        E --> F["Section Parsing Loop"]
    end

    subgraph "Factory Registration Layer"
        MF["MoverFactory<br/>(Singleton)"]
        FF["FilterFactory<br/>(Singleton)"]
        SF["ScoreFunctionFactory"]
        TOF["TaskOperationFactory"]
        RSF["ResidueSelectorFactory"]
        PP["PackerPaletteFactory"]
    end

    subgraph "Output"
        PP2["ParsedProtocol<br/>(extends Mover)"]
        DM["DataMap<br/>(shared object store)"]
        STEP1["Step 1: Mover → Filter → Metrics"]
        STEP2["Step 2: Mover → Filter → Metrics"]
        STEPN["Step N: Mover → Filter → Metrics"]
    end

    XML --> A
    INCL --> A
    SV --> A
    F --> MF
    F --> FF
    F --> SF
    F --> TOF
    F --> RSF
    F --> PP
    MF --> PP2
    FF --> PP2
    SF --> DM
    TOF --> DM
    E --> DM
    F --> PP2
    PP2 --> STEP1 --> STEP2 --> STEPN
```

The parser itself lives in `source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/` and coordinates all of these operations. Its constructor triggers `register_factory_prototypes()` and reads the inclusion recursion limit from options [RosettaScriptsParser.cc](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/RosettaScriptsParser.cc#L102-L106). The class exposes multiple `generate_mover()` overloads accepting file paths, XML strings, script variables, and resource managers, providing flexible entry points for both command-line and programmatic usage [RosettaScriptsParser.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/RosettaScriptsParser.hh#L75-L105).

## XML Document Structure

Every RosettaScript must be wrapped in a top-level `<ROSETTASCRIPTS>` element. Within this root, several top-level sections define the objects available to the protocol. The sections are parsed independently, but **only `<PROTOCOLS>` is order-sensitive** — it defines the execution sequence of mover-filter pairs. All other sections function as declarative registries.

```xml
<ROSETTASCRIPTS>
    <SCOREFXNS>
        <!-- ScoreFunction definitions -->
    </SCOREFXNS>
    <FILTERS>
        <!-- Filter definitions -->
    </FILTERS>
    <MOVERS>
        <!-- Mover definitions -->
    </MOVERS>
    <TASKOPERATIONS>
        <!-- TaskOperation definitions -->
    </TASKOPERATIONS>
    <RESIDUE_SELECTORS>
        <!-- ResidueSelector definitions -->
    </RESIDUE_SELECTORS>
    <SIMPLE_METRICS>
        <!-- SimpleMetric definitions -->
    </SIMPLE_METRICS>
    <PROTOCOLS>
        <!-- Order-sensitive execution steps -->
        <Add mover="some_mover" name="step1"/>
        <Filter filter="some_filter" name="step2"/>
    </PROTOCOLS>
    <OUTPUT />
</ROSETTASCRIPTS>
```

The `generate_mover_for_protocol()` method in the parser orchestrates the traversal of these sections [RosettaScriptsParser.cc](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/RosettaScriptsParser.cc#L474-L500). It first calls `initialize_data_map()` to populate the DataMap with predefined objects (default score functions, task operations, etc.), then iterates over the tag's children, dispatching each section to the appropriate instantiation method. The parser's documentation explicitly notes that xi:include statements can be placed anywhere and will be replaced with the contents of the included file [RosettaScriptsParser.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/RosettaScriptsParser.hh#L73-L87).

The following table summarizes each top-level section and its role:

| Section | Order-Sensitive | Purpose | Factory Used |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<SCOREFXNS>` | No | Register named ScoreFunction objects | `ScoreFunctionFactory` |
| `<FILTERS>` | No | Register named Filter objects | `FilterFactory` |
| `<MOVERS>` | No | Register named Mover objects | `MoverFactory` |
| `<TASKOPERATIONS>` | No | Register named TaskOperation objects | `TaskOperationFactory` |
| `<RESIDUE_SELECTORS>` | No | Register named ResidueSelector objects | `ResidueSelectorFactory` |
| `<SIMPLE_METRICS>` | No | Register named SimpleMetric objects | `SimpleMetricFactory` |
| `<PROTOCOLS>` | **Yes** | Define ordered execution sequence | Direct instantiation |
| `<RESOURCES>` | No | Load ResourceManager resources | `ResourceManager` |
| `<OUTPUT>` | No | Configure output behavior | `OutputMover` |
| `<APPLY_TO_POSE>` | N/A | **Deprecated/Removed** — raises error if non-empty | N/A |

## The Tag Abstraction Layer

The `utility::tag::Tag` class is Rosetta's unified representation of an XML element. Each Tag has a name (the element name), a map of string key-value pairs (attributes/options), and an ordered vector of child Tags (sub-elements). The class derives from both `utility::VirtualBase` and `enable_shared_from_this<Tag>`, making it reference-counted and suitable for shared ownership across the object graph [Tag.hh](source/src/utility/tag/Tag.hh#L73-L78).

Type-safe attribute access is provided through templated `getOption<T>()` methods. A required variant throws if the key is missing, while an optional variant accepts a default value. All access is tracked internally — the `accessed_options_` set records which options have been read, enabling the framework to warn about unrecognized XML attributes [Tag.hh](source/src/utility/tag/Tag.hh#L100-L170). Type conversion is handled by `boost::lexical_cast`, with clear error messages on failure:

```cpp
template< class T >
T getOption(std::string const& key, T const& t_default) const {
    auto i = mOptions_.find(key);
    if ( i == mOptions_.end() ) {
        accessed_options_[key]= key;
        return t_default;
    }
    accessed_options_[key]= i->second;
    try {
        return boost::lexical_cast<T>(i->second);
    } catch(boost::bad_lexical_cast &) {
        // Throws descriptive error message
    }
}
```

The Tag class also supports the PyRosetta Python bindings through dedicated `get_option_bool()` and `get_option_int()` methods that bypass the templated approach for interoperability [Tag.hh](source/src/utility/tag/Tag.hh#L188-L192).

## Factory Pattern and Component Registration

Every component type that RosettaScripts can instantiate (Movers, Filters, TaskOperations, ResidueSelectors, SimpleMetrics, etc.) uses the same factory pattern. Each factory is a **SingletonBase** subclass that maintains a `std::map<string, CreatorOP>` mapping human-readable keynames to Creator objects. The Creator pattern separates object creation from object use: each concrete component class has a corresponding Creator class that knows how to instantiate it.

The **MoverFactory** exemplifies this pattern clearly. It stores a `MoverMap` (a map of `MoverCreatorOP`s keyed by string) and provides `newMover()` methods — one that creates a Mover by name, and another that creates one by parsing a Tag while also accepting a DataMap for dependency resolution [MoverFactory.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverFactory.hh#L51-L111). The abstract `MoverCreator` base class requires three methods [MoverCreator.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverCreator.hh#L32-L46):

| Method | Return Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `create_mover()` | `MoverOP` | Construct and return a new default instance |
| `keyname()` | `std::string` | Return the XML tag name (e.g., `"MinMover"`) |
| `provide_xml_schema()` | `void` | Write the XML Schema definition for this Mover |

Registration happens at static initialization time through the **Registrator** pattern. Each Mover's `.cc` file typically contains a static global variable:

```cpp
static protocols::moves::MoverRegistrator< MyMoverCreator > reg_MyMover( "MyMover" );
```

The `MoverRegistrator<T>` template derives from `utility::factory::WidgetRegistrator<MoverFactory, T>`, which calls `MoverFactory::factory_register()` in its constructor at program startup [MoverFactory.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverFactory.hh#L41-L48). This ensures all Movers are available before any XML parsing occurs. The identical pattern is replicated for Filters (`FilterRegistrator`), TaskOperations, ResidueSelectors, and other component types [FilterFactory.hh](source/src/protocols/filters/FilterFactory.hh#L49-L56).

> [!TIP]
> The static-registration-via-Registrator pattern is fundamental to Rosetta's extensibility. Any new Mover you create automatically becomes available in RosettaScripts XML simply by including its Registrator in a linked translation unit — no manual factory registration code is needed.

## ParsedProtocol: The Executable Pipeline

`ParsedProtocol` is the runtime representation of a RosettaScript protocol. It extends `protocols::moves::Mover` (so it can itself be nested in other protocols), implements `ResId` for residue-level targeting, and observes `JobOutputterObserver` for JD2 score reporting integration [ParsedProtocol.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/ParsedProtocol.hh#L56-L62). Internally, it maintains an ordered vector of `ParsedProtocolStep` objects, each containing a Mover, an optional Filter, optional SimpleMetrics, and a `FilterReportTime` enum controlling when filter results are reported [ParsedProtocol.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/ParsedProtocol.hh#L74-L96).

The `FilterReportTime` enum offers three modes:

| Enum Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `AT_END` | Re-run all filters at protocol completion |
| `AFTER_APPLY` | Re-run each filter immediately after application |
| `NONE` | Never re-run filters after initial apply |

During execution, `ParsedProtocol::apply()` iterates through its steps sequentially. For each step, it applies the Mover (if present), then the Filter (if present), and finally any SimpleMetrics. If a filter fails (returns `false`), the protocol can optionally halt or continue depending on configuration. The `apply_step()` method returns a boolean indicating success, and `finish_protocol()` handles any post-processing including final scoring [ParsedProtocol.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/ParsedProtocol.hh#L155-L170).

Critically, `ParsedProtocol` can also be constructed **programmatically** — the `add_step()` methods accept Mover/Filter pairs directly, enabling C++ code to build protocol pipelines that reuse the same execution semantics as XML-defined protocols [ParsedProtocol.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/ParsedProtocol.hh#L122-L133).

## The DataMap: Shared State and Dependency Injection

The `basic::datacache::DataMap` is the central repository through which all RosettaScripts components share named objects. It is a nested map structure (`DataMap::DataMap_map`) where the outer key is a category string (e.g., `"scorefxns"`, `"filters"`, `"movers"`, `"task_operations"`) and the inner key is the user-assigned name. Values are stored as `DataMapObjOP` — type-erased smart pointers to `DataMapObj<T>` instances.

When a Mover's XML tag references `scorefxn="ref2015"`, the parser looks up `data["scorefxns"]["ref2015"]`, casts it to `ScoreFunctionOP`, and passes it to `parse_my_tag()`. The same mechanism connects Movers to TaskOperations (`task_operations="..."`), Filters to ScoreFunctions, and any other named dependency. The `initialize_data_map()` method pre-populates the DataMap with default objects read from command-line options before any user-defined objects are instantiated [RosettaScriptsParser.cc](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/RosettaScriptsParser.cc#L484).

## Script Variables and Include Processing

RosettaScripts supports two powerful composability features: **script variable substitution** and **xi:include directives**. Script variables are passed via `-parser:script_vars var1=val1,var2=val2` and substituted into the XML text wherever `%%var1%%` appears before parsing begins. This allows parameterized protocols without XML modifications. The parser provides dedicated `create_tag_from_xml()` and `create_tag_from_xml_string()` overloads accepting either an `OptionCollection` or explicit `vector1<string>` of `key=value` pairs [RosettaScriptsParser.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/RosettaScriptsParser.hh#L234-L255).

The include system uses standard xi:include syntax. The `read_in_and_recursively_replace_includes()` method performs recursive file inclusion with circular dependency detection by maintaining a copy-on-include stack of parent filenames. Recursion depth is bounded by `parser::inclusion_recursion_limit` [RosettaScriptsParser.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/RosettaScriptsParser.hh#L332-L345).

## XML Schema Generation and Validation

RosettaScripts includes a comprehensive **schema validation** subsystem built on libxml2. The `RosettaScriptsSchemaValidator` is a singleton that aggregates XML Schema definitions from every registered Mover, Filter, and other component type. Each component's `provide_xml_schema()` method contributes its attribute types, sub-element rules, and restrictions to a shared `XMLSchemaDefinition` object [RosettaScriptsSchemaValidator.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/RosettaScriptsSchemaValidator.hh#L27-L74).

The `utility::tag::XMLSchemaGeneration` module provides the C++ abstraction for constructing XSD documents programmatically — elements, complex types, attributes, model groups, and restrictions can all be composed without touching raw XML Schema syntax [XMLSchemaGeneration.hh](source/src/utility/tag/XMLSchemaGeneration.hh#L13-L80). At validation time, the generated schema is compiled into an `XMLSchemaValidator` that checks user XML files against the complete RosettaScripts grammar, providing early and precise error messages for typos, missing required attributes, or unrecognized elements.

The static method `xsd_for_rosetta_scripts()` returns the complete XSD as a string, and `write_ROSETTASCRIPTS_complex_type()` defines the root element's structure including all legal top-level sections [RosettaScriptsSchemaValidator.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/RosettaScriptsSchemaValidator.hh#L39-L43).

## XmlObjects: Programmatic XML-to-Object Conversion

The `XmlObjects` class provides a standalone interface for instantiating individual Rosetta components from XML fragments, independent of the full RosettaScripts protocol machinery. It supports three usage patterns as documented in its header [XmlObjects.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/XmlObjects.hh#L26-L35):

1. **File-based**: `XmlObjects::create_from_file("my_objects.xml")` returns an `XmlObjectsCOP` whose `get_*()` methods retrieve named components
2. **String-based**: `XmlObjects::create_from_string(xml_text)` wraps incomplete XML with `<ROSETTASCRIPTS>` and `<PROTOCOLS>` tags as needed
3. **Static single-object**: `XmlObjects::static_get_score_function("<ScoreFunction .../>")` instantiates a single component from an XML fragment

The class exposes typed getters for all major component types — ScoreFunctions, ResidueSelectors, SimpleMetrics, Movers, Filters, TaskOperations, PackerPalettes, and JumpSelectors — each with both OptionCollection-aware and backwards-compatible overloads [XmlObjects.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/XmlObjects.hh#L110-L200). This makes `XmlObjects` particularly valuable in PyRosetta workflows where you want to construct a single Mover from XML without executing an entire protocol.

## Multi-Pose Processing and Selectors

Beyond single-pose pipelines, RosettaScripts supports multi-pose workflows through the `MultiplePoseMover` and its supporting `PoseSelector` and `PosePropertyReporter` classes. A `PoseSelector` receives a vector of `PoseOP`s and returns a boolean mask indicating which poses to retain, while a `PosePropertyReporter` computes per-pose properties that selectors can reference [PoseSelector.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/PoseSelector.hh#L28-L77). The `PoseSelectorFlags` enum allows selectors to declare whether they need access to the full pose set upfront (`PSF_NEED_FULL_POSE_SET`) or can evaluate poses independently.

The `PoseSelectorFactory` mirrors the MoverFactory pattern — each selector has a Creator and a `parse_my_tag()` method for XML-driven configuration [PoseSelector.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/PoseSelector.hh#L57-L61). Selectors are registered in their own XML section and referenced by name from the `MultiplePoseMover`.

## Summary of Key Source Locations

| Component | Header | Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| XML Parser | `protocols/rosetta_scripts/RosettaScriptsParser.hh` | `.cc` |
| Protocol Executor | `protocols/rosetta_scripts/ParsedProtocol.hh` | `.cc` |
| Object Loader | `protocols/rosetta_scripts/XmlObjects.hh` | `.cc` |
| XML Tag | `utility/tag/Tag.hh` | `Tag.cc` |
| Schema Validation | `utility/tag/XMLSchemaValidation.hh` | `.cc` |
| Schema Generation | `utility/tag/XMLSchemaGeneration.hh` | `.cc` |
| Schema Validator | `protocols/rosetta_scripts/RosettaScriptsSchemaValidator.hh` | `.cc` |
| Mover Factory | `protocols/moves/MoverFactory.hh` | `MoverFactory.cc` |
| Mover Creator | `protocols/moves/MoverCreator.hh` | `MoverCreator.cc` |
| Filter Factory | `protocols/filters/FilterFactory.hh` | `FilterFactory.cc` |
| Pose Selector | `protocols/rosetta_scripts/PoseSelector.hh` | `PoseSelector.cc` |
| Pose Reporter | `protocols/rosetta_scripts/PosePropertyReporter.hh` | `.cc` |
| Multi-Pose Mover | `protocols/rosetta_scripts/MultiplePoseMover.hh` | `.cc` |

## Navigating Further

This page covered the XML parsing, object instantiation, and execution machinery of RosettaScripts. For related topics in the codebase architecture:

- **[Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy)** — the base classes that all RosettaScripts components implement, including the `parse_my_tag()` interface contract
- **[Factory Pattern Architecture](15-factory-pattern-architecture)** — a deeper look at Rosetta's singleton factory system, WidgetRegistrator, and static initialization ordering
- **[ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework)** — how score functions are constructed and used as named dependencies within XML
- **[PyRosetta Python Bindings](16-pyrosetta-python-bindings)** — how the Tag and XmlObjects classes are exposed to Python, enabling XML-driven protocols from interactive sessions

# Factory Pattern Architecture



Rosetta's extensibility rests on a comprehensive, self-registering factory system that allows hundreds of protocol components to be instantiated by name at runtime—primarily from XML input via the RosettaScripts framework. This system eliminates the need for centralized switch statements or manual registration calls; instead, every Mover, Filter, TaskOperation, and other pluggable component registers itself into a global singleton factory through static initialization. Understanding this architecture is essential for anyone extending Rosetta with new protocol components or debugging registration failures.

## Architectural Overview

The factory system is a layered design built on three foundational templates: a **WidgetFactory** base, a **WidgetRegistrator** for load-time registration, and a **Creator** abstract interface for each component domain. Each domain (Movers, Filters, etc.) instantiates this pattern into a concrete singleton factory that maps string identifiers to Creator objects. The registration happens before `main()` executes, driven by static global variables declared in dedicated initialization headers.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    direction TB

    class WidgetFactory~Creator~ {
        <<template>>
        #CreatorMap creators_
        +factory_register("CreatorOP")
        #creators() CreatorMap
        +factory_name() string*
    }

    class WidgetRegistrator~Factory, Creator~ {
        <<template>>
        +WidgetRegistrator()
    }

    class SingletonBase~T~ {
        <<utility>>
        +get_instance() "T&"
    }

    class MoverFactory {
        -MoverMap mover_creator_map_
        -"set~string~" forbidden_names_
        +factory_register("MoverCreatorOP")
        +newMover(string) "MoverOP"
        +newMover("TagCOP, DataMap") "MoverOP"
        +mover_exists(string) bool
        +provide_xml_schema(string, "XSD")
        +define_mover_xml_schema("XSD")
    }

    class FilterFactory {
        -FilterMap filter_creator_map_
        +factory_register("FilterCreatorOP")
        +newFilter(string) "FilterOP"
        +newFilter("TagCOP, DataMap") "FilterOP"
        +filter_exists(string) bool
    }

    class DataLoaderFactory {
        -LoaderMap dataloader_creator_map_
        +factory_register("DataLoaderCreatorOP")
        +newDataLoader(string) "DataLoaderOP"
    }

    class MoverCreator {
        <<abstract>>
        +create_mover() "MoverOP*"
        +keyname() string*
        +provide_xml_schema("XSD")*
    }

    class MoverRegistrator~T~ {
        <<template>>
    }

    class DsspMoverCreator {
        +create_mover() "MoverOP*"
        +keyname() string*
        +provide_xml_schema("XSD")*
    }

    WidgetFactory <|-- MoverFactory
    WidgetFactory <|-- FilterFactory
    WidgetFactory <|-- DataLoaderFactory
    SingletonBase <|-- MoverFactory
    SingletonBase <|-- FilterFactory
    SingletonBase <|-- DataLoaderFactory

    WidgetRegistrator <|-- MoverRegistrator
    MoverCreator <|-- DsspMoverCreator

    MoverRegistrator --> MoverFactory : registers into
    MoverFactory --> MoverCreator : holds map of
    DsspMoverCreator --> MoverFactory : registered by MoverRegistrator
```

## The Three-Layer Template Foundation

At the base of the entire system lies `utility::factory::WidgetFactory<Creator>`, a CRTP-style template that holds a `std::map<std::string, CreatorOP>` mapping component key names to owning pointers of their Creator objects. The `factory_register()` method inserts new Creators into this map, with an assertion that rejects duplicate names by calling `utility_exit_with_message()`. A comment in the source explicitly notes where mutex locking should occur for thread safety, though the base template does not implement it—concrete factories like `FilterFactory` include `#ifdef MULTI_THREADED` guards for mutex support.

Sources: [WidgetFactory.hh](source/src/utility/factory/WidgetFactory.hh#L39-L79)

The `utility::factory::WidgetRegistrator<Factory, Creator>` template is the mechanism that drives load-time self-registration. Its constructor body contains a single statement: `FACTORY::get_instance()->factory_register(make_shared<CREATOR>())`. Because each domain-specific Registrator (e.g., `MoverRegistrator<T>`) derives from `WidgetRegistrator<MoverFactory, T>`, and is declared as a `static` global variable, C++ static initialization guarantees that every Registrator's constructor runs before `main()`, populating the factory map before any XML parsing begins.

Sources: [WidgetRegistrator.hh](source/src/utility/factory/WidgetRegistrator.hh#L34-L45)

The Singleton pattern is applied through `utility::SingletonBase<T>`, which all concrete factories inherit from. This ensures a single global instance of each factory. The `MoverFactory`, for instance, declares `SingletonBase<MoverFactory>` as its base and `friend class utility::SingletonBase<MoverFactory>` to grant the singleton access to its private constructor.

Sources: [MoverFactory.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverFactory.hh#L58-L60)

## Domain-Specific Factories and Creators

Each component domain in Rosetta follows an identical structural pattern. The table below catalogs the major factory/creator pairs and their locations:

| Domain | Factory Class | Creator Base Class | Registrator Alias |
|--------|--------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| **Movers** | `protocols::moves::MoverFactory` | `MoverCreator` | `MoverRegistrator<T>` |
| **Filters** | `protocols::filters::FilterFactory` | `FilterCreator` | `FilterRegistrator<T>` |
| **Task Operations** | `core::pack::task::operation::TaskOperationFactory` | `TaskOperationCreator` | `TaskOperationRegistrator<T>` |
| **Residue Selectors** | `core::select::residue_selector::ResidueSelectorFactory` | `ResidueSelectorCreator` | `ResidueSelectorRegistrator<T>` |
| **Data Loaders** | `protocols::parser::DataLoaderFactory` | `DataLoaderCreator` | `DataLoaderRegistrator<T>` |
| **Pose Selectors** | `protocols::rosetta_scripts::PoseSelectorFactory` | `PoseSelectorCreator` | `PoseSelectorRegistrator<T>` |
| **Simple Metrics** | `core::simple_metrics::SimpleMetricFactory` | `SimpleMetricCreator` | `SimpleMetricRegistrator<T>` |

Each Creator base class defines the same three pure virtual methods: a factory method (`create_mover()`, `newFilter()`, etc.), a key name accessor (`keyname()`), and an XML schema provider (`provide_xml_schema()`). The concrete Creator implementation supplies these: the key name must match the XML tag name used in RosettaScripts, the factory method returns a fresh instance of the concrete component, and the schema method defines the XSD complex type for XML validation.

Sources: [MoverCreator.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverCreator.hh#L35-L47), [DsspMoverCreator.hh](source/src/protocols/moves/DsspMoverCreator.hh#L23-L33)

## Registration Mechanism: From Static Globals to Factory Maps

The registration pipeline flows through four stages that connect a concrete component to its runtime availability:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CC as ConcreteCreator.hh
    participant IR as init.*Registrators.ihh
    participant RS as register*.cc
    participant WR as WidgetRegistrator
    participant MF as MoverFactory (Singleton)

    CC->>IR: Developer adds #include
    Note over IR: static MoverRegistrator<ConcreteCreator> reg_ConcreteCreator;
    IR->>RS: Included via init.hh → register.cc
    RS->>WR: Static initialization triggers constructor
    WR->>MF: get_instance()->factory_register(make_shared<ConcreteCreator>())
    MF->>MF: Insert into mover_creator_map_[keyname()]
    Note over MF: Factory now resolves "ConcreteCreator" → ConcreteCreator
```

The init headers in `source/src/protocols/init/` come in two varieties per domain: `init.*Creators.ihh` (which includes the Creator header files) and `init.*Registrators.ihh` (which declares the static `Registrator` instances). For Movers, there are four `register*.cc` files that include these headers, partitioned alphabetically to reduce per-compilation-unit load time. Each `init.MoverRegistrators.ihh` contains hundreds of static declarations like `static MoverRegistrator<abinitio::DomainAssemblyCreator> reg_DomainAssemblyCreator;`, maintaining alphabetical order across 698 lines.

Sources: [init.MoverRegistrators.ihh](source/src/protocols/init/init.MoverRegistrators.ihh#L1-L100)

The MoverFactory adds a layer of protection with a `forbidden_names_` set containing five historically reserved names (`quick_ccd`, `sdwindow`, `quick_ccd_moves`, `perturb_ccd`, `perturb_kic`) that originated from the legacy LoopMoverFactory. Attempting to register a Mover with one of these names throws a `RosettaScriptsOptionError`.

Sources: [MoverFactory.cc](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverFactory.cc#L45-L55)

## Object Creation and XML Parsing Pathways

Factories expose two creation pathways. The simple form `newMover(string const&)` performs a map lookup and calls `creator->create_mover()`, returning a default-configured instance. The XML-aware form `newMover(TagCOP, DataMap&)` additionally calls `mover->parse_my_tag(tag, data)` to populate the component from XML attributes, then registers the mover's citations with the `CitationManager`. The error path is particularly informative: when a key name is not found, the factory iterates the entire creator map and prints all known names to the tracer, then throws an exception with explicit instructions pointing to the init header files that need modification.

Sources: [MoverFactory.cc](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverFactory.cc#L135-L178)

The XML schema system provides two layers of validation. Individual Creators define their own complex type schemas via `provide_xml_schema()`, and the factory's `define_mover_xml_schema()` method aggregates all registered movers into an XML Schema Definition group named `"mover"` using `utility::tag::define_xml_schema_group()`. This enables RosettaScripts to validate entire XML protocols against the schema before execution begins, catching typos and missing attributes at parse time rather than at runtime.

> [!TIP]
> When a Mover is reported as "not known to the MoverFactory," the error message explicitly names the two init files that must be updated: `src/protocols/init/init.MoverCreators.ihh` (add the `#include`) and `src/protocols/init/init.MoverRegistrators.ihh` (add the `static MoverRegistrator` declaration). This diagnostic exists in both `newMover()` and `provide_xml_schema()` error paths.

Sources: [MoverFactory.cc](source/src/protocols/moves/MoverFactory.cc#L98-L108)

## Implementing a New Factory-Registered Component

Adding a new Mover to Rosetta requires creating four artifacts and modifying two init files:

| Step | Artifact | Responsibility |
|------|----------|----------------|
| 1 | `ConcreteMover.hh/.cc` | The Mover implementation with `parse_my_tag()` and `apply()` |
| 2 | `ConcreteMoverCreator.hh/.cc` | Creator returning `keyname()`, `create_mover()`, and `provide_xml_schema()` |
| 3 | Edit `init.MoverCreators.ihh` | Add `#include <path/ConcreteMoverCreator.hh>` |
| 4 | Edit `init.MoverRegistrators.ihh` | Add `static MoverRegistrator<ConcreteMoverCreator> reg_ConcreteMoverCreator;` |

The same pattern applies identically for Filters (editing `init.FilterCreators.ihh` and `init.FilterRegistrators.ihh`), TaskOperations, ResidueSelectors, and every other factory-registered domain.

> [!TIP]
> The static Registrator variables must use globally unique names. The convention `reg_ConcreteCreator` prevents linker collisions but collisions are still possible across domains. Keep names specific to both the class and its namespace.

## Relationship to the XML Framework and JD2/JD3

The factory architecture is the backbone of the [RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework) and is consumed by the `RosettaScriptsParser` during protocol loading. The parser calls `newMover(TagCOP, DataMap)` for each `<MOVERS>` sub-tag, `newFilter()` for each `<FILTERS>` sub-tag, and so forth. The `ParsedProtocol` (a Mover itself, registered as `"ParsedProtocol"`) orchestrates the sequential execution of these factory-created components against each Pose produced by the job distribution system. The JD3 job queen (`RosettaScriptsJobQueen`) uses the same factories but through a different code path, reflecting the architectural evolution documented in the job distribution system.

Sources: [RosettaScriptsParser.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/RosettaScriptsParser.hh), [ParsedProtocol.hh](source/src/protocols/rosetta_scripts/ParsedProtocol.hh)

## Scope and Limitations

This factory system is limited to components that are parseable from XML and needed at protocol definition time. It does not cover energy methods (which use a separate `EnergyMethodCreator`/`EnergyMethodFactory` system), scoring functions, or rotamer libraries—those have their own registration pathways described in the [ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework) and [Energy Methods](10-energy-methods) pages. The architecture also does not address component discovery at runtime (plugin DLLs); registration is determined entirely at compile time through static linking of the init headers.

For protocol authors, the practical implication is that any component not appearing in the init headers is invisible to RosettaScripts, even if the source is compiled into the binary. This is the single most common source of "X is not known to the Factory" errors in practice.

# PyRosetta Python Bindings



PyRosetta bridges the Rosetta molecular modeling suite and the Python ecosystem, enabling rapid prototyping of structural biology protocols without C++ compilation cycles. This page dissects its four-layer architecture — the **C++ binding generation pipeline**, the **native pybind11 interface**, the **Pythonic enrichment layer**, and the **distributed computing framework** — and provides practical guidance for intermediate developers who need to understand how the bindings work under the hood or extend them.

## Architecture Overview

PyRosetta is not a hand-maintained wrapper around selected Rosetta functions. It is an **automatically generated, near-complete Python binding** of the entire Rosetta C++ codebase, produced by a custom LLVM-based binder tool. The resulting compiled shared library exposes virtually every class, function, and enum in Rosetta's `core` and `protocols` namespaces, which is then enriched with a pure-Python layer providing idiomatic interfaces.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Build-Time Pipeline"
        A["Rosetta C++ Headers<br/>(core, protocols, numeric, ...)"] --> B["Binder Tool<br/>(LLVM Clang Plugin)"]
        B --> C["Generated .cpp Binding Sources"]
        C --> D["CMake + Ninja Build"]
        D --> E["_rosetta.so<br/>(compiled shared library)"]
    end

    subgraph "Runtime Layers"
        E --> F["pyrosetta.rosetta<br/>(native pybind11 module)"]
        F --> G["pyrosetta.bindings<br/>(Pythonic enrichment)"]
        G --> H["pyrosetta.toolbox<br/>(high-level utilities)"]
        G --> I["pyrosetta.io<br/>(file I/O convenience)"]
        G --> J["pyrosetta.distributed<br/>(parallel computing)"]
        H --> K["User Code"]
        I --> K
        J --> K
    end

    subgraph "Developer Support"
        B -.-> L["rosetta_binders.hpp<br/>(custom type adapters)"]
        E -.-> M["pybind11-stubgen<br/>(type stubs / IDE support)"]
    end

    style A fill:#f9e79f,stroke:#d4ac0d
    style E fill:#aed6f1,stroke:#2980b9
    style K fill:#a9dfbf,stroke:#27ae60
```

This architecture separates concerns cleanly: the C++ pipeline handles bulk binding generation with zero manual maintenance, while the Python layer selectively overrides and enriches specific classes where a more Pythonic interface is warranted.

## Build-Time Binding Generation

### The Binder Tool Pipeline

The binding generation system lives in `build.py` and orchestrates a multi-stage pipeline that transforms the entire Rosetta C++ codebase into a compilable Python extension module. At its core is a **custom LLVM Clang plugin** called "binder" that performs AST-level analysis of Rosetta headers to produce pybind11 binding code.
Sources: [build.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/build.py#L1-L200)

The build script identifies all eligible headers by walking the Rosetta source tree (`ObjexxFCL`, `utility`, `numeric`, `basic`, `core`, `protocols`) while filtering out implementation files (`.impl.hh`, `.fwd.hh`, `.py.hh`) and explicitly banned headers — notably GPU code, deprecated database session loaders, and JD3 output writers. All remaining headers are aggregated into a single `all_rosetta_includes.hh` umbrella file, which the binder tool consumes in a single compilation pass.
Sources: [build.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/build.py#L637-L685)

A content-hash signature mechanism avoids redundant binder runs: the build script computes an MD5 hash of all include file paths, their modification times, and the binder configuration. If this signature matches the cached value from the previous run, the generation step is skipped entirely, significantly reducing rebuild times during iterative development.
Sources: [build.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/build.py#L671-L692)

### Compilation Defines and Conditional Binding

The generated bindings respect Rosetta's preprocessor feature flags, controlled through the `get_defines()` function. Key defines include `PYROSETTA` (enabling PyRosetta-specific code paths), `NOCRASHREPORT` (disabling C++ crash reporters that would terminate the Python process), and optional flags for `SERIALIZATION`, `MULTI_THREADED`, `USE_TORCH`, and `USE_TENSORFLOW`. When serialization is enabled, the build system additionally scans `.cc` files for `SAVE_AND_LOAD_SERIALIZABLE` macros and rewrites them as `EXTERN_SAVE_AND_LOAD_SERIALIZABLE` to ensure serialization templates are instantiated in the binding module.
Sources: [build.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/build.py#L117-L136)

### Build Invocation

Building PyRosetta requires Clang 3.4+ or GCC 4.8+, CMake, Ninja, and Python 3.8+. The standard build invocation is straightforward, with the build script handling LLVM/binder toolchain installation, binding generation, CMake configuration, and Ninja compilation as a single operation.
Sources: [README.md](source/src/python/PyRosetta/README.md#L13-L18)

```bash
cd source/src/python/PyRosetta
python3 build.py -j8
```

Useful flags include `--create-package` (produces a `setup.py`-based installable package), `--create-wheel` (produces a `.whl` file), and `--skip-namespaces N` (binds only the first N of the six Rosetta namespaces, useful for faster iteration). During development, the `--print-build-root` flag reveals the build output directory, allowing direct `PYTHONPATH` manipulation without full package installation — all Python files at the build location are symlinks to the originals, so code changes take effect immediately.
Sources: [README.md](source/src/python/PyRosetta/README.md#L25-L33), [build.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/build.py#L369-L400)

> [!TIP]
> **Development workflow**: Use `python3 build.py -j8 --print-build-root` to get the build directory, then set `PYTHONPATH` to that directory. The build system symlinks Python source files, so edits to `pyrosetta/bindings/pose.py` etc. are reflected immediately without rebuilding. Only C++ changes require re-running `build.py`.

### CMake Integration and Library Assembly

After binder generates the `.cpp` source files, the build system produces per-library CMake files from Rosetta's SCons `.src.settings` files, converting each into an `add_library(... OBJECT ...)` directive with `POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE` enabled. These object libraries are then consumed by the main `rosetta.cmake` template, which links everything into the final `_rosetta.so` shared module. External dependencies (sqlite3, cppdb, and optionally others) are handled through parallel `.external.settings` parsing.
Sources: [build.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/build.py#L442-L599)

## The Native pybind11 Module: `pyrosetta.rosetta`

### Bulk Auto-Generated Bindings

The compiled `_rosetta.so` is imported as `pyrosetta.rosetta` and exposes the near-complete Rosetta C++ API. Every class in `core`, `protocols`, `numeric`, `basic`, `utility`, and `ObjexxFCL` namespaces is available, typically with its original C++ name preserved. Enum types, typedefs, and free functions are also bound. The module serves as the **single source of truth** for all Rosetta functionality — nothing is hidden behind a Python-only facade.
Sources: [pyrosetta/__init__.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/__init__.py#L24-L38)

### Custom C++ Binders for Special Types

While the binder tool handles the vast majority of types automatically, certain Rosetta template-heavy types require **hand-written binders** defined in [`rosetta_binders.hpp`](source/src/python/PyRosetta/include/rosetta_binders.hpp). This header provides specialized pybind11 adapters for three categories of types:

**Utility vectors** — Rosetta's `utility::vector0<T>` and `utility::vector1<T>` (0-based and 1-based indexed vectors) receive full Python sequence protocol support including `__getitem__`, `__setitem__`, `__len__`, `__iter__`, `append`, `extend`, `pop`, `remove`, `__contains__`, and `__repr__`. The binder uses SFINAE-based compile-time introspection (`has_equal_operator_s`) to conditionally enable equality comparisons and containment testing only for element types that support them. The 1-based indexing of `vector1` is preserved at the C++ level — Python code using `pose.residues[1]` accesses the first residue correctly.
Sources: [rosetta_binders.hpp](source/src/python/PyRosetta/include/rosetta_binders.hpp#L146-L283)

**xyzVector and xyzMatrix** — These geometric types receive property-based attribute access (`vector.x`, `vector.y`, `vector.z`, `matrix.xx`, `matrix.xy`, etc.), arithmetic operator overloads, and Python index protocol support (`v[0]`, `v[1]`, `v[2]`).
Sources: [rosetta_binders.hpp](source/src/python/PyRosetta/include/rosetta_binders.hpp#L388-L475)

**Standard containers** — `std::set`, `std::map`, and `std::list` receive analogous Pythonic treatment with appropriate protocol methods.
Sources: [rosetta_binders.hpp](source/src/python/PyRosetta/include/rosetta_binders.hpp#L94-L142)

The following table summarizes how major Rosetta C++ types map to their Python representations:

| C++ Type | Python Access | Indexing | Python Protocol |
|---|---|---|---|
| `utility::vector1<T>` | `rosetta.utility.vector1_<T>` | 1-based | Full sequence (`len`, `iter`, slicing`) |
| `utility::vector0<T>` | `rosetta.utility.vector0_<T>` | 0-based | Full sequence |
| `numeric::xyzVector<double>` | `rosetta.numeric.xyzVector_double_t` | 0-based (`v[0]`, `v[1]`, `v[2]`) | Properties: `.x`, `.y`, `.z` |
| `numeric::xyzMatrix<double>` | `rosetta.numeric.xyzMatrix_double_t` | 0-based (rows) | Properties: `.xx`, `.xy`, ... `.zz` |
| `core::pose::Pose` | `rosetta.core.pose.Pose` | — | Enriched by Python layer |
| `core::scoring.ScoreFunction` | `rosetta.core.scoring.ScoreFunction` | — | Direct access |

## Pythonic Enrichment Layer: `pyrosetta.bindings`

The `pyrosetta.bindings` subpackage applies selective Pythonic enhancements to the raw pybind11 bindings. Rather than re-wrapping entire classes, it uses a `bind_method` utility to **monkey-patch additional methods** onto the existing C++ classes. This approach preserves full access to the native API while adding convenience features where they matter most.
Sources: [bindings/__init__.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/__init__.py#L1-L7)

### Pose Enrichments

The [`pose.py`](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/pose.py) module provides the most extensive enrichment, adding several Python-native interfaces to the core `Pose` class:

**PoseResidueAccessor** — A collection-like wrapper accessed via `pose.residues` that provides Pythonic iteration, slicing with 1-based index translation, and even in-place append (`pose.residues += residue`). Slicing such as `pose.residues[2:6]` returns a generator yielding `Residue` objects for positions 2 through 5, respecting Rosetta's 1-based convention. A zero-index access raises `IndexError` with a clear message about the 1-based indexing requirement.
Sources: [pose.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/pose.py#L117-L188)

**residue_pairs() generator** — A composable method that yields permutations of residue pairs filtered by `ResidueSelector` instances and optional cartesian/sequence distance cutoffs. It composes `NeighborhoodResidueSelector` and `PrimarySequenceNeighborhoodSelector` internally, providing a high-level interface for tasks like interface analysis.
Sources: [pose.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/pose.py#L78-L115)

**Pose pickling support** — Custom `__getstate__`/`__setstate__` methods enable serialization of Pose objects through Python's `pickle` protocol (used by `pyrosetta.distributed`). Sequence constraints are explicitly unsupported with a warning; the implementation strips them before pickling. The serialization itself uses cereal, Rosetta's C++ serialization framework.
Sources: [pose.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/pose.py#L61-L76)

### Energy Array Bindings

The [`energies.py`](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/energies.py) module adds NumPy integration to the `Energies` class, providing methods that return structured NumPy arrays of energy decompositions:

- **`residue_pair_energies_array()`** — Returns a 2D structured array of shape `(n_residues, n_residues)` where each entry contains named fields for every non-zero-weight energy type. This enables direct NumPy-based analysis of pairwise interaction energies.
- **`residue_onebody_energies_array()`** and **`residue_total_energies_array()`** — Return per-residue energy decompositions as 1D structured arrays.
- **`total_energies_array()`** and **`active_total_energies()`** — Provide total energy summaries.
- **`nonzero_weights()`** — Returns the set of energy terms with non-zero weights, used to determine which fields appear in the structured arrays.

All array methods accept optional residue selection arguments (indices or boolean masks) for focused analysis. The structured dtype is dynamically constructed from `ScoreType` enum members whose weights are non-zero in the active `ScoreFunction`.
Sources: [energies.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/energies.py#L1-L215)

> [!TIP]
> **NumPy energy analysis**: Use `pose.energies().residue_total_energies_array()` to get a structured NumPy array where each row is a residue and each column is a named energy term. This enables vectorized operations like `array['fa_atr'].mean()` for rapid statistical analysis without Python loops.

### ResidueSelector Operator Overloads

The [`residue_selectors.py`](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/residue_selectors.py) module overloads Python bitwise operators on all `ResidueSelector` subclasses, enabling combinatorial selection logic with familiar syntax:

| Python Operator | Rosetta Equivalent | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `&` | `AndResidueSelector` | `chainA & near_active_site` |
| `\|` | `OrResidueSelector` | `polar_residues \| charged_residues` |
| `~` | `NotResidueSelector` | `~glycines` |
| `^` | XOR composition | `selectorA ^ selectorB` |
| `&=`, `\|=`, `^=` | In-place variants | `selection &= backbone` |

A `get_residues(pose)` convenience method is also added, returning a plain Python `list` of selected residue indices (in Rosetta 1-based numbering).
Sources: [residue_selectors.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/residue_selectors.py#L24-L91)

### Homogeneous Transform and RT Bindings

The [`homogeneous_transform.py`](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/homogeneous_transform.py) module and [`rt.py`](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/rt.py) module bridge Rosetta's rigid-body transform types to NumPy arrays. The `RT.as_array()` method converts a `core.kinematics.RT` object into a 4×4 homogeneous transformation matrix (`numpy.ndarray`), combining the rotation and translation components. An `is_homog_xform()` validation function verifies the matrix properties. This integration enables direct use of Rosetta transforms within NumPy/SciPy linear algebra pipelines.
Sources: [rt.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/rt.py#L1-L18)

## Initialization and Configuration

### The `pyrosetta.init()` Function

The `init()` function is the mandatory entry point for any PyRosetta session. It accepts command-line-style option strings, resolves the Rosetta database location, initializes global scoring data, and sets up logging. The default flags `-ex1 -ex2aro` enable extra chi1 rotamers and extra aromatic chi sampling — these are nearly always desirable for production protocols.
Sources: [pyrosetta/__init__.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/__init__.py#L113-L173)

```python
import pyrosetta
pyrosetta.init()                                    # defaults: -ex1 -ex2aro
pyrosetta.init(extra_options='-pH')                 # append flags
pyrosetta.init('-pH -database /path/to/database')   # override all defaults
pyrosetta.init(silent=True)                         # suppress output
```

Database resolution follows a priority chain: the `PYROSETTA_DATABASE` environment variable, then the package installation directory, the current working directory, the user's home directory, and standard system paths.
Sources: [pyrosetta/__init__.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/__init__.py#L68-L110)

### Logging Integration

The `set_logging_handler` parameter controls how Rosetta's C++ tracing system routes output through Python's `logging` module. In interactive contexts (REPLs, Jupyter notebooks), it defaults to `"interactive"` mode, which registers a Python log handler and displays output. For batch scripts, the default is `None`, which writes through C++ file handles. The `"logging"` mode registers the handler without modifying the logging configuration, suitable for integration with existing logging setups.
Sources: [pyrosetta/__init__.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/__init__.py#L127-L145)

## I/O Convenience Layer: `pyrosetta.io`

The `pyrosetta.io` subpackage provides Pythonic wrappers around Rosetta's PDB I/O functions, handling compressed file formats and providing generator-based interfaces for multi-file operations:

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `pose_from_pdb(filename)` | Load a single PDB file (supports `.bz2`, `.gz`, `.xz` compression) |
| `pose_from_sequence(seq)` | Create a Pose from an amino acid letter sequence |
| `poses_from_files(file_list)` | Generator yielding Poses from multiple files |
| `poses_from_silent(filename)` | Generator yielding Poses from a Rosetta silent file |
| `poses_from_multimodel_pdb(filename)` | Generator yielding Poses from multi-model PDB files |
| `dump_pdb(pose, filename)` | Write Pose to PDB file |
| `dump_cif(pose, filename)` | Write Pose to mmCIF format |
| `dump_silent(...)` | Write Poses to Rosetta silent file format |
| `create_score_function(name)` | Factory for named ScoreFunction presets |

The `pose_from_sequence()` function goes beyond `make_pose_from_sequence()` by setting all torsion angles to 180° and attaching `PDBInfo`, producing a properly initialized Pose suitable for immediate scoring or manipulation.
Sources: [io/__init__.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/io/__init__.py#L82-L117)

## The Distributed Computing Framework

PyRosetta includes a first-class distributed computing framework under `pyrosetta.distributed`, designed for cluster and cloud-scale structural modeling. It integrates with **Dask** for task scheduling, **blosc** for efficient pose serialization, and provides its own `PackedPose` container for network-transparent pose transport. The framework is declared as an optional dependency in `setup.py` (under the `distributed` extra), requiring `numpy`, `pandas`, `blosc`, and `traitlets`.
Sources: [setup.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/setup.py#L61-L76)

Key components include a cluster management module (`pyrosetta.distributed.cluster`), task definitions (`pyrosetta.distributed.tasks`), an I/O system for distributed file handling (`pyrosetta.distributed.io`), a `packed_pose` serialization format, and a `viewer` module for result visualization. Pose pickling within the distributed framework uses cereal-based serialization through the custom `__getstate__`/`__setstate__` methods defined in the bindings layer.
Sources: [pyrosetta/__init__.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/__init__.py#L55-L58), [pose.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/bindings/pose.py#L61-L76)

## Toolbox and Utility Modules

The `pyrosetta.toolbox` subpackage collects high-level convenience functions commonly needed in structural biology workflows. Notable modules include: Sources: [pyrosetta/__init__.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/pyrosetta/__init__.py#L93-L94)

| Module | Key Functions |
|---|---|
| `cleaning.py` | PDB structure cleanup and preparation |
| `generate_resfile.py` | Resfile generation for packing/design |
| `load_ligand.py` | Param file loading for small molecules |
| `mutants.py` | Point mutation generation |
| `numpy_utils.py` | NumPy conversion utilities for Rosetta types |
| `py_jobdistributor.py` | Python-native job distribution loop |
| `rcsb.py` | Download structures directly from the RCSB PDB |
| `atom_pair_energy.py` | Atom-pair energy decomposition |
| `extract_coords_pose.py` | Coordinate extraction utilities |

## Package Distribution and Installation

PyRosetta is distributed as a native Python package via `setup.py`, which uses a custom `PyRosettaDistribution` class that declares the package as containing non-pure (compiled) extension modules. The package requires `numpy` as a core dependency and optionally depends on `pandas`, `blosc`, and `traitlets` for the distributed framework. The `package_data` specification includes compiled `.so` files, Markdown documentation, type stubs (`.pyi`), and the Rosetta database directory.
Sources: [setup.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/src/setup.py#L19-L86)

Type stubs are generated post-build using `pybind11-stubgen`, which introspects the compiled module to produce `.pyi` files that enable IDE autocompletion and static type checking. This is critical for developer experience given that the bulk of PyRosetta's API lives in the compiled module where standard Python introspection is limited.
Sources: [build.py](source/src/python/PyRosetta/build.py#L763-L775)

PyRosetta's bindings provide access to every core Rosetta concept. To deepen your understanding of what the bindings expose and how to use them effectively:

- **[Pose and Conformation](8-pose-and-conformation)** — Understanding the central data structure that PyRosetta's `pose.py` bindings enrich
- **[ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework)** — The scoring system that `energies.py` bridges to NumPy
