- **[Docker and Conda Setup](4-docker-and-conda-setup)** — Pre-built PyRosetta environments for quick start without source compilation

# De Novo Protein Design



De novo protein design in Rosetta addresses the inverse folding problem: given a desired structure or topology, generate amino acid sequences that fold into that conformation with high stability. Unlike comparative modeling or refinement, de novo design constructs entirely new proteins from first principles using parameterized backbone geometries, fragment-based folding, and sequence optimization. This page documents the core framework in `protocols/denovo_design` — the component-based architecture that decomposes structure creation into composable phases of topology specification, pose building, folding, connection, and perturbation.

## Architectural Overview

The de novo design system follows a **pipeline architecture** where each stage is encapsulated by a pluggable interface. The central orchestrator is `FoldArchitectMover`, which coordinates the entire flow from topology definition through folded pose generation. This design mirrors the Mover/Filter hierarchy described in [Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy) but specializes it for the unique requirements of building proteins from scratch rather than modifying existing ones.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Topology["1. Topology Specification"]
        Architect["DeNovoArchitect<br/>(abstract)"]
        BP["BlueprintArchitect"]
        HA["HelixArchitect"]
        BS["BetaSheetArchitect"]
        MA["MotifArchitect"]
        CA["CompoundArchitect"]
        SA["StructureArchitect"]
        PA["PoseArchitect"]
        STA["StrandArchitect"]
        Architect --> BP
        Architect --> HA
        Architect --> BS
        Architect --> MA
        Architect --> CA
        Architect --> SA
        Architect --> PA
        Architect --> STA
    end

    subgraph Data["Blueprint Data Model"]
        SD["StructureData<br/>(SegmentMap)"]
        Seg["Segment<br/>(SS, ABEGO, length)"]
        SP["SegmentPairing<br/>(HELIX, STRAND)"]
        SD --> Seg
        SD --> SP
    end

    subgraph Build["2. Pose Construction"]
        Builder["PoseBuilder<br/>(abstract)"]
        EPB["ExtendedPoseBuilder"]
        Builder --> EPB
    end

    subgraph Fold["3. Conformation Sampling"]
        Folder["PoseFolder<br/>(abstract)"]
        RPF["RandomTorsionPoseFolder"]
        NPF["NullPoseFolder"]
        RLM["RemodelLoopMoverPoseFolder"]
        Folder --> RPF
        Folder --> NPF
        Folder --> RLM
    end

    subgraph Connect["4. Segment Connection"]
        Conn["ConnectionArchitect"]
        Conn --> SD
    end

    subgraph Perturb["5. Topology Perturbation"]
        Pertr["StructureDataPerturber"]
        CP["ConnectionPerturber"]
        NP["NullPerturber"]
        Pertr --> CP
        Pertr --> NP
    end

    subgraph Orchestrator["Orchestration"]
        FAM["FoldArchitectMover"]
    end

    Topology -->|"design()"| Data
    Data -->|"apply()"| Build
    Build -->|"apply()"| Fold
    Connect -->|"apply()"| Data
    Perturb -->|"apply()"| Data
    FAM -->|"coordinates"| Topology
    FAM -->|"uses"| Build
    FAM -->|"uses"| Fold
    FAM -->|"uses"| Connect
    FAM -->|"uses"| Perturb
```

The pipeline flows through five logically distinct phases. The **Topology Specification** phase uses an `DeNovoArchitect` to produce a `StructureData` blueprint containing named `Segment` objects with secondary structure, ABEGO conformation codes, and `SegmentPairing` relationships. The **Pose Construction** phase materializes this blueprint into a physical `Pose` via `ExtendedPoseBuilder`. The **Conformation Sampling** phase folds the extended pose into 3D space using a `PoseFolder` strategy. **Connection** and **Perturbation** phases optionally modify the topology blueprint and re-fold, enabling iterative refinement.

Sources: [FoldArchitectMover.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/movers/FoldArchitectMover.hh#L49-L119), [DeNovoArchitect.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/architects/DeNovoArchitect.hh#L47-L87), [PoseBuilder](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/components/ExtendedPoseBuilder.hh#L40-L65), [PoseFolder.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/components/PoseFolder.hh#L48-L97)

## The StructureData Blueprint Model

At the heart of every de novo design is `StructureData` — a serializable, cacheable data structure stored as `WriteableCacheableData` on the Pose. It acts as the authoritative blueprint from which all geometry and connectivity are derived. A `StructureData` is essentially an ordered map of `Segment` objects, plus metadata for pairings, aliases, covalent bonds, and user-defined data fields.

### Segment: The Atomic Unit of Topology

Each `Segment` encapsulates a contiguous block of residues with shared structural intent. A segment carries three defining properties:

| Property | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| `ss` | `std::string` | Secondary structure string (one char per residue: H, E, L) |
| `abego` | `std::string` | ABEGO backbone torsion bins per residue |
| `id` | `std::string` | Unique name used for pairing and referencing |

Segments also track pose-coordinate mapping (`set_pose_start()`, `segment_to_pose()`, `pose_to_segment()`) and boundary inclusion flags (`nterm_included_`, `cterm_included_`) that control whether padding residues are considered part of the designable segment. The `parse_motif()` method accepts compact strings like `"1LX-10HA-1LA-1LB"`, describing a 1-residue loop, 10-residue helix, and two 1-residue loops — a common pattern in blueprint notation.

Sources: [Segment.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/components/Segment.hh#L47-L200), [ResidueDihedrals](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/components/Segment.hh#L47-L93)

### SegmentPairing: Defining Inter-Segment Geometry

When segments must adopt specific relative orientations — such as parallel or antiparallel helix pairings, or strand hydrogen-bonding registers — `SegmentPairing` objects encode these constraints. The base class defines four pairing types through an enum: `HELIX`, `STRAND`, `HELIX_SHEET`, and `UNKNOWN`. Derived classes `HelixPairing` and `StrandPairing` carry the specific geometric parameters. The `pairing_string()` method serializes the pairing into the classic Rosetta pairing notation used by constraints and filters.

Sources: [SegmentPairing.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/components/SegmentPairing.hh#L35-L139)

### StructureData Operations

`StructureData` provides a rich manipulation API organized into several categories. **Segment management** includes `add_segment()`, `delete_segment()`, `rename_segment()`, `move_segment()`, `merge_segments()`, and `replace_segment()`. **Connectivity** is controlled through `connect_segments()`, `disconnect_segments()`, and `declare_covalent_bond()` using the `BondInfo` class. **Alias** support allows naming specific residues (`set_alias()`) for convenient cross-referencing in movers and filters. **Arbitrary user data** (integers, reals, strings) can be attached per-segment via the `set_data_*()` / `get_data_*()` family of methods. The `slice()` method extracts a subset of segments into a new `StructureData`, and `merge()` / `merge_before()` combine two blueprints — critical for modular assembly.

Sources: [StructureData.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/components/StructureData.hh#L106-L327)

## The Architect Hierarchy: Blueprint Generation

`DeNovoArchitect` is the abstract interface whose `design()` method produces a `StructureDataOP` from an optional input pose. The class extends `StructureArchitect` and provides the critical `apply()` method that internally calls `design()`, making it usable both programmatically and within the [RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework). Each concrete architect encodes a different strategy for topology creation.

### Concrete Architect Implementations

| Architect | Source | Topology Strategy |
|-----------|--------|-------------------|
| `BlueprintArchitect` | Blueprint file | Parses the classic Rosetta blueprint format including HHPAIR lines for helix-helix contacts |
| `HelixArchitect` | Parameterized | Generates helical bundle topologies with controllable helix count, lengths, and packing angles |
| `BetaSheetArchitect` | Parameterized | Constructs β-sheet topologies with strand count, register, and orientation specifications |
| `MotifArchitect` | PDB fragments | Extracts structural motifs from input poses and wraps them into segments |
| `CompoundArchitect` | Composite | Chains multiple child architects to combine their output into a single `StructureData` |
| `PoseArchitect` | Input pose | Converts an existing pose into a `StructureData` by extracting its secondary structure and geometry |
| `StrandArchitect` | Parameterized | Creates individual strand segments with specific strand pairing constraints |

`BlueprintArchitect` deserves special attention: it wraps the legacy `BluePrint` parser and additionally handles `HHPAIR` lines that specify helix-helix pairings with orientation (P/A = parallel/antiparallel) and register offsets. Template segments — residues with non-zero residue numbers in the blueprint — are extracted from the input pose and anchored in the blueprint via `set_template_segments()`, enabling hybrid templated/de novo design.

Sources: [BlueprintArchitect.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/architects/BlueprintArchitect.hh#L37-L103), [DeNovoArchitectFactory](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/architects/DeNovoArchitectFactory.hh#L1-L50)

## Pose Building: From Blueprint to Extended Chain

Once `StructureData` is defined, `ExtendedPoseBuilder` materializes it into a physical `Pose`. The builder operates in two stages. First, `create_template_pose()` extracts segments that have template conformations (stored via `set_template_pose()`) and assembles them into a partial pose with correct chain boundaries. Then `extend_pose()` inserts de novo segments as extended-chain residues (glycines or poly-alanine) at the appropriate positions, guided by the `ResidueDihedrals` helper for dihedral anchoring at junctions. The `FoldTree` is constructed to reflect the segment connectivity encoded in the blueprint.

The `PoseBuilder` base class provides a `debug` flag that, when enabled, outputs intermediate PDB files at each build stage — invaluable for diagnosing topology issues. The standalone functions `prepend_new_residues()` and `append_new_residues()` handle the low-level mechanics of residue insertion with proper variant type assignment at cutpoints.

Sources: [ExtendedPoseBuilder.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/components/ExtendedPoseBuilder.hh#L67-L104)

## Pose Folding: Sampling 3D Conformations

The `PoseFolder` abstract interface defines the contract for conformation sampling. Its `apply()` method receives a pose (with all residues already present), a `ResidueSubset` marking which residues are movable, and a `Loops` object defining foldable regions. Critically, residues not marked as movable and not contained within any loop must not be modified — this ensures template segments remain fixed while de novo segments are folded.

| Folder | Strategy |
|--------|----------|
| `RemodelLoopMoverPoseFolder` | Wraps the Remodel loop modeling mover for kinematics-based loop closure |
| `RandomTorsionPoseFolder` | Assigns random backbone torsions within ABEGO constraints |
| `NullPoseFolder` | No-op folder; leaves the pose as-is for scenarios where only sequence design is needed |

The `FoldGraph` class plays a supporting role here: it constructs a graph representation of segment connectivity from `StructureData`, enabling computation of optimal fold trees and loop definitions. The `compute_best_solution()` method identifies movable segment groups that minimize the number of independent folding subproblems — essentially a graph partitioning problem solved via `create_loops()`.

> [!TIP]
> The `EXCN_Fold` exception class signals folding failures. Derived `PoseFolder` implementations should throw this exception rather than silently producing invalid conformations, allowing `FoldArchitectMover` to trigger retries with perturbed topologies.

Sources: [PoseFolder.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/components/PoseFolder.hh#L41-L97), [FoldGraph.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/components/FoldGraph.hh#L45-L80)

## Segment Connection and Loop Closure

`ConnectionArchitect` addresses the challenge of covalently joining separate chain segments (e.g., closing a cutpoint between two helices). It operates on `StructureData` rather than the Pose, modifying the blueprint to add connecting loop segments. The architect maintains lists of `segment1_ids()` and `segment2_ids()` specifying which segment pairs are candidates for connection, and `compute_connection_candidates()` evaluates feasible loop motifs by length and geometry.

Connection architects are consumed by `FoldArchitectMover` as a vector of `ConnectionArchitectCOPs`, applied sequentially to the `StructureData` before folding. The `BridgeChainsMover` provides an alternative Pose-level implementation that uses kinematic closure (KIC) to bridge chain termini, and `DeclareStructureDataCovalentBondMover` handles non-peptide covalent bonds between arbitrary atoms.

Sources: [ConnectionArchitect.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/connection/ConnectionArchitect.hh#L48-L93), [BridgeChainsMover](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/movers/BridgeChainsMover.hh#L1-L50)

## StructureData Perturbation: Topology Search

`StructureDataPerturber` enables systematic exploration of topology space by modifying the blueprint between folding attempts. The base class defines `enumerate()` which returns a set of `Permutation` objects (lists of replacement `Segment` COPs), and `apply()` replaces segments in the current `StructureData` with the selected permutation.

The `ConnectionPerturber` subclass "mutates" existing connections by varying loop lengths and ABEGO patterns, while `NullPerturber` serves as the identity operation. The `EnumeratedVectorSelector` used internally cycles through permutations, enabling controlled enumeration without replacement — essential for thorough sampling in large topology spaces. The `ignore_segments()` mechanism allows excluding template or fixed segments from perturbation.

Sources: [StructureDataPerturber.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/components/StructureDataPerturber.hh#L39-L88)

## The FoldArchitectMover Orchestrator

`FoldArchitectMover` is the primary entry point that wires together all the components described above. It implements the standard `moves::Mover` interface, making it directly usable from RosettaScripts, PyRosetta, and the job-distribution system. The mover manages the complete lifecycle:

1. **Topology generation**: Calls `DeNovoArchitect::apply()` to produce `StructureData`
2. **Perturbation**: Optionally applies `StructureDataPerturber` to explore topology variants
3. **Connection**: Runs `ConnectionArchitect` instances to close chain gaps
4. **Build**: Uses `PoseBuilder` to create the extended-chain pose
5. **Constraint setup**: Applies `ConstraintGenerator` instances for folding guidance
6. **Fold**: Invokes `PoseFolder` to sample backbone conformations
7. **Post-processing**: Runs secondary `Mover` and `Filter` pipelines for refinement and quality assessment

The `DivideAndConqueror` component referenced in the mover's interface handles the strategy of folding complex topologies by decomposing them into independently foldable subproblems based on the `FoldGraph` connectivity analysis.

> [!TIP]
> `FoldArchitectMover` stores both an architect and a folder as mutable state. When configuring via RosettaScripts, use `set_architect()` and `set_folder()` separately to compose different topology strategies with different folding strategies — e.g., pair `BlueprintArchitect` with `RemodelLoopMoverPoseFolder` for classic blueprint-based design, or `HelixArchitect` with `RandomTorsionPoseFolder` for parametric bundle exploration.

Sources: [FoldArchitectMover.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/movers/FoldArchitectMover.hh#L49-L119)

## Design-Time Filters and Quality Assessment

The `denovo_design` module provides specialized filters that evaluate design quality during the RosettaScripts pipeline:

| Filter | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `CavityVolumeFilter` | Detects buried cavities via the `CavityCalculator` — large cavities indicate poor packing |
| `ExposedHydrophobicsFilter` | Flags solvent-exposed hydrophobic residues that destabilize the design |
| `PreProlineFilter` | Ensures pre-proline residues adopt favorable backbone conformations |
| `SSPredictionFilter` | Validates that predicted secondary structure matches design intent |
| `SSShapeComplementarityFilter` | Evaluates shape complementarity at secondary structure element interfaces |

These filters complement the broader Rosetta filter system and are typically chained after the design mover in a RosettaScripts protocol. The `ConsensusLoopDesignOperation` task operation provides loop-specific sequence design constraints that prefer consensus loop geometries.

Sources: [filters/](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/filters/CavityVolumeFilter.cc#L1-L10), [task_operations/ConsensusLoopDesignOperation](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/task_operations/ConsensusLoopDesignOperation.hh#L1-L10)

## Related Modules and Complementary Systems

De novo design in Rosetta extends well beyond the `denovo_design` module. Several related subsystems provide specialized capabilities that integrate with or complement the core framework.

### Topology Analysis (fldsgn)

The `protocols/fldsgn` module provides secondary structure topology analysis infrastructure, including `StrandPairing`, `HelixPairing`, `HSSTriplet` (helix-strand-strand motifs), and `Sheet` topology objects. The `BluePrintBDR` mover is a legacy topology builder, and `SheetConstraintGenerator` / `SheetRemodelConstraintGenerator` enforce β-sheet geometry during folding. The `potentials/` subdirectory contains `AACompositionEnergy` and `SetSecStructEnergies` — energy functions that bias the [ScoreFunction](9-scorefunction-framework) toward designed secondary structure patterns.

Sources: [fldsgn/](source/src/protocols/fldsgn/topology/StrandPairing.hh#L1-L10), [fldsgn/potentials](source/src/protocols/fldsgn/potentials/AACompositionEnergy.hh#L1-L10)

### Helical Bundle Design (helical_bundle)

The `protocols/helical_bundle` module provides a parametric framework for coiled-coil and helical bundle design, built around `MakeBundle` (creates bundles from Crick parameterization), `PerturbBundle` / `PerturbBundleHelix` (searches parameter space), and `BundleGridSampler` (systematic parameter exploration). `helical_bundle_predict.cc` is the standalone application. This system can feed into the de novo framework via `HelixArchitect` or operate independently for symmetric bundle design.

### Residue Selectors

The `NamedSegmentSelector` and `PairedSheetResidueSelector` provide `ResidueSelector` implementations that select residues based on `StructureData` segment names or β-sheet pairing membership, enabling design task operations targeted to specific structural elements within a de novo design.

Sources: [residue_selectors/NamedSegmentSelector](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/residue_selectors/NamedSegmentSelector.hh#L1-L10)

## Component Interaction Pattern

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User as RosettaScripts / PyRosetta
    participant FAM as FoldArchitectMover
    participant Arch as DeNovoArchitect
    participant SD as StructureData
    participant Pert as StructureDataPerturber
    participant Conn as ConnectionArchitect
    participant Build as ExtendedPoseBuilder
    participant Fold as PoseFolder
    participant Pose as Pose

    User->>FAM: apply(pose)
    FAM->>Arch: apply(empty_pose)
    Arch->>SD: design() → StructureDataOP
    SD-->>FAM: blueprint

    loop Until acceptance or max attempts
        FAM->>Pert: apply(sd)
        Pert-->>FAM: modified blueprint

        FAM->>Conn: apply(sd)
        Conn-->>FAM: connected blueprint

        FAM->>Build: apply(sd)
        Build->>Pose: create_template_pose() + extend_pose()
        Pose-->>Build: extended pose with fold tree

        Build-->>FAM: PoseOP

        FAM->>Fold: apply(pose, movable, loops)
        Fold-->>FAM: folded pose

        FAM->>FAM: run filters
        alt Filters pass
            FAM-->>User: accepted design
        else Filters fail
            Note over FAM: retry with new perturbation
        end
    end
```

This sequence diagram illustrates the iterative nature of the de novo design process. Each iteration perturbs the topology, rebuilds the pose, and re-folds — with filter evaluation determining acceptance. The separation of topology (StructureData) from conformation (Pose) enables this efficient exploration, as blueprint modifications are far cheaper than rebuilding and refolding from scratch.

Sources: [FoldArchitectMover.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/movers/FoldArchitectMover.hh#L78-L86), [DeNovoArchitect.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/architects/DeNovoArchitect.hh#L84-L87), [StructureDataPerturber.hh](source/src/protocols/denovo_design/components/StructureDataPerturber.hh#L58-L66)

## Navigating Further

The de novo design system sits at the intersection of several architectural layers in Rosetta. Understanding its neighbors provides fuller context:

- **[Pose and Conformation](8-pose-and-conformation)** — The Pose object that StructureData materializes into, and the conformational representations used during folding
- **[ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework)** — Energy functions that evaluate and drive the design toward stable, well-packed structures
- **[RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework)** — How to compose de novo design protocols using XML; all architects, folders, and filters support `parse_my_tag()` / `provide_xml_schema()` for declarative configuration
- **[Monte Carlo Sampling](12-monte-carlo-sampling)** — The stochastic acceptance framework that governs topology perturbation iterations
- **[Fragment Picking System](26-fragment-picking-system)** — Fragment libraries used by folding strategies like `RemodelLoopMoverPoseFolder`
- **[Structure Relaxation](18-structure-relaxation)** — Post-folding refinement that polishes de novo designs into physically realistic structures
- **[ProteinMPNN Integration](22-proteinmpnn-integration)** — Modern sequence design methods that can replace Rosetta's native packing for sequence optimization of de novo backbones

# Structure Relaxation



Structure relaxation is the computational process of reducing steric clashes, improving hydrogen bonding geometry, and optimizing backbone and sidechain conformations of a protein model. Within Rosetta, relaxation serves as both a standalone refinement protocol and a critical post-processing step woven into nearly every major workflow — from ab initio folding to comparative modeling to design. This page documents the architectural foundations, protocol variants, and script-driven orchestration system that collectively form Rosetta's relaxation framework.

## Architecture Overview

The relaxation subsystem is built on a disciplined class hierarchy that separates *policy* (which degrees of freedom to move, which scoring to use) from *orchestration* (the order and repetition of packing/minimization cycles). All production relax movers descend from `RelaxProtocolBase`, which itself inherits from the foundational `moves::Mover` class, while specialized variants like `LocalRelax` operate independently at the `Mover` level for fundamentally different algorithmic approaches.

Sources: [RelaxProtocolBase.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/RelaxProtocolBase.hh#L45-L52)

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Mover {
        <<abstract>>
        +"apply(Pose&)"*
        +"get_name()"*
        +"clone()"*
        +"parse_my_tag()"*
    }
    class RelaxProtocolBase {
        #scorefxn_: ScoreFunctionOP
        #movemap_: MoveMapOP
        #task_factory_: TaskFactoryOP
        #cartesian_: bool
        #min_type_: string
        #max_iter_: Size
        #constrain_coords_: bool
        #ramp_down_constraints_: bool
        +constrain_relax_to_native_coords()
        +constrain_relax_to_start_coords()
        +cartesian(bool)
        +min_type(string)
        +max_iter(Size)
    }
    class FastRelax {
        -default_repeats_: Size
        -script_: vector~RelaxScriptCommand~
        +"apply(Pose&)"
        +"batch_apply(vector~SilentStructOP~&)"
        +dualspace(bool)
        +"set_script_from_lines(vector~string~&)"
        +set_script_to_batchrelax_default()
    }
    class ClassicRelax {
        -lj_ramp_cycles: int
        -stage2_cycles: int
        +"apply(Pose&)"
        +set_lj_ramp_cycles(int)
        +set_stage2_cycles(int)
    }
    class MiniRelax {
        -scorefxn_: ScoreFunctionOP
        +"apply(Pose&)"
    }
    class LocalRelax {
        -NCYC_: Size
        -pack_sfxn_: ScoreFunctionOP
        -min_sfxn_: ScoreFunctionOP
        +"apply(Pose&)"
        +optimization_loop()
    }

    Mover <|-- RelaxProtocolBase
    RelaxProtocolBase <|-- FastRelax
    RelaxProtocolBase <|-- ClassicRelax
    RelaxProtocolBase <|-- MiniRelax
    Mover <|-- LocalRelax
```

The `RelaxProtocolBase` class codifies the shared vocabulary for all script-driven relax protocols. It manages the **MoveMap** (controlling which torsions and bond angles are free to move), the **ScoreFunction** (defining the energy landscape), the **TaskFactory** (governing which residues may be repacked or redesigned), and an extensive set of boolean flags for constraint behavior and minimization geometry. These settings are the knobs that every downstream protocol either respects or overrides.

Sources: [RelaxProtocolBase.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/RelaxProtocolBase.hh#L142-L183)

## Protocol Variants

Rosetta provides four distinct relaxation implementations, each optimized for different scenarios. Understanding their trade-offs is essential for choosing the right tool.

| Protocol | Class | Strategy | Use Case | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **FastRelax** | `FastRelax` | Script-driven repack/minimize cycles with ramped repulsive weights | Default refinement; most general-purpose | Moderate |
| **ClassicRelax** | `ClassicRelax` | Three-phase protocol with explicit Lennard-Jones ramping | Legacy Rosetta++ compatibility | Slow |
| **MiniRelax** | `MiniRelax` | Minimal-cycle relaxation using base-class settings | Lightweight post-processing | Fast |
| **LocalRelax** | `LocalRelax` | Iterative Cartesian relaxation on clustered residue subsets | Large structures; local strain relief | Variable |

### FastRelax — The Standard Protocol

`FastRelax` is the workhorse of Rosetta refinement. It operates by interpreting a *relax script* — a sequence of declarative commands that specify how many times to repeat a cycle, what coordinate constraint weights to apply, how to scale the repulsive term (`fa_rep`), and when to repack versus minimize. The script language acts as a domain-specific orchestrator decoupling the sequence of operations from their implementation.

Sources: [FastRelax.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/FastRelax.hh#L74-L102)

A `RelaxScriptCommand` struct captures each parsed line of the script, storing the command name, up to four numeric parameters, and a vector for variable-length parameter lists. This design allows the `apply()` method to dispatch commands through a simple switch-like structure without re-parsing on every iteration.

Sources: [FastRelax.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/FastRelax.hh#L50-L66)

FastRelax supports both **dihedral-space** and **Cartesian-space** minimization. When `dualspace(true)` is called, the minimizer operates in both dihedral and Cartesian coordinates simultaneously, using the `lbfgs_armijo_nonmonotone` algorithm. This is particularly effective for correcting severe geometric distortions (e.g., from homology models) because Cartesian minimization can directly improve bond angles and lengths, while dihedral minimization preserves the protein's chain connectivity intuition. The documentation recommends setting `max_iter` to 200 and enabling `minimize_bond_angles` when using dualspace mode.

Sources: [FastRelax.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/FastRelax.hh#L115-L122)

### ClassicRelax — Legacy Three-Phase Relaxation

`ClassicRelax` implements the original Rosetta++ `pose_relax` protocol. It operates in three explicit phases — phase 1 (high repulsive weight, coarse repacking), phase 2 (ramped repulsive, rotamer trials), and phase 3 (full repulsive, final minimization) — controlled by configurable cycle counts and Lennard-Jones ramp parameters. While superseded by FastRelax for most applications, ClassicRelax remains available for backward compatibility and for cases where its explicit phase structure provides useful control points.

Sources: [ClassicRelax.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/ClassicRelax.hh#L55-L107)

### LocalRelax — Cluster-Based Local Optimization

`LocalRelax` takes a fundamentally different approach. Rather than relaxing the entire structure simultaneously, it computes a neighbor interaction graph, clusters spatially proximate residues, and performs iterative Cartesian relaxation on each cluster independently. This is particularly useful for very large structures or for relieving local strain without perturbing well-folded regions. It maintains separate `pack_sfxn_` and `min_sfxn_` score functions, allowing different scoring regimes for packing and minimization phases within each local cluster.

Sources: [LocalRelax.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/LocalRelax.hh#L34-L99)

## Relax Script System

The relax script is the central orchestration mechanism for FastRelax. Scripts are text files containing one command per line, supporting conditional repetition and weight scaling. They reside in the Rosetta database at `database/sampling/relax_scripts/` and are managed by the `RelaxScriptManager` singleton.

Sources: [RelaxScriptManager.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/RelaxScriptManager.hh#L124-L128)

### Script Command Language

Below is a representative FastRelax script (`MonomerRelax2019.txt`) annotated with the role of each command:

```
repeat %%nrepeats%%          ← Outer loop; %%nrepeats%% is substituted at load time
coord_cst_weight 1.0         ← Set coordinate constraint weight (full tethering)
scale:fa_rep 0.040           ← Scale repulsive term to 4% of full weight
repack                        ← Perform full rotamer packing
scale:fa_rep 0.051           ← Slightly raise repulsive weight
min 0.01                     ← Minimize with tolerance 0.01
coord_cst_weight 0.5         ← Halve coordinate constraint strength
scale:fa_rep 0.265           ← Continue ramping repulsive
repack                        ← Repack again at higher repulsive
scale:fa_rep 0.280
min 0.01
coord_cst_weight 0.0         ← Release coordinate constraints entirely
scale:fa_rep 0.559
repack
scale:fa_rep 0.581
min 0.01
coord_cst_weight 0.0
scale:fa_rep 1               ← Full repulsive weight
repack
min 0.00001                  ← Final tight minimization
accept_to_best               ← Accept if this is the best score seen
endrepeat
```

Sources: [MonomerRelax2019.txt](database/sampling/relax_scripts/MonomerRelax2019.txt#L1-L22)

The key architectural insight is the **repulsive ramping** pattern. The `fa_rep` (full-atom repulsive) term starts at a very low fraction of its full weight, allowing the structure to resolve severe clashes through gradual rearrangement. As the weight increases, the structure settles into the correct energy basin. Simultaneously, the **coordinate constraint** weight is ramped *down* — the structure starts tightly tethered to its input coordinates and is progressively released. This dual-ramping prevents the minimizer from wandering into unrelated conformational space while still allowing significant structural improvement.

### Available Database Scripts

The `database/sampling/relax_scripts/index.dat` file catalogs all available scripts and indicates which ones are scorefunction-specialized:

| Script | Scorefunction-Specific | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `MonomerRelax2019` | No | Default monomer refinement (relax only, no design) |
| `MonomerDesign2019` | No | Monomer refinement with sequence design enabled |
| `InterfaceRelax2019` | No | Multi-chain interface refinement |
| `InterfaceDesign2019` | No | Interface refinement with design |
| `PolarDesign2019` | Yes (score12, talaris2013/4, ref2015, beta_nov16) | Design with polar residue optimization |
| `legacy` | No | Original FastRelax default script |
| `no_cst_ramping` | No | Relaxation without coordinate constraint ramping |
| `rosettacon2018` | No | RosettaCon 2018 experimental script |

Sources: [index.dat](database/sampling/relax_scripts/index.dat#L1-L14)

Each script with scorefunction-specific variants has additional files named `<title>.<scorefxn>.txt` and `<title>.<scorefxn>.dualspace.txt`. For example, `PolarDesign2019` exists as `PolarDesign2019.ref2015.txt`, `PolarDesign2019.beta_nov16.txt`, and so on. The `RelaxScriptManager` automatically selects the closest matching variant based on the score function's weight composition.

Sources: [index.dat](database/sampling/relax_scripts/index.dat#L1-L5)

### RelaxScriptManager — Singleton Script Loader

The `RelaxScriptManager` is a thread-safe singleton that ensures each relax script is loaded from disk exactly once, regardless of how many `FastRelax` instances reference it. It implements lazy loading with a three-tier caching strategy:

1. **Script file contents** are cached in a `std::map` keyed by a tuple of `(filename, nearest_sfxn_name, dualspace)`.
2. **Database script metadata** from `index.dat` is loaded once into `relax_scripts_in_database_`.
3. **Energy maps** for scorefunction distance computation are cached separately in `energy_maps_map_`.

When a `FastRelax` instance requests a script via `get_relax_script()`, the manager first checks whether the script is a database script with scorefunction-specific variants. If so, it computes the squared Euclidean distance between the caller's score function weights and each candidate's cached energy map to select the best match. This ensures that `PolarDesign2019` used with `ref2015` automatically loads `PolarDesign2019.ref2015.txt` without any manual configuration.

Sources: [RelaxScriptManager.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/RelaxScriptManager.hh#L131-L182)

> [!TIP]
> The `%%nrepeats%%` variable in relax scripts is substituted at load time with the `standard_repeats` parameter passed to `FastRelax`. The default for `MonomerRelax2019` is 5 repeats, but the `FastRelax(scorefxn, standard_repeats, script_file)` constructor allows explicit control. The `batch_apply()` method provides an optimized path for relaxing large batches of structures by sharing constraint sets across poses.

## Coordinate Constraint System

Coordinate constraints are the primary mechanism by which relaxation balances structural improvement against deviation from the input model. The `AtomCoordinateCstMover` provides standalone functionality for adding harmonic constraints to protein atoms, while `RelaxProtocolBase` integrates constraint management directly into the relaxation pipeline through its `set_up_constraints()` method.

Sources: [AtomCoordinateCstMover.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/AtomCoordinateCstMover.hh#L39-L50)

The `AtomCoordinateCstMover` supports several configuration options that control constraint behavior:

| Parameter | Method | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cst_sd` | `cst_sd(Real)` | — | Standard deviation of harmonic constraint (lower = tighter) |
| `bounded` | `bounded(bool)` | — | Whether constraints are bounded (flat-bottom potential) |
| `cst_width` | `cst_width(Real)` | — | Width of the bounded constraint flat region |
| `cst_sidechain` | `cst_sidechain(bool)` | — | Whether to constrain sidechain atoms |
| `ambiguous_hnq` | `ambiguous_hnq(bool)` | — | Ambiguous HNQ atom handling for HIS/ASN/GLN |
| `func_groups` | `func_groups(bool)` | — | Whether to use functional group constraints |

Sources: [AtomCoordinateCstMover.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/AtomCoordinateCstMover.hh#L67-L84)

Within the relaxation pipeline itself, `RelaxProtocolBase` provides a complementary set of constraint controls through boolean flags. `constrain_relax_to_native_coords` and `constrain_relax_to_start_coords` determine the reference structure for constraints. The `ramp_down_constraints` flag — when true — instructs the script interpreter to gradually reduce constraint weights across relaxation cycles, which is the default behavior in all 2019-era scripts. The `constrain_relax_segments` flag enables segment-specific constraint behavior, useful when only certain loops or domains should be mobile.

Sources: [RelaxProtocolBase.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/RelaxProtocolBase.hh#L77-L108)

> [!TIP]
> When relaxing homology models or RosettaCM outputs, always enable coordinate constraints (`constrain_coords(true)`) and ramp them down. Without tethering, minimization can cause large-scale domain movements that destroy the model's global fold. The 2019 default scripts handle this automatically via the `coord_cst_weight` command sequence.

## Minimization Infrastructure

The relaxation framework delegates actual energy minimization to Rosetta's minimization movers in `protocols/minimization_packing/`. `FastRelax` creates and configures `MinMover` instances internally through its `do_minimize()` method, passing the current `MoveMap`, `ScoreFunction`, and tolerance from the script command. The choice of minimization algorithm is controlled by the `min_type_` string — typically `lbfgs_armijo_nonmonotone` for dualspace/Cartesian or the default `dfpmin` for dihedral-space.

Sources: [FastRelax.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/FastRelax.hh#L191-L196)

The `RelaxProtocolBase` class exposes fine-grained control over what degrees of freedom the minimizer may alter:

| Setting | Method | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `minimize_bond_lengths` | `minimize_bond_lengths(bool)` | Allow bond length changes during minimization |
| `minimize_bond_angles` | `minimize_bond_angles(bool)` | Allow bond angle changes during minimization |
| `minimize_bondlength_subset` | `minimize_bondlength_subset(int)` | Subset-specific bond length minimization |
| `minimize_bondangle_subset` | `minimize_bondangle_subset(int)` | Subset-specific bond angle minimization |
| `fix_omega` | `fix_omega(bool)` | Prevent ω dihedral rotation (peptide bonds) |
| `limit_aroma_chi2` | `limit_aroma_chi2()` | Restrict aromatic χ2 angles |
| `cartesian` | `cartesian(bool)` | Use Cartesian vs. dihedral minimization |

Sources: [RelaxProtocolBase.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/RelaxProtocolBase.hh#L72-L86)

The `max_iter_` parameter (default varies by context) limits the number of minimizer iterations per step. For dualspace relaxation, the documentation explicitly recommends increasing this to 200, as Cartesian minimization converges more slowly than dihedral minimization for the same tolerance threshold. The `dry_run_` flag, when set, bypasses all cycles entirely — useful for validating script parsing and constraint setup without spending compute time.

Sources: [RelaxProtocolBase.hh](source/src/protocols/relax/RelaxProtocolBase.hh#L74-L101)

## End-to-End Relaxation Flow

The following diagram illustrates the complete lifecycle of a `FastRelax.apply()` call, from script loading through the iterative repack-minimize cycles to final output:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["FastRelax.apply(pose)"] --> B["RelaxScriptManager.get_relax_script()"]
    B --> C{"Script cached?"}
    C -->|Yes| D["Return cached RelaxScriptFileContents"]
    C -->|No| E["Load from database/sampling/relax_scripts/"]
    E --> F{"Scorefunction-specific variant exists?"}
    F -->|Yes| G["Select closest matching sfxn variant"]
    F -->|No| H["Load base script"]
    G --> I["Cache and return"]
    H --> I
    D --> J["Parse script into RelaxScriptCommand vector"]
    I --> J
    J --> K["set_up_constraints() — add coordinate constraints"]
    K --> L["Begin outer repeat loop"]
    L --> M{"Next command?"}
    M -->|coord_cst_weight| N["Scale coordinate constraint weight"]
    M -->|scale:fa_rep| O["Scale repulsive term in score function"]
    M -->|repack| P["PackRotamersMover.apply()"]
    M -->|min| Q["MinMover.apply() with tolerance"]
    M -->|accept_to_best| R["Compare to best pose; accept if improved"]
    M -->|endrepeat| S{"More repeats?"}
    S -->|Yes| L
    S -->|No| T["Return relaxed pose"]
    N --> M
    O --> M
    P --> M
    Q --> M
    R --> M
```

## Integration with the Broader Framework

Relaxation does not exist in isolation — it is deeply integrated with several other subsystems covered elsewhere in this documentation:

- **[ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework)**: Relaxation's effectiveness depends critically on the choice of score function. The `ref2015` weight set is the standard pairing with the 2019 relax scripts, while `beta_nov16` is commonly used for design-oriented relaxation.
- **[Side-Chain Packing](13-side-chain-packing)**: The `repack` command in relax scripts invokes `PackRotamersMover`, which performs the full rotamer packing algorithm including dead-end elimination and simulated annealing over rotamer combinations.
- **[Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy)**: All relax protocols are `Mover` subclasses and can be composed within RosettaScripts pipelines, chained with filters, and controlled by the job distribution system.
- **[RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework)**: `FastRelax` exposes itself via `parse_my_tag()` with full XML Schema support (`provide_xml_schema()`), enabling declarative configuration within XML protocol files.
- **[Membrane Protein Modeling](25-membrane-protein-modeling)**: Specialized relax variants exist under `source/src/protocols/relax/membrane/` that incorporate membrane-specific energy terms and constraints.
- **[Monte Carlo Sampling](12-monte-carlo-sampling)**: The `accept_to_best` command introduces a Monte Carlo acceptance criterion within the relaxation loop, allowing the protocol to escape local minima.

## Recommended Reading Progression

For developers seeking to extend or customize relaxation behavior, the following sequence provides the most efficient learning path:

1. **[ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework)** — understand the energy landscape that relaxation optimizes
2. **[Side-Chain Packing](13-side-chain-packing)** — understand the rotamer packing engine invoked by `repack` commands
3. **[Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy)** — understand the base class interface all relax protocols implement
4. **[Monte Carlo Sampling](12-monte-carlo-sampling)** — understand the acceptance criteria used during relaxation
5. **[RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework)** — learn to compose relaxation into larger protocol pipelines

# Ligand Docking



Rosetta's ligand docking subsystem provides a multi-layered framework for predicting how small molecules bind to protein targets. It spans from grid-accelerated genetic algorithm search to high-resolution Monte Carlo refinement, with a rich ecosystem of filters, scoring utilities, and integration points for enzyme design constraints. This page dissects the two primary docking paradigms — the classic `LigandDockProtocol` and the genetic-algorithm-driven `GALigandDock` — alongside the shared infrastructure that supports pose preparation, interface detection, and scoring.

Sources: [LigandDockProtocol.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/LigandDockProtocol.hh#L48-L64), [GALigandDock.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/GALigandDock/GALigandDock.hh#L1-L66)

## Architectural Overview

The ligand docking system is organized around two complementary docking engines, unified by a shared layer of utility functions, interface analysis, and filter movers. The architecture follows Rosetta's Mover/Filter paradigm, enabling seamless composition within RosettaScripts pipelines and JD2 job distribution.


## Classic Docking: LigandDockProtocol

The `LigandDockProtocol` (authored by Ian W. Davis) is the traditional Monte Carlo–based docking engine. It extends `LigandBaseProtocol` and implements a multi-stage search that begins with soft repulsive scoring and transitions to hard repulsion for final refinement. The protocol orchestrates rigid-body perturbation, side-chain repacking, and ligand torsion minimization within a simulated annealing framework.

### Protocol Initialization and Parameters

The constructor accepts a comprehensive set of parameters that define docking behavior. These can be supplied programmatically or read from the option system via `-docking:ligand:*` flags.

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `protocol` | `string` | Protocol mode: `"classic"`, `"shear_min"`, `"rescore"`, or `"unbound"` |
| `minimize_ligand` | `bool` | Whether to minimize ligand internal degrees of freedom |
| `minimize_backbone` | `bool` | Whether to minimize protein backbone near the interface |
| `tether_ligand` | `bool` | Apply harmonic tether to prevent ligand from drifting far |
| `mutate_same_name3` | `bool` | Allow ligand protonation state changes |
| `ligand_chi_stddev_deg` | `Real` | Standard deviation for harmonic torsion restraints (degrees) |
| `protein_CA_stddev_Ang` | `Real` | Standard deviation for backbone CA restraints (Å) |
| `ligand_tether_stddev_Ang` | `Real` | Tether spring constant (Å); -1 disables tether |
| `ligand_shear_moves` | `Size` | Number of ligand shear (fragment) moves per cycle |

Sources: [LigandDockProtocol.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/LigandDockProtocol.hh#L54-L64), [LigandDockProtocol.cc](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/LigandDockProtocol.cc#L100-L136)

### Multi-Stage Docking Pipeline

The `apply()` method implements the full docking pipeline. It begins by loading unbound rotamer bonuses via `core::pack::dunbrack::load_unboundrot()`, switches between soft and hard repulsive score functions, detects the ligand jump ID, and dispatches to one of the protocol variants. The soft-rep stage enables coarse exploration while the hard-rep stage provides accurate final scoring.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Input Pose] --> B[Load Unbound Rotamers<br/>load_unboundrot]
    B --> C{Protocol?}
    C -->|rescore| Z[Return - score only]
    C -->|unbound| U[Score unbound ligand]
    C -->|classic / shear_min| D[Set Soft-Rep ScoreFunction]
    
    D --> E[Save FoldTree]
    E --> F[Get Ligand Jump ID]
    F --> G[Score Pose]
    G --> H{iphold cycles?}
    
    H -->|yes| H1[LoopRelaxMover<br/>cen_cycles]
    H1 --> H2[LoopRelaxMover<br/>fa_cycles]
    H2 --> I
    H -->|no| I[Random Conformer Sampling]
    
    I --> J{Start-from points?}
    J -->|yes| K[Place ligand at<br/>start_from_pts_]
    J -->|no| L[Optimize Orientation]
    
    K --> L
    L --> M{Protocol variant}
    M -->|classic| N[classic_protocol<br/>MC + Repack + Minimize]
    M -->|shear_min| O[shear_min_protocol<br/>Shear moves + Minimize]
    
    N --> P[Restore FoldTree]
    O --> P
    P --> Q[Final Minimization<br/>Hard-Rep ScoreFunction]
    Q --> R[Append Docking Scores]
    R --> S[Output Docked Pose]
```

Sources: [LigandDockProtocol.cc](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/LigandDockProtocol.cc#L194-L250), [LigandDockProtocol.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/LigandDockProtocol.hh#L88-L107)

### Classic Protocol vs. Shear-Min Protocol

The two core protocol variants differ fundamentally in how they explore conformational space. The **classic protocol** uses a Monte Carlo cycle with random conformer sampling, rigid-body perturbation via `DockingInitialPerturbation`, and periodic repacking. The **shear-min protocol** (selected when `ligand_shear_moves_ > 0`) incorporates ligand fragment replacement moves that require ambiguous torsion constraints to maintain chemical validity.

The classic protocol constructs a composite mover through `make_dockmcm_mover()`, which chains together repack movers, rigid-body movers, and minimization movers under a Monte Carlo acceptance criterion. The shear-min variant replaces this with a specialized fragment insertion + minimization loop that can bridge larger torsion barriers.

Sources: [LigandDockProtocol.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/LigandDockProtocol.hh#L88-L107), [LigandDockProtocol.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/LigandDockProtocol.hh#L120-L129), [LigandDockProtocol.cc](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/LigandDockProtocol.cc#L133-L135)

### Ligand Torsion Restraints

Torsion restraints prevent the ligand from deviating too far from energetically favorable rotamers during docking. The `ligand_functions` utility provides two mechanisms: `torsion_constraints_from_rotamers()` generates ambiguous dihedral constraints from a set of reference conformations, while `torsion_constraints_from_chi_rotamers()` derives them from the `ResidueType`'s intrinsic `chi_rotamers()` data. Both are invoked by `get_ligand_torsion_constraints()` and aggregated into `ResidueTorsionRestraints` objects managed by the protocol.

> [!TIP]
> When using shear moves, the protocol enforces that ambiguous torsion constraints must be enabled (`-docking:ligand:use_ambig_constraints true`). This is a hard requirement validated at construction time — violating it triggers `utility_exit_with_message()`.

Sources: [ligand_functions.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/ligand_functions.hh#L34-L71), [LigandDockProtocol.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/LigandDockProtocol.hh#L131-L134)

## GA-Based Docking: GALigandDock

The `GALigandDock` subsystem (authored by Hahnbeom Park and Frank DiMaio) implements a fundamentally different search strategy: a multi-stage genetic algorithm that operates on a compact **gene representation** of the docking problem. This approach trades the full-atom accuracy of the classic protocol for dramatically faster exploration of binding poses, making it particularly effective for large-scale virtual screening.

### Gene Representation: LigandConformer

The central data structure is `LigandConformer`, which encodes a complete docking solution as a compact gene. Rather than storing full Cartesian coordinates, it parameterizes the pose through:

- **Rigid body transform** (`rb_`): a 6-DOF representation (3 translational + 3 rotational) of the ligand's position and orientation relative to the receptor
- **Ligand chi angles** (`ligandchis`): internal torsion degrees of freedom
- **Receptor chi angles** (`receptorchis`): side-chain torsions of flexible residues near the binding site

This gene representation enables efficient mutation and crossover operations — the fundamental genetic algorithm operators — directly in torsion/rotation space without needing to reconstruct full atom coordinates for intermediate evaluation. Friend functions `mutate()`, `crossover()`, and `distance_fast()`/`distance_slow()` implement these operations, with the slow variant accounting for symmetric atom equivalences.

Sources: [LigandConformer.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/GALigandDock/LigandConformer.hh#L39-L99), [LigandConformer.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/GALigandDock/LigandConformer.hh#L61-L82)

### Grid-Based Scoring: GridScorer

The `GridScorer` class is the computational engine that makes the genetic algorithm tractable. Rather than evaluating the full Rosetta energy function for each candidate pose, it pre-computes a three-dimensional grid representation of the receptor's scoring potential and evaluates ligand poses by simple grid lookups. This grid encodes van der Waals interactions (via `Etable`), hydrogen bonding (`HBondDatabase`), Lennard-Jones solvation (`LK_BallEnergy`), and Coulomb electrostatics (`Coulomb`).

The grid workflow consists of three phases: `prepare_grid()` calculates the bounding box around the binding site, `get_grid_atomtypes()` determines which atom types to encode based on the ligand's chemistry, and `calculate_grid()` populates the 3D grid values. During optimization, `score()` evaluates a `LigandConformer` gene by interpolating atom positions into the pre-computed grid, while `score_init()` adds an electron density correlation term for guided initial placement.

Sources: [GridScorer.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/GALigandDock/GridScorer.hh#L58-L120)

### Multi-Stage Genetic Algorithm: GAOptimizer

The `GAOptimizer` orchestrates the evolutionary search through a configurable multi-stage protocol. Each stage is defined by `GADockStageParams`, which controls population size, mutation rate, convergence thresholds, and scoring ramping schedules.

| Stage Parameter | Type | Role |
|----------------|------|------|
| `repeats` | `Size` | Number of generations to apply this stage |
| `pool` | `Size` | Population size for this stage |
| `rmsthreshold` | `Real` | Minimum RMSD between pool members (diversity enforcement) |
| `pmut` | `Real` | Per-gene mutation probability |
| `maxiter` | `Real` | Maximum minimization iterations per evaluation |
| `packcycles` | `Real` | Side-chain packing iterations |
| `smoothing` | `Real` | Grid smoothing factor |
| `elec_scale` | `Real` | Scaling factor for electrostatic terms |
| `ramp_schedule` | `vector1<Real>` | `fa_rep` weight ramping schedule |

The algorithm proceeds through `optimize_generation()` which performs selection, mutation (`mutate` / `mutate_ft`), crossover (`crossover` / `crossover_ft`), and pool update with RMSD-based diversity filtering. The `fa_rep` ramping schedule gradually increases the repulsive weight, transitioning from permissive exploration to precise refinement within a single run.

Sources: [GAOptimizer.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/GALigandDock/GAOptimizer.hh#L28-L59), [GAOptimizer.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/GALigandDock/GAOptimizer.hh#L67-L88)

### Output Management and Scoring Metrics

The `OutputStructureStore` maintains a priority queue of the best-scoring structures, ranked by either total energy or binding enthalpy (ΔH = complex score − receptor score − ligand score). Each stored result includes per-component scores (receptor, ligand, complex), RMSD to native, and the full constraint set, enabling comprehensive post-docking analysis. The store supports resizing to retain only the top-N results.

Sources: [GALigandDock.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/GALigandDock/GALigandDock.hh#L59-L105), [GALigandDock.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/GALigandDock/GALigandDock.hh#L156-L180)

## HighResDocker: Modular Refinement Mover

The `HighResDocker` provides a composable, RosettaScripts-friendly alternative to the monolithic `LigandDockProtocol`. It encapsulates a single high-resolution refinement stage — Monte Carlo cycles alternating between rigid-body perturbation, side-chain repacking, and minimization — that can be embedded within larger XML protocols.

The mover manages three key internal workflows: `setup_ligands_to_minimize()` configures per-ligand minimization parameters, `tether_ligands()` applies harmonic spatial restraints, and `make_packer_task()` builds interface-aware packing tasks using the `Interface` analysis system. It supports both chain-based and interface-distance-based residue selection for controlling repacking scope.

Sources: [HighResDocker.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/HighResDocker.hh#L56-L120), [HighResDocker.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/HighResDocker.hh#L138-L154)

## Interface Detection and Analysis

The `Interface` class in the `ligand_options` namespace classifies every residue in the receptor according to its proximity to the ligand chain. Each residue is tagged as `non_interface`, `near_interface`, or `is_interface`, forming a partition that controls which residues are permitted to repack or minimize during docking. This classification drives the `MoveMapBuilder` and packer task construction in both `HighResDocker` and `LigandDockProtocol`.

The interface detection uses distance-based heuristics with configurable padding. The `Interface` class extends `utility::vector1<InterfaceInfo>`, providing methods like `get_interface_residues()` and `get_near_interface_residues()` for downstream consumption, plus `enforce_minimum_length()` to ensure contiguous interface regions meet a minimum window size.

Sources: [Interface.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/ligand_options/Interface.hh#L39-L91)

## Ligand Scoring Utilities

The `ligand_scores` module provides a suite of scoring functions that decompose the binding interaction into interpretable metrics. `get_interface_deltas()` computes the difference between bound and separated energy components, while `get_ligand_travel()` measures how far the ligand centroid has moved — a diagnostic for detecting docking failures where the ligand escapes the binding site. `get_ligand_grid_scores()` evaluates poses against QSAR scoring grids for pharmacophore-aware assessment, and `get_radius_of_gyration()` quantifies ligand compactness, since ligands tend to bind in extended conformations.

The `grid_functions` module offers lower-level grid-based operations: `grid_score()` evaluates a residue against a `CartGrid`, `grid_rotamer_trials()` selects the optimal rotamer by grid scoring, and `rb_grid_score_atr_rep()` separates attractive and repulsive grid contributions for rigid-body regions. These utilities underpin both the classic protocol's coarse screening and GALigandDock's fast evaluation.

Sources: [ligand_scores.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/ligand_scores.hh#L35-L118), [grid_functions.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/grid_functions.hh#L33-L95)

## Ligand Input Pipeline

Rosetta's ligand docking ingests small molecules through the chemical data layer. The `core/chemical/sdf/` subsystem provides SDF and MOL file parsers supporting both V2000 and V3000 CTAB formats, while the `core/chemical/rdkit/` integration enables conversion between RDKit molecular representations and Rosetta's `MutableResidueType` — the core abstraction for parametrized small molecules. The Gasteiger atom typer (`core/chemical/gasteiger/`) assigns partial charges, and the ring conformer system (`core/chemical/rings/`) provides enumeration of valid ring pucker states.

The function `get_ligand_seqpos()` scans a pose for all non-polymer residues, identifying which residue indices correspond to ligands — essential for any docking operation that needs to determine which chain/jump to manipulate.

Sources: [ligand_functions.hh](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/ligand_functions.hh#L73-L77), [source/src/core/chemical/sdf/](source/src/core/chemical/sdf/), [source/src/core/chemical/rdkit/](source/src/core/chemical/rdkit/)

## Comparison of Docking Paradigms

| Feature | LigandDockProtocol | GALigandDock | HighResDocker |
|---------|-------------------|--------------|---------------|
| **Search strategy** | Monte Carlo + minimization | Multi-stage genetic algorithm | Single-stage MC refinement |
| **Scoring** | Full Rosetta energy function | Pre-computed 3D grids | Full Rosetta energy function |
| **Speed** | Moderate (~minutes/pose) | Fast (~seconds/pose for GA stage) | Moderate |
| **Ligand flexibility** | Full torsion + rigid body | Full torsion + rigid body (gene) | Configurable via MoveMap |
| **Receptor flexibility** | Backbone + side-chain (limited) | Side-chain only (flex SCs in gene) | Side-chain + backbone (configurable) |
| **Best for** | Accurate single-pose docking | High-throughput screening | Protocol composition |
| **RosettaScripts** | Via LigandDockProtocol Mover | Via GALigandDock Mover | Native support |
| **Output metrics** | Interface deltas, travel | dH, RMS, per-component scores | Standard Rosetta scores |

## Application Entry Point

The `ligand_dock_main()` function in `ligand_dock_impl.cc` serves as the application entry point. It instantiates `LigandDockMain` (a subclass of `LigandDockProtocol` that adds native pose handling and enzyme constraint support), configures AtomTreeDiff output precision for compact silent files, and delegates to the JD2 `JobDistributor`. The `LigandDockMain` override of `apply()` adds enzyme design constraints if a constraint file is specified via `-enzdes:cstfile`, automatically enabling coordinate, atom pair, angle, and dihedral constraint weights.

> [!TIP]
> The `ligand_dock` application requires `-run:preserve_header true` — without it, the application exits immediately with an error message. This preserves PDB header information critical for correct ligand parametrization across job distribution.

Sources: [ligand_dock_impl.cc](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/ligand_dock_impl.cc#L57-L80), [ligand_dock_impl.cc](source/src/protocols/ligand_docking/ligand_dock_impl.cc#L164-L190)
