# Ab Initio Folding



Rosetta's **ab initio folding** protocol predicts three-dimensional protein structures from amino acid sequence alone, using fragment assembly guided by a low-resolution centroid representation. The system constructs conformations by repeatedly inserting short peptide fragments (typically 3- and 9-mers) harvested from known structures, accepting or rejecting moves via Monte Carlo criteria against progressively more discriminating score functions. For developers building on or extending this pipeline, understanding the four-stage architecture and its extensible class hierarchy is essential.

## Architectural Overview

The ab initio subsystem lives primarily under `source/src/protocols/abinitio/` and operates through a deep inheritance chain rooted in Rosetta's Mover framework. The core relationship is `moves::Mover` → `Protocol` → `ClassicAbinitio` → `KinematicAbinitio`, with each level adding domain-specific behavior — evaluation hooking, staged score functions, and loop/jump closure respectively. A parallel XML-accessible pathway exists through `AbscriptMover`, which uses the environment/claims system for declarative configuration.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    direction TB
    class Mover {
        <<protocols::moves::Mover>>
        +apply(Pose)
        +clone() MoverOP
    }
    class Protocol {
        <<protocols::abinitio::Protocol>>
        #scorefxn_fa_ : ScoreFunctionOP
        #scorefxn_centroid_ : ScoreFunctionOP
        #use_trRosetta_constraints_ : bool
        +init(Pose)
        +set_fullatom_scorefxn()
        +set_centroid_scorefxn()
    }
    class ClassicAbinitio {
        <<protocols::abinitio::ClassicAbinitio>>
        #stage1_cycles_ : Size
        #stage2_cycles_ : Size
        #stage3_cycles_ : Size
        #stage4_cycles_ : Size
        #stage5_cycles_ : Size
        #mc_ : MonteCarloOP
        #brute_move_small_ : FragmentMoverOP
        #brute_move_large_ : FragmentMoverOP
        #smooth_move_small_ : FragmentMoverOP
        +apply(Pose)
        +set_score_weight(ScoreType, Real, StageID)
        #do_stage1_cycles(Pose) bool
        #do_stage2_cycles(Pose) bool
        #do_stage3_cycles(Pose) bool
        #do_stage4_cycles(Pose) bool
        #prepare_stage1(Pose) bool
        #prepare_stage2(Pose) bool
        #prepare_stage3(Pose) bool
        #prepare_stage4(Pose) bool
    }
    class KinematicAbinitio {
        <<protocols::abinitio::KinematicAbinitio>>
        #bRampChainbreaks_ : bool
        #closure_protocol_ : SlidingWindowLoopClosureOP
        +set_max_seq_sep(Pose, Size)
    }
    class FoldConstraints {
        <<protocols::abinitio::FoldConstraints>>
    }
    class AbscriptMover {
        <<protocols::abinitio::abscript::AbscriptMover>>
        +yield_claims(Pose, DataMap) EnvClaims
        +parse_my_tag(TagCOP, DataMap)
        +provide_xml_schema(XSD)
    }

    class FragmentMover {
        <<protocols::simple_moves::FragmentMover>>
        #fragset_ : FragSetCOP
        #movemap_ : MoveMapCOP
        #insert_map_ : InsertMap
        +apply(Pose, Size) bool
        +apply_at_all_positions(Pose) Size
    }
    class ClassicFragmentMover {
        <<protocols::simple_moves::ClassicFragmentMover>>
        +apply(Pose)
        +set_check_ss(bool)
    }
    class SmoothFragmentMover {
        <<protocols::simple_moves::SmoothFragmentMover>>
    }

    Mover <|-- Protocol
    Protocol <|-- ClassicAbinitio
    FoldConstraints <|-- KinematicAbinitio
    ClassicAbinitio <|-- KinematicAbinitio
    Mover <|-- AbscriptMover
    FragmentMover <|-- ClassicFragmentMover
    FragmentMover <|-- SmoothFragmentMover
    ClassicAbinitio --> FragmentMover : "brute_move_small_, brute_move_large_, smooth_move_small_"
```

Sources: [ClassicAbinitio.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.hh#L80-L165), [Protocol.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/Protocol.hh#L1-L100), [KinematicAbinitio.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/KinematicAbinitio.hh#L1-L80), [AbscriptMover.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/abscript/AbscriptMover.hh#L1-L131)

## The Four-Stage Folding Pipeline

The `ClassicAbinitio` protocol implements a sequential, multi-stage Monte Carlo search. Each stage uses a progressively richer centroid score function and different fragment insertion strategies. The stage progression is encoded as an enum within the class itself.

Sources: [ClassicAbinitio.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.hh#L81-L96)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Extended Chain\n(Centroid Representation)"] --> B["Stage 1\nscore0 — VDW only"]
    B --> C["Stage 2\nscore1 — VDW + pair + env"]
    C --> D["Stage 3\nscore2 ↔ score5 alternating"]
    D --> E["Stage 4\nscore3 — full centroid terms\n+ smooth 3mer insertions"]
    E --> F{"return_centroid?"}
    F -- "Yes" --> G["Centroid Output"]
    F -- "No" --> H["Resolution Switch\nto Full-Atom + Relax"]
    
    style B fill:#f9f,stroke:#333
    style D fill:#ff9,stroke:#333
    style E fill:#9f9,stroke:#333
```

Each stage follows a consistent **prepare-then-cycle** pattern. The `prepare_stageN()` virtual method sets the score function and may modify the pose (e.g., applying constraints, switching weights), while `do_stageN_cycles()` executes the Monte Carlo loop. This design enables fine-grained customization — subclasses can override preparation, the mover composition within a stage, or the cycling logic independently.

Sources: [ClassicAbinitio.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.hh#L259-L326), [ClassicAbinitio.cc](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.cc#L286-L354)

### Stage Parameters

| Stage | Score Function | Fragment Size | Default Cycles | Purpose |
|-------|---------------|---------------|----------------|---------|
| **Stage 1** | `score0` (VDW only) | 9-mer (large) | ~2000 | Rapid chain compaction from extended conformation |
| **Stage 2** | `score1` (VDW + pair + env) | 9-mer (large) | ~2000 | Early secondary structure formation |
| **Stage 3a/3b** | `score2` ↔ `score5` alternating | 3-mer + 9-mer | Tunable loops | Topology search with full centroid scoring |
| **Stage 4** | `score3` (all centroid terms) | 3-mer (smooth) | ~4000 | Refinement with GunnCost-weighted local moves |

The cycle counts are configurable at runtime via the `abinitio::increase_cycles` option and the `set_cycles()` method, which scales all stages by a multiplier. The `set_score_weight()` method allows per-stage weight overrides, where `stage == -1` applies a change globally across all stages. The `prepare_loop_in_stage3()` and `prepare_loop_in_stage4()` hooks are invoked within inner iteration loops, enabling dynamic weight ramping during a single stage.

Sources: [ClassicAbinitio.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.hh#L208-L210), [ClassicAbinitio.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.hh#L314-L326), [ClassicAbinitio.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.hh#L393-L399)

> [!TIP]
> The `recover_low()` method is called after each stage to reset the pose to the best (lowest-energy) conformation encountered during that stage's Monte Carlo trajectory. The set of stages at which recovery occurs is controlled by the `recover_low_stages_` member, configurable via the `-abinitio:recover_low_in_stages` flag. Checkpointing is integrated at stage boundaries via the `CheckPointer` system, allowing recovery from `stage_1` or `stage_2` checkpoints on restart.

Sources: [ClassicAbinitio.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.hh#L246-L247), [ClassicAbinitio.cc](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.cc#L331-L344)

## Fragment Mover Taxonomy

The fragment movers that drive conformational sampling are defined in `source/src/protocols/simple_moves/` and are composed into the ab initio protocol through three named slots. The `FragmentMover` abstract base class manages the fragment set, move map, and insert position bookkeeping. It computes an `InsertMap` and `InsertSize` during `update_insert_map()` to track valid insertion sites, respecting the move map's mobility constraints.

Sources: [FragmentMover.hh](source/src/protocols/simple_moves/FragmentMover.hh#L50-L105)

| Mover Class | Base Class | Sampling Strategy | Typical Role |
|-------------|-----------|-------------------|--------------|
| `ClassicFragmentMover` | `FragmentMover` | Uniform random selection from frame | `brute_move_small_`, `brute_move_large_` |
| `SmoothFragmentMover` | `FragmentMover` | `GunnCost`-biased local fragment selection | `smooth_move_small_` |
| `SymmetricFragmentMover` | `ClassicFragmentMover` | Uniform + symmetry replication | Symmetric folding |
| `LoggedFragmentMover` | `ClassicFragmentMover` | Uniform + fragment logging | Debug/tracing |
| `ResTypeFragmentMover` | `FragmentMover` | Residue-type restricted insertion | Constrained folding |

The constructor in `ClassicAbinitio` selects among these implementations based on command-line flags. When `abinitio::symmetry_residue` is set, `SymmetricFragmentMover` instances are created for all three slots. When `abinitio::log_frags` is active (requires `abinitio::debug`), `LoggedFragmentMover` is used for brute-force slots. Otherwise, standard `ClassicFragmentMover` and `SmoothFragmentMover` (with `GunnCost`) are instantiated. The `end_bias` parameter, defaulting to 30.0, is applied uniformly across all three movers to penalize fragment insertions near chain termini.

Sources: [ClassicAbinitio.cc](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.cc#L164-L219)

## The ClassicAbinitio Execution Flow

The `apply()` method in `ClassicAbinitio` orchestrates the full pipeline. After delegating to `Parent::apply()`, it optionally adds trRosetta-generated distance constraints (when compiled with TensorFlow), then proceeds through stages 1–4 sequentially. Each stage block follows an identical pattern: check skip flag → start profiler → call `prepare_stageN()` → execute `do_stageN_cycles()` → call `recover_low()` → dump MC counters → checkpoint. A `success` flag gates progression — if any stage returns failure (via `FAIL_RETRY`), the entire protocol aborts early.

Sources: [ClassicAbinitio.cc](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.cc#L286-L354), [ClassicAbinitio.cc](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.cc#L411-L457)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START["apply(Pose)"] --> PARENT["Parent::apply(pose)"]
    PARENT --> DRY{"dry_run?"}
    DRY -- Yes --> END["Return"]
    DRY -- No --> TR{"use_trRosetta\nconstraints?"}
    TR -- Yes --> ADDCST["Add trRosetta constraints\nto pose"]
    TR -- No --> S1
    ADDCST --> S1
    
    S1{"bSkipStage1?"} -->|No| PREP1["prepare_stage1()"]
    PREP1 --> DO1["do_stage1_cycles()"]
    DO1 --> REC1["recover_low(STAGE_1)"]
    REC1 --> CHK1["checkpoint('stage_1')"]
    
    S1 -->|Yes| S2
    CHK1 --> S2{"bSkipStage2?"}
    S2 -->|No| PREP2["prepare_stage2()"]
    PREP2 --> DO2["do_stage2_cycles()"]
    DO2 --> REC2["recover_low(STAGE_2)"]
    REC2 --> S3
    
    S2 -->|Yes| S3{"bSkipStage3?"}
    S3 -->|No| PREP3["prepare_stage3()"]
    PREP3 --> DO3["do_stage3_cycles()"]
    DO3 --> REC3["recover_low(STAGE_3b)"]
    REC3 --> S4
    
    S3 -->|Yes| S4{"bSkipStage4?"}
    S4 -->|No| PREP4["prepare_stage4()"]
    PREP4 --> DO4["do_stage4_cycles()"]
    DO4 --> DONE["Protocol Complete"]
    S4 -->|Yes| DONE
```

> [!TIP]
> Stage 3 is unique in that it alternates between two score functions (`score2` and `score5`) across inner loop iterations. The `prepare_loop_in_stage3()` hook — called at the start of each inner iteration — is responsible for switching the active score function. This design supports the "temperature annealing" strategy where weaker scoring (score5) permits exploration while stronger scoring (score2) enforces progressively tighter geometric constraints. The `replace_scorefxn()` virtual method provides a final opportunity to modify weight terms before each iteration begins.

Sources: [ClassicAbinitio.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.hh#L249-L250), [ClassicAbinitio.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.hh#L314-L319), [ClassicAbinitio.cc](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.cc#L416-L452)

## KinematicAbinitio: Loop Closure and Jump Sampling

`KinematicAbinitio` extends `FoldConstraints` (which itself extends `ClassicAbinitio`) to add **kinematic loop closure** and **jump move sampling** for multi-domain or template-guided folding. The critical extensions are:

1. **Jump-aware stage movers** — `stage1_mover()`, `stage2_mover()`, `stage3_mover()`, and `stage4_mover()` are all overridden to wrap the standard fragment trial mover with jump moves via `create_jump_moves()`, which combines the jump mover with the standard backbone moves into a `SequenceMover`.

2. **Chainbreak weight ramping** — `bRampChainbreaks_` and `bOverlapChainbreaks_` flags control progressive ramping of chainbreak penalties during stages 3 and 4, ensuring that loop geometry tightens gradually as the fold matures.

3. **Loop closure protocol** — An optional `SlidingWindowLoopClosureOP` can be attached via `closure_protocol()`. When present, it is invoked during stage preparation to close kinematic loop gaps opened by jump moves.

4. **Maximum sequence separation** — The `set_max_seq_sep()` method controls the distance constraint cutoff for residue pairs, a parameter critical for contact-order-based folding. This is overridden from `FoldConstraints`.

Sources: [KinematicAbinitio.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/KinematicAbinitio.hh#L52-L140)

## AbscriptMover: Declarative RosettaScripts Integration

For XML-driven workflows, `AbscriptMover` provides an alternative entry point that uses Rosetta's environment/claims system. Rather than hardcoding a fixed stage sequence, `AbscriptMover` parses XML tags to dynamically register sub-movers and preparers against specific `StageID` values. The `parse_my_tag()` method processes sub-tags, while `register_submover()` and `register_preparer()` associate mover instances with stage sets and optional weights. The `calculate_iterations()` method computes the number of Monte Carlo iterations per stage based on pose properties.

`AbscriptMover` inherits from `ClientMover` (not from `ClassicAbinitio`), meaning it uses a fundamentally different coordination mechanism — environment claims and initialization gates rather than direct sequential invocation. It delegates stage execution to `AbscriptStageMover` instances stored in a `std::map<StageID, AbscriptStageMoverOP>`. This design supports fully declarative folding protocol composition, where users specify fragment sources, movers, and stage-level parameters entirely through XML without C++ intervention.

Sources: [AbscriptMover.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/abscript/AbscriptMover.hh#L47-L131)

## Specialized Protocol Variants

The ab initio module contains several specialized variants that extend the core pipeline for specific structural contexts:

| Variant | Purpose | Key Extension |
|---------|---------|---------------|
| `DoubleLayerKinematicAbinitio` | Two-pass folding with coarse-to-fine refinement | Dual-pass stage execution |
| `MembraneAbinitio` | Transmembrane protein folding | Membrane-specific score functions |
| `ConstraintFragmentSampler` | Folding guided by experimental constraints | External constraint integration |
| `IterativeAbrelax` | Iterative centroid ↔ full-atom switching | `IterativeBase` multi-resolution cycles |
| `FragmentSampler` | Standalone fragment sampling without full pipeline | Lightweight single-stage execution |
| `DomainAssembly` | Multi-domain assembly from individual ab initio predictions | Domain-level docking and assembly |
| `BrokeringFold` (`BrokerMain`) | Fragment broker-based conformational sampling | Constraint broker pattern for fragment selection |

Sources: [source/src/protocols/abinitio/](source/src/protocols/abinitio/)

## trRosetta Constraint Integration

When Rosetta is compiled with TensorFlow support (`extras=tensorflow`), `ClassicAbinitio` supports injecting inter-residue distance and orientation constraints predicted by the trRosetta neural network. The `Protocol` base class holds a `trRosettaConstraintGeneratorOP` and a boolean flag `use_trRosetta_constraints_`. During `apply()`, if this flag is set, constraints are generated and added to the pose before stage 1 begins, biasing the fragment assembly toward the predicted contact map. The `supports_trRosetta_constraints()` virtual method is overridden to `true` in `ClassicAbinitio`, while the base `Protocol` class returns `false` — a pattern that allows downstream protocols to opt in selectively.

Sources: [Protocol.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/Protocol.hh#L82-L100), [Protocol.hh](source/src/protocols/abinitio/Protocol.hh#L164-L175), [ClassicAbinitio.cc](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.cc#L300-L311)

## Command-Line Options

`ClassicAbinitio::register_options()` exposes the key runtime-tunable parameters. These must be registered before `core::init::init()` by calling `ClassicAbinitio::register_options()` from the application's main function.

| Option Flag | Type | Purpose |
|------------|------|---------|
| `-abinitio:increase_cycles` | Real | Multiplier for all stage cycle counts |
| `-abinitio:smooth_cycles_only` | Boolean | Skip stages 1–3, run only stage 4 |
| `-abinitio:debug` | Boolean | Enable debug output and structure dumps |
| `-abinitio:skip_convergence_check` | Boolean | Disable convergence-based early termination |
| `-abinitio:log_frags` | Boolean | Enable fragment insertion logging |
| `-abinitio:only_stage1` | Boolean | Execute only stage 1 |
| `-abinitio:end_bias` | Real | Bias penalty for terminal fragment insertions (default: 30.0) |
| `-abinitio:symmetry_residue` | Integer | Enable symmetric folding with given pivot residue |
| `-abinitio:vdw_weight_stage1` | Real | Override VDW weight during stage 1 |
| `-abinitio:override_vdw_all_stages` | Real | Override VDW weight across all stages |
| `-abinitio:recover_low_in_stages` | IntegerVector | Stages at which low-energy recovery occurs |
| `-abinitio:close_chbrk` | Boolean | Enable chainbreak closure during stage 4 |

Sources: [ClassicAbinitio.cc](source/src/protocols/abinitio/ClassicAbinitio.cc#L110-L126)

## Key Extension Points for Developers

The `ClassicAbinitio` class is designed for extensibility through well-defined virtual methods organized by granularity level. Understanding which hook to override is critical for building custom folding protocols.

**Mover-level customization** — Override `stage1_mover()` through `stage4_mover()` to inject custom trial movers (e.g., backbone perturbation moves, constraint-aware movers). The `create_bb_moves()` helper in `KinematicAbinitio` demonstrates this pattern by wrapping standard fragment trials with jump perturbation moves.

**Score function customization** — Override `set_default_scores()` to change the patch files loaded for each stage, or override `replace_scorefxn()` to dynamically adjust weights during transitions. The `set_score_weight()` public API allows post-construction weight adjustments without subclassing.

**Stage lifecycle customization** — Override `prepare_stageN()` to modify pose state before sampling (e.g., adding/removing constraints, changing fold trees), or override `prepare_loop_in_stageN()` for per-iteration adjustments within a stage's inner loop.

**Full protocol replacement** — For XML-based protocols, use `AbscriptMover` with custom `AbscriptStageMover` implementations registered per-stage, avoiding C++ inheritance entirely.

For developers needing the fragment supply chain itself, the [Fragment Picking System](26-fragment-picking-system) provides the upstream machinery for generating the 3-mer and 9-mer fragment libraries consumed by these protocols. The scoring functions used at each stage are detailed in [ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework), and the Monte Carlo acceptance criteria governing trial evaluation are described in [Monte Carlo Sampling](12-monte-carlo-sampling). For ML-augmented folding that bypasses the classical fragment pipeline entirely, see [trRosetta Deep Learning](21-trrosetta-deep-learning).

# trRosetta Deep Learning



This page documents Rosetta's C++ integration of the **trRosetta** deep learning method — a transformer-based protein structure prediction pipeline originally published by Yang et al. (2020) and subsequently ported into Rosetta by Vikram K. Mulligan. The implementation wraps TensorFlow inference behind Rosetta-native abstractions, converting predicted inter-residue geometry distributions into Rosetta constraints that drive gradient-based folding. The entire subsystem is gated behind the `USE_TENSORFLOW` compile-time flag, making it an optional but deeply integrated ML extension.

Sources: [trRosettaProtocolBase.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/trRosettaProtocolBase.hh#L1-L100), [trRosettaProtocolMover.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/movers/trRosettaProtocolMover.hh#L10-L13)

## Architectural Overview

The trRosetta subsystem is decomposed into two logical layers: a **TensorFlow inference core** (`protocols/trRosetta/`) that encapsulates the neural network session, MSA preprocessing, and output tensor management; and a **Rosetta protocol layer** (`protocols/trRosetta_protocols/`) that exposes this functionality through Rosetta's standard `Mover` and `ConstraintGenerator` interfaces. This separation ensures that the low-level TensorFlow interaction can evolve independently of the protocol-level orchestration.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Rosetta Protocol Layer"
        TM["trRosettaProtocolMover<br/>(Full Folding Protocol)"]
        CG["trRosettaConstraintGenerator<br/>(Constraint Generation)"]
    end

    subgraph "TensorFlow Inference Core"
        PB["trRosettaProtocolBase"]
        PV1["trRosettaProtocol_v1"]
        OB["trRosettaOutputsBase"]
        OV1["trRosettaOutputs_v1"]
        MSA["trRosettaMultipleSequenceAlignment"]
    end

    subgraph "Rosetta Infrastructure"
        TFB["RosettaTensorflowProtocolBase"]
        MM["MinMover / FastRelax"]
        SF["ScoreFunction"]
    end

    TM --> CG
    TM --> MM
    CG --> PV1
    PV1 --> PB
    PV1 --> OB
    PV1 -.-> OV1
    PB --> TFB
    CG --> MSA
    PV1 --> MSA
    OV1 --> OB
    MM --> SF
```

The `trRosettaProtocolMover` orchestrates the complete folding pipeline — from MSA ingestion through staged constraint-guided minimization to optional fullatom refinement — while `trRosettaConstraintGenerator` offers a modular, reusable component that can be embedded in arbitrary RosettaScripts workflows. Both consume the inference core, which is rooted in Rosetta's `RosettaTensorflowProtocolBase` abstract class.

Sources: [trRosettaProtocolBase.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/trRosettaProtocolBase.hh#L37-L97), [trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/constraint_generators/trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh#L44-L68)

## TensorFlow Inference Core

### Protocol Hierarchy

The inference core follows a versioned inheritance pattern. `trRosettaProtocolBase` extends `RosettaTensorflowProtocolBase` and declares the contract that all concrete trRosetta models must fulfill: MSA file loading, TensorFlow session initialization, and output generation. The sole concrete implementation, `trRosettaProtocol_v1`, provides the Yang et al. 2020 model.

The base class manages two key pieces of state behind `#ifdef USE_TENSORFLOW` guards: a `RosettaTensorflowSessionContainerCOP` for the live TensorFlow session, and a `trRosettaMultipleSequenceAlignmentOP` for the parsed MSA data. The `set_input_msa_file()` method triggers an immediate disk read and populates the MSA object, while `init_tensorflow_session()` is called once during construction to load the serialized model graph from disk.

Sources: [trRosettaProtocolBase.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/trRosettaProtocolBase.hh#L37-L97), [trRosettaProtocol_v1.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/trRosettaProtocol_v1.hh#L40-L95)

### MSA Input Processing

The `trRosettaMultipleSequenceAlignment` class is responsible for transforming a raw multiple sequence alignment file into the three-tensor input format expected by the TensorFlow model. Its constructor takes a string of file contents and produces a `vector1` of `RosettaTensorflowTensorContainer<int32_t>` containing: (1) a 1-D tensor for the number of columns (sequence length), (2) a 1-D tensor for the number of rows (number of sequences), and (3) a 2-D rows×columns tensor with one-hot encodings of each aligned residue. Lowercase characters in the alignment — which typically represent insertions relative to the query sequence — are stripped during preprocessing via the private `remove_lcase()` method.

Sources: [trRosettaMultipleSequenceAlignment.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/trRosettaMultipleSequenceAlignment.hh#L36-L74)

### Output Tensor Structure

The output side mirrors the input versioning strategy. `trRosettaOutputsBase` is a minimal `VirtualBase` subclass providing only cloning semantics. `trRosettaOutputs_v1` carries the full set of geometry predictions for version 1, stored as four `RosettaTensorflowTensorContainer<float>` objects corresponding to the four predicted geometric distributions.

Sources: [trRosettaOutputsBase.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/trRosettaOutputsBase.hh#L28-L43), [trRosettaOutputs_v1.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/trRosettaOutputs_v1.hh#L41-L131)

## Inter-Residue Geometry Predictions

The v1 model predicts four types of inter-residue geometric probability distributions for every pair of residues in the input sequence. These are the core geometric descriptors that enable gradient-based structure prediction. Each distribution is discretized into bins, and individual bin probabilities can be accessed through 1-based index accessors.

| Distribution | Atom Definition | Symmetry | Bins | Bin Count Macro |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Distance** | Cβ–Cβ distance | Symmetric (dist(a,b) = dist(b,a)) | 37 | `trRosetta_v1_expected_dist_bins` |
| **Phi (ϕ)** | Angle CA₁–CB₁–CB₂ | Asymmetric (ϕ(a,b) ≠ ϕ(b,a)) | 13 | `trRosetta_v1_expected_phi_bins` |
| **Theta (θ)** | Dihedral N₁–CA₂–CB₁–CB₂ | Asymmetric (θ(a,b) ≠ θ(b,a)) | 25 | `trRosetta_v1_expected_theta_bins` |
| **Omega (ω)** | Dihedral CA₁–CB₁–CB₂–CA₂ | Symmetric (ω(a,b) = ω(b,a)) | 25 | `trRosetta_v1_expected_omega_bins` |

An important caveat: the **phi** and **omega** predicted by trRosetta are **not** the backbone dihedral torsions of the same names. They are inter-residue side-chain orientation angles. The phi distribution describes the angle at CB₂ between CA₁–CB₁ and CB₂ (with CB₂ as the vertex), while omega describes the dihedral defined by CA₁–CB₁–CB₂–CA₂. This distinction is critical when interpreting constraint outputs.

> [!TIP]
> Symmetric distributions (distance, omega) generate one constraint per residue pair, while asymmetric distributions (phi, theta) generate two constraints per pair (one for (i,j) and one for (j,i)), unless i == j which is always skipped.

Sources: [trRosettaOutputs_v1.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/trRosettaOutputs_v1.hh#L34-L131), [trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/constraint_generators/trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh#L98-L122)

## Constraint Generation

### The trRosettaConstraintGenerator

The `trRosettaConstraintGenerator` is the bridge between TensorFlow inference outputs and Rosetta's constraint system. It extends `protocols::constraint_generator::ConstraintGenerator`, making it directly usable in RosettaScripts XML as well as programmatically. Its `apply()` method takes a `Pose` and returns a `ConstraintCOPs` vector.

The generator is lazy: the neural network is only executed when `apply()` is first called (via the private `load_msa_and_run_neural_network()` method). The `reset()` method invalidates cached outputs, forcing re-execution on the next call. This design is important for workflows where the same generator might be used with different poses or settings.

Four boolean flags control which constraint types are generated, all enabled by default:

| Flag | Constraint Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `generate_dist_constraints_` | Cβ–Cβ atom pair distance constraints | `true` |
| `generate_omega_constraints_` | CA₁–CB₁–CB₂–CA₂ dihedral constraints | `true` |
| `generate_theta_constraints_` | N₁–CA₂–CB₁–CB₂ dihedral constraints | `true` |
| `generate_phi_constraints_` | CA₁–CB₁–CB₂ angle constraints | `true` |

Each constraint type has an independent probability cutoff that controls which predicted bins are translated into Rosetta constraints, and an independent weight that scales the constraint's contribution to the score function.

Sources: [trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/constraint_generators/trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh#L86-L141), [trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/constraint_generators/trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh#L293-L354)

### Probability Cutoffs and Constraint Weights

The generator uses per-distribution probability thresholds to filter noisy predictions. Only bins exceeding the cutoff are translated into constraints. The defaults are tuned to balance constraint density with prediction confidence:

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `dist_prob_cutoff_` | 0.05 | Probability threshold for distance constraints |
| `omega_prob_cutoff_` | 0.55 | Probability threshold for omega dihedral constraints |
| `theta_prob_cutoff_` | 0.55 | Probability threshold for theta dihedral constraints |
| `phi_prob_cutoff_` | 0.65 | Probability threshold for phi angle constraints |
| `distance_constraint_weight_` | 1.0 | Weight for distance constraints in the score function |
| `omega_constraint_weight_` | 1.0 | Weight for omega dihedral constraints |
| `theta_constraint_weight_` | 1.0 | Weight for theta dihedral constraints |
| `phi_constraint_weight_` | 1.0 | Weight for phi angle constraints |

The notably lower distance cutoff (0.05 vs 0.55–0.65 for angle/dihedral constraints) reflects the larger bin count and sharper probability distributions typical of distance predictions.

Sources: [trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/constraint_generators/trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh#L324-L354)

## Full Folding Protocol: trRosettaProtocolMover

### Protocol Phases

The `trRosettaProtocolMover` implements the complete trRosetta folding pipeline as a single Rosetta `Mover`. This is the entry point for end-to-end structure prediction. The protocol proceeds through several distinct phases, each orchestrated by private helper methods.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Load Sequence<br/>(FASTA or inline)"] --> B["Validate Sequence"]
    B --> C["Build Extended Pose<br/>(Centroid)"]
    C --> D["Backbone Randomization"]
    D --> E{"Gly→Ala mutation?"}
    E -->|Yes| F["Mutate Gly to Ala<br/>(centroid phase)"]
    E -->|No| G["Skip mutation"]
    F --> H["Generate trRosetta<br/>Constraints"]
    G --> H
    H --> I{"Minimization Mode"}
    I -->|classic0| J["Stage 1: Short-range<br/>Stage 2: +Medium<br/>Stage 3: +Long-range"]
    I -->|classic1| K["Stage 1: Short+Medium<br/>Stage 2: +Long-range"]
    I -->|classic2| L["All constraints<br/>simultaneously"]
    J --> M{"Fullatom<br/>Refinement?"}
    K --> M
    L --> M
    M -->|Yes| N["FastRelax with<br/>shifted cutoffs"]
    M -->|No| O["Output Centroid"]
    N --> P["Output Fullatom"]
```

> [!TIP]
> The Mover defers MSA file reading to `apply()` time rather than construction time, avoiding disk I/O during mover registration. However, the `trRosettaConstraintGenerator`'s neural network execution is cached after the first `apply()` call — set a new MSA file to trigger `reset()` and re-execution.

Sources: [trRosettaProtocolMover.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/movers/trRosettaProtocolMover.hh#L69-L72), [trRosettaProtocolMover.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/movers/trRosettaProtocolMover.hh#L374-L499)

### Backbone Randomization Modes

The initial conformation is generated by randomizing backbone dihedrals of the extended pose. Three strategies are available, enumerated by `trRosettaProtocolBackboneRandomizationMode`:

| Mode | Enum Value | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **classic** | 1 | The original Yang et al. method. Matches the published protocol exactly. |
| **ramachandran** | 2 | Randomization biased by Ramachandran preferences of each amino acid. Supports configurable cis-probability for pre-proline and non-pre-proline positions. |
| **bins** | 3 | Randomization based on observed frequency of residue i in bin X and residue i+1 in bin Y (φ/ψ bin co-occurrence). |

The `classic` mode is the default and the one used in the original publication. The `ramachandran` and `bins` modes provide alternative sampling distributions that may improve convergence for specific protein families.

Sources: [trRosettaProtocolMover.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/movers/trRosettaProtocolMover.hh#L45-L55)

### Staged Constraint-Guided Minimization

The core of the trRosetta protocol is a staged minimization where constraints are progressively added based on sequence separation. This hierarchical approach mirrors the physics of protein folding: short-range interactions form first, then medium-range, and finally long-range contacts drive the final topology.

Three minimization modes are available via `trRosettaProtocolBackboneMinimizationMode`:

| Mode | Enum Value | Constraint Stages |
|---|---|---|
| **classic0** | 1 | Stage 1: short-range only → Stage 2: +medium-range → Stage 3: +long-range |
| **classic1** | 2 | Stage 1: short+medium-range → Stage 2: +long-range |
| **classic2** | 3 | All constraints applied simultaneously in a single stage |

The `add_constraints_to_pose()` private method filters the full constraint set by sequence separation range for each stage. It also accepts a `skip_glycine_positions` flag — when enabled alongside `mutate_gly_to_ala_`, glycine constraints are excluded during the centroid phase to avoid biasing the small side chain. Each stage uses a separate `MinMover` with its own `ScoreFunction`, allowing per-stage weight tuning via `set_scorefunction_for_minimization_stage()`.

Sources: [trRosettaProtocolMover.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/movers/trRosettaProtocolMover.hh#L57-L67), [trRosettaProtocolMover.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/movers/trRosettaProtocolMover.hh#L474-L499)

### Fullatom Refinement

After centroid minimization, an optional fullatom refinement step applies Rosetta's `FastRelax` protocol. This step is enabled by default (`fullatom_refinement_ = true`). During refinement, the probability cutoffs are shifted by an offset parameter passed to `generate_trRosetta_constraints()`, allowing tighter constraint thresholds for the more physically accurate all-atom representation. The score function for refinement is configured separately via `set_scorefunction_for_fullatom_refinement()`, which automatically enables `atom_pair_constraint`, `dihedral_constraint`, and `angle_constraint` score terms if they are absent in the loaded weights file.

Sources: [trRosettaProtocolMover.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/movers/trRosettaProtocolMover.hh#L226-L260), [trRosettaProtocolMover.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/movers/trRosettaProtocolMover.hh#L384-L392)

## Build and Configuration

The entire trRosetta subsystem requires the `USE_TENSORFLOW` compile-time flag. Without it, all TensorFlow-dependent code paths are compiled out via `#ifdef` guards, and the protocol classes reduce to empty shells with stub methods. This means Rosetta can be built without TensorFlow for standard structural biology workflows while still maintaining source-level compatibility.

The TensorFlow model graphs and associated data are stored in `database/protocol_data/tensorflow_graphs/`, which serves as the repository for all TensorFlow-based protocol models in Rosetta. The trRosetta-specific model data is loaded at session initialization time by `trRosettaProtocol_v1::init_tensorflow_session()`.

Sources: [trRosettaProtocolBase.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/trRosettaProtocolBase.hh#L22-L28), [tensorflow_graphs directory](database/protocol_data/tensorflow_graphs/)

## RosettaScripts Integration

Both the `trRosettaProtocolMover` and `trRosettaConstraintGenerator` support RosettaScripts XML configuration. The Mover registers itself through the standard `MoverCreator` pattern (see [trRosettaProtocolMoverCreator.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/movers/trRosettaProtocolMoverCreator.hh)), while the ConstraintGenerator registers through `ConstraintGeneratorCreator` (see [trRosettaConstraintGeneratorCreator.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/constraint_generators/trRosettaConstraintGeneratorCreator.hh)). Both classes implement `provide_xml_schema()` for XSD validation and `parse_my_tag()` for XML attribute parsing.

The standalone constraint generator is particularly useful in composite protocols where trRosetta predictions augment Rosetta's native constraint system without invoking the full folding pipeline. For example, it can be combined with Rosetta's ab initio or comparative modeling protocols to provide ML-guided restraints.

Sources: [trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/constraint_generators/trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh#L70-L80), [trRosettaProtocolMover.hh](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/movers/trRosettaProtocolMover.hh#L135-L160)

## Source File Reference

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| [`trRosettaProtocolBase.hh/cc`](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/) | Abstract base for TensorFlow protocols; manages MSA and session state |
| [`trRosettaProtocol_v1.hh/cc`](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/) | Concrete v1 model; loads graph and executes inference |
| [`trRosettaOutputsBase.hh/cc`](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/) | Abstract output container |
| [`trRosettaOutputs_v1.hh/cc`](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/) | V1 output tensors (dist, phi, theta, omega) with bin accessors |
| [`trRosettaMultipleSequenceAlignment.hh/cc`](source/src/protocols/trRosetta/) | MSA parser and one-hot tensor constructor |
| [`trRosettaConstraintGenerator.hh/cc`](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/constraint_generators/) | ConstraintGenerator bridging NN outputs to Rosetta constraints |
| [`trRosettaConstraintGeneratorCreator.hh`](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/constraint_generators/) | Factory registration for RosettaScripts |
| [`trRosettaProtocolMover.hh/cc`](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/movers/) | Full folding protocol as a Rosetta Mover |
| [`trRosettaProtocolMoverCreator.hh`](source/src/protocols/trRosetta_protocols/movers/) | Factory registration for RosettaScripts |

# ProteinMPNN Integration



Rosetta's ProteinMPNN integration embeds the Dauparas et al. deep learning inverse folding model directly into the native C++ framework via LibTorch (PyTorch's C++ API), enabling sequence design and per-residue probability estimation as first-class protocol operations. This integration is conditionally compiled behind `#ifdef USE_TORCH` and requires building Rosetta with `extras=pytorch`.

## Architectural Overview

The integration is organized into three conceptual layers: a **core neural network interface**, a **Mover for sequence threading**, and a **SimpleMetric for probability extraction**. Together they bridge Rosetta's [Pose and Conformation](8-pose-and-conformation) data structures to the ProteinMPNN TorchScript model loaded once from the Rosetta database.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "User-Facing Protocol Layer"
        PM["ProteinMPNNMover<br/>(Mover)"]
        PPM["ProteinMPNNProbabilitiesMetric<br/>(SimpleMetric)"]
    end

    subgraph "Core NN Interface"
        PN["ProteinMPNN<br/>(Singleton)"]
        PO["ProteinMPNNOptions<br/>(Config Struct)"]
    end

    subgraph "Tensor Conversion"
        UT["util.hh/cc<br/>(Pose → Tensor)"]
    end

    subgraph "External Dependencies"
        TS["TorchScript Model<br/>ProteinMPNN.pt"]
        DB["Rosetta Database<br/>protocol_data/protein_mpnn/"]
    end

    PM -->|"creates options"| PO
    PM -->|"calls sample()"| PN
    PPM -->|"calls get_probabilities_and_logits()"| PN
    PO -->|"passed to"| PN
    PN -->|"converts Pose → Tensors"| UT
    PN -->|"loads once"| DB
    DB -->|"serves"| TS
    PN -->|"invokes model"| TS
    PM -->|"threads sequence"| STM["SimpleThreadingMover"]
```

## Core Neural Network Interface: The `ProteinMPNN` Singleton

The `ProteinMPNN` class ([ProteinMPNN.hh](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNN.hh#L87-L109)) is implemented as a `utility::SingletonBase<ProteinMPNN>`, guaranteeing that the pre-trained TorchScript model is loaded exactly once per process lifetime. The model file — `ProteinMPNN.pt` — is located in the Rosetta database at `protocol_data/protein_mpnn/` and loaded via `basic::database::full_name()` in [ProteinMPNN.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNN.cc#L213-L220).

The singleton exposes three inference methods:

| Method | Signature | Purpose |
|--------|-----------|---------|
| `sample` | `(Pose, Options) → string` | Sample a single sequence from the model |
| `sample` | `(Pose) → string` | Sample with default options (temperature 0.1, all positions designable) |
| `sample_batch` | `(Pose, Options) → vector1<string>` | Sample multiple sequences (currently batch_size=1 only) |
| `get_probabilities_and_logits` | `(Pose, Options, probs_map, logits_map) → void` | Extract per-residue probability and logit tensors |

The inference pipeline follows a precise sequence: option validation via `verify_options()`, tensor preparation via `generate_sample_inputs()` and `generate_sample_optional_inputs()`, method dispatch (choosing between `sample` and `tied_sample` based on whether tied positions exist), and output parsing from the returned dictionary containing keys `"S"` (sampled sequences) and `"probs"` (probability tensors) as shown in [ProteinMPNN.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNN.cc#L59-L113).

### The `ProteinMPNNOptions` Configuration Struct

The `ProteinMPNNOptions` struct ([ProteinMPNN.hh](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNN.hh#L39-L82)) encapsulates all configurable inference parameters. It is **pose-dependent**: the constructor requires a `Pose` reference to initialize mask arrays with the correct dimensions. Defaults are established in the `reset()` method at [ProteinMPNN.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNN.cc#L411-L455):

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `sequence` | `string` | Pose sequence (non-protein → 'X') | Starting sequence; unrecognized residues become 'X' |
| `coord_mask` | `vector1<bool>` | All true (protein only) | Which residue coordinates to pass; non-protein residues masked to `false` |
| `chain_mask` | `vector1<bool>` | All true | Which chains to predict; indexed by chain ID (not PDB letter) |
| `pos_mask` | `vector1<bool>` | All true (protein only) | Which positions are designable |
| `omit_AAs` | `vector1<char>` | `{'X'}` | Globally disallowed amino acid types |
| `omit_AAs_pos` | `vector1<vector1<char>>` | Per-position `{'X'}` | Position-specific disallowed types |
| `bias_AAs` | `vector1<Real>` | All zeros (length 21) | Global amino acid biases |
| `temperature` | `Real` | `0.1` | MCMC sampling temperature; >1.0 triggers a warning |
| `tied_positions` | `vector1<vector1<Size>>` | Empty | Groups of residues forced to share identity |
| `batch_size` | `Size` | `1` | Currently only 1 is supported |
| `deterministic_flag` | `bool` | `false` | When true, overrides temperature for greedy decoding |

> [!TIP]
> The `AA_ALPHABET` constant in [util.hh](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/util.hh#L49) is defined as `"ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWYX"` — note the 21st character is the unknown residue 'X'. Every `omit_AAs` configuration **must** include 'X', which the validator enforces at [ProteinMPNN.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNN.cc#L359-L363). This prevents nonsensical predictions of unknown residue types.

## Pose-to-Tensor Conversion Pipeline

The `util.hh`/`util.cc` module ([util.hh](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/util.hh), [util.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/util.cc)) contains the complete data marshaling layer that translates Rosetta's in-memory protein representation into the tensor format expected by the TorchScript model. Each conversion function produces a `torch::Tensor` with the correct shape and dtype.

The critical backbone coordinate extraction operates on the first four atom indices per residue (N, CA, C, O) as shown in [util.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/util.cc#L43-L78):

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Rosetta Pose"
        CONF["Conformation"]
    end

    subgraph "Tensor Conversion (util.cc)"
        BB["bb_coords_to_tensor<br/>(batch × nres × 4 × 3, float32)"]
        SEQ["seq_to_tensor<br/>(batch × nres, int64)"]
        CE["chain_encoding_to_tensor<br/>(batch × nres, int64)"]
        RI["residue_idx_to_tensor<br/>(batch × nres, int64)"]
        CM["coord_mask_to_tensor<br/>(batch × nres, float32)"]
        PM["pos_mask_to_tensor<br/>(batch × nres, float32)"]
        OM["omit_AAs_to_tensor<br/>(21, float32)"]
        TP["convert_tied_positions<br/>(List of List of int64)"]
    end

    CONF --> BB
    CONF --> SEQ
    CONF --> CE
    CONF --> RI

    BB -->|"Input 0"| MODEL["TorchScript Model"]
    SEQ -->|"Input 2"| MODEL
    CE -->|"Input 4"| MODEL
    RI -->|"Input 5"| MODEL
    CM -->|"Input 6"| MODEL
    OM -->|"Input 7"| MODEL
    PM -->|"Input 9"| MODEL
    TP -->|"Input 10"| MODEL
```

Notably, `residue_idx_to_tensor` at [util.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/util.cc#L118-L130) adds a 100-position offset per chain break (`residue_index + 100 * (chain_id - 1)`), mirroring the Python implementation's convention for distinguishing chain boundaries. Non-protein residues receive zero-filled coordinates and are automatically masked out of both `coord_mask` and `pos_mask` during `ProteinMPNNOptions::reset()` at [ProteinMPNN.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNN.cc#L449-L453).

## ProteinMPNNMover: Sequence Design as a Protocol Step

The `ProteinMPNNMover` ([ProteinMPNNMover.hh](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNNMover.hh), [ProteinMPNNMover.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNNMover.cc)) integrates with Rosetta's [Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy) as a standard `protocols::moves::Mover`, making it directly usable in RosettaScripts XML, PyRosetta, and programmatic C++ workflows. Its `apply()` method orchestrates a multi-phase pipeline:

1. **Option construction** — Creates `ProteinMPNNOptions` from the pose
2. **ResidueSelector application** — Converts `design_selector` and `coord_selector` into boolean masks
3. **Tied position resolution** — Translates `TiedPositions` subtags (each specifying comma-separated ResidueSelectors) into residue index lists
4. **TaskOperations integration** — If a `TaskFactory` is provided, per-residue allowed types are converted to `omit_AAs_pos` constraints
5. **Symmetry handling** — For symmetric poses, automatically ties equivalent residues across subunits and replicates masks/taskops
6. **Inference** — Calls `ProteinMPNN::get_instance()->sample()`
7. **Sequence threading** — Uses `SimpleThreadingMover` with packing disabled to thread the predicted sequence onto the pose backbone

The symmetry support at [ProteinMPNNMover.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNNMover.cc#L228-L248) is particularly important: it iterates over independent residues in the asymmetric unit, collects symmetric clones across all subunits, pushes each group as a tied set, and replicates the design mask and `omit_AAs_pos` to all symmetric copies.

### RosettaScripts XML Interface

The Mover exposes the following XML attributes, defined in `provide_xml_schema()` at [ProteinMPNNMover.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNNMover.cc#L331-L371):

```xml
<ROSETTASCRIPTS>
    <RESIDUE_SELECTORS>
        <Index name="core" resnums="10-30,45-60"/>
        <Index name="surface" resnums="1-9,31-44,61-80"/>
    </RESIDUE_SELECTORS>
    <MOVERS>
        <ProteinMPNNMover name="design_mpnn"
            temperature="0.1"
            omit_AAs="XC"
            design_selector="core"
            coord_selector="surface"
            deterministic_flag="false">
            <TiedPositions residue_selectors="rs1,rs2"/>
        </ProteinMPNNMover>
    </MOVERS>
    <PROTOCOLS>
        <Add mover="design_mpnn"/>
    </PROTOCOLS>
</ROSETTASCRIPTS>
```

| XML Attribute | Type | Default | Description |
|---------------|------|---------|-------------|
| `deterministic_flag` | `bool` | `false` | Greedy decoding; overrides temperature |
| `temperature` | `Real` | `0.1` | Sampling temperature |
| `omit_AAs` | `string` | `"X"` | Globally disallowed types as concatenated single-letter codes |
| `design_selector` | `string` | (none) | ResidueSelector name for designable positions |
| `coord_selector` | `string` | (none) | ResidueSelector name for coordinate input |
| `TiedPositions` (subelement) | — | — | Repeatable; `residue_selectors` attribute takes comma-separated ResidueSelector names |

TaskOperations can also be attached via the standard `<TaskOperations>` subtags, providing fine-grained per-residue type control as an alternative to the simpler `design_selector` approach.

> [!TIP]
> When `ProteinMPNNMover` threads the predicted sequence, virtual residues and unchanged positions are replaced with `'-'` characters before calling `SimpleThreadingMover`, which instructs the threading mover to skip those positions entirely. Packing is explicitly disabled (`set_pack_neighbors(false)`, `set_pack_rounds(0)`) to preserve the ML-predicted identity without Rosetta's physics-based repacking interference. See [ProteinMPNNMover.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNNMover.cc#L263-L271).

## ProteinMPNNProbabilitiesMetric: Per-Residue Probability Analysis

The `ProteinMPNNProbabilitiesMetric` ([ProteinMPNNProbabilitiesMetric.hh](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNNProbabilitiesMetric.hh), [ProteinMPNNProbabilitiesMetric.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNNProbabilitiesMetric.cc)) extends `core::simple_metrics::PerResidueProbabilitiesMetric`, enabling integration with Rosetta's SimpleMetrics reporting system for detailed per-residue analysis without modifying the pose sequence. Its `calculate()` method returns a `map<Size, map<AA, Real>>` — a nested map from residue position to amino acid type to predicted probability.

The metric delegates to `ProteinMPNN::get_probabilities_and_logits()` to obtain raw tensors, then converts probabilities to logits via `torch::logit()`. A static helper `fill_return_map()` maps the 21-element probability vectors (indexed by the `AA_ALPHABET` constant) into the Rosetta `chemical::AA` enum-keyed return structure.

```xml
<SIMPLE_METRICS>
    <ProteinMPNNProbabilitiesMetric name="mpnn_probs"
        residue_selector="core"
        coord_selector="all"
        deterministic_flag="true"
        write_pssm="output.pssm"/>
</SIMPLE_METRICS>
```

| XML Attribute | Type | Default | Description |
|---------------|------|---------|-------------|
| `write_pssm` | `string` | `""` | If non-empty, writes a PSI-BLAST–style PSSM file (usable with `FavorSequenceProfile`) |
| `residue_selector` | `string` | (none) | Limits returned probabilities to selected residues |
| `coord_selector` | `string` | (none) | Selects coordinates passed as input to the model |
| `sequence_mask_selector` | `string` | (none) | Masks specific positions in the input sequence |
| `deterministic_flag` | `bool` | `false` | Enables deterministic (greedy) inference |

The PSSM output option bridges ProteinMPNN predictions into Rosetta's traditional scoring pipeline — the generated PSSM file can be consumed by the `FavorSequenceProfile` score term, enabling hybrid ML-physics energy functions.

## Conditional Compilation and Build Requirements

The entire integration is gated by the `USE_TORCH` preprocessor macro. Without it, the `ProteinMPNNMover::apply()` method calls `utility_exit_with_message()` with a clear error instructing the user to recompile with `extras=pytorch` and run a binary with `pytorch` in the name (e.g., `rosetta_scripts.pytorch.linuxgccrelease`) as documented at [ProteinMPNNMover.cc](source/src/protocols/protein_mpnn/ProteinMPNNMover.cc#L102-L104). The `ProteinMPNNProbabilitiesMetric` follows the same guard pattern in its `calculate()` method.

## Relationship to Related Systems

ProteinMPNN sits alongside two related ML integrations in Rosetta. The [trRosetta Deep Learning](21-trrosetta-deep-learning) integration uses TensorFlow to predict distance/angle distributions for structure prediction — a complementary forward-folding task. The `MIFST` module in the `inverse_folding/` directory provides an alternative inverse-folding approach. ProteinMPNN differentiates itself through its message-passing neural network architecture that operates on the graph of backbone Cα coordinates, making it particularly effective for fixed-backbone sequence design within Rosetta's [De Novo Protein Design](17-de-novo-protein-design) and [Side-Chain Packing](13-side-chain-packing) workflows.

## Next Steps

- **[RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework)** — Understand the XML parsing and `MoverCreator` registration that makes `ProteinMPNNMover` available as a tag
- **[Side-Chain Packing](13-side-chain-packing)** — Compare ML-based sequence design via ProteinMPNN with Rosetta's traditional physics-based packing
- **[De Novo Protein Design](17-de-novo-protein-design)** — See how ProteinMPNN fits into end-to-end design pipelines that combine backbone generation with sequence optimization
- **[trRosetta Deep Learning](21-trrosetta-deep-learning)** — Explore the complementary TensorFlow-based distance prediction integration


# Runtime Database System



Rosetta's Runtime Database System provides a unified abstraction layer for accessing, constructing, and managing large, immutable data objects—called **Resources**—from heterogeneous data stores during protocol execution. Rather than having each protocol independently manage file I/O or database connections, the system centralizes resource lifecycle management through a declarative XML configuration model, factory-driven instantiation, and inter-resource dependency tracking. This architecture is critical for the JD3 job-distribution framework, where expensive data (poses, fragment sets, score functions) must be shared safely across distributed tasks.

Sources: [ResourceManager.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.hh#L1-L221), [types.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/types.hh#L1-L39)

## Architectural Overview

The Runtime Database System comprises two closely integrated subsystems: the **Resource Manager** (responsible for declarative resource construction and lifecycle) and the **Database Session Manager** (responsible for connection pooling and transaction management across multiple database backends). These subsystems operate through a layered pipeline: XML declarations are parsed and validated, resource locators resolve data streams from arbitrary backends, and resource loaders construct immutable objects from those streams.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Declarative Layer
        XML["XML Resource<br/>Definition Files"]
        XSD["XSD Schema<br/>Validation"]
    end

    subgraph ResourceManager ["ResourceManager (Singleton-like)"]
        RM["ResourceManager Core"]
        FL["ResourceLocatorFactory"]
        FAL["ResourceLoaderFactory"]
    end

    subgraph Resolution Layer
        FSL["FileSystemResourceLocator"]
        DBL["DatabaseResourceLocator"]
        FLL["FileListResourceLocator"]
        NUL["NullResourceLocator"]
    end

    subgraph Database Layer
        DSM["DatabaseSessionManager<br/>(Singleton)"]
        SQL["cppdb::session"]
    end

    subgraph Output
        RES["Immutable Resource<br/>(utility::VirtualBaseCOP)"]
    end

    XML --> XSD --> RM
    RM --> FL
    FL --> FSL & DBL & FLL & NUL
    DBL --> DSM
    DSM --> SQL
    FSL & DBL & FLL -->|"ResourceStream<br/>(istream)"| RM
    RM --> FAL -->|"create_resource()"| RES

    style ResourceManager fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32
    style Database Layer fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e65100
    style Output fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0
```

Sources: [ResourceManager.cc](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.cc#L80-L115), [ResourceLocator.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceLocator.hh#L56-L128)

## Core Abstractions

### Resource — The Immutable Data Contract

A Resource is defined simply as `utility::VirtualBaseCOP`—a const owning pointer to any Rosetta-recognized object [types.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/types.hh#L29-L31). Once constructed, a resource is **bitwise immutable** for its entire lifetime. This design choice is deliberate: because resources cannot be modified after creation, they can be shared across multiple threads without race conditions, making the system naturally compatible with JD3's multi-threaded job execution. A resource may itself depend on other resources (for example, a pose resource might require a fragment set resource during its construction), and the ResourceManager tracks these interdependencies to ensure correct deallocation ordering.

Sources: [types.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/types.hh#L19-L31)

### ResourceManager — Central Orchestrator

The `ResourceManager` class ([ResourceManager.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.hh#L35-L153)) serves as the system's central orchestrator. It is initialized from the command line via the `-resource_definitions` flag (mapped to `jd3::resource_definition_files`), which accepts one or more XML files [ResourceManager.cc](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.cc#L48-L67). Its primary responsibilities include:

- **Parsing and validating** XML resource definition files against an internally generated XSD schema
- **Lazily constructing** resources on first access via `get_resource()`
- **Tracking inter-resource dependencies** so that deallocating a parent resource cascades to dependent resources
- **Preventing circular dependencies** by maintaining a construction stack that detects infinite recursion

The ResourceManager stores resource declarations as `TagCOP` objects (deferred XML parse trees), locators as instantiated `ResourceLocatorOP` objects, and constructed resources in a `map<string, ResourceCOP>`. This separation between declaration and instantiation enables the lazy-loading pattern central to the system's efficiency.

Sources: [ResourceManager.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.hh#L160-L221), [ResourceManager.cc](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.cc#L162-L200)

## Resource Locators — The Resolution Strategy Pattern

Resource Locators implement the **Strategy pattern** to abstract data retrieval from arbitrary backends. Each locator receives a `locator_id` (a string identifying the data source) and returns a `ResourceStream`—a polymorphic wrapper around `std::istream` that the ResourceLoader consumes [ResourceLocator.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceLocator.hh#L43-L51). The base class defines two pure virtual methods: `locate_resource_stream()` for stream creation and `parse_my_tag()` for XML configuration.

### Locator Comparison

| Locator | Backend | `locator_id` Semantics | Key Use Case |
|---------|---------|----------------------|--------------|
| **FileSystemResourceLocator** | Local filesystem | File path (resolved against `search_paths`) | Standard PDB/silent file loading |
| **DatabaseResourceLocator** | SQLite3, MySQL, PostgreSQL | Value bound to a parameterized SQL `SELECT` statement | Retrieving structures from features databases |
| **FileListResourceLocator** | Local filesystem | Whitespace-delimited list of file paths, concatenated into one stream | Constructing poses from multiple PDB segments |
| **NullResourceLocator** | None | Ignored | Testing and placeholder resources |

Sources: [FileSystemResourceLocator.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/locator/FileSystemResourceLocator.hh#L88-L144), [DatabaseResourceLocator.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/locator/DatabaseResourceLocator.hh#L43-L100), [FileListResourceLocator.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/locator/FileListResourceLocator.hh#L48-L88)

### DatabaseResourceLocator in Detail

The `DatabaseResourceLocator` is the most architecturally interesting locator because it bridges the Resource Manager with the Database Session Manager. It requires two pieces of configuration: the name of a database session resource (itself a resource managed by the ResourceManager), and a **partially-formatted SQL SELECT statement** with a single `?` placeholder [DatabaseResourceLocator.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/locator/DatabaseResourceLocator.hh#L50-L63). When `locate_resource_stream()` is invoked, the locator:

1. Requests the database session resource from the ResourceManager
2. Binds the `locator_id` to the SQL parameter
3. Executes the query
4. Packages the result set as a string stream

This design enables a single DatabaseResourceLocator instance to retrieve arbitrary rows from a database table simply by varying the `locator_id` passed by the resource declaration, making it highly reusable across multiple resource definitions.

Sources: [DatabaseResourceLocator.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/locator/DatabaseResourceLocator.hh#L43-L100)

## Database Session Manager — Connection Abstraction

The `DatabaseSessionManager` ([DatabaseSessionManager.hh](source/src/utility/sql_database/DatabaseSessionManager.hh#L97-L245)) is a singleton that provides a unified interface for acquiring database sessions across three backend engines. It wraps the **cppdb** library (a C++ database connectivity layer) and extends it with Rosetta-specific metadata including transaction mode, partitioning support, and schema search paths.

### Supported Database Backends

| Backend | Session Method | Typical Use Case |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| **SQLite3** | `get_session_sqlite3()` | Local features databases, offline analysis |
| **MySQL** | `get_session_mysql()` | Shared structure repositories |
| **PostgreSQL** | `get_session_postgres()` | Large-scale production databases with schema partitioning |

Each `session` object ([DatabaseSessionManager.hh](source/src/utility/sql_database/DatabaseSessionManager.hh#L19-L95)) carries metadata including `DatabaseMode` (sqlite3/mysql/postgres), `TransactionMode` (standard/chunked), `db_name`, `pq_schema` (PostgreSQL schema name), and `db_partition` (for horizontal partitioning). The session class also provides `begin_transaction()`, `commit_transaction()`, and `force_commit_transaction()` methods that implement chunked transaction semantics—transactions are batched according to `chunk_size` to balance write performance against data integrity.

Sources: [DatabaseSessionManager.hh](source/src/utility/sql_database/DatabaseSessionManager.hh#L19-L95), [DatabaseSessionManager.hh](source/src/utility/sql_database/DatabaseSessionManager.hh#L128-L245)

## Resource Dependency Tracking

A distinctive feature of the ResourceManager is its built-in dependency tracking system. When a resource is being constructed and requests another resource from the ResourceManager, the system records the parent-child relationship using three data structures [ResourceManager.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.hh#L208-L219):

- **`resources_being_constructed_stack_`** — detects circular dependencies by maintaining a stack of resources currently under construction
- **`resources_a_resource_depends_on_`** — maps each resource to the set of resources it depends on
- **`living_resources_dependent_on_a_resource_`** — reverse mapping used during deallocation

When `deallocate_resource()` is called on a parent, the ResourceManager recursively deallocates all dependent resources—**unless** a dependent has been explicitly marked to persist via `require_explicit_deallocation_for_resource()`. Circular dependencies are detected at runtime and result in an exception with a diagnostic message listing the full construction chain [ResourceManager.cc](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.cc#L162-L200).

> [!TIP]
> **Thread-safety through immutability**: Resources are stored as `ResourceCOP` (const owning pointers). Since they are bitwise immutable after creation, the ResourceManager can safely hand out the same resource to multiple concurrent consumers without locks. However, the ResourceManager itself is **not** thread-safe for concurrent writes—resource construction and deallocation must be serialized.

Sources: [ResourceManager.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.hh#L208-L219), [ResourceManager.cc](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.cc#L162-L200)

## Factory Registration Pattern

Both ResourceLocators and ResourceLoaders are instantiated through the factory registration pattern used throughout Rosetta. The `ResourceLocatorFactory` and `ResourceLoaderFactory` are singletons that maintain a `map<string, CreatorOP>` mapping type-name strings to creator objects [ResourceLocatorFactory.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceLocatorFactory.hh#L43-L92). Concrete locator/loader classes register themselves at load time using `ResourceLocatorRegistrator` and `ResourceLoaderRegistrator` template classes, typically placed in library `init.cc` files. This pattern allows new data backends to be added without modifying the ResourceManager core—simply implement the interface, create a Creator, and add a registration line.

Sources: [ResourceLocatorFactory.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceLocatorFactory.hh#L43-L92), [ResourceLoaderFactory.hh](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceLoaderFactory.hh#L40-L88)

## XML Resource Definition Format

Resource definitions are specified in XML files following the internally generated XSD schema. The top-level `<ResourceDefinitions>` element contains two repeatable sub-blocks: `<ResourceLocators>` and `<Resources>`. The schema is dynamically constructed by iterating over all registered locators and loaders, ensuring that adding a new backend automatically extends the valid XML vocabulary [ResourceManager.cc](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.cc#L230-L350).

```xml
<ResourceDefinitions>
  <ResourceLocators>
    <FileSystem name="std" search_paths="/data/inputs/" />
    <Database name="features_db"
              database_session_resource="features_session"
              sql_command="SELECT structure FROM structures WHERE tag = ?" />
  </ResourceLocators>
  <Resources>
    <Resource name="native_pose" input_id="1l2yH.pdb" locator="std">
      <PoseResource>
        <PDB><PoseLoaderOptions skip_conect_info="false"/></PDB>
      </PoseResource>
    </Resource>
  </Resources>
</ResourceDefinitions>
```

Multiple resource definition files may be loaded, and resources in one file may reference locators declared in another—provided the locator's file is parsed first. Name collisions across files throw an exception that reports both the conflicting name and the originating file paths [ResourceManager.cc](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.cc#L436-L470).

> [!TIP]
> **Lazy construction semantics**: Resources are not instantiated when the XML is parsed. The ResourceManager stores only the XML `TagCOP` objects. Actual construction occurs on the first call to `get_resource(name)`, and the resulting `ResourceCOP` is cached for subsequent access. This means configuration errors in a resource that is never requested will go undetected until runtime.

Sources: [ResourceManager.cc](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.cc#L230-L350), [ResourceManager.cc](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.cc#L436-L470)

## System Initialization Flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Application / JD3
    participant RM as ResourceManager
    participant XSD as XSD Validator
    participant RLF as ResourceLocatorFactory
    participant RL as ResourceLocator
    participant RLF2 as ResourceLoaderFactory
    participant DB as DatabaseSessionManager

    App->>RM: initialize_from_commandline()
    RM->>RM: Read -resource_definitions files
    RM->>XSD: validate_input_against_xsd()
    XSD-->>RM: schema_for_resource_definition_file()
    RM->>RM: read_resource_locators_tags()
    Note over RM: Store TagCOP, defer instantiation

    App->>RM: get_resource("my_pose")
    RM->>RM: create_resource("my_pose")
    RM->>RLF: create_resource_locator(type, tag)
    RLF-->>RM: ResourceLocatorOP
    RM->>RL: locate_resource_stream(input_id)
    alt Database Backend
        RL->>RM: get_resource(db_session)
        RM->>DB: get_session_sqlite3/mysql/postgres()
        DB-->>RM: sessionOP
    end
    RL-->>RM: ResourceStreamOP (istream)
    RM->>RLF2: create_resource_loader(loader_type)
    RLF2-->>RM: ResourceLoaderOP
    RM->>RM: loader.create_resource(...)
    RM-->>App: ResourceCOP
```

Sources: [ResourceManager.cc](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.cc#L48-L115), [ResourceManager.cc](source/src/basic/resource_manager/ResourceManager.cc#L475-L520)
