# Symmetry Modeling



Rosetta's symmetry modeling framework enables the modeling, scoring, docking, and design of symmetric macromolecular assemblies — from simple cyclic homomers to complex multi-component architectures. Rather than representing every subunit explicitly during optimization, the system tracks a single **asymmetric unit (ASU)** and propagates all conformational changes through clone mappings, dramatically reducing the search space while preserving exact geometric symmetry.

## Architectural Overview

The symmetry system operates as a layered architecture that intercepts core Rosetta abstractions at the conformation, scoring, and optimization levels. A `.sym` definition file is parsed into a `SymmData` object, which initializes a `SymmetryInfo` registry inside a `SymmetricConformation`. From that point, every conformational mutation, energy evaluation, and minimization step is symmetry-aware.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph Definition Layer
        SYM["<b>.sym Definition File</b><br/>C3_Z.sym, etc."]
        SD["<b>SymmData</b><br/>Parsed symmetry definition"]
    end

    subgraph Conformation Layer
        SC["<b>SymmetricConformation</b><br/>Overrides Conformation setters"]
        SI["<b>SymmetryInfo</b><br/>Clone mappings, DOF independence,<br/>score multipliers"]
        MS["<b>MirrorSymmetricConformation</b><br/>Mirror-symmetric variant"]
    end

    subgraph Scoring Layer
        SE["<b>SymmetricEnergies</b><br/>Symmetry-aware energy storage"]
        SSF["<b>SymmetricScoreFunction</b><br/>Weighted interface scoring"]
    end

    subgraph Optimization Layer
        SATM["<b>SymAtomTreeMinimizer</b><br/>Constrained DOF minimization"]
        SMM["<b>SymMinimizerMap</b><br/>DOF dependency resolution"]
    end

    subgraph Protocol Layer
        SDP["<b>SymDockProtocol</b><br/>Low/High-res symmetric docking"]
        SPM["<b>SymPackRotamersMover</b><br/>Symmetry-aware rotamer packing"]
        SMM2["<b>SymMinMover</b><br/>Symmetry-aware minimization"]
    end

    SYM -->|"read_symmetry_data_from_file"| SD
    SD -->|"initialize"| SI
    SI -->|"composes"| SC
    SI -->|"composes"| MS
    SC -->|"produces"| SE
    SE -->|"used by"| SSF
    SC -->|"provides DOF deps"| SMM
    SMM -->|"feeds"| SATM
    SC -->|"manages pose for"| SDP
    SC -->|"manages pose for"| SPM
    SC -->|"manages pose for"| SMM2

    style SYM fill:#4a86c8,color:#fff
    style SC fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff
    style SI fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff
```

The critical architectural insight is that `SymmetricConformation` **overrides every conformational setter** in `Conformation` — `set_dof`, `set_torsion`, `set_jump`, `set_xyz`, `replace_residue`, `set_bond_angle`, `set_bond_length`, `set_torsion_angle` — to automatically propagate changes from independent residues to all their clones. This means any protocol operating through the standard `Pose` API gains symmetry support transparently.

Sources: [SymmetricConformation.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetricConformation.hh#L47-L200), [SymmetricConformation.cc](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetricConformation.cc#L146-L237)

## Symmetry Definition Files (`.sym`)

Symmetry definitions live under `database/symmetry/` and use a declarative text format that completely describes the geometric arrangement, degrees of freedom, and scoring behavior of a symmetric assembly. The current repository ships with 98 pre-defined cyclic symmetry files spanning C2 through C99.

Sources: [C3_Z.sym](/database/symmetry/cyclic/C3_Z.sym#L1-L25)

### File Format Reference

A complete symmetry definition consists of the following sections:

**Metadata section** — declares the symmetry group and global parameters.

| Directive | Description | Example |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| `symmetry_name` | Human-readable symmetry group identifier | `symmetry_name C3` |
| `subunits` | Total number of subunits in the assembly | `subunits 3` |
| `number_of_interfaces` | Count of unique inter-subunit interface types | `number_of_interfaces 2` |
| `anchor_residue` | Residue or COM used as the coordinate origin | `anchor_residue COM` |

**Energy equation** — defines how the total energy is computed from subunit and interface terms. This controls which interactions are scored and how many times, preventing double-counting while ensuring all unique interfaces are evaluated. The format `E = N*S_self + M*(Si:Sj)` specifies subunit self-energy weights and interface weights.
Sources: [C3_Z.sym](/database/symmetry/cyclic/C3_Z.sym#L4)

**Virtual coordinates block** — defines the Cartesian frames for each subunit's virtual root and the symmetry centers. The `xyz` directive specifies a named coordinate system with an X-axis, Y-axis, and origin triplet.

**Connection directives** — wire virtual residues together through named jumps. `connect_virtual` links virtual residue pairs, and the special target `SUBUNIT` attaches a virtual root to the first residue of its subunit.

**DOF and grouping directives** — `set_dof` specifies which translational and rotational degrees of freedom each jump is allowed to explore. `set_jump_group` binds multiple jumps into coordinated groups that move in lockstep during sampling.

### C3 Cyclic Symmetry Example

The following definition file for C3 symmetry illustrates the complete format:

```
symmetry_name C3
subunits 3
number_of_interfaces 2
E = 2*S1  + 1*(S1:S2) + 1*(S1:S3)
anchor_residue COM
virtual_coordinates_start
xyz C1 0,0,1 +0.0000000,+1.0000000,0 0,0,0
xyz S1 0,0,1 +0.0000000,+1.0000000,0 0,0,0
xyz C2 0,0,1 +0.8660254,-0.5000000,0 0,0,0
xyz S2 0,0,1 +0.8660254,-0.5000000,0 0,0,0
xyz C3 0,0,1 -0.8660254,-0.5000000,0 0,0,0
xyz S3 0,0,1 -0.8660254,-0.5000000,0 0,0,0
virtual_coordinates_stop
connect_virtual JS1 C1 S1
connect_virtual JS1S S1 SUBUNIT
connect_virtual JC2 C1 C2
connect_virtual JS2 C2 S2
connect_virtual JS2S S2 SUBUNIT
connect_virtual JC3 C1 C3
connect_virtual JS3 C3 S3
connect_virtual JS3S S3 SUBUNIT
set_dof JS1 x y angle_x angle_y angle_z
set_jump_group JGS JS1 JS2 JS3
set_jump_group JGSS JS1S JS2S JS3S
```

Three subunits are arranged at 120° intervals (cos60° ≈ 0.866, sin60° ≈ 0.5) around the Z-axis. Virtual residues `C1`–`C3` define symmetry centers, `S1`–`S3` anchor each subunit, and the energy equation weights subunit 1's self-energy by 2 and evaluates both unique interfaces exactly once. The `set_dof` line grants the JS1 jump full rigid-body freedom (x, y, and all three rotational angles), while `set_jump_group` coordinates the three corresponding jumps across subunits.

Sources: [C3_Z.sym](/database/symmetry/cyclic/C3_Z.sym#L1-L25)

## SymmetryInfo: The Clone Registry

`SymmetryInfo` is the central runtime data structure that maintains all mappings between independent (master) degrees of freedom and their dependent clones. It is constructed from a `SymmData` object using the asymmetric unit's residue count and jump count.

Sources: [SymmetryInfo.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetryInfo.hh#L53-L358)

### Independence and Clone Mapping

Every residue, torsion, and jump in the symmetric pose is classified as either **independent** (part of the ASU) or **dependent** (a clone). The registry provides three parallel mapping systems:

| Mapping System | Key Method | Purpose |
|----------------|------------|---------|
| Backbone clones | `bb_follows(res)`, `bb_clones(res)` | Maps each dependent residue to its ASU master; lists all clones of an independent residue |
| Chi clones | `chi_follows(res)`, `chi_clones(res)` | Same mapping for side-chain torsion DOFs |
| Jump clones | `jump_follows(j)`, `jump_clones(j)` | Maps symmetric jumps; supports **weighted clones** for partial propagation |

The distinction between `bb_clones` and `chi_clones` is critical: backbone and side-chain independence can diverge when, for example, a symmetric backbone has asymmetric side-chain packing. The `jump_clone_wts_` map stores per-clone weights, allowing derivative propagation to be scaled — essential for symmetric docking where not all subunit interfaces carry identical geometric relationships.

Sources: [SymmetryInfo.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetryInfo.hh#L122-L203)

### Score Multiplier System

`SymmetryInfo` implements a sophisticated scoring correction to avoid energy double-counting in symmetric assemblies. The energy equation from the `.sym` file is compiled into per-residue-pair multipliers stored in `score_multiply_`. The method `score_multiply(res1, res2)` returns the weight for any inter-residue energy term, and `score_multiply_factor()` returns the global normalization factor that scales the total energy to approximate a full-assembly value.

The `reset_score_multiply_to_reasonable_default()` method provides a fallback when explicit multipliers are absent: it assigns weight 1 to intra-subunit interactions and weight 1/N to inter-subunit interactions, where N is the number of subunits. The `set_score_multiply_from_subunit_factors()` method allows fine-grained per-subunit weighting for hetero-oligomeric systems.

Sources: [SymmetryInfo.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetryInfo.hh#L157-L235)

### Multi-Component Support

Beyond simple homomeric symmetry, `SymmetryInfo` supports **multi-component** assemblies (hetero-oligomers, coiled-coils with distinct chains). The component system tracks:

- `num_components_` — number of distinct chain types
- `components_` — per-residue component assignment vector
- `component_bounds_` — residue ranges `[lower, upper]` for each component in the ASU
- `jname2components_` / `jname2subunits_` — maps jump names to the components and subunit indices they connect

This enables protocols to reason about inter-component interfaces distinctly from intra-component symmetry.

Sources: [SymmetryInfo.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetryInfo.hh#L249-L273)

## SymmData: Parsing the Definition File

`SymmData` is the raw data container produced by parsing a `.sym` file. It stores the complete symmetry specification before any optimization-specific preprocessing occurs.

Sources: [SymmData.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmData.hh#L40-L200), [SymmData.cc](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmData.cc#L38-L597)

### Parsing Architecture

The parser in `read_symmetry_data_from_stream()` operates as a state machine with distinct reading modes:

1. **Normal mode** — processes top-level directives (`symmetry_name`, `subunits`, `E =`, `set_dof`, `connect_virtual`)
2. **Virtual coordinates mode** — between `virtual_coordinates_start` / `virtual_coordinates_stop`, parses `xyz` directives into `VirtualCoordinate` objects stored in the `virtual_coordinates_` map
3. **Transform mode** — between `virtual_transforms_start` / `virtual_transforms_stop`, reads rotation (`rot` with `Rx`, `Ry`, `Rz`, `Rx_angle`, `Ry_angle`, `Rz_angle`) and translation (`trans`) operations to procedurally generate subunit coordinate frames

The parser supports two coordinate specification strategies: **explicit** (listing every `xyz` line as in the C3 example) and **procedural** (specifying rotational symmetry operators that are composed to generate subunit frames). In the procedural mode, each `rot Rz N` directive creates an N-fold rotation matrix, and these are composed sequentially to place each successive subunit.

### Virtual Coordinate Graph

Virtual coordinates form a directed graph: each `VirtualCoordinate` stores an X-axis vector, Y-axis vector, and origin. The `connect_virtual` directives create edges in this graph. The `jump_string_to_virtual_pair_` map links jump names to `(parent_virtual, child_virtual)` pairs, while `jump_string_to_jump_num_` assigns sequential numeric IDs. The special target `SUBUNIT` in a `connect_virtual` directive links a virtual residue to the actual protein chain of the corresponding subunit.

Sources: [SymmData.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmData.hh#L79-L88), [SymmData.cc](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmData.cc#L430-L597)

## SymDof: Degrees of Freedom Control

The `SymDof` class encodes which translational and rotational DOFs are permitted for each symmetric jump, along with their motion bounds. Each DOF type corresponds to one of six rigid-body parameters defined in the `dof_type` enum.

Sources: [SymDof.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymDof.hh#L32-L156)

### DOF Types and Bounds

| DOF Constant | Value | Description |
|-------------|-------|-------------|
| `X_DOF` | 1 | Translation along X |
| `Y_DOF` | 2 | Translation along Y |
| `Z_DOF` | 3 | Translation along Z |
| `X_ANGLE_DOF` | 4 | Rotation around X |
| `Y_ANGLE_DOF` | 5 | Rotation around Y |
| `Z_ANGLE_DOF` | 6 | Rotation around Z |

Each DOF supports **two independent range pairs** (`range1` and `range2`), with separate lower/upper bounds and presence flags. The `range2_is_bound_` flag distinguishes between periodic ranges (e.g., angular limits) and hard bounds (e.g., translational limits). The `jump_dir_` field stores the direction of each DOF's jump (upstream vs. downstream), which is critical for correct derivative propagation during minimization. The `allowed_dof_jumps_` vector is the primary gate: only DOFs with `allow_dof(i) == true` are sampled.

Sources: [SymDof.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymDof.hh#L32-L143)

## SymmetricConformation: Transparent Symmetry Propagation

`SymmetricConformation` extends `Conformation` by overriding every mutation method to maintain symmetric invariants automatically. It holds a `SymmetryInfoOP` and a mutable vector of `SymmetryTransform` objects (`Tsymm_`) that cache the homogeneous transforms between subunit frames.

Sources: [SymmetricConformation.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetricConformation.hh#L47-L200)

### Setter Override Pattern

Every conformational setter follows the same three-step pattern:

1. **Resolve the independent master** — if the requested residue/DOF is dependent, look up its master via `bb_follows()`, `chi_follows()`, or `jump_follows()`
2. **Apply the change to the master** — delegate to the base `Conformation::set_*` method on the independent residue
3. **Propagate to all clones** — iterate over the clone list from `SymmetryInfo` and apply the same change

This pattern is exemplified by `set_torsion`: when a torsion is set on an independent residue, the same value is immediately applied to all clones listed in `dependent_torsions()`. For jumps, `set_jump` propagates rigid-body transformations across all jump clones. Crucially, after any jump change or when `torsion_changes_move_other_monomers_` is true, the cached transforms (`Tsymm_`) are cleared via `clear_Tsymm()`, forcing recomputation on the next geometry query.

Sources: [SymmetricConformation.cc](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetricConformation.cc#L146-L287)

### Coordinate Transformation System

`SymmetricConformation` provides methods to transform coordinates between subunit frames:

- `get_transformation(resid)` returns the `HomogeneousTransform<Real>` mapping the ASU frame to the frame of residue `resid`
- `apply_transformation(Xin, from, to)` remaps a point from one subunit's frame to another's
- `recalculate_transforms()` forces recomputation of all cached transforms from the current atom positions

These transforms are lazy-computed and cached, then invalidated whenever a jump changes. This system is essential for protocols that need to evaluate distances or orientations across subunit boundaries.

Sources: [SymmetricConformation.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetricConformation.hh#L173-L191)

> [!TIP]
> The `torsion_changes_move_other_monomers_` flag in `SymmetryInfo` controls a critical performance tradeoff. When true, any backbone torsion change invalidates the subunit transform cache, ensuring geometric correctness but at the cost of frequent recomputation. For protocols that only modify side chains, leaving this flag false avoids unnecessary cache invalidation.

## Symmetry-Aware Scoring

Scoring symmetric assemblies requires careful handling to avoid both double-counting inter-subunit interactions and under-counting intra-subunit terms.

Sources: [SymmetricEnergies.hh](/source/src/core/scoring/symmetry/SymmetricEnergies.hh), [SymmetricScoreFunction.hh](/source/src/core/scoring/symmetry/SymmetricScoreFunction.hh)

### Score Multiplier Mechanism

`SymmetricEnergies` extends the base `Energies` class to incorporate the `score_multiply` weights from `SymmetryInfo`. When the scoring system evaluates a pairwise energy term between residues `i` and `j`, it queries `SymmetryInfo::score_multiply(i, j)` to determine the effective weight. This weight can be 0 (interaction should not be scored), 1 (scored once), or a fractional value for weighted interface contributions. The `get_residue_weight()` method in `SymmetricConformation` exposes this system to the scoring machinery.

Sources: [SymmetricConformation.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetricConformation.hh#L141-L145)

### Residue Masking

`SymmetricConformation::get_residue_mask()` returns a `vector1<bool>` that identifies which residues in the full symmetric pose are "real" versus virtual, enabling scoring methods to skip virtual residues entirely. Combined with the score multiplier system, this ensures that only physically meaningful interactions contribute to the total energy.

Sources: [SymmetricConformation.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetricConformation.hh#L141-L142)

## Symmetry-Constrained Optimization

Minimization of symmetric structures operates on a drastically reduced DOF space. The `SymAtomTreeMinimizer` works with a `SymMinimizerMap` that only exposes independent DOFs to the optimizer, while `SymAtomTreeMultifunc` evaluates the objective function including all clone contributions.

Sources: [SymAtomTreeMinimizer.hh](/source/src/core/optimization/symmetry/SymAtomTreeMinimizer.hh), [SymMinimizerMap.hh](/source/src/core/optimization/symmetry/SymMinimizerMap.hh)

### Derivative Propagation

The `get_dof_derivative_weight()` method in `SymmetryInfo` is the key to correct gradient computation. For independent DOFs, the weight is 1. For dependent non-jump DOFs, the weight is 0 (they are not free variables). For dependent jump DOFs, the weight can be any real number stored in `jump_clone_wts_`. This allows the minimizer to compute gradients only with respect to the true free variables while correctly accounting for their effect on the full assembly energy.

The protocol-layer `SymMinMover` wraps `SymAtomTreeMinimizer` as a standard Mover, and `TaskAwareSymMinMover` additionally respects packing task restrictions. Both are drop-in replacements for their asymmetric counterparts in any RosettaScripts workflow.

Sources: [SymmetryInfo.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmetryInfo.hh#L179-L184), [SymMinMover.hh](/source/src/protocols/minimization_packing/symmetry/SymMinMover.hh), [TaskAwareSymMinMover.hh](/source/src/protocols/minimization_packing/symmetry/TaskAwareSymMinMover.hh)

## Symmetry-Aware Packing

Rotamer packing for symmetric assemblies must respect the constraint that equivalent positions across subunits carry identical rotamers. The `SymPackRotamersMover` and `SymRotamerTrialsMover` override their base classes to restrict rotamer sampling to independent residues only, then propagate selected rotamers to all clones.

Sources: [SymPackRotamersMover.hh](/source/src/protocols/minimization_packing/symmetry/SymPackRotamersMover.hh), [SymRotamerTrialsMover.hh](/source/src/protocols/minimization_packing/symmetry/SymRotamerTrialsMover.hh)

The `SymRestrictTaskForDocking` utility further refines the packing task by identifying interface residues and restricting packing to those positions, which is essential for symmetric docking protocols where only the interface should be repacked.

Sources: [SymRestrictTaskForDocking.hh](/source/src/protocols/symmetric_docking/SymRestrictTaskForDocking.hh)

## Symmetric Docking Protocols

The symmetric docking framework provides a complete pipeline from low-resolution rigid-body search through high-resolution refinement, implemented across several dedicated classes.

Sources: [SymDockProtocol.hh](/source/src/protocols/symmetric_docking/SymDockProtocol.hh), [SymDockingLowRes.hh](/source/src/protocols/symmetric_docking/SymDockingLowRes.hh), [SymDockingHiRes.hh](/source/src/protocols/symmetric_docking/SymDockingHiRes.hh)

### Protocol Hierarchy

| Protocol | Purpose | Resolution |
|----------|---------|------------|
| `SymDockBaseProtocol` | Common initialization and scoring setup | — |
| `SymDockProtocol` | Full docking pipeline orchestration | Both |
| `SymDockingLowRes` | Centroid-level rigid-body sampling with Monte Carlo | Low |
| `SymDockingHiRes` | All-atom refinement with side-chain repacking and minimization | High |
| `SymFoldandDockMoveRbJumpMover` | Coupled folding and docking move set | Both |
| `SymFoldandDockSlideTrialMover` | Sliding symmetry trial moves for cyclic symmetry | Both |

The low-resolution phase uses a coarse-grained score function and explores the rigid-body DOFs defined in the `.sym` file via `SymDof` constraints. The high-resolution phase switches to a full-atom score function, repacks interface side chains using `SymPackRotamersMover`, and runs `SymMinMover` to relax the interface. The `SymFoldandDock*` movers integrate ab initio folding with symmetric docking, allowing simultaneous exploration of backbone conformation and subunit arrangement.

The `membrane/MPSymDockMover` extends symmetric docking to membrane proteins, adding membrane-aware scoring and orientation constraints.

Sources: [MPSymDockMover.hh](/source/src/protocols/symmetric_docking/membrane/MPSymDockMover.hh)

## Utility Functions

The `core::pose::symmetry` namespace and `core::conformation::symmetry::util` provide essential helper functions for working with symmetric poses, including detecting whether a pose is symmetric, extracting the ASU, and converting between symmetric and asymmetric representations.

Sources: [util.hh](/source/src/core/pose/symmetry/util.hh), [util.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/util.hh)

The `SymmDataLoader` class integrates with Rosetta's resource loader framework, allowing `.sym` files to be referenced by name and loaded from the database search path. This enables protocols to specify symmetry by group name rather than absolute file path.

Sources: [SymmDataLoader.hh](/source/src/core/conformation/symmetry/SymmDataLoader.hh)

## Module File Map

The symmetry system spans multiple directories in the Rosetta codebase. The following table provides a complete map for targeted code exploration:

| Directory | Purpose | Key Classes |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `core/conformation/symmetry/` | Core data structures | `SymmData`, `SymmetryInfo`, `SymmetricConformation`, `SymDof`, `VirtualCoordinate`, `SymSlideInfo`, `MirrorSymmetricConformation`, `SymmetryTransform` |
| `core/scoring/symmetry/` | Symmetry-aware scoring | `SymmetricEnergies`, `SymmetricScoreFunction` |
| `core/optimization/symmetry/` | Constrained minimization | `SymAtomTreeMinimizer`, `SymMinimizerMap`, `SymAtomTreeMultifunc` |
| `core/pose/symmetry/` | Pose-level utilities | Symmetry detection, ASU extraction |
| `protocols/minimization_packing/symmetry/` | Symmetry-aware movers | `SymMinMover`, `SymPackRotamersMover`, `SymRotamerTrialsMover` |
| `protocols/symmetric_docking/` | Docking protocols | `SymDockProtocol`, `SymDockingLowRes`, `SymDockingHiRes`, `SymFoldandDock*` |
| `database/symmetry/cyclic/` | Pre-built definitions | C2 through C99 cyclic `.sym` files |

## Integration with RosettaScripts

All symmetry-aware movers are registered as RosettaScripts Movers via their respective `Creator` classes (`SymMinMoverCreator`, `SymPackRotamersMoverCreator`, `SymDockProtocolCreator`, etc.), making them directly usable in XML protocol definitions. Symmetry is typically activated by the `-symmetry:definition` command-line option, which triggers `SymmDataLoader` to parse the `.sym` file and construct the `SymmetricConformation` before the protocol begins.

> [!TIP]
> When debugging symmetry issues, the `symmetry_info` conformation attribute is your primary diagnostic. Call `pose.conformation().Symmetry_Info()->show()` to dump the complete clone mapping, DOF settings, and score multiplier table. The `independent_residues()` method returns a boolean vector useful for quickly identifying which residues are ASU masters.

## Navigating Further

Symmetry modeling intersects with several other Rosetta subsystems. For protocol composition fundamentals, see [Mover and Filter Hierarchy](11-mover-and-filter-hierarchy). The optimization layer depends on the core minimization infrastructure described in [Structure Relaxation](18-structure-relaxation). Scoring integration follows the patterns in [ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework). For the XML interface used to compose symmetric protocols, consult [RosettaScripts XML Framework](14-rosettascripts-xml-framework). Membrane protein symmetry extends the membrane framework covered in [Membrane Protein Modeling](25-membrane-protein-modeling).

# Membrane Protein Modeling



Rosetta's membrane protein modeling framework — **RosettaMP** — provides a biophysically grounded implicit membrane environment for folding, docking, design, and relaxation of transmembrane proteins. Rather than simulating individual lipid molecules, the framework represents the bilayer as a continuous solvent-like potential whose physical parameters are derived from all-atom MD simulations and X-ray/neutron scattering data. This page dissects the architectural layers that enable membrane-aware scoring, protein-membrane embedding optimization, and topology-driven constraint enforcement, equipping advanced developers to extend or customize any component of the pipeline.

Sources: [AddMembraneMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/AddMembraneMover.hh#L1-L40), [MembraneInfo.hh](source/src/core/conformation/membrane/MembraneInfo.hh#L1-L40)

## Architecture Overview

RosettaMP is structured across four concentric layers: a **conformation data layer** that attaches membrane metadata to the Pose, a **geometry engine** that computes spatial relationships between atoms and the implicit bilayer, an **energy method layer** that scores atoms based on their membrane depth and local environment, and a **protocol mover layer** that orchestrates setup, transformation, and optimization workflows. These layers communicate through the `MembraneInfo` object, which is stored directly in the `Conformation` and accessed exclusively via `pose.conformation().membrane_info()`. The implicit membrane itself is represented by a virtual MEM residue — a root-level `Residue` appended to the Pose whose orientation defines the bilayer normal and center.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Protocol Mover Layer"
        AM[AddMembraneMover]
        OM[OptimizeMembranePositionMover]
        OE[OptimizeProteinEmbeddingMover]
        MP[MPQuickRelaxMover]
        TM[TiltMover / TranslationRotationMover]
        AP[AqueousPoreFinder]
        SC[SpanConstraints]
    end

    subgraph "Energy Method Layer"
        WTBE[FaWaterToBilayerEnergy]
        EFLL[ElectricfieldLipidlayer]
        MEP[MEnvAtomParams]
    end

    subgraph "Geometry Engine"
        MG[MembraneGeometry]
        SL[Slab]
        VS[Vesicle]
        BC[Bicelle]
        DV[DoubleVesicle]
        ED[EmbeddingDef]
        EB[Embedding]
    end

    subgraph "Conformation Data Layer"
        MI[MembraneInfo]
        ILI[ImplicitLipidInfo]
        ST[SpanningTopology]
        AP2[AqueousPoreParameters]
        MEM[MEM Virtual Residue]
    end

    subgraph "Database"
        ILP[implicit_lipid_parameters.txt]
        LEF[lipid_electric_field_params.txt]
        MFP[memb_fa_params_2019.txt]
    end

    AM --> MI
    OM --> MI
    OE --> ED
    MP --> WTBE
    AP --> AP2
    TM --> MG

    WTBE --> MEP
    EFLL --> MG
    WTBE --> ILI

    MI --> ST
    MI --> ILI
    MI --> MG
    MI --> MEM

    ILI --> ILP
    EFLL --> LEF
    MEP --> MFP

    MG --> SL
    MG --> VS
    MG --> BC
    MG --> DV

    EB --> ED
```

Sources: [MembraneGeometry.hh](source/src/core/conformation/membrane/MembraneGeometry.hh#L1-L80), [Embedding.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/geometry/Embedding.hh#L50-L130), [FaWaterToBilayerEnergy.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/scoring/FaWaterToBilayerEnergy.hh#L1-L60)

## Conformation Data Layer

The conformation data layer is the architectural foundation that makes any Pose "membrane-aware." Once initialized, `pose.conformation().is_membrane()` returns `true` and the full membrane scoring pipeline becomes available. The central class is `MembraneInfo`, which aggregates four pieces of essential state: the MEM residue index (sequence position of the membrane virtual residue), the membrane jump number (the FoldTree jump connecting protein chains to MEM), a `SpanningTopology` object describing which residues form transmembrane helices, and an `ImplicitLipidInfo` object encoding the physical properties of the lipid bilayer. This design enforces a single source of truth — all geometry queries, scoring methods, and movers route through `MembraneInfo` rather than maintaining independent membrane state.

Sources: [MembraneInfo.hh](source/src/core/conformation/membrane/MembraneInfo.hh#L46-L80)

### MembraneInfo

`MembraneInfo` provides the canonical API for all membrane spatial queries. Key methods include `membrane_center()` and `membrane_normal()` which compute the bilayer's position and orientation from the MEM residue's current coordinates, `in_membrane()` and `in_membrane_atom()` which classify residues and atoms as intramembrane or extramembrane based on the transition zone, and `residue_z_position()` / `atom_z_position()` which return the signed distance along the membrane normal. The constructor accepts either legacy thickness/steepness parameters directly or a lipid composition name and temperature, delegating to `ImplicitLipidInfo` for parameter lookup. The `MP_GEOMETRY_TRANSITION` enum selects among `Slab`, `Vesicle`, `Bicelle`, or `DoubleVesicle` membrane topologies, each of which provides a different thickness profile function.

> [!TIP]
> **MEM residue is a FoldTree root anchor.** The MEM virtual residue is always positioned at the root of the FoldTree. All downstream kinematic transformations — jumps, minimization, backbone sampling — propagate through this root, meaning the membrane and protein move as a coupled system unless a mover explicitly modifies the membrane jump. This is why `AddMembraneMover` accepts an `anchor_rsd` parameter: it redesigns the FoldTree so the specified protein residue becomes the root, with MEM as its immediate child.

Sources: [MembraneInfo.hh](source/src/core/conformation/membrane/MembraneInfo.hh#L80-L160), [AddMembraneMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/AddMembraneMover.hh#L98-L120)

### SpanningTopology and Span

`SpanningTopology` stores a collection of `Span` objects, each representing a single transmembrane segment defined by a start residue, end residue, and an `Orientation` enum (`IN` for N-to-C cytoplasmic orientation, `OUT` for the reverse). The topology can be loaded from a spanfile (a whitespace-delimited text file with columns for start, end, and orientation) or constructed programmatically. Topology drives two critical downstream behaviors: it determines which residues are classified as transmembrane for span-based constraints, and it provides the span boundaries used by `Embedding::from_spans()` to compute per-helix embedding vectors that feed into the optimization movers.

Sources: [Span.hh](source/src/core/conformation/membrane/Span.hh#L1-L30), [AddMembraneMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/AddMembraneMover.hh#L71-L90)

### ImplicitLipidInfo

`ImplicitLipidInfo` encapsulates the biophysical parameters of the lipid bilayer, loaded at runtime from `database/membrane/implicit_lipid_parameters.txt`. The file contains experimentally-derived measurements for over 90 lipid composition/temperature combinations across four headgroup types (PC, PE, PG, ToCdl). Each entry specifies: `WATER_THK` (half the distance between Gibbs dividing surfaces), `PARAM_A` (a thickness proxy), `WATER_STP` (the steepness of the water density gradient), `TEMP`, and `DOS` (degrees of saturation). The `ImplicitLipidInfo` constructor looks up the matching row by lipid name and temperature (default: DLPC at 37°C) and exposes these values through accessor methods used by the geometry engine's transition functions.

Sources: [ImplicitLipidInfo.hh](source/src/core/conformation/membrane/ImplicitLipidInfo.hh#L1-L30), [implicit_lipid_parameters.txt](database/membrane/implicit_lipid_parameters.txt#L1-L30)

## Membrane Geometry Engine

The geometry engine translates the abstract membrane parameters into concrete per-atom spatial classifications. This is where the "implicit" in implicit membrane becomes computationally real: every atom receives a continuous hydration score between 0 (fully buried in lipid) and 1 (fully exposed to water) based on its position relative to the bilayer.

Sources: [MembraneGeometry.hh](source/src/core/conformation/membrane/MembraneGeometry.hh#L1-L200)

### Transition Functions

The geometry engine provides two mathematically distinct transition functions that map an atom's z-coordinate (distance along the membrane normal) to a continuous [0, 1] hydration value:

- **`f_imm1(z)`** — The classic Lazaridis IMM1 function, an exponential sigmoid that models the water-to-lipid interface as a smooth step. This is the default for `Slab` and `Vesicle` geometries and is controlled by the `steepness` parameter.
- **`f_franklin(z, τ, κ)`** — A newer transition function introduced by Alford, Fleming, and Gray (2020) with lipid-type-dependent parameters τ (transition midpoint) and κ (transition sharpness). This provides better discrimination for different headgroup chemistries and is selected when `use_franklin()` returns true.

The base `MembraneGeometry` class computes `f_thickness()` as the flat-membrane transition value, then `f_hydration()` composes it with `f_cavity()` to account for aqueous pore effects. The `corrected_xyz()` method transforms atom coordinates from lab frame into membrane-local frame (thickness axis, binormal axis, normal axis) for geometric queries.

Sources: [MembraneGeometry.hh](source/src/core/conformation/membrane/MembraneGeometry.hh#L140-L200)

### Membrane Geometry Variants

The `MembraneGeometry` class hierarchy supports four distinct membrane topologies, each modeling a physically different environment:

| Geometry Class | Description | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| `Slab` | Infinite planar bilayer (default) | Standard α-helical membrane proteins |
| `Vesicle` | Single spherical shell | Monotopic/peripheral proteins, vesicle-bound peptides |
| `Bicelle` | Discoidal bilayer patch | Nanodisc or bicelle-embedded systems |
| `DoubleVesicle` | Concentric double shell | Vesicle fusion intermediates, dual-membrane systems |

Each subclass overrides `clone()`, `show()`, and the core `f_thickness()` / `f_hydration()` virtual methods to implement geometry-specific thickness profiles. All subclasses inherit the pore correction machinery from the base class through `f_cavity()` and `f_hydration()`.

Sources: [membrane_geometry/](source/src/core/conformation/membrane/membrane_geometry/)

### Embedding System

The embedding subsystem — located in `protocols/membrane/geometry/` rather than `core/conformation/membrane/` — provides a higher-level abstraction for representing how transmembrane helices are positioned relative to the bilayer. `EmbeddingDef` is the atomic unit: a struct holding a `center` (3D point) and `normal` (3D unit vector) that together define a helical segment's position and tilt. It can be constructed from a pose and residue range, automatically computing the Cα centroid and principal axis. `Embedding` aggregates multiple `EmbeddingDef` objects (one per transmembrane span) and maintains a `total_embed_` — the average embedding across all spans — which is used by `OptimizeProteinEmbeddingMover` as the optimization target.

Sources: [EmbeddingDef.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/geometry/EmbeddingDef.hh#L55-L109), [Embedding.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/geometry/Embedding.hh#L90-L130)

## Energy Method Layer

RosettaMP provides two custom one-body energy methods that score membrane-embedded atoms based on their depth-dependent solvation environment. Both are registered as `ContextDependentOneBodyEnergy` methods, meaning they compute per-residue scores that depend on the full pose context (specifically, the membrane position).

Sources: [FaWaterToBilayerEnergy.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/scoring/FaWaterToBilayerEnergy.hh#L50-L60), [ElectricfieldLipidlayer.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/scoring/ElectricfieldLipidlayer.hh#L50-L60)

### FaWaterToBilayerEnergy (fa_wtbe)

This energy method implements the water-to-bilayer transfer free energy, the core scoring term of RosettaMP. For each atom, it retrieves `MEnvAtomParams` containing `dGfreeW` (solvation free energy in water), `dGfreeB` (solvation free energy in bilayer), and a `hydration` value from the geometry engine. The per-atom energy is computed by `eval_fa_wtbe()` as a weighted interpolation between the water and bilayer reference states, modulated by the atom's membrane depth. The method supports full derivative computation through `eval_atom_derivative()`, which produces F1/F2 force vectors for gradient-based minimization. An internal flag `use_fleming_de_` toggles between the original and a revised dielectric formulation.

Sources: [FaWaterToBilayerEnergy.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/scoring/FaWaterToBilayerEnergy.hh#L70-L139), [MEnvAtomParams.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/scoring/MEnvAtomParams.hh#L40-L79)

### ElectricfieldLipidlayer (f_elec_lipidlayer)

This method captures the electrostatic contribution of the lipid headgroup dipole field. Real lipid bilayers generate a substantial electric field in the headgroup region due to oriented carbonyl and phosphate dipoles; this field influences the energetics of charged and polar residues near the membrane interface. `ElectricfieldLipidlayer` computes a per-atom electrostatic penalty/reward based on the atom's z-position using `MEnvElectroAtomParams`, providing both energy values and gradient derivatives for optimization.

Sources: [ElectricfieldLipidlayer.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/scoring/ElectricfieldLipidlayer.hh#L70-L122)

### MEnvAtomParams

The `MEnvAtomParams` container is the parameter bridge between the scoring methods and the database files. Each instance stores: `atom_type_name` (the Rosetta atom type), `dGfreeW` and `dGfreeB` (pair of reference solvation energies), `hyd_` (the continuous hydration value computed by the geometry engine at scoring time), and F1/F2 derivative vectors. Parameters are loaded from `database/membrane/memb_fa_params_2019.txt` during score function initialization and indexed by atom type name. The hydration field is populated dynamically during `setup_for_scoring()` based on the current membrane geometry, making the energy method fully responsive to membrane position changes during optimization.

Sources: [MEnvAtomParams.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/scoring/MEnvAtomParams.hh#L30-L79)

## Protocol Mover Layer

The protocol layer provides the end-user-facing API for membrane protein workflows. All membrane movers extend `protocols::moves::Mover` and are fully RosettaScripts-compatible with XML schema definitions and `Creator` classes following the [Factory Pattern Architecture](15-factory-pattern-architecture).

Sources: [AddMembraneMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/AddMembraneMover.hh#L55-L70)

### Initialization: AddMembraneMover

`AddMembraneMover` is the gateway to RosettaMP — every membrane protocol must invoke it first. Its `apply()` method performs six sequential initialization steps documented in the class header: (1) creates and appends a MEM virtual residue to the pose, (2) constructs a `SpanningTopology` object from the spanfile or inline span definitions, (3) sets up initial membrane coordinates (default: centered at origin), (4) optionally initializes per-atom lipid accessibility data, (5) optionally initializes aqueous pore dimensions, and (6) creates the `ImplicitLipidMembraneInfo` and attaches it to the conformation. The mover offers multiple constructor overloads for common initialization patterns: from a spanfile path, from an existing MEM residue number, from a pre-built `SpanningTopologyOP`, or via RosettaScripts XML tags.

> [!TIP]
> **Constructor overload resolution is non-trivial.** Several `AddMembraneMover` constructors have overlapping signature patterns when `membrane_rsd=0` (auto-detect). The version with `(anchor_rsd, bool, bool, membrane_rsd)` uses the two boolean dummy parameters purely to disambiguate from `(membrane_rsd, lipid_composition, temperature)`. When calling from C++, always use the explicit constructor forms or the RosettaScripts interface to avoid accidental overload selection.

Sources: [AddMembraneMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/AddMembraneMover.hh#L55-L135)

### Membrane Position and Embedding Optimization

Once initialized, the membrane position can be optimized through two complementary movers:

- **`OptimizeMembranePositionMover`** — Adjusts the membrane (MEM residue) relative to a fixed protein by minimizing a scoring function that includes `fa_wtbe` and `f_elec_lipidlayer`. This is used when the protein structure is trusted and the membrane placement needs refinement.
- **`OptimizeProteinEmbeddingMover`** — Adjusts the protein position relative to a fixed membrane by modifying the protein-MEM jump. This uses the `Embedding` system to define per-span targets and optimizes the global transform to match the computed average embedding.

Both movers operate on the FoldTree jump connecting the protein root to MEM, but from opposite perspectives. `SetMembranePositionMover` and `RandomMembranePositionMover` provide non-optimizing alternatives for explicit positioning or stochastic initialization. `MembranePositionFromTopologyMover` computes an initial placement purely from spanning topology and ideal helix geometry.

Sources: [OptimizeMembranePositionMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/OptimizeMembranePositionMover.hh), [OptimizeProteinEmbeddingMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/OptimizeProteinEmbeddingMover.hh)

### Transformation and Sampling Movers

The framework provides fine-grained movers for exploring membrane protein conformational space:

| Mover | Operation | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `TiltMover` | Rotates protein around the membrane normal | Tilt angle range, angle increment |
| `TranslationRotationMover` | Full rigid-body transform of protein in membrane | Translation magnitude, rotation angle |
| `SpinAroundPartnerMover` | Rotates protein around a partner protein | Partner chain, angular range |
| `FlipMover` | Inverts membrane orientation (inside ↔ outside) | None (stateless) |
| `TransformIntoMembraneMover` | Applies a computed transformation to embed protein into membrane | Embedding target |

Each mover modifies the protein-MEM jump while preserving the MEM residue's position, effectively repositioning the protein within the fixed bilayer reference frame.

Sources: [TiltMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/TiltMover.hh), [TranslationRotationMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/TranslationRotationMover.hh), [SpinAroundPartnerMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/SpinAroundPartnerMover.hh)

### Relaxation and Constraints

`MPQuickRelaxMover` provides a membrane-aware relaxation protocol that wraps the standard FastRelax with membrane-specific score function weights and fold-tree constraints. Unlike the general-purpose [Structure Relaxation](18-structure-relaxation) pipeline, it ensures the membrane jump is preserved during minimization and that `fa_wtbe` gradients are properly included in the optimization.

Span-based constraints are added by `AddMembraneSpanConstraint` (penalizes deviation from idealized transmembrane geometry) and `AddMembraneSpanTermZConstraint` (keeps span termini near the membrane interface). These constraints work in concert with the energy methods to maintain physically realistic membrane embeddings during aggressive backbone sampling.

Sources: [MPQuickRelaxMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/MPQuickRelaxMover.hh), [AddMembraneSpanConstraint.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/AddMembraneSpanConstraint.hh)

### Aqueous Pore System

For transmembrane proteins with water-filled channels (ion channels, porins, transporters), the framework provides `AqueousPoreFinder` and `AqueousPoreParameters`. The pore finder detects channel-like voids in the protein structure and initializes pore geometry parameters (radius, taper, axis). The geometry engine then uses `f_cavity()` to modify the hydration profile: atoms inside the pore receive higher hydration values even when their z-coordinate places them nominally within the bilayer, correctly modeling the fact that channel-lining residues face water rather than lipid.

Sources: [AqueousPoreFinder.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/AqueousPoreFinder.hh), [AqueousPoreParameters.hh](source/src/core/conformation/membrane/AqueousPoreParameters.hh)

### Symmetry Support

`SymmetricAddMembraneMover` extends `AddMembraneMover` for symmetric membrane protein assemblies. It handles the additional complexity of symmetric FoldTrees, ensuring that the MEM residue is correctly placed in the asymmetric unit and that the symmetry definition propagates the membrane across all subunits. The utility functions in `protocols/membrane/symmetry/util.hh` provide helpers for setting up symmetric membrane poses compatible with the [Symmetry Modeling](24-symmetry-modeling) framework.

Sources: [symmetry/SymmetricAddMembraneMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/symmetry/SymmetricAddMembraneMover.hh)

## Database Parameter Files

The membrane framework depends on three runtime database files located in `database/membrane/`:

| File | Content | Consumers |
|---|---|---|
| `implicit_lipid_parameters.txt` | 90+ lipid composition entries with thickness, steepness, temperature, saturation data | `ImplicitLipidInfo` |
| `lipid_electric_field_params.txt` | Electric field parameters per lipid type | `ElectricfieldLipidlayer` |
| `memb_fa_params_2019.txt` | Per-atom-type water/bilayer solvation energies | `MEnvAtomParams` / `FaWaterToBilayerEnergy` |

The implicit lipid parameters file covers four headgroup families (PC, PE, PG, cardiolipin) across chain lengths from 12:0 to 22:6 and temperatures from 20°C to 60°C. This breadth allows users to model membrane proteins in physiologically relevant bilayer compositions by specifying `-mp:lipids:composition DOPC -mp:lipids:temperature 37` on the command line.

Sources: [implicit_lipid_parameters.txt](database/membrane/implicit_lipid_parameters.txt#L19-L30)

## Lipid Composition Reference

The following table summarizes the most commonly used lipid compositions available in the framework, showing how bilayer thickness varies with chain length, headgroup type, and temperature:

| Lipid | Headgroup | Chains | Thickness (Å) @ 30°C | Thickness (Å) @ 37°C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DLPC | PC | 12:0/12:0 | 16.3–16.5 | 17.25 |
| DMPC | PC | 14:0/14:0 | 18.35–19.7 | 17.974 |
| DOPC | PC | 18:1/18:1 | 18.0 | 18.639 |
| POPC | PC | 16:0/18:1 | 19.55 | 19.1 |
| DPPC | PC | 16:0/16:0 | — | 20.029 |
| DLPE | PE | 12:0/12:0 | — | 16.454 |
| POPE | PE | 16:0/18:1 | — | 19.397 |
| DOPG | PG | 18:1/18:1 | 17.85 | 17.974 |
| POPG | PG | 16:0/18:1 | 18.3 | 18.688 |

PE and PG headgroups produce systematically thicker effective hydrophobic layers compared to PC lipids of the same chain length, reflecting their smaller headgroup cross-sections and tighter packing.

Sources: [implicit_lipid_parameters.txt](database/membrane/implicit_lipid_parameters.txt#L23-L92)

## Visualization and Debugging

The `protocols/membrane/visualize/` subdirectory provides two diagnostic movers: `VisualizeEmbeddingMover` outputs per-span embedding vectors (center + normal) as PDB B-factor records or via PyMOL/ChimeraX session files, while `VisualizeMembraneMover` renders the implicit membrane boundary as a mesh or series of planes at the user-specified hydration contour level. These are invaluable for validating that the membrane is correctly positioned relative to the protein before launching expensive sampling protocols.

Sources: [visualize/VisualizeEmbeddingMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/visualize/VisualizeEmbeddingMover.hh), [visualize/VisualizeMembraneMover.hh](source/src/protocols/membrane/visualize/VisualizeMembraneMover.hh)

## Integration with Broader Rosetta Frameworks

RosettaMP intersects several other subsystems in the Rosetta architecture. The membrane energy methods integrate into the [ScoreFunction Framework](9-scorefunction-framework) as standard `EnergyMethod` plugins, activated by including `fa_wtbe` and `f_elec_lipidlayer` terms. The Environment framework (`core::environment` and `protocols::environment`) provides a general mechanism for controlling degrees of freedom through a claims-based system (`XYZClaim`, `JumpClaim`, `TorsionClaim`) and `DofPassport` objects — this is the infrastructure that allows membrane movers to lock and unlock specific FoldTree jumps during coordinate manipulation. For machine-learning-assisted membrane modeling, the framework is compatible with [ProteinMPNN Integration](22-proteinmpnn-integration) for sequence design of transmembrane regions.


# Fragment Picking System



The Fragment Picking System is one of Rosetta's most critical preprocessing pipelines — it is the engine that selects short protein backbone fragments (typically 3-mers and 9-mers) from a massive structural database to serve as the sampling building blocks for ab initio folding, comparative modeling, and hybridization protocols. Without high-quality fragments, downstream conformational search is blind; with them, Rosetta can efficiently explore native-like conformational space by assembling pre-validated local structural motifs.

## Architectural Overview

The fragment picker follows a **plugin-based pipeline architecture** where a central orchestrator (`FragmentPicker`) coordinates data ingestion, chunk filtering, scoring, collection, and final selection through composable, swappable components. The entire system lives under `source/src/protocols/frag_picker/` and draws structural data from the **Vall** database — a comprehensive library of protein backbone torsion angles extracted from the PDB.

Sources: [FragmentPicker.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.hh#L83-L106), [FragmentPicker.cc](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.cc#L16-L46)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Input["Input Layer"]
        Query["Query Sequence<br/>& Profile"]
        SS["SS Predictions<br/>(PsiPred, Talos, Spine-X)"]
        VallDB["Vall Database<br/>(database/sampling/)"]
    end

    subgraph Core["FragmentPicker Orchestrator"]
        VP["VallProvider<br/>Chunk Reader"]
        VF["VallChunkFilter<br/>PDB ID filter"]
        PCC["pick_candidates()<br/>Per-position scoring"]
        SM["FragmentScoreManager<br/>Weighted scoring"]
    end

    subgraph Storage["CandidatesCollector"]
        BC["BoundedCollector<br/>Top-N per position"]
        QC["QuotaCollector<br/>SS-pool diversity"]
        GA["GrabAllCollector<br/>Keep everything"]
    end

    subgraph Selection["Fragment Selection"]
        BTS["BestTotalScoreSelector"]
        CS["CustomScoreSelector"]
        DS["DiversifyCrmsdSelector"]
        QS["QuotaSelector"]
    end

    subgraph Output["Output"]
        FF["Fragment Files<br/>.200.3mers / .200.9mers"]
        FS["FragSet<br/>(in-memory)"]
    end

    Query --> Core
    SS --> Core
    VallDB --> VP
    VP --> VF --> PCC
    PCC --> SM
    SM --> Storage
    Storage --> Selection --> Output
```

## Core Classes and Data Flow

### FragmentPicker — The Central Orchestrator

`FragmentPicker` is the main entry point for the entire system. It manages query data (sequence profiles, secondary structure predictions, phi/psi angles, solvent accessibility), orchestrates the scoring pipeline, and drives the three picking protocols. The class supports multithreaded operation via `set_max_threads()`, with one `FragmentScoreManager` per thread to avoid cache contention on chunk-level scoring data. It maintains a map of `CandidatesCollector` instances keyed by fragment size and thread index, enabling parallel scoring of different fragment lengths simultaneously.

Sources: [FragmentPicker.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.hh#L89-L121), [FragmentPicker.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.hh#L451-L475)

### FragmentCandidate — A Potential Fragment

Each `FragmentCandidate` represents a contiguous X-mer extracted from a Vall chunk that aligns to a specific position in the query sequence. It stores three critical indices: the query residue index, the Vall residue index, and the fragment length. Critically, **scores are stored separately** in a `FragmentScoreMap` object rather than on the candidate itself — this separation allows the same candidate to be evaluated by different scoring schemes without mutation. The candidate can produce a `FragData` object for direct integration with Rosetta's fragment framework via `get_frag_data()`.

Sources: [FragmentCandidate.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentCandidate.hh#L41-L58), [FragmentCandidate.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentCandidate.hh#L132-L148)

### VallProvider — Structural Database Reader

`VallProvider` reads the Vall database file (e.g., `filtered.vall.dat.2006-05-05.gz`) and partitions it into `VallChunk` objects — contiguous segments from the same PDB entry. Each chunk contains `VallResidue` entries with backbone torsion angles (φ, ψ, ω), secondary structure assignments, B-factors, and residue depth information. The provider supports lazy loading with configurable line ranges, profile caching, and pose caching to avoid redundant computation when the same chunk is scored against multiple query positions.

Sources: [VallProvider.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/VallProvider.hh#L38-L128)

### FragmentScoreManager — Pluggable Scoring Engine

`FragmentScoreManager` is the extensible scoring subsystem that evaluates how well a fragment candidate matches the query's predicted properties. It maintains an ordered list of `FragmentScoringMethod` instances, each with a weight. Methods are sorted by priority (higher priority scored first) to enable early rejection of poor candidates before expensive scores are computed. The manager implements a caching protocol via the `CachingScoringMethod` interface — chunk-level data that doesn't change per-candidate (e.g., Gunn costs) is precomputed once per chunk, then reused across all fragments derived from that chunk. The total score is a simple weighted sum: `Σ(weight_i × score_i)`.

Sources: [FragmentScoreManager.cc](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/scores/FragmentScoreManager.cc#L101-L144), [FragmentScoreManager.cc](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/scores/FragmentScoreManager.cc#L146-L167)

## Scoring Methods Catalog

The scoring subsystem contains over 40 pluggable scoring methods organized under `source/src/protocols/frag_picker/scores/`. Each implements the `FragmentScoringMethod` base class with a `score()` virtual method and participates in the priority-ordered evaluation pipeline.

| Category | Scoring Method | Purpose |
|----------|---------------|---------|
| **Sequence** | `ProfileScoreL1`, `ProfileScoreBlosum62`, `SequenceIdentity` | Compare query sequence profile against Vall fragment sequence |
| **Secondary Structure** | `SecondarySimilarity`, `SecondaryIdentity`, `TalosSSSimilarity`, `PartialSecondarySimilarity`, `ABEGO_SS_Score` | Match predicted vs. observed secondary structure |
| **Torsion Angles** | `RamaScore`, `PhiPsiRmsd`, `PhiPsiSquareWell`, `TorsionBinSimilarity`, `Phi`, `Psi` | Evaluate backbone torsion angle agreement |
| **Geometry** | `FragmentCrmsd`, `FragmentAllAtomCrmsd`, `FragmentCrmsdResDepth`, `FragmentDME`, `GunnCostScore` | Structural similarity metrics |
| **Experimental (NMR)** | `JCoupling`, `RDCScore`, `CSScore`, `AmbigCSScore`, `PCS_FragDistance` | Restraint-based scoring from NMR data |
| **Environment** | `SolventAccessibility`, `BFactor`, `Faraggi_SA`, `HydrophobicitySimilarity`, `HydrophobicityProfileSimilarity` | Solvent and physico-chemical context |
| **Constraints** | `AtomPairConstraintsScore`, `DihedralConstraintsScore`, `InterbondAngleScore` | Custom distance/angle restraints |
| **Special** | `DisulfideIdentity`, `DisulfideDistance`, `ProlinePhiScore`, `MidPhiOut`, `MidPsiOut` | Residue-specific checks |

Sources: [FragmentScoreManager.cc](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/scores/FragmentScoreManager.cc#L22-L64), [FragmentScoringMethod.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/scores/FragmentScoringMethod.hh#L34-L93)

The `FragmentScoringMethod` base class defines a critical **early rejection** mechanism: each method declares a `lowest_acceptable_value_` threshold and a `use_lowest_` flag. If a candidate's score falls below this threshold, it can be discarded before remaining (potentially expensive) scores are evaluated — a key optimization when scanning millions of Vall residues.

Sources: [FragmentScoringMethod.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/scores/FragmentScoringMethod.hh#L69-L85)

## Three Picking Protocols

The `FragmentPicker` exposes three distinct protocols that differ in how they manage candidate storage and memory consumption. Each is suited to different computational scenarios.

Sources: [FragmentPicker.cc](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.cc#L113-L218)

### Keep-All Protocol

The `keep_all_protocol()` is a **position-by-position** approach. For each query position, it scans the entire Vall, scores every candidate, stores all candidates that pass filters, then selects the top-N fragments and writes them immediately. Storage is flushed after each position, making this the most memory-efficient option. However, it is **incompatible with multithreading** — each Vall chunk must be processed sequentially per position. It processes fragment sizes in an outer loop, writing separate output files per size.

Sources: [FragmentPicker.cc](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.cc#L160-L218)

### Bounded Protocol

The `bounded_protocol()` is the **default and recommended approach** for production use. It scores all Vall data against all query positions in parallel (multi-threaded), keeping only the top-K candidates per position using a `BoundedCollector` — a template class parameterized by a `StrictWeakOrdering` comparator that maintains a lazy-sorted bounded priority queue with configurable buffer factor. This protocol uses significantly more memory (O(query_length × max_candidates_per_position)) but enables full thread parallelism and produces higher-quality fragment sets because it sees all Vall candidates before making final selections.

Sources: [FragmentPicker.cc](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.cc#L113-L117), [BoundedCollector.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/BoundedCollector.hh#L48-L79)

### Quota Protocol

The `quota_protocol()` is the most sophisticated approach, designed to ensure **secondary structure diversity** in the final fragment set. Instead of selecting the globally best N fragments per position, it distributes fragments across secondary structure pools (e.g., H, E, L for helix, strand, loop) using `QuotaCollector` and `QuotaPool`. Each pool receives a proportional allocation based on predicted secondary structure, preventing the picker from over-representing one structure type. The `ABEGO_SS_Config` extension further classifies fragments by ABEGO backbone torsion bins within each secondary structure category.

Sources: [FragmentPicker.cc](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.cc#L119-L158), [QuotaCollector.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/quota/QuotaCollector.hh#L40-L113)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph KeepAll["keep_all_protocol()"]
        KA1["Position 1"] --> KA2["Score all Vall"]
        KA2 --> KA3["Select top-N"]
        KA3 --> KA4["Flush & write"]
        KA4 --> KA5["Position 2"]
    end

    subgraph Bounded["bounded_protocol()"]
        B1["All positions × All threads"]
        B1 --> B2["BoundedCollector<br/>(top-K per pos)"]
        B2 --> B3["Select final top-N"]
        B3 --> B4["Write all"]
    end

    subgraph Quota["quota_protocol()"]
        Q1["All positions × All threads"]
        Q1 --> Q2["QuotaCollector<br/>(SS-pooled storage)"]
        Q2 --> Q3["QuotaSelector<br/>(diversity-aware pick)"]
        Q3 --> Q4["Write all"]
    end
```

| Property | Keep-All | Bounded | Quota |
|----------|----------|---------|-------|
| Memory usage | Low (per-position) | Medium (O(Q×K)) | Medium (O(Q×P×K)) |
| Thread-safe | No | Yes | Yes |
| Output quality | Good | Better | Best (diversity) |
| Typical use case | Debugging, small queries | Default production | SS-diverse fragment sets |
| Storage type | Any `CandidatesCollector` | `BoundedCollector` | `QuotaCollector` |

## CandidatesCollector Hierarchy

All three protocols share the `CandidatesCollector` abstract interface, which defines `add()`, `clear()`, `insert()`, `count_candidates()`, and `get_candidates()` operations. The three concrete implementations provide fundamentally different storage strategies:

- **`GrabAllCollector`** — Stores every candidate without limit; useful for debugging and when external selection logic is needed. Found in [GrabAllCollector.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/GrabAllCollector.hh).
- **`BoundedCollector<StrictWeakOrdering>`** — A templated class using `LazySortedVector1` to maintain a bounded priority queue per query position. The `buffer_factor` (default 5) controls internal buffer size vs. the exposed max candidates. [BoundedCollector.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/BoundedCollector.hh#L48-L163)
- **`QuotaCollector`** — A two-level storage structure: per-position arrays of `QuotaPool` objects, where each pool tracks candidates belonging to a specific secondary structure or ABEGO category. Pools can be renormalized dynamically. [QuotaCollector.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/quota/QuotaCollector.hh#L40-L113)

Sources: [CandidatesCollector.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/CandidatesCollector.hh#L43-L73), [BoundedCollector.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/BoundedCollector.hh#L44-L79), [QuotaCollector.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/quota/QuotaCollector.hh#L40-L113)

## Fragment Selection Rules

After candidates are collected, a `FragmentSelectingRule` determines the final fragment set. The picker supports four selection strategies:

- **`BestTotalScoreSelector`** — Selects the N fragments with the lowest weighted total score. This is the default for bounded and keep-all protocols.
- **`CustomScoreSelector`** — Allows users to define arbitrary selection criteria beyond the total score.
- **`DiversifyCrmsdSelector` / `DiversifyDihedralsSelector`** — Enforces structural diversity among selected fragments by filtering out candidates that are too similar (measured by Cα RMSD or backbone dihedral angles) to already-selected fragments.
- **`QuotaSelector`** — Selects fragments proportionally from each `QuotaPool` to maintain secondary structure balance. Used exclusively by the quota protocol.

> [!TIP]
> When using the `DiversifyCrmsdSelector`, note that diversity filtering happens **after** scoring but **before** final output. A common mistake is to request more fragments than the diversity filter can produce, resulting in fewer than expected output fragments. Increase `n_candidates` (the collector capacity) to compensate.

Sources: [FragmentPicker.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.hh#L210-L213), [FragmentPicker.cc](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.cc#L24-L34)

## Query Data Inputs

The fragment picker ingests multiple types of predictive query data to evaluate fragment candidates:

| Input | Method | Description |
|-------|--------|-------------|
| Sequence profile | `set_query_seq()` / `set_query_profile()` | PSI-BLAST or similar PSSM |
| Secondary structure (PsiPred) | `read_psipred_ss2()` | Helix/strand/loop probabilities per residue |
| Secondary structure (Talos) | `read_talos_ss()` | NMR-derived SS from TALOS+ |
| Phi/Psi/Solvent accessibility | `read_spine_x()` | SPINE-X predictions |
| Residue depth | `read_depth()` | DEPTH algorithm output |
| Phi/Psi angles & confidence | `set_query_phi()` / `set_query_psi()` / `set_query_phi_conf()` / `set_query_psi_conf()` | Direct angle predictions |

These inputs feed into the corresponding scoring methods. For example, `ProfileScoreL1` uses the sequence profile, `SecondarySimilarity` uses PsiPred predictions, and `RamaScore` uses Spine-X phi/psi predictions. The picker supports multiple secondary structure predictions simultaneously via a map keyed by prediction name.

Sources: [FragmentPicker.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.hh#L235-L328), [FragmentPicker.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.hh#L215-L233)

## Vall Database and Chunk Filtering

The Vall database is stored under `database/sampling/` with files like `filtered.vall.dat.2006-05-05.gz` (full PDB-derived library) and `small.vall.gz` (testing subset). Additional specialized databases exist for RNA (`rna/`), antibodies (`antibodies/Fragments/`), and secondary-structure-specific fragments (`ss_fragfiles/` with 27 files covering all 3-letter SS combinations from EEE to LLL).

Before fragments are extracted, `VallChunkFilter` instances can reject entire chunks. The most common filter is `PdbIdChunkFilter`, which excludes chunks derived from specific PDB entries (e.g., the query protein itself to avoid homology bias). Filters are registered via `add_chunk_filter()` on the picker.

Sources: [FragmentPicker.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.hh#L441-L444), [FragmentPicker.cc](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.cc#L31)

## Integration with Core Fragment Framework

Selected fragments ultimately become `ConstantLengthFragSet` objects — the standard in-memory fragment representation used throughout Rosetta's sampling protocols. The `FragmentPicker::getFragSet()` method performs this conversion, producing a vector of `ConstantLengthFragSetOP` instances (one per fragment size). Each `FragSet` contains `Frame` objects at each query position, and each Frame holds the selected `FragData` entries with backbone torsion angles. These `FragSet` objects are then consumed by the ab initio folding, comparative modeling, and loop modeling protocols described in other pages of this documentation.

On disk, fragments are written in Rosetta's standard fragment format with files named `{prefix}.{n_frags}.{size}mers` (e.g., `frags.200.3mers` and `frags.200.9mers`), which can be loaded via `-in:file:fraglist` or the `FragmentSetLoader` class.

Sources: [FragmentPicker.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.hh#L392-L394), [FragmentCandidate.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentCandidate.hh#L132-L148)

## Nonlocal Fragments and Contact Prediction

Beyond standard local fragment picking, the system supports **nonlocal fragment pairs** — pairs of fragments from distant positions in the query sequence that are predicted to be in spatial contact. The `nonlocal_pairs()` and `nonlocal_pairs_at_position()` methods identify such pairs by analyzing side-chain contact geometry from top-scoring local fragments. This functionality integrates with Rosetta's nonlocal folding protocols and contact prediction pipelines, using `NonlocalPair` objects that wrap two `FragmentCandidate` instances plus a contact count score.

Sources: [FragmentPicker.hh](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.hh#L170-L173), [FragmentPicker.cc](source/src/protocols/frag_picker/FragmentPicker.cc#L221-L250)

## Source Code Layout

```
source/src/protocols/frag_picker/
├── FragmentPicker.hh/cc          # Central orchestrator
├── FragmentCandidate.hh/cc       # A potential fragment (Vall → query mapping)
├── CandidatesCollector.hh        # Abstract collector interface
├── BoundedCollector.hh           # Top-K bounded priority queue (templated)
├── GrabAllCollector.hh           # Unlimited storage collector
├── VallProvider.hh/cc            # Vall database reader & chunk manager
├── VallChunk.hh/cc               # Contiguous PDB segment from Vall
├── VallResidue.hh/cc             # Single residue with torsion data
├── VallChunkFilter.hh/cc         # Chunk pre-screening base + PdbId filter
├── FragmentScoreFilter.hh/cc     # Score-based candidate filtering
├── FragmentSelectingRule.hh      # Selection base class
├── BestTotalScoreSelector.hh/cc  # Select by lowest total score
├── CustomScoreSelector.hh/cc     # User-defined selection logic
├── DiversifyCrmsdSelector.hh/cc  # Diversity by Cα RMSD
├── DiversifyDihedralsSelector.hh # Diversity by dihedral angles
├── scores/                       # 40+ scoring method implementations
│   ├── FragmentScoringMethod.hh  # Base class for all scorers
│   ├── CachingScoringMethod.hh   # Chunk-level caching interface
│   ├── FragmentScoreManager.hh/cc# Scoring engine with weighted sum
│   ├── PValuedFragmentScoreManager.hh/cc # P-value based scoring
│   ├── AdaptiveScoreHistogram.hh/cc     # Dynamic score calibration
│   └── ...
├── quota/                        # Quota-based diversity system
│   ├── QuotaCollector.hh/cc      # SS-pooled collector
│   ├── QuotaSelector.hh/cc       # Proportional pool selection
│   ├── QuotaPool.hh              # Single SS category storage
│   ├── QuotaConfig.hh/cc         # Pool configuration parser
│   ├── ABEGO_SS_Pool.hh/cc       # ABEGO+SS combined pools
│   ├── ABEGO_SS_Map.hh/cc        # ABEGO↔SS mapping logic
│   └── SecondaryStructurePool.hh/cc # SS-based pool implementation
└── nonlocal/                     # Nonlocal fragment pair support
    ├── NonlocalFrags.hh/cc       # Nonlocal fragment finder
    ├── NonlocalPair.hh           # Pair of distant fragments
    └── NonlocalFragsMain.hh/cc   # Entry point for nonlocal picking
```
